The primary cues are binaural: the Interaural Time Difference (ITD) and the Interaural Level Difference (ILD), both arising from the geometry of the head and the spatial separation of the ears [macpherson2002listener, middlebrooks2015sound]. ITD reflects the difference in arrival time between the two ears and is highly reliable for localizing low-frequency sounds whose long wavelengths exceed head size. Conversely, ILD captures sound pressure level differences caused by head-shadowing effects and serves as a dominant cue for high-frequency localization where such attenuation is more pronounced. However, binaural cues alone cannot fully resolve depth, elevation, or front-back ambiguities.

To address these limitations, the auditory system further exploits monaural spectral cues and environmental reverberation. Direction-dependent spectral filtering produced by the torso, head, and pinnae introduces characteristic notches and peaks, enabling inference of elevation and disambiguation of positions on the cone of confusion [gardner19983]. In addition, the room impulse response (RIR) shaped by early reflections, late reverberation, and surface materials encodes information about source distance, enclosure geometry, and environmental structure [kuttruff2016room, blauert1997spatial]. These monaural and environmental cues complement binaural information, jointly supporting robust spatial inference under naturalistic conditions.

Computational models formalize these perceptual cues through structured acoustic representations. Head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) [wightman1989headphone] capture listener-specific spectral filtering and are foundational to perceptual research and spatial audio rendering. In parallel, spherical-harmonics–based ambisonics representations [zotter2019ambisonics] provide a scene-centric encoding of the sound field around a point in space, with controllable angular resolution. Together, these representations describe how sound interacts with the body and the environment, enabling principled approaches to spatial reasoning, source localization, and scene reconstruction. Taken together, the ability of the auditory system to integrate binaural, monaural, and environmental cues demonstrates that sound carries rich implicit structure about the spatial configuration of sources and the surrounding environment.

Recent learning-based approaches aim to capture spatial structure directly from raw audio, going beyond analytic models. Neural encoders trained on spatially annotated or simulated data learn to infer direction, distance, and environmental geometry from multi-channel waveforms or spectrograms [chen2022soundspaces, yuksel2025general]. Learning frameworks further exploit the relation between sound and space: SoundSpaces [chen2020soundspaces] provides audio-visual simulation for embodied navigation, while VisualEchoes [gao2020visualechoes] uses image–echo correspondences for self-supervised spatial representation learning. These learned representations encode not only spatial acoustics but also grounding in surrounding geometry, forming a key component of spatially aware representation.

In real-world environments, spatial audio interacts closely with other sensory modalities. Audio–visual models align acoustic cues with visual observations to localize sounding objects and understand where events occur [morgado2018self, afouras2020self, morgado2020learning]. Embodied agents further leverage auditory signals to perceive layout and navigate toward acoustic targets, as demonstrated in audio–visual navigation [chen2020soundspaces] and egocentric audio reasoning [zheng2024bat, biswas2025owl]. Through such cross-modal grounding, audio provides complementary spatial cues that enhance robustness under visual occlusion and enable reasoning about events beyond the agent’s field of view. This makes audio a powerful complementary modality for spatial representation, especially in scenarios where visual information is partial, noisy, or unavailable.

4.6 Domain-Specific Representations

The representations surveyed so far are organized by modality, each general enough to span many applications. A large body of practice, however, develops representations tailored to a specific sensor or downstream task rather than to a modality as such, and these are collected here. What unites them is not a shared signal but a shared design logic: each encodes the inductive biases of its data and trades spatial fidelity against semantic compressibility in the way its sensors and target tasks demand. This section walks through five such domains: embodied robotics, virtual reality, geospatial and remote sensing, clinical and scientific imaging, and indoor intelligent assistants, examining in each the representations that have become canonical and the constraints that shaped them. Beginning with robot perception and planning, systems commonly take as input RGB-D sequences and point clouds (often fused over time into geometric maps that ground observations into a common 3D frame [newcombe2011kinectfusion, dai2017bundlefusion]), and enable tracking, map building, and manipulation. Many such systems also encode visual input into compressed spatial representations, such as keypoints, dense correspondences [florencemanuelli2018dense], and point tracks, used to parameterize 6-DoF grasps [mousavian20196] and object-centric actions. When available, free space is typically represented with occupancy grids [Moravec1985SonarMaps, hornung2013octomap] and signed-distance representations [curless1996volumetric], and is often additionally augmented with semantic labels such as traversability and cost for planning. To further enable action from perception, planners frequently operate on affordance representations [mo2021where2act] over parts and candidate contact points, encoding feasible interactions such as graspability or predicted contact quality, thereby enabling policies to execute tasks successfully.

Real-time virtual reality systems often represent scenes with triangle meshes and physically based rendering (PBR) materials, where geometry, normals, and texture define appearance, while 6-DoF camera poses keep virtual content registered to the environment. To enable flexible interaction, such systems include captured geometry (e.g., , spatial meshes, planes, or TSDF and SDF volumes [curless1996volumetric, newcombe2011kinectfusion]) and depth-based occlusion layers, which are often paired with collision proxies and semantic labels. Toward photoreal view synthesis, methods increasingly use neural scene representations (e.g., , NeRF-style radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splats [mildenhall2021nerf, kerbl20233d]), to support novel-view rendering and relighting. Additionally, for the purposes of enabling characters in virtual reality systems, such characters are commonly represented with skeletal pose and expression parameters (e.g., , SMPL-style body models [loper2015smpl] or Blendshapes), and their navigation relies on navmeshes combined with acceleration structures (e.g., , octrees), to handle moving agents in simulation at high frame rates.

In remote sensing applications, geographic information systems typically represent the world (the Earth) as georeferenced raster fields, for example, optical multispectral and hyperspectral imagery as well as SAR backscatter. These fields are aligned to explicit coordinate reference systems and sensor geometry metadata. Such systems encode terrain through multiple elevation products (e.g., , DEM, DTM, DSM), and compress human infrastructure into vector networks (e.g., , roads, power grids, pipelines), often across scales. And increasingly, they use LiDAR to not only output raw point clouds, but also to output rasterized height maps that support flexible 3D reasoning. These frameworks also commonly operate on multi-temporal stacks and spatiotemporal data with validity masks, which can generate change maps for land-use dynamics and disaster response, as well as feed digital-twin pipelines that generate orthomosaics and photogrammetric point clouds [schonberger2016structure], for simulation and virtual modeling.

Clinical and scientific imaging operate on volumetric scans (e.g., , CT and MRI), in which 3D voxel grids capture geometry and intensities [cciccek20163d], and explicit spatial transforms (e.g., , rigid, affine, and nonlinear deformation fields) align subjects and modalities into a shared atlas space. In addition, functional measurements (e.g., , fMRI BOLD and calcium imaging) are often stored as 4D spatiotemporal tensors, but are frequently compressed into time series and activation maps after parcellation. When available, such systems represent structural delineations (e.g., , tissue, organ, lesion) as segmentation masks and labeled maps [ronneberger2015unet], which are often paired with surface meshes (e.g., , cortical surfaces) that enable surface-based topological comparison across subjects. For diffusion imaging applications, tensor and orientation fields encode local diffusion directions and magnitudes, while tractography streamlines use these fields to reconstruct fiber pathways and uncover possible structural connectivity. These diverse representations across granularities and temporal scales are often mapped onto one another through atlas spaces and parcellations, enabling multimodal fusion and cross-subject analysis.

Intelligent assistants that operate in indoor environments typically ground language in 3D space using multi-scale maps, for example, 3D reconstructions and floorplans anchored by an estimated 6-DoF agent pose [savva2019habitat, straub2019replica, chang2017matterport3d], which are often combined with semantic maps that encode navigable routes. Context for interactions is captured in structured world models (e.g., , scene graphs with typed entities and relations [armeni20193dsg, wald2020learning, wu2021scenegraphfusion]), which can be augmented with additional semantics like anchors, keypoints, and regions of interest. For the purposes of intelligent and persistent assistance, representations that encode some form of memory are necessary, for example, episodic records and long-horizon object trajectories, which are often represented as probabilistic beliefs over object locations in a room. In addition, assistant systems can optionally contain geofences and occupancy masks, to help define actionable regions for planning.

In summary, many domains have developed representations specifically designed for specialized sensors and encoding the inductive biases of the underlying data structure. We see that these representations model a tradeoff between (spatial) fidelity and (semantic) compressibility, reflecting how the aforementioned sensors sample space, what priors are built in, and what downstream tasks are to be supported.

Chapter 5 Cross-Modal Spatial Representation

The aim of cross-modal spatial representation is a latent space in which heterogeneous perceptual signals, images, 3D scenes, video, audio, and language are aligned so that the spatial structure each carries is preserved rather than averaged away. Where the previous chapter asked how much geometry a single modality holds on its own, the concern here is the opposite and harder one: how signals that encode space in incompatible formats (a pixel grid, a world-frame point set, a waveform, a sentence) can be brought into correspondence without the alignment itself distorting what it aligns.

No single recipe achieves this. Methods differ in what they treat as the unit of alignment, in the objective that binds one modality to another, in how tightly they anchor the space to physical geometry, and in the linguistic interface through which it is queried. These choices are not independent, and the chapter first makes them explicit as a small set of design axes before turning to the individual cross-modal pairings in which they play out.

5.1 Overview

We define four axes that structure this cross-modal representation learning problem, which we use to organize the remainder of the chapter. The first axis is the alignment strategy, which we categorize into contrastive alignment, generative alignment, and programmatic alignment. Contrastive alignment learns a shared embedding space by pushing together paired samples and pulling away negative samples. Such alignment scales to weakly paired data and enables retrieval and coarse grounding, but often needs additional spatial supervision to understand fine-grained relations grounded to specific visual regions. In contrast, generative alignment predicts across modalities (e.g., , captioning from vision or language-conditioned decoding into images, 3D, or video), which gives rich supervision and coverage, but also tends to drift from true underlying geometry unless it is further constrained, for example, by multi-view consistency. Finally, programmatic alignment aligns visual entities to explicit symbols (e.g., , attributes, relation graphs, or concepts in domain-specific languages), which define spatial semantics and naturally interface with program-based, verifiable reasoning, but often requires stronger supervision and trades off expressiveness for structure.

The second axis is spatial modality, which ranges from view-aligned 2D to world-aligned 4D. Here, two-dimensional tokens (e.g., , pixels, patches) are expressive and broadly applicable, but rely on some form of geometric structure to capture faithful spatial relationships. Three-dimensional tokens (e.g., , points, meshes, implicit fields, Gaussian primitives) better encode metric scale and rigid-body invariance (i.e., SE(3) consistency: rotations and translations of the scene do not change the underlying semantics), so that linguistic queries are grounded in world coordinates rather than in image projections. However, they are less ubiquitous and often rely on partial and noisy reconstructions of geometry. Extending 3D through time yields 4D traces (e.g., , tracks), that bind actions to expressive motion and change, but significantly increase computational complexity and require reliable alignment data, while being sensitive to tracking errors such as identity switches. These different spatial modalities correspond to and build upon the single-modality representations of Chapter 4.

The third axis is the language interface, from free-form text to structured interfaces. Free-form text (e.g., , natural language) enables open-vocabulary understanding for referring expressions, retrieval, and instruction following, but comes with corresponding ambiguity in terms of frames of reference, scale, and units. In contrast, structured interfaces (e.g., , programs) reduce such ambiguity by explicitly describing spatial semantics, enabling integration with symbolic reasoning, but are less flexible in capturing the full range of natural language descriptions.

The fourth axis is the training regime, which defines both the level of supervision and coverage. Paired supervision, for example, from captioned videos or referring expressions in 3D scenes, gives strong alignment, but is expensive and can be biased toward frequent compositions and co-occurrences. Weakly paired internet data, for example, from alt-text or transcripts, enable diversity, but, due to low signal-to-noise ratios, often yield noisier spatial grounding.

Below, we organize the chapter by cross-modal pair, using spatial modality (which pair) and alignment strategy (which objective) as the primary organisational axes; the language interface and training regime axes recur as cross-cutting attributes referenced throughout. We give an overview of 2D-text alignment (Section 5.2), 3D-text alignment (Section 5.3), audio-text alignment (Section 5.4), and vision-vision alignment (Section 5.5); each follows the scope and axes defined here.

5.2 2D-text

The most developed cross-modal setting pairs images with language. Its defining tension is that a text-aligned 2D representation lives in the image projection, not the world: appearance and layout sit on the pixel grid, yet the relations a caption asserts (left of, above, behind) are only implicit there. How faithfully those relations survive alignment turns on two choices: the granularity at which the image is represented, and the objective that binds it to text, and this section is organized around them. Models often fall into three broad families of visual representations, across different levels of granularity. First are global embeddings that compress an entire image into a single vector paired with a sentence embedding. Here, dual-encoder approaches such as CLIP [radford2021learning] and ALIGN [jia2021scaling] show that large-scale contrastive pretraining over noisy web data yields strong zero-shot classification and retrieval performance. Second, many works have proposed local tokens tied to image subregions, in which vision-language models, often transformers (e.g., , ViLBERT [lu2019vilbert], LXMERT [tan2019lxmert], UNITER [chen2020uniter], OSCAR [li2020oscar]) input region features extracted by bottom-up detectors (e.g., , Faster R-CNN [ren2015faster]) into cross-modal attention blocks, enabling word-region alignment, and hence fine-grained reasoning over object proposals. A third class of methods makes relations explicit; here, models extract intermediate representations that are directly aligned with spatial predicates such as “left-of” or “on.” NSCL [mao2019neuro] and LEFT [hsu2023s] learn hybrid representations that explicitly bind named visual concepts with latent features. This representational spectrum, from global to region to relation-based, forms the basis for the objectives below.

Contrastive retrieval serves as a common objective for large-scale pretraining, as it learns a shared metric space, without requiring dense and expensive supervision. As representative examples, CLIP [radford2021learning] and ALIGN [jia2021scaling] maximize agreement between paired image and text embeddings, enabling robust zero-shot transfer; LiT [zhai2022lit] shows that contrastively tuning only the text encoder on top of a locked image encoder can further improve such transfer; and CoCa [yu2022coca] fuses contrastive learning with captioning in a single encoder-decoder architecture to combine discriminative and generative strengths. Another line of work adapts contrastive alignment to more fine-grained regions. RegionCLIP [zhong2022regionclip] lifts global contrast to region-text pairs, FILIP [yao2021filip] proposes late token-token interaction to align words with patches efficiently, X-VLM [zeng2021multi] learns multi-grained alignment such that entities and attributes can be localized and described consistently across granularities, and ALBEF [li2021align] conducts image-text contrast with cross-modal fusion and momentum-distilled pseudo-targets to stabilize learning on noisy web data.

In addition, masked modeling with textual conditioning has been shown to provide a complementary self-supervised signal that encourages cross-modal consistency. LXMERT [tan2019lxmert] and UNITER [chen2020uniter] pretrain with masked language modeling, masked region modeling, and image-text matching to build word-region alignment. VLMo [bao2022vlmo] generalizes this idea with mixture-of-modality experts, and BEiT-3 [wang2023image] performs masked data modeling over images, text, and image-text pairs in a single multiway transformer.

With more labels, generative objectives can be applied for this representation learning problem, and also complement self-supervised ones. Here, methods teach models to produce language conditioned on images, intuitively, to generate tokens that act as spatially grounded explanations. As representative examples, SimVLM [wang2021simvlm] shows that a prefix language-modeling objective trained on weak supervision can improve performance on captioning and visual question answering, BLIP [li2022blip] adds caption bootstrapping to denoise web supervision, and GIT [wang2022git] simplifies a scalable image-encoder and text-decoder architecture.

In a more fine-grained manner, grounding objectives can directly optimize spatial correspondence between language and 2D pixels, points, or boxes. Here, text-conditioned detection and phrase grounding unify detection and language. MDETR [kamath2021mdetr] learns a DETR-style [carion2020end] detector modulated by text, GLIP [li2022grounded] pretrains on both detection and grounding corpora and self-generates boxes from image-text pairs to scale supervision, and Grounding DINO [liu2024grounding] augments strong detection backbones with grounded pretraining for open-set detection. At the pixel level, DenseCLIP [rao2022denseclip] adapts image-text matching to pixel-text matching for dense prediction, and GroupViT [xu2022groupvit] shows that segmentation structure can appear from text supervision alone.

Across these categories, we see that 2D-text representations can emerge from diverse approaches, for example, differing in whether spatial structure is implicit (e.g., , in attention over patches) or explicit (e.g., , in region tokens), and whether supervision is weakly paired and contrastive, generative, or explicitly grounded. Models that learn 2D vision-language representations now increasingly combine all contrastive, captioning, grounding, and masked objectives to solve a wide range of downstream tasks, from (more semantic) referring expression comprehension to (more visually grounded) localization.

5.3 3D-text

Moving from the image plane to the scene itself removes the projection gap that limits 2D-text alignment: language is now bound to geometry expressed in world coordinates, so that metric scale and the invariance of meaning under rotation and translation become properties the representation can actually enforce. The difficulty shifts accordingly, from recovering relations that pixels hide to obtaining and aligning 3D structure that is often partial, noisy, and expensive to annotate. As before, the representation families and the alignment objectives acting on them jointly organize the section. Two complementary families of representations have emerged in this domain. First, object-centric and scene-centric encoders learn world-aligned tokens, then align them to language via contrastive or generative objectives. ULIP [xue2023ulip] instantiates this paradigm by aligning point-cloud features to an image-text space, scaling supervision through synthetic triplets. OpenShape [liu2023openshape] extends this direction further with curated 3D corpora and hard negative mining to support open-world 3D retrieval, and OpenScene [peng2023openscene] co-embeds dense features for 3D scenes with text and image pixels in CLIP feature space. Additional projection strategies have also been explored, for example, adapting 2D vision-language models to 3D by rendering depth or multi-view images and transferring CLIP’s alignment to point clouds; PointCLIP [zhang2022pointclip] and CLIP2Point [huang2023clip2point] do so and enable adapters for cross-modal transfer.

A second family binds language to implicit scene fields. Here, LERF [kerr2023lerf] optimizes a dense 3D language field inside NeRF [mildenhall2021nerf] by rendering CLIP embeddings across views, enabling open-vocabulary queries that return relevancy volumes. CLIP-Fields [shafiullah2022clip] similarly distills 2D vision-language cues into 3D implicit maps to support semantic search and view localization. In addition, replacing NeRF with 3D Gaussian Splatting [kerbl20233d] yields efficient language fields; for example, LangSplat [qin2024langsplat] combines CLIP features with Gaussians for fast, precise open-vocabulary querying. These methods build on advances in explicit 3D primitives and real-time rendering to maintain high-fidelity representations while training efficiently.

In this 3D-text domain, objectives also follow the representation choices. Contrastive alignment remains common, for example, ULIP trains with InfoNCE [oord2018representation] over point clouds-images-text, while OpenShape scales both data and hard-negative mining. Projection-based approaches transfer contrastive objectives to depth and multi-view renders to align point clouds with text labels. Grounded objectives enforce explicit 3D correspondence between language and geometry. 3D referring expression datasets and models (e.g., , ScanRefer [chen2020scanrefer], ReferIt3D [achlioptas2020referit3d], 3D-VisTA [zhu20233d], BUTD-DETR [jain2022bottom], NS3D [hsu2023ns3d], InstanceRefer [yuan2021instancerefer]) localize targets from language descriptions and learn to understand complex relations dependent on viewpoints.

Here, geometry-aware representations are critical for aligning language with the physical world. Ideal 3D-text representations should respect SE(3) structure (e.g., , rotations and translations should not spuriously change semantics), yet cross-modal alignment should still encode view-dependent language (e.g., , “the chair to the left of the table”). To this end, priors from equivariant architectures, such as the SE(3)-Transformer [fuchs2020se] and Vector Neurons [deng2021vector], can be integrated into 3D-text models. Implicit fields enable different options; while NeRF-based language fields are not strictly equivariant, multi-view consistency and cross-view regularization can improve their spatial coherence. Alternatively, Gaussian splatting uses a canonical world frame and enables efficient supervision during language-field optimization. Overall, these representation choices and objectives give rise to a wide range of approaches for 3D-text alignment, from tri-modal contrastive pretraining to implicit or splat-based language fields.

5.4 Audio-text

Sound aligns to language along a different primary dimension than vision does. What an acoustic signal encodes first is time, the sequence of events as they unfold, and only secondarily, and coarsely, does it carry spatial attributes such as direction of arrival or distance. Audio-text representation learning therefore aims for embeddings that are open-vocabulary and temporally grounded, with spatial awareness added where the labels permit. The section again moves from the representation granularity to the objectives that align it with text. One such direction is to embed audio-text representations at a coarse level, for example, with global encoders mapping an entire audio clip and a full sentence into a joint space, enabling zero-shot retrieval. Here, CLAP [elizalde2023clap] and LAION-CLAP [wu2023large] scale contrastive language-audio pretraining with curated datasets, and show strong transfer across retrieval benchmarks. In addition, AudioCLIP [guzhov2022audioclip] extends CLIP to a tri-modal image-text-audio setting, to leverage visual-text semantics, and Wav2CLIP [wu2022wav2clip] distills CLIP’s alignment into an audio encoder when audio-text pairs are scarce.

Beyond global representations, a line of work that aims to extract representations at a more fine-grained scale learns temporally local structure, for example, by operating on spectrogram patch tokens with transformer architectures. The Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) [gong2021ast] and PaSST [koutini2021efficient] show that attention over time-frequency patches captures long-range temporal dependencies, and HTS-AT [chen2022hts] further returns frame-level maps that are useful for event localization. These tokenizations make it straightforward to bind subclip semantics to text (e.g., , “a door slams, then footsteps echo”). Self-supervised masked objectives, e.g., , SSAST [gong2022ssast], MAE-AST [baade2022mae], and Audio-MAE [huang2022masked], additionally pretrain such backbones by reconstructing masked patches, while BEATs [chen2022beats] adds an iterative tokenizer-encoder scheme that encourages high-level semantic abstraction.

Across advances in representations and objectives, an emergent and increasingly common paradigm is to first pretrain an audio backbone with masked modeling, then align embeddings to text via contrastive losses, and finally, optionally add a captioning head to increase supervision. In tasks where spatial semantics is important, incorporating spatial labels, such as direction-of-arrival, helps refine the audio-text representation space. By leveraging these approaches, models can learn to align predicates such as “left-of” or “far” with meaningful acoustic features. These methods enable models to learn embeddings that are not only open-vocabulary and temporally grounded, but also (coarsely) spatially aware.

5.5 Vision-vision

A common approach to improving vision-language alignment is to first align vision with vision, intuitively, enforcing geometric consistency such that visual features are anchored to a persistent world model before combining with language. Concretely, the goal of vision-vision representation learning is to fuse visual inputs (e.g., , multiview RGB) into a set of world-aligned scene tokens, such that they are invariant to viewpoint changes and can be later queried by language. Here, we discuss three broad families of approaches: lifting 2D features into 3D scene tokens, projecting these 3D tokens back into 2D for supervision, and using audiovisual correspondence to add constraints that further anchor the world model.

Lifting 2D to 3D follows two complementary directions. The most classical and canonical approach first estimates camera poses and geometry with structure-from-motion (SfM) and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), then adds semantics to the generated map. Here, commonly used frameworks include COLMAP for SfM [schonberger2016structure], KinectFusion and ElasticFusion for dense RGB-D mapping [newcombe2011kinectfusion, whelan2015elasticfusion], and ORB-SLAM2 for SLAM [mur2017orb]. Learning-based reconstructions build upon this direction by back-projecting per-view features into a 3D volume and predicting TSDF or occupancy directly from posed images, for example, as in NeuralRecon [sun2021neuralrecon]. Though components may differ, all of these approaches output view-agnostic scene tokens that can later be guided by linguistic supervision and queries.

Projecting 3D back to 2D provides self-supervision. Differentiable rendering in neural fields anchors world-aligned tokens to multiview observations, and enforces cross-view consistency [mildenhall2021nerf]. Distilling 2D foundation features into 3D fields adds semantic knowledge without manual, expensive 3D labels. Here, works typically transfer 2D features into a co-registered 3D feature volume, which can be rendered to any view [shen2023distilled, ye2023featurenerf]. In addition, distillation is not limited to 2D language targets alone; for example, ImageBind [girdhar2023imagebind] proposes a multisensor feature target (image-text-audio-depth-thermal-IMU), which enables transfer of cross-sensor semantics even when there are few explicit labels. Although these distillations are vision-vision processes, they are explicitly designed for language alignment later. The key benefit is that now vision-language alignment is conducted on a geometry-consistent representation, rather than directly on view-specific features.

Audio-visual alignment can further constrain this vision-vision world model; self-supervised objectives have been designed to enforce consistency between audio and visual motion, which allows models to localize sound sources and disambiguate co-occurring events [arandjelovic2017look, owens2018audio, zhao2018sound]. Such cues provide directional or timing semantics that help anchor linguistic queries to specific world-aligned entities, especially in cases with multiple candidate entities. Across this variety of approaches, vision-vision representation learning methods all aim to learn a persistent world model that is geometrically and temporally consistent before adding any linguistic supervision, therefore making downstream cross-modal alignment more data-efficient and spatially faithful to the physical world.

Part III Spatial Intelligence: From Perception to Generation

If the previous part asked how space is represented, this one asks what a system does with that representation. Under the definition of Chapter 2, this use resolves into three capabilities that build on one another: perceiving space, reasoning over it, and generating it, the generative side of prediction. These are less separate subfields than three phases of a single loop running from sensory input to spatial artifact.

Perception comes first because everything downstream depends on it: it converts raw observation into structured spatial evidence, answering what is present, where it lies, and how it moves. Reasoning takes that evidence as given and draws consequences from it, inferring relations, planning routes and actions, and predicting how a configuration will change under intervention. Generation closes the loop by running the process in reverse, mapping an intent (a prompt, a constraint, a partial observation) back into concrete spatial content: an image, a shape, a scene, a motion, an entire simulated world. Read in sequence, the three chapters trace the path from a scene that is given, to one that is understood, to one that is made.

Each of the three rests on the representations built in the previous part and supplies capabilities that the applications of the next will draw on; together they are the core of what makes a system spatially intelligent.

Chapter 6 Spatial Perception

Spatial perception is the foundational layer of spatial intelligence: it turns raw sensory input into the structured spatial evidence that everything downstream depends on, answering what is present, where it lies, and how it moves. It is what stands between an agent and a scene, and the reliability of every later inference is bounded by the reliability of what perception delivers.

The chapter follows a single progression, from the elemental to the structured. It begins with recognizing the discrete entities that populate a scene, grounds them in metric geometry, then binds them into relational and scene-level structure, extends that structure across time, and finally broadens it beyond vision by fusing complementary modalities. Each step presupposes the ones before it, so that perception builds from isolated percepts toward a dynamic, multimodal model of space that reasoning and generation can act on.

6.1 Spatial Entity Recognition

Before space can be measured or organized, its contents must be named. Spatial entity recognition is that entry point: it answers what is present, and every later geometric and relational step builds on the entities it names. Recognition operates at several granularities, and the section is ordered accordingly: detecting discrete object instances, delineating dense regions of pixels or points by segmentation, pinning down sparse keypoints and landmarks, and finally assigning a holistic scene label. What unites them is that they recover identity and category, not yet geometry; where each entity sits and how it is oriented is taken up next.

6.1.1 Object Detection
6.1.1.1 Task Definition

Given a 2D image II, 2D object detection identifies instances of predefined object classes and localizes each one in the image plane. The output is a set of detections

𝒟={(ci,bi,si)}i=1N,\mathcal{D}=\{(c_{i},b_{i},s_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, (6.1)

where cic_{i} is the predicted class, bi=(xi,yi,wi,hi)b_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i},w_{i},h_{i}) a 2D bounding box parameterized by center and size, and si∈[0,1]s_{i}\in[0,1] a confidence score. In short, the task answers what objects are where. Figure 6.1 summarizes the 2D task and its detector families.

3D object detection keeps the same set-of-detections output but places each box in metric 3D space. The input is a LiDAR point cloud 𝒫={𝐩j}j=1M\mathcal{P}=\{\mathbf{p}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} with 𝐩j∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} (often with an intensity channel), one or more calibrated images, or both, and each box becomes

bi=(xi,yi,zi,li,wi,hi,θi),b_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i},\;l_{i},w_{i},h_{i},\;\theta_{i}), (6.2)

a 3D center, the physical length, width, and height, and a heading angle θi\theta_{i} about the vertical axis; indoor benchmarks often use axis-aligned boxes and drop θi\theta_{i}. Because the box is expressed in the sensor or ego frame rather than the image plane, a 3D detection already carries metric position and heading, which is why driving and robotics stacks consume it directly.

6.1.1.2 Methodology
Before Deep Learning.

Early detectors [zou2019object] ran a sliding window over multi-scale image pyramids and classified each candidate region with hand-crafted features and shallow models. Viola–Jones [viola_jones_2001] combined Haar-like features with an AdaBoost cascade for real-time face detection; HOG features with linear SVMs [dalal_triggs_2005] became the standard pipeline for pedestrians and generic objects; and deformable part-based models (DPMs) [felzenszwalb_dpm_2010] represented an object as parts connected by deformable constraints. Manual feature design, dense-window evaluation, and limited robustness to pose, scale, and occlusion capped this line and motivated the move to learned features.

Two-stage Detectors.

R-CNN [girshick2014rcnn] first generates category-independent region proposals and then classifies each with a CNN, a large accuracy gain over hand-crafted pipelines bought with high computational cost. Fast R-CNN [girshick2015fast] shares convolutional computation across proposals through ROI pooling and trains classification and box regression jointly; Faster R-CNN [ren2015faster] adds a Region Proposal Network so that proposals are nearly free and the whole detector trains end-to-end. Sparse R-CNN [sun2021sparsercnn] later replaced dense anchors with a small set of learnable proposals, reaching end-to-end detection without a transformer.

One-stage Detectors.

One-stage detectors drop the proposal step and predict classes and boxes directly from the feature map. YOLO [redmon2016yolo] casts detection as a single regression over the whole image, trading localization accuracy for speed; YOLOv2 and YOLOv3 [redmon2017yolo9000, redmon2018yolov3] add anchors, multi-scale prediction, and stronger backbones, and later versions [bochkovskiy2020yolov4, jocher2020yolov5] refine training and deployment. SSD [liu2016ssd] predicts from multiple feature maps at different scales, and RetinaNet [lin2017focal] introduces the focal loss to counter the extreme foreground–background imbalance, bringing one-stage accuracy level with two-stage methods. Recent YOLO models move to anchor-free, decoupled heads (YOLOv8 [jocher2023yolov8]) and NMS-free end-to-end training (YOLOv10 [wang2024yolov10]), converging with the set-prediction detectors below.

Transformer-based Detectors.

DETR [carion2020end] reformulates detection as direct set prediction with a transformer encoder–decoder, removing anchors and non-maximum suppression at the price of slow convergence and weak small-object performance. Deformable DETR [Zhu2021DeformableDETR] attends to a sparse set of sampling points, which fixes both; Conditional DETR [meng2021conditional] conditions decoder attention on spatial queries for faster training; DINO [zhang2023dino] adds denoising training and better query initialization; and RT-DETR [zhao2024detrs] brings the family to real-time speed.

Open-Vocabulary Detection.

Open-vocabulary detection (OVD) recognizes objects outside a fixed label set by aligning region features with text embeddings. The line evolved from embedding distillation to large-scale vision–language pretraining to data-driven vocabulary expansion: ViLD [gu2021open] and OVR-CNN [zareian2021ovrcnn] distill or learn a shared region–text embedding space from image–text pairs; GLIP [li2022grounded] unifies detection with phrase grounding under grounded language–image pretraining; and Detic [zhou2022detecting] shows that image-level labels over a large vocabulary suffice to train the classifier of an open-vocabulary detector. OWL-ViT [minderer2022simple], Grounding DINO [liu2024grounding], and YOLO-World [cheng2024yoloworld] push the same idea toward simpler transfer, tighter grounding, and real-time speed; see the surveys [zhu2024survey, wu2024towards] for a fuller account.

3D Object Detection.

3D detectors differ mainly in how they turn sensor data into something a network can process; the detection heads on top largely reuse the 2D families above. On LiDAR, VoxelNet [zhou2018voxelnet] learns features inside voxels and runs 3D convolutions over the grid, and PointPillars [lang2019pointpillars] collapses the vertical axis into pillars so that an ordinary 2D CNN on the bird’s-eye-view (BEV) plane does the rest at real-time speed. Point-based detectors keep the raw points: PointRCNN [shi2019pointrcnn] generates proposals from PointNet++ features [qi2017pointnetplus] of segmented foreground points, PV-RCNN [shi2020pvrcnn] combines voxel and point features. CenterPoint [yin2021center] replaces anchors with BEV center heatmaps, the 3D counterpart of anchor-free 2D detection. Indoor scenes are cluttered and object centers often fall in empty space, which favors voting: in VoteNet [qi2019votenet] surface points vote for object centers before grouping, and 3DETR [misra20213detr] carries DETR-style set prediction over to point clouds.

Camera-only 3D detection has to infer the depth that LiDAR measures. Monocular detectors regress depth, size, and orientation on top of a 2D detection (Section 6.2.3 treats them as metric estimation). Pseudo-LiDAR [wang2019pseudolidar] instead converts a predicted depth map into a point cloud and runs a LiDAR detector on it, showing that much of the camera–LiDAR gap came from the representation rather than from depth quality alone. Multi-camera systems lift image features into a shared BEV space, either bottom-up, as Lift-Splat-Shoot [philion2020lss] does by predicting a depth distribution per pixel and splatting features onto the ground plane, or top-down, as DETR3D [wang2022detr3d] and BEVFormer [LiWLXSLQD22] do by projecting 3D queries or BEV cells into the images to sample features. Fusion combines both sensors, from Frustum PointNets [qi2018frustum], which crops the point cloud with 2D image detections, to BEVFusion [liu2023bevfusion], which merges camera and LiDAR features on a common BEV map. Cube R-CNN [Omni3D-Brazil0SR0G23] trains a single image-based detector across indoor and outdoor domains on Omni3D. Deployment constraints for driving are discussed in Section 9.2, and video detection, which adds cross-frame association to the same output set, under tracking in Section 6.4.2.

6.1.1.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.1 summarizes the benchmarks that shaped the field. PASCAL VOC [everingham2010pascal] fixed the evaluation protocol and remained the reference through the early deep-learning era despite its modest scale. MS COCO [lin2014microsoft], with complex everyday scenes and segmentation masks alongside boxes, then became the standard for both detection and segmentation. Open Images [kuznetsova2020open], Objects365 [shao2019objects365], and LVIS [gupta2019lvis] scale the vocabulary to hundreds and then over a thousand categories, with LVIS deliberately emphasizing rare classes, which turned it into the canonical long-tail and open-world benchmark.

Evaluation follows the precision–recall framework. A detection (c^,b^,s^)(\hat{c},\hat{b},\hat{s}) is correct when it matches a previously unmatched ground-truth instance of class c^\hat{c}, whose box bb overlaps b^\hat{b} at or above the required Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold

IoU⁢(b^,b)=|b^∩b||b^∪b|.\mathrm{IoU}(\hat{b},b)=\frac{|\hat{b}\cap b|}{|\hat{b}\cup b|}. (6.3)

Sorting the detections of a class by confidence traces a precision–recall curve whose area is the Average Precision (AP); the mean Average Precision (mAP) averages AP over classes. Benchmarks differ chiefly in the IoU threshold: PASCAL VOC uses a single IoU=0.5\mathrm{IoU}=0.5 (AP50), whereas COCO averages over ten thresholds from 0.50.5 to 0.950.95 to obtain its primary AP and reports AP50 and AP75 as diagnostic slices. COCO further stratifies by object size into APS (area <322<32^{2} pixels), APM (32232^{2}–96296^{2}), and APL (>962>96^{2}), which exposes the persistent difficulty of small objects.

3D detection is benchmarked mainly on driving data, KITTI [KITTI-GeigerLU12], nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes], and the Waymo Open Dataset [WaymoOpen-SunKDCPTGZCCVHN20], and indoors on SUN RGB-D [song2015sunrgbd] and ScanNet [dai2017scannet]; Omni3D (Table 6.1) pools image-based 3D annotations from both. The IoU above is computed between 3D boxes or their BEV footprints: KITTI reports 3D and BEV AP at IoU 0.70.7 for cars and 0.50.5 for pedestrians and cyclists, and indoor benchmarks report mAP at 3D IoU 0.250.25 and 0.50.5. nuScenes matches detections by center distance on the ground plane (0.50.5, 11, 22, and 44 m) instead of IoU and folds translation, scale, orientation, velocity, and attribute errors into its nuScenes Detection Score (NDS); Waymo weights AP by heading accuracy (APH).

Table 6.2 collects reported COCO results across the detector families. On the canonical ResNet-50 backbone, AP has climbed from 37.437.4 for Faster R-CNN to 53.153.1 for RT-DETR over roughly a decade, with much of the recent gain attributable to transformer-based set prediction (DETR →\rightarrow Deformable DETR →\rightarrow DINO) and improved denoising-style query initialization. The APS column highlights the well-documented small-object weakness of vanilla DETR (20.520.5); deformable attention and denoising progressively close this gap (Deformable DETR 26.426.4, DINO 32.032.0, RT-DETR 34.834.8). On the efficiency frontier, the modern YOLO line (YOLOv8-x at 53.953.9, YOLOv10-l at 53.253.2) matches RT-DETR in accuracy at substantially higher throughput, so the traditional accuracy–speed divide between CNN one-stage detectors and transformer set prediction has largely closed.

6.1.1.4 Challenges

The accuracy–efficiency trade-off remains unresolved. The transformer-based detectors that top COCO and open-vocabulary leaderboards are still expensive at inference: even with deployment stacks such as TensorRT, their latency and parameter counts rule out most mobile and embedded targets, while the lightweight real-time detectors that fit those budgets trail them in accuracy. The same tension recurs for every recognition task in this section. Open-world detection degrades on the hardest instances. Open-vocabulary detectors extend recognition beyond a fixed label set, yet still miss small objects and mislabel rare categories, precisely the long-tail regime that motivated LVIS. Detection inside multimodal large language models is still immature. Recent systems fold detection into MLLMs as a grounding primitive that ties image regions to language, but even the strongest closed-source models post markedly lower numbers than specialist detectors on standard benchmarks [zhu2024survey, wu2024towards]. 3D detection is bounded by depth. For camera-only detectors, localization error is dominated by depth error, which grows with distance [ma2021delving]; LiDAR measures depth directly but its returns thin out with range, so distant and small objects are seen through a handful of points.

6.1.2 Segmentation

Segmentation partitions an image, a video, or a 3D scan into meaningful regions. Before deep learning it was a mid-level grouping problem, clustering pixels by similarity somewhere between low-level edge detection and high-level recognition; learned models turned it into dense prediction, with class labels, instance identities, and temporal consistency attached to every region. Figure 6.2 shows the principal segmentation map types produced on a common scene.

6.1.2.1 Task Definition

Semantic Segmentation: Given an input image I∈ℝH×W×3I\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}, semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel, producing a dense label map

S∈{1,…,C}H×W,S\in\{1,\dots,C\}^{H\times W}, (6.4)

where CC is the number of classes; instances of the same class are not distinguished.

Instance and Panoptic Segmentation: Instance segmentation detects and segments each object instance separately. The output is a set of labeled masks

𝒴={(mi,ci)}i=1N,\mathcal{Y}=\{(m_{i},c_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, (6.5)

where mi∈{0,1}H×Wm_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} is the binary mask of the ii-th instance and cic_{i} its class; masks may overlap, and only countable thing classes are covered. Panoptic segmentation keeps the same output form but requires the NN masks to form a non-overlapping partition of the image that covers thing instances and stuff regions alike, each stuff class as a single mask.

Video Segmentation: Given a video clip V∈ℝT×H×W×3V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times H\times W\times 3}, video segmentation predicts temporally consistent masks across frames, output as a set of mask tubes

𝒴={(mi,ci)}i=1N,mi∈{0,1}T×H×W,\mathcal{Y}=\{(m_{i},c_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N},\quad m_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{T\times H\times W}, (6.6)

each tracking an object or region over time, with semantic, instance, and panoptic variants as above.

3D Segmentation: Given a point cloud 𝒫={𝐩j}j=1M\mathcal{P}=\{\mathbf{p}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} with 𝐩j∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and optional color or intensity, 3D semantic segmentation labels every point,

S∈{1,…,C}M,S\in\{1,\dots,C\}^{M}, (6.7)

and 3D instance and panoptic segmentation predict point masks mi∈{0,1}Mm_{i}\in\{0,1\}^{M} under the same set form and overlap constraints as their image counterparts; voxels or mesh vertices take the place of points for other 3D representations. The definitions carry over unchanged. What changes is the input: the points are unordered, unevenly spaced, and sparse, and that is where 3D methods depart from image methods.

6.1.2.2 Methodology

Figure 6.3 summarizes the method families surveyed below.

Before Deep Learning.

Classical segmentation grouped pixels either by appearance or by minimizing an energy. The first family includes thresholding of pixel intensities [otsu1979threshold], region growing that merges similar neighbors [adams1994region], kk-means clustering in feature space [macqueen1967kmeans], and the watershed transform, which treats the image as a topographic surface and segments by catchment basins [vincent1991watersheds]. The second family includes active contours (snakes) that evolve a curve toward object boundaries [kass1988snakes], graph cuts that solve certain segmentation energies to global optimality [boykov2001graphcuts], and Markov and conditional random fields that impose spatial coherence probabilistically [geman1984mrf, lafferty2001crf]; the last of these carried over directly into early learning-based segmenters.

Fully Convolutional Networks.

FCNs [long2015fcn] replace fully connected layers with convolutions, enabling end-to-end dense prediction at arbitrary input size. U-Net [ronneberger2015unet] adds a symmetric encoder–decoder with skip connections that fuse low- and high-level features, SegNet [badrinarayanan2017segnet] reuses max-pooling indices for cheap upsampling and boundary recovery, and PSPNet [zhao2017pspnet] aggregates global and local context through pyramid pooling.

Dilated and Multi-Scale Context Modeling (DeepLab Series).

The DeepLab series introduces atrous (dilated) convolution to enlarge the receptive field without losing resolution (v1 [chen2015deeplab]), Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling for multi-scale context (v2 [chen2017deeplabv2], refined with batch normalization and stronger backbones in v3 [chen2017deeplabv3]), and an encoder–decoder that recovers boundary detail from low-level features (v3+ [chen2018deeplabv3plus]).

Region-Based Mask Prediction (Mask R-CNN Family).

Mask R-CNN [he2017mask] extends Faster R-CNN with a parallel mask branch and ROIAlign, which removes the quantization error of ROI pooling and makes pixel-accurate masks possible. PANet [liu2018panet], Hybrid Task Cascade [chen2019htc], and PointRend [kirillov2020pointrend] refine it through better feature flow, cascaded box–mask prediction, and point-wise boundary rendering respectively; this two-stage, region-based family dominated instance segmentation until transformers arrived.

Transformer Backbones and Representation Learning.

Transformer-based segmentation, following DETR, favors unified query-based formulations that bridge detection and segmentation, predict masks end-to-end without hand-crafted post-processing, and allow joint learning across tasks and modalities. The first step was the backbone: SETR [zheng2021setr] applies a pure ViT to semantic segmentation with a simple decoder, SegFormer [xie2021segformer] pairs a lightweight hierarchical transformer with an MLP decoder for a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off, and Swin Transformer [liu2021swin] uses shifted-window attention to produce CNN-like multi-scale features and has become a default segmentation backbone. Self-supervised pretraining such as MAE [he2022masked] supplies ViT backbones that transfer well to dense prediction.

Query-based Transformer Segmentation.

Query-based methods cast segmentation as set prediction with object or mask queries. MaX-DeepLab [wang2021maxdeeplab] is the first purely mask-based panoptic framework without box supervision; MaskFormer [cheng2021maskformer] unifies semantic and panoptic segmentation by predicting mask embeddings with class labels; K-Net [zhang2021knet] treats segmentation as kernel prediction with iterative refinement; and Mask2Former [cheng2022mask2former] adds masked cross-attention and multi-scale decoding, setting a strong baseline across all three tasks. QueryInst [fang2021queryinst] and Panoptic SegFormer [li2022panopticsegformer] are variants that respectively generate instance-specific kernels from queries and decouple semantic from instance queries.

Video and Multimodal Transformer-based Segmentation.

VisTR [wang2021vistr] predicts spatio-temporal mask tubes end-to-end from object queries; Video K-Net [li2022videoknet] unifies video semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation by associating queries across time; and TubeFormer [wang2022tubeformer] adds tube-level attention for long-term consistency. X-Decoder [zou2023xdecoder] unifies image segmentation with language-based prediction, while OMGSeg [OMGSeg] covers image and video segmentation across open-vocabulary and class-agnostic settings within one model.

SAM series.

SAM [kirillov2023sam] made segmentation promptable: trained on the SA-1B dataset of over one billion masks, it decouples a heavy image encoder from a light prompt-conditioned mask decoder and produces masks from points, boxes, or text with strong zero-shot generalization. SAM 2 [ravi2024sam2] extends this to video, propagating masks across frames with a memory mechanism while keeping interactive control.

3D Point Cloud Segmentation.

Point-cloud segmenters split by how they impose structure on the points (Section 4.2.3). Point-based networks consume raw points: PointNet [qi2017pointnet] applies a shared MLP to every point and pools symmetrically, PointNet++ [qi2017pointnetplus] adds hierarchical neighborhoods, DGCNN [wang2019dgcnn] builds kk-nearest-neighbor graphs that are recomputed in feature space at every layer, KPConv [thomas2019kpconv] defines convolution kernels by points placed in space, and RandLA-Net [hu2020randlanet] relies on random sampling to scale to scenes of millions of points. Sparse voxel networks such as MinkowskiNet [choy2019minkowski] and SPVNAS [tang2020searching] quantize the points and convolve only occupied voxels, which keeps 3D convolution affordable on room- and street-scale scans. Projection methods take the opposite route: RangeNet++ [milioto2019rangenet] unrolls a LiDAR sweep into a range image, runs a 2D segmenter in real time, and projects the labels back onto the points. Transformers entered with Point Transformer [zhao2021point], and Point Transformer V3 [wu2024ptv3] replaces exact neighbor search with serialized point orderings so that attention scales to large scenes.

Instance segmentation in 3D retraces the 2D history. PointGroup [jiang2020pointgroup] predicts per-point offsets toward instance centers and clusters the shifted points, a bottom-up grouping; Mask3D [schult2023mask3d] applies Mask2Former-style queries to sparse voxel features and predicts instance masks directly. Because 3D labels remain scarce, open-vocabulary 3D segmentation mostly borrows from 2D foundation models: OpenScene [peng2023openscene] distills CLIP-aligned pixel features into points, and OpenMask3D [takmaz2023openmask3d] classifies class-agnostic 3D instance masks with CLIP features aggregated over multi-view images.

6.1.2.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.3 summarizes the main benchmarks. PASCAL VOC [everingham2010pascal] anchored the classical semantic-segmentation era with 20 foreground classes plus background. MS COCO [lin2014microsoft], with semantic, instance, box, and panoptic annotations over complex object-centric scenes, is the shared testbed for all three modern task types. Cityscapes [cordts2016cityscapes] and Mapillary Vistas [neuhold2017mapillary] specialize to street scenes, the latter stressing long-tail classes and diverse geographies, and ADE20K [zhou2017ade20k] targets holistic scene parsing over 150 object and stuff classes. The 3D rows of the table cover indoor RGB-D scans (NYU-D V2, SUN RGB-D, ScanNet) and outdoor LiDAR (SemanticKITTI), and S3DIS [armeni2016s3dis] is a further indoor standard.

Segmentation evaluation reuses IoU (Section 6.1.1) with masks in place of boxes. For semantic segmentation the headline metric is the mean Intersection over Union (mIoU),

mIoU=1C⁢∑k=1CTPkTPk+FPk+FNk,\mathrm{mIoU}=\frac{1}{C}\sum_{k=1}^{C}\frac{\mathrm{TP}_{k}}{\mathrm{TP}_{k}+% \mathrm{FP}_{k}+\mathrm{FN}_{k}}, (6.8)

where CC is the number of classes and TPk\mathrm{TP}_{k}, FPk\mathrm{FP}_{k}, FNk\mathrm{FN}_{k} count the true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative pixels for class kk. Because the average is unweighted, mIoU is sensitive to rare classes, which is one motivation behind ADE20K and Mapillary Vistas; pixel accuracy is dominated by frequent classes (e.g., , sky, road) and is less informative.

For instance segmentation, the COCO mask-AP protocol matches predictions to ground truth by mask IoU and averages AP over IoU thresholds 0.50.5–0.950.95. For panoptic segmentation, Panoptic Quality [kirillov2019panoptic] is PQ=SQ×RQ\mathrm{PQ}=\mathrm{SQ}\times\mathrm{RQ}, the average IoU of matched segments times the F1 score over matched, false-positive, and false-negative segments, treating things and stuff uniformly. For video object segmentation, the DAVIS 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} metric averages region similarity (𝒥\mathcal{J}, mask IoU) and contour accuracy (ℱ\mathcal{F}, computed on mask boundaries). 3D semantic segmentation reports the same mIoU computed over points or voxels, and 3D instance segmentation on ScanNet reports AP at mask IoU thresholds averaged over 0.50.5–0.950.95, with AP50 and AP25 as looser slices.

Table 6.4 reports results across these four protocols. The clearest trend is on semantic segmentation, where ADE20K mIoU has roughly doubled in under a decade, from FCN-8s’s 29.429.4 to Mask2Former’s 57.757.7; the largest single jumps track two shifts, first to transformer backbones (SETR, SegFormer, Swin-L) and then to universal query-based formulations. That second shift is what unifies the table: MaskFormer is the first entry to report semantic mIoU and panoptic PQ within one framework, and Mask2Former extends the same architecture to all three tasks with competitive results on each. Instance segmentation followed a partly separate path, climbing from Mask R-CNN (35.435.4) and HTC (38.438.4) on R50-FPN to 50.150.1 once Mask2Former is paired with a Swin-L backbone, which confirms that transformer backbones lift mask quality at the instance level as well, not only semantic accuracy.

6.1.2.4 Challenges

The cost of self-attention at high resolution, over long video, and on dense 3D data sharpens the accuracy–speed tension noted for detection, and two problems are specific to segmentation. Long-video, multi-object consistency is hard. Holding spatial precision and temporal coherence together remains difficult in cluttered scenes, particularly for video panoptic segmentation and segmentation-based multi-object tracking, where objects enter, leave, and occlude one another over long horizons. Segmentation is moving toward the open world. The field is shifting from fixed label sets to class-agnostic, open-vocabulary, and multimodal settings, in which language and other auxiliary signals are folded in to improve spatial reasoning and adaptability, a direction that SAM, X-Decoder, and OMGSeg already anticipate.

6.1.3 Keypoint and Landmark Detection

Keypoint and landmark detection localizes a set of semantically consistent, precisely positioned points that characterize object geometry in images or videos: eye corners, skeletal joints, or structurally distinctive parts of man-made objects. Compared with region-based representations, keypoints give a sparser, explicitly geometric encoding that often survives deformation, rotation, and partial occlusion. Figure 6.4 summarizes the task families and the method families surveyed below.

6.1.3.1 Task Definition

Given an input image II, a parametric model fθf_{\theta} estimates a set of point locations

fθ⁢(I)={𝐩i}i=1N,𝐩i∈ℝ2,f_{\theta}(I)=\{\mathbf{p}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\quad\mathbf{p}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, (6.9)

where each 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} is the image coordinate of a salient visual or structural element. Landmark detection fixes a predefined semantic identity for each point (a particular eye corner, a particular joint); the two terms are otherwise used interchangeably.

3D keypoint detection predicts 𝐩i∈ℝ3\mathbf{p}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} instead. From images, the depth of each point must be inferred; from depth maps or point clouds 𝒫\mathcal{P}, surface geometry is observed, but occluded or internal landmarks still require inference. For human pose, 3D joints are usually expressed in camera coordinates relative to a root joint (the pelvis), which leaves global depth unconstrained, as a single image cannot fix it.

The task varies along three axes. The input modality sets what geometry is directly available: most detectors work on 2D images (RGB, grayscale, or infrared), where keypoints must be inferred from appearance alone, whereas point clouds expose spatial structure directly; RGB-D or RGB-infrared fusion adds robustness in clutter and poor lighting, and video supplies temporal continuity through motion blur and transient occlusion. The prediction target ranges from planar image coordinates, which underpin most benchmarks, to 3D keypoints required in robotics and autonomous driving, to 4D trajectories tracked over time. The application scenario fixes what the points mean. Research has concentrated on humans: body joints for pose estimation, facial landmarks for expression recognition and identity verification, and finger joints for gesture-based interaction and sign language recognition [ko2019neural]. Keypoints are also defined on everyday items, industrial parts, and vehicles for manipulation, inspection, and driving (e.g., , monocular 3D detection from vehicle keypoints [li2020rtm3d]), on animals for behavior analysis (multi-animal DeepLabCut [lauer2022multi]), and on anatomical structures in medical imaging, where universal landmark detectors cover several modalities and anatomies [zhu2021you].

6.1.3.2 Methodology

Classical pipelines combined local feature detectors with statistical shape models that handled occlusion and deformation through explicit geometric constraints. Moravec [moravec1980obstacle], Harris [harris1988combined], and Shi–Tomasi [shi1994good] corners were followed by feature detectors and descriptors such as SIFT [lowe2004distinctive], SURF [bay2006surf], FAST [rosten2006machine], BRIEF [calonder2010brief], and ORB [rublee2011orb], which improved scale invariance, speed, and robustness. For faces and hands, active shape models [cootes1995asm], active appearance models [cootes1998active], and constrained local models with regularized mean-shift fitting [saragih2011deformable] provided the parametric frameworks.

Learning-based detection began with supervised descent for face alignment [xiong2013supervised] and, in 2014, with DeepPose [toshev2014deeppose], which regressed human joints directly with a deep network. Heatmap regression then dominated through 2020: Tompson et al. [tompson2014joint, tompson2015efficient] coupled convolutional networks with graphical models, convolutional pose machines [wei2016convolutional] and stacked hourglass networks [newell2016stacked] refined heatmaps over repeated stages, and HRNet [wang2020deep] kept a high-resolution branch throughout the network for precise localization.

Multi-person estimation splits into two strategies. Top-down methods detect each person first and then estimate keypoints inside the box, which is accurate but scales with the number of people; bottom-up methods predict all keypoints at once and then group them, which is faster but makes grouping the hard part. Part Affinity Fields [cao2017realtime], consolidated as OpenPose [CaoHSWS21], are the canonical bottom-up design; YOLO-Pose [maji2022yolo], RTMPose [jiang2023rtmpose], and RTMO [lu2024rtmo] advance real-time multi-person estimation through one-stage and top-down designs.

Vision transformers and foundation models made keypoint detection general-purpose: ViTPose [xu2022vitpose] set simple transformer baselines for human pose in 2022, and Sapiens [khirodkar2024sapiens] in 2024 provides a single foundation model for human-centric vision tasks.

3D human pose estimation grew out of these 2D detectors. Lifting methods take detected 2D keypoints as input and regress the 3D joints: a fully connected network on 2D joints alone was a strong baseline [martinez2017simple], temporal convolutions over 2D pose sequences (VideoPose3D [pavllo2019videopose3d]) and spatio-temporal transformers (MotionBERT [zhu2023motionbert]) use motion to reduce the depth ambiguity, and DiffPose [gong2023diffpose] casts lifting as diffusion. Direct methods predict 3D from pixels, as in the volumetric heatmaps of Pavlakos et al. [pavlakos2017coarse]. With a calibrated multi-view rig most of the ambiguity disappears, and learnable triangulation [iskakov2019learnable] fuses per-view heatmaps into a 3D estimate. Recovering a full body mesh rather than a joint set is taken up with human motion in Section 8.4.

Classical corner detectors were in turn replaced by learned ones: SuperPoint [detone2018superpoint] learns detection and description jointly under self-supervised homographic adaptation, DISK [tyszkiewicz2020disk] selects keypoints with a reinforcement-style objective, and SuperGlue [sarlin2020superglue] matches sparse keypoints; the detector-free LoFTR [Sun2021LoFTR] instead produces semi-dense correspondences. These serve as correspondence rather than semantic points and are the workhorses of the structure-from-motion, visual-odometry, and SLAM pipelines in the spatial-localization section that follows.

On point clouds, keypoints mostly serve registration and pose estimation. Intrinsic Shape Signatures [zhong2009iss] select points whose local neighborhood has a distinctive eigenvalue structure; USIP [li2019usip] learns, without labels, detectors that stay stable under rigid transformation, and D3Feat [bai2020d3feat] predicts a detection score and a descriptor for every point, the 3D analogue of SuperPoint. Category-level 3D keypoints are a different kind: Suwajanakorn et al. [suwajanakorn2018discovery] discover keypoints that are consistent across instances of a category through a relative-pose objective, and kPAM [manuelli2019kpam] uses such keypoints as the interface for robotic manipulation. Keypoint-based 6D object pose, which predicts the 2D projections of 3D model keypoints and solves PnP, belongs to pose estimation (Section 6.2.5).

Table 6.5 reports COCO Keypoints (val2017) results for the CNN, transformer, and real-time families.

6.1.3.3 Datasets and Metrics

Keypoint datasets are mostly embedded in broader pose and action benchmarks rather than built in isolation; Table 6.6 lists the most used. Human body datasets are the most mature and trace the field’s expansion: MPII [andriluka20142d] and COCO Keypoints [lin2014microsoft] fixed in-the-wild 2D evaluation, PoseTrack [andriluka2018posetrack] added temporal association in video, Human3.6M [IonescuPOS14] supplies controlled multi-view 3D ground truth for 2D-to-3D lifting, DensePose [guler2018densepose] replaces sparse joints with dense surface correspondences, and CrowdPose [li2019crowdpose] stresses crowded, occluded scenes. Face datasets moved from large pose variation (AFLW [koestinger2011annotated]) and high-density annotation (HELEN [le2012interactive]) to occlusion (COFW [burgos2013robust]), the standardized 68-point protocol of 300-W [sagonas2013300] and its large-pose synthetic extension 300-W-LP [zhu2016face], and the 98-point, hard-condition WFLW [wu2018look]. Hand datasets contend with fine articulation and self-occlusion through multi-view capture (CMU Panoptic HandDB [simon2017hand]), synthetic 3D labels (RHD [zimmermann2017learning]), real 3D pose and shape (FreiHAND [zimmermann2019freihand]), and interacting hands (InterHand2.6M [moon2020interhand2]). Animal-Pose [cao2019cross] and AP-10K [yu2021ap] carry the human recipe to animals across species, while ApolloCar3D [song2019apollocar3d] and KeypointNet [you2020keypointnet] define keypoints on rigid vehicles and 3D object categories.

Metrics measure raw or scale-normalized distances between predicted and ground-truth points. The End-Point Error (EPE) is the raw Euclidean distance. The Normalized Mean Error (NME) divides it by a reference length:

NME=1N⁢∑i=1N∥𝐱^i−𝐱i∥2d,\mathrm{NME}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-\mathbf% {x}_{i}\rVert_{2}}{d}, (6.10)

where 𝐱^i\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i} and 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} denote the predicted and ground-truth locations of the ii-th keypoint, and dd is a task-dependent normalization factor (e.g., , inter-ocular distance for faces). The Percentage of Correct Keypoints (PCK) instead thresholds the error,

PCK⁢@⁢α=1N⁢∑i=1N𝕀⁢(∥𝐱^i−𝐱i∥2≤α⋅s),\mathrm{PCK@}\alpha=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}\!\left(\lVert\hat{% \mathbf{x}}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq\alpha\cdot s\right), (6.11)

where α\alpha controls the tolerance and ss is the reference scale, giving an accuracy rate that is easy to compare across methods; the Cumulative Error Distribution (CED) curve and its Area Under the Curve (AUC) summarize behavior across thresholds.

For large-scale benchmarks, Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS) incorporates object scale and keypoint-specific uncertainty,

OKS=∑iexp⁡(−∥𝐱^i−𝐱i∥222⁢s2⁢κi2)⁢δ⁢(vi>0)∑iδ⁢(vi>0).\mathrm{OKS}=\frac{\sum_{i}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{i}-% \mathbf{x}_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}}{2s^{2}\kappa_{i}^{2}}\right)\delta(v_{i}>0)}{% \sum_{i}\delta(v_{i}>0)}. (6.12)

Here ss denotes the object scale (the square root of the segmented area), κi\kappa_{i} is a per-keypoint normalization constant calibrating the fall-off, and vi∈{0,1,2}v_{i}\in\{0,1,2\} is the ground-truth visibility flag for keypoint ii, where vi=0v_{i}=0 indicates unlabeled, vi=1v_{i}=1 indicates labeled but occluded, and vi=2v_{i}=2 indicates labeled and visible. OKS plays the role of IoU in computing average precision and recall on MS COCO [lin2014microsoft]. For 3D human pose, the Mean Per-Joint Position Error (MPJPE) averages the Euclidean joint error in millimeters after aligning the root joints; PA-MPJPE applies a Procrustes alignment of scale, rotation, and translation first, and 3DPCK thresholds the error at 150150 mm, as on MPI-INF-3DHP [mehta2017monocular]. Point-cloud keypoint detectors are scored by repeatability under rigid transformation and, downstream, by registration recall on benchmarks such as 3DMatch [zeng20173dmatch].

6.1.3.4 Challenges

Robustness in unconstrained scenes is still the first problem [fisal2025reported, guo2025survey]: occlusion, extreme pose, and non-rigid deformation leave partial or ambiguous configurations, and symmetric parts (left versus right limbs, the fingers of a self-occluded hand) are routinely swapped. Generalization is the second [kappan2026survey, ma20252d, jiang2022animal]: keypoint definitions differ across datasets even for the same object class, so models trained on one benchmark transfer poorly to another, and the gap widens for animals, objects, and anatomical structures, where annotation is scarce and demographic or species bias enters the training data. The accuracy–speed tension discussed for detection applies here as well [khabarlak2021fast, alvarez2021real]: high-precision models are too heavy for embedded targets, and lightweight ones lose accuracy precisely under occlusion and fast motion.

6.1.4 Scene Classification

Going beyond objects, regions, and keypoints, scene classification (SC) assigns a single semantic label to a whole image describing the environment it portrays [zeng2021deep]. Where object recognition names the things in a picture (“car”, “tree”, “person”), scene classification names the where: “a busy street”, “a serene beach”, “a modern kitchen”. It asks “What kind of place is this?”, a judgment that rests on the global layout and gist of the image rather than on any single object [henderson1999high, epstein2005cortical], and it supplies the holistic prior on which an embodied or virtual agent conditions its later behavior [liao2016understand, ni2022improved, muhammad2022vision, Zhang2024UrbanVI].

6.1.4.1 Task Definition

Formally, scene classification learns a mapping f:I↦y∈𝒴f:I\mapsto y\in\mathcal{Y} from an image II to a label yy in a predefined category set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, or, in the multi-label case, to a subset Y⊆𝒴Y\subseteq\mathcal{Y} covering several facets of the scene [boutell2004learning] (“urban” for area, “parking lot” for place, “night” for condition). Beyond the single-/multi-label split, the task is instantiated by domain, with indoor [quattoni2009recognizing] and outdoor [6724252] scenes, remote-sensing imagery [nogueira2017towards, cheng2017remote], and driving contexts such as highways and tunnels [ni2022improved], and by modality, extending from still images to video [huang1999integration] and acoustic scenes [mesaros2018multi].

6.1.4.2 Methodology

Figure 6.5 summarizes the progression from hand-crafted global descriptors through deep features to vision–language models.

Early methods summarized the whole image into one discriminative vector of low-level texture, color, and gradient statistics. The Spatial Envelope model [oliva2001modeling] describes a scene by a few perceptual dimensions (naturalness, openness, roughness, expansion, ruggedness), a descriptor commonly called GIST. Bag-of-Visual-Words (BoVW) [csurka2004visual] treats the image as a histogram of quantized local features such as SIFT [lowe2004distinctive], discarding most spatial information [7025553]; Spatial Pyramid Matching (SPM) [lazebnik2006beyond] restores coarse layout by computing BoVW histograms over a pyramid of sub-regions and concatenating them.

Deep networks learn scene features end to end. CNNs [krizhevsky2012imagenet, o2015introduction] such as AlexNet [krizhevsky2012imagenet], VGG [simonyan2014very], ResNet [he2016deep], and DenseNet [huang2017densely], pre-trained on ImageNet [ImageNet, krizhevsky2012imagenet], proved to be strong global feature extractors for scenes, and Places-CNN [zhou2014learning] re-trained them on the large-scale Places benchmark to establish the standard transfer recipe. Vision Transformers [vit] match or exceed CNNs with a class-token embedding that attends over all patches, in the manner of BERT [devlin2019bert].

A separate line models layout explicitly, since a stadium is recognized by its global oval while a classroom differs from an office by the mid-scale arrangement of desks and blackboard. Multi-scale pooling over the CNN feature hierarchy (FPN-style [lin2017feature]) captures structure at several scales, and scene graphs [johnson2015image] make objects and their relations explicit, so that propagating over them with graph convolutional networks [kipf2017semisupervised] yields layout-aware scene features [Liang2020ADN].

Vision–language models (VLMs) turn scene classification into open-vocabulary, zero-shot matching. Contrastive models such as CLIP [radford2021learning] embed the image and the textual names of all candidate classes in one space and pick the most similar class [li2023rs], needing no fine-tuning beyond prompt design [sahoo2024systematic]; the recipe extends to 3D point clouds [huang2023clip2point]. Autoregressive multimodal large language models (MLLMs; LLaVA [liu2023llava], Qwen-VL [bai2023qwen], Gemma 3 [team2025gemma]) instead generate the label as text in response to an instruction [Saha_2024_CVPR]. With rich semantics available for free, the research focus has shifted from one global label toward compositional understanding of what is inside the scene [chen2023clip2scene].

6.1.4.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.7 lists the standard benchmarks. The small early sets, Scene 15 [lazebnik2006beyond] and the indoor MIT 67 [quattoni2009recognizing], were superseded by SUN 397 [XiaoHEOT10, Xiao2014SUNDE], which fixed a near-exhaustive category list, and by Places [zhou2014learning, zhou2017places], which scaled scene recognition to millions of images across its Places205, Places88, Places365-Standard, and Places365-Challenge subsets. NYU Depth v2 [silberman2012nyudv2] and SUN RGB-D [song2015sunrgbd] add aligned depth and a scene category per image for indoor RGB-D classification.

Scene classification is evaluated primarily with top-1 accuracy (the fraction of images for which the highest-scoring predicted class matches the ground truth) and top-5 accuracy (the fraction of images where the ground-truth class is among the top five predictions), with the latter especially useful on long-tail benchmarks such as Places-365 and SUN 397. For multi-label settings, the mean Average Precision (mAP) and class-wise F1 are reported instead, mirroring the protocol used in multi-label image recognition.

Table 6.8 reports results on the two most-cited scene benchmarks. Supervised CNNs on Places-365 cluster in a narrow band of roughly 5353–55%55\% top-1, with diminishing returns from AlexNet to ResNet, while CLIP reaches 63.2%63.2\% top-1 on SUN 397 zero-shot [radford2021learning], on par with supervised scene classifiers without any target-set training.

6.1.4.4 Challenges

Closed-set accuracy on Places-365, SUN 397, and MIT 67 is now recovered zero-shot by CLIP [radford2021learning] and by MLLMs (LLaVA [liu2023llava], Qwen-VL [bai2023qwen], Gemma 3 [team2025gemma]), so “what kind of place is this” is no longer the frontier. The task has climbed a granularity ladder, from one label to attribute sets to grounded, compositional description across image, video, and 3D, and the open problems sit at that richer end, where MLLMs are weaker than their coarse-label accuracy suggests.

Fine-grained and long-tail discrimination. MLLMs still trail dedicated classifiers and CLIP-style models on fine-grained and long-tail categories, where the distinction between, e.g., , a “bistro” and a “brasserie” turns on subtle cues [NEURIPS2024_5c702404].
