Such rules are cheap but brittle: 2D-to-3D back-projection misplaces occluded or oddly posed objects (a rear vehicle whose centroid lands ambiguously on the BEV plane), fixed rules cannot express functional or contextual relations (“person riding bicycle”, a book more likely on a shelf than under it), and every new domain needs its rules rewritten.

Learning-based approaches.

Zhao et al. [zhao2022visual] decoupled spatial relation generation from generic captioning and trained it with a joint visual–spatial objective; 3DVSD [zhao2023generating] moved the same task into 3D scene modeling and added structure-aware sampling that holds up under occlusion.

MLLM-based approaches.

Multimodal large language models carried the line from image-level predicates toward finer and more metric grounding. SpatialVLM [chen2024spatialvlm] used monocular-depth-derived spatial QA supervision to train a vision-language model so the model answers metric queries such as “How far is A from B?”, outperforming GPT-4V on spatial VQA. SpatialBot [cai2024spatialbot] exposes pixel-level depth queries through a depth API and trains progressively, translating spatial reasoning into higher robotic grasping success. SpatialRGPT [cheng2024spatialrgpt] sharpens granularity from the whole image to regions, accepting boxes or masks and auto-generating 8.7M region-level spatial samples through scene-subgraph sampling (S3). SpatialLLM [ma2025spatialllm] pairs a hybrid CLIP–DINOv2 encoder with staged data injection to hold qualitative and quantitative capabilities in one model.

6.3.1.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.17 lists the benchmarks. They differ mainly in how relations were collected: manual labeling of robot-captured lab scenes in SpatialAwareRobot [wang2025spatial]; adversarial crowdsourcing in SpatialSense [yang2019spatialsense], where annotators propose relations that fool a baseline and only those count, which makes the dataset deliberately hard; the merge of SpatialSense and Visual Genome [krishna2017visual] into VSD [zhao2022visual], whose VSD-v1 version contains over 143K descriptions; the 34-preposition, English–French annotations of SpatialVOC2K [belz2018spatialvoc2k]; and the automatically generated, depth-aware SpaceSGG [xu2025llava], released as 10K scene descriptions, 20K question–answer pairs, and 20K multi-turn conversations over 20K scenes.

Each subtask has its own evaluation regime, and the metrics are not comparable across them. VSC is scored as classification: SpatialSense [yang2019spatialsense] measures binary accuracy for given object–predicate pairs, with the driving-scene systems Roadscene2Vec [malawade2022roadscene2vec] and HKT-SG [zhou2024hktsg] reporting per-relation F1 or accuracy on their own data; results on SpatialSense’s adversarial split lag well behind those on conventional crowdsourced data, which is the contextual-relation difficulty taken up under Challenges. VSD is scored as generation: VSDNet [zhao2022visual] and 3DVSD [zhao2023generating] report BLEU-4, METEOR, and CIDEr on the VSD datasets, and LLaVA-SpaceSGG [xu2025llava] reports QA accuracy on SpaceSGG. Quantitative understanding is the newest regime: SpatialVLM [chen2024spatialvlm] and SpatialRGPT [cheng2024spatialrgpt] evaluate metric estimates using human-annotated spatial questions and answers (SpatialVLM) or questions derived from ground-truth 3D cuboid annotations (SpatialRGPT-Bench), SpatialLLM [ma2025spatialllm] reports combined qualitative and quantitative VQA accuracy, and SpatialBot [cai2024spatialbot] adds robotic grasp success as an embodied proxy. MLLM-based models dominate the qualitative leaderboards but still fall short on metric-scale reasoning, which motivates the unified representations discussed next.

6.3.1.4 Challenges

Spatial relations are not purely geometric. “A cup on a table” is plausible and “a cup on a wall” is not, yet the two differ only in object identity, so rule-based and purely geometric methods cannot capture functional or commonsense constraints; a model needs to know what objects are for and where they tend to be, not just their boxes or point coordinates. Metric grounding is the second gap. MLLMs handle contextual and functional predicates well but judge distances, sizes, and angles poorly; injecting geometry and depth during pre- or post-training, or exposing dedicated spatial tools, is the current route, and the longer-term goal is a representation that holds discrete predicates (“near”) and continuous quantities (“2 meters away”) together, since navigation and manipulation need both. Generalization is the third. SpatialSense [yang2019spatialsense] and VSD [zhao2022visual] cover a small slice of real scenes, and models trained on them degrade under new object appearances, scene complexity, lighting, and occlusion; SpatialVLM [chen2024spatialvlm] and its successors generalize better, but unseen and dynamic environments remain largely untested.

6.3.2 Scene Graph Generation

Scene graph generation (SGG) [xu2017scene, chang2021comprehensive, li2024scene] parses visual content into a graph of triplets, each joining a subject and an object through a predicate, for example (person,rides,horse)(\text{person},\text{rides},\text{horse}). The graph records not only which objects are present but how they interact, which is what retrieval [johnson2015image, miao2024scenegraphloc], captioning [zhong2020comprehensive, lu2025benchmarking], autonomous driving [zhou2022toward, liu2023learning, malawade2022roadscene2vec], and robotics [nguyen2025generating, werby2024hierarchical, garg2024robohop] consume downstream.

6.3.2.1 Task Definition

Given a visual scene, SGG produces a graph

𝒢={(si,pi,oi)}i=1M,si,oi∈𝒪,pi∈𝒫,\mathcal{G}=\{(s_{i},p_{i},o_{i})\}_{i=1}^{M},\qquad s_{i},o_{i}\in\mathcal{O}% ,\;p_{i}\in\mathcal{P}, (6.35)

where each entity in 𝒪\mathcal{O} is an object instance with a localization (a bounding box, or a mask in the panoptic setting) and a class label, and pip_{i} is a predicate from a relation vocabulary 𝒫\mathcal{P} describing how sis_{i} and oio_{i} interact.

The task is instantiated by input modality. Image SGG (ISG) [krishna2017visual, zellers2018neural] on static 2D images is the original and most studied setting and anchors most benchmarks. Video SGG (VSG) [teng2021target, cong2021spatial] adds time, so relations become dynamic and temporally extended, and temporal context disambiguates interactions a single frame leaves open. Textual SGG (TSG) [li2023factual, choi2022scene] parses a sentence (“A person is riding a horse in a field”) into a graph, treating SGG as structured language parsing. 3D SGG (3DSG) [wald2020learning, wu2021scenegraphfusion] operates on point clouds or meshes and models relations in metric 3D space, free of the perspective ambiguity of images. Universal SGG (USG) [wu2025universal] aims at one graph from several simultaneous modalities (image, video, 3D, text). Two further variants change the level of detail rather than the modality. Human–Object Interaction detection (HOI) [li2019transferable, wang2020learning] restricts the subject to humans and has become a field of its own because of pose variability and the subtlety of intent. Panoptic SGG (PSG) [yang2022panoptic, yang2023panoptic] grounds nodes on panoptic segmentation masks instead of boxes, so relations can involve “stuff” (sky, road) and are localized without the imprecision of boxes.

6.3.2.2 Methodology

Figure 6.14 illustrates the five modality settings and the two specializations with a representative input and output each.

Two-stage methods.

Two-stage methods [xu2017scene, zellers2018neural, li2021bipartite, lin2020gps, li2023compositional, zhou2024hierarchical] were the standard for years: a pre-trained detector such as Faster R-CNN [ren2015faster] produces boxes and per-object features, and a separate relation model predicts a predicate for each pair. Specializing each stage made the graphs accurate, but detector errors propagate uncorrected into relation prediction, the two models are trained and tuned separately, and object interactions are only modeled after detection has already committed.

One-stage methods.

One-stage methods [im2024egtr, wang2024oed, newell2017pixels, liu2021fully] fold detection and relation prediction into one end-to-end network. Pixel-based [newell2017pixels] and fully convolutional [liu2021fully] formulations came first; after DETR [carion2020end], most one-stage SGG adopted set prediction with learned queries, and the methods differ in what the queries represent. RelTR [cong2023reltr] uses paired subject–object queries so the Transformer predicts relations between pairs directly; SGTR [li2022sgtr] decouples subject, object, and predicate queries and composes them, which lets each component be predicted on its own; and PSGTR [yang2022panoptic] uses triplet queries that emit scene-graph triplets without a detector at all.

Prior knowledge.

Because predicates are long-tailed and many relations are not visually decidable, SGG has long imported priors. Language priors [liang2017deep, lu2016visual, cui2018context] supply semantic embeddings that help rare predicates; statistical priors [yu2017visual, zhou2023learning, zhou2024hierarchical] model object-pair co-occurrence; knowledge graphs such as ConceptNet [speer2017conceptnet] add commonsense [zhang2024hiker, chen2023more]; and LLMs bring world knowledge [chen2024scene, kim2024llm4sgg].

Beyond images.

The non-image settings reuse these designs and add modality-specific machinery. Video SGG tracks object tubes and aggregates relations over time: TRACE [teng2021target] decomposes relation prediction by temporal segment and STTran [cong2021spatial] applies a spatio-temporal Transformer over frame-level graphs. Textual SGG is a parsing problem, for which the FACTUAL parser [li2023factual] fine-tunes a sequence-to-sequence model to emit faithful triples. 3D SGG predicts relations from point-cloud or mesh segments with graph networks [wald2020learning], and SceneGraphFusion [wu2021scenegraphfusion] does so incrementally from an RGB-D stream so the graph grows with the reconstruction. Panoptic SGG is served by the triplet-query PSGTR [yang2022panoptic] and its video extension [yang2023panoptic], and USG [wu2025universal] shares one graph decoder across image, video, 3D, and text inputs.

6.3.2.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.1811 1 The table is extended from the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ChocoWu/Awesome-Scene-Graph-Generation lists the benchmarks by modality. The image benchmarks run from the small precursors Visual Phrase [Sadeghi2011VisualPhrases], Scene Graph [johnson2015image], and VRD [lu2016visual], which first exposed the long-tailed predicate distribution, to Visual Genome [krishna2017visual], Open Images [kuznetsova2020open], and GQA [hudson2019gqa], with VrR-VG [liang2019vrr] and UnRel [peyre2017weakly] carved out to test visually relevant and zero-shot relations respectively. Visual Genome is the primary benchmark but its raw release (33,877 object and 40,480 relationship synsets) is noisy and heavily long-tailed, so the community works with cleaned subsets: the broad cleaning in Table 6.18 keeps roughly 6K object and 1K predicate classes, and the de-facto SGG benchmark VG150 restricts these to the 150 most frequent object and 50 most frequent predicate classes. Spatial-only relations are covered by SpatialSense and SpatialVOC2K (see the preceding subsection), panoptic grounding by PSG [yang2022panoptic], and non-standard viewpoints by the overhead AUG [li2024aug], the satellite STAR [li2025star], ReCon1M [yan2025recon1m], and instruction-based SkySenseGPT [luo2024skysensegpt], and the traffic-scene graphs of [zhou2022toward]. Video benchmarks began with ImageNet-VidVRD [shang2017video] and the trajectory-annotated VidOR [shang2019annotating], then specialized to human activity (Action Genome [ji2020action]), drone footage (AeroEye [nguyen2024cyclo]), panoptic video (PVSG [yang2023panoptic]), fine topological interlacements (ASPIRe [nguyen2024hig]), egocentric capture (Ego-EASG [rodin2024action]), and imminent traffic events (IESG [liu2023learning]). 3DSSG [wald2020learning] is the standard 3D benchmark; PSG4D [yang20234d] adds time, and the operating-room sets 4D-OR [ozsoy20224d], MM-OR [ozsoy2025mm], and EgoExOR [ozsoy2025egoexor] bring multimodal (RGB-D, audio, robot logs) and egocentric surgical scenes. On the text side, TSG Bench [yang2025llm] evaluates LLMs on graph generation from narratives, while FACTUAL [li2023factual] and DiscoSG-DS [lin2025discosg] pair images with text for factually consistent, cross-modal graphs.

Evaluation separates what is given from what is predicted. In Predicate Classification (PredCls) boxes and object labels are given and only predicates are predicted; in Scene Graph Classification (SGCls) boxes are given and both object labels and predicates are predicted; in Scene Graph Generation (SGGen, also SGDet) everything is predicted, and a triplet counts only if both boxes overlap their ground truth at IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5, with Phrase Detection relaxing this to the union box and SGGen+ also crediting correctly detected singleton nodes. Panoptic SGG replaces box IoU with mask IoU. The standard metric is recall of ground-truth triplets among the top-KK predictions,

R⁢@⁢K=|T⁢o⁢pK∩G⁢T||G⁢T|,R@K=\frac{|Top_{K}\cap GT|}{|GT|}, (6.36)

under a graph constraint (one predicate per pair) or without it. Because R⁢@⁢KR@K is dominated by frequent predicates, mean Recall@K (m⁢R⁢@⁢KmR@K) averages recall per predicate class and has become the long-tail metric of record; the gap between R⁢@⁢KR@K and m⁢R⁢@⁢KmR@K drove much of the debiasing literature [lin2020gps, li2021bipartite, zhou2024hierarchical]. Weighted triplet recall, micro- versus macro-averaging over images, the stricter m⁢A⁢Pr⁢e⁢lmAP_{rel} / m⁢A⁢Pp⁢h⁢rmAP_{phr} of the Open Images challenge, and retrieval-based R-Precision are reported in specific settings.

Each modality has its own benchmark and protocol, so leaderboards are not comparable across types: video SGG uses trajectory-based evaluation on ImageNet-VidVRD and VidOR, while Action Genome commonly uses frame-level PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet; textual SGG uses set F1 over triples on FACTUAL and LLM-judged action coverage on TSG Bench; 3D SGG uses object-, predicate-, and triplet-level recall on 3DSSG; panoptic SGG uses mask-IoU R⁢@⁢KR@K on PSG and PVSG. Table 6.19 therefore reports only the image setting, where VG150 SGDet is shared.

Table 6.19 shows the trade-off that still shapes image SGG. The two-stage Motifs baseline keeps the highest overall recall, but its mean recall is the lowest, which is the frequent-predicate bias in numbers; BGNN’s debiasing doubles mean recall at a small cost in R⁢@⁢KR@K. The one-stage DETR-style models start several recall points lower, since they must detect and relate in one pass with a weaker backbone, yet SGTR and RelTR reach the best mean recall of the group, and EGTR closes most of the overall-recall gap to two-stage methods while running end to end.

6.3.2.4 Challenges
From single-modality to universal SGG.

Methods are built per modality, yet real scenes are multimodal, with images carrying visual detail and text carrying abstract concepts and events. A universal scene graph [wu2025universal] would express all of them in one cross-modal representation; the hard part is identifying the same objects, events, and relations across modalities and suppressing cross-modal noise, and granularity has to follow the application rather than a fixed ontology, since robotic interaction or driving may need relations at a level of detail that image-level graphs do not provide.

Integrating SGG with MLLMs.

MLLMs are strong at language and weaker at structured visual understanding. Scene graphs offer a way in: pretraining objectives that mask and predict graph nodes (objects, attributes, relations) across image, video, and text inputs would teach a language model to read structure rather than only the next token, and the scene-graph-guided MLLMs of the preceding subsection [xu2025llava] are an early instance.

From images to embodied use.

Most SGG analyzes static images or videos, but the graph is most useful when it is kept live: robots update it as they act [nguyen2025generating, werby2024hierarchical, garg2024robohop], and driving systems read relations among lanes, signs, and pedestrians from it [zhou2022toward, liu2023learning, malawade2022roadscene2vec]. As these uses grow, the scene graph shifts from a product of perception to the state on which decision and interaction operate.

6.3.3 Layout Estimation and Room Parsing

Layout estimation recovers the structural geometry of an indoor space, the corners, walls, floor, and ceiling that bound it, as a simplified 3D “wireframe” called the room layout. Room parsing extends this by also detecting, localizing, and labeling the objects inside (furniture and fixtures), giving a complete description of the scene. For outdoor scenes, the analogous problem is recovering a road layout in bird’s-eye view from a street image [YangLLYMHP21]. Figure 6.15 shows the inputs and output representations for the structural part of the task.

6.3.3.1 Task Definition

Given an image 𝐈∈ℝH×W×3\mathbf{I}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} (a perspective view, a 360∘360^{\circ} panorama, or a multi-view or video capture), layout estimation recovers the dominant surfaces that bound the navigable volume of a room as a room layout ℒ={Pk}k=1K\mathcal{L}=\{P_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}, where each PkP_{k} is a planar polygon in 3D; equivalently the output may be plane parameters (𝐧k,dk)(\mathbf{n}_{k},d_{k}) or a per-pixel structural-surface label map. Under a vertical-wall model, the layout compresses to a floor-plan polygon with floor and ceiling heights yf,ycy_{f},y_{c}. Outdoor road-layout methods instead predict road regions and vehicle occupancy in bird’s-eye view. Room parsing adds per-object instance masks {mi}\{m_{i}\} or boxes with class labels, drawn from a fixed ontology or, in the open-vocabulary setting, from free-form language.

6.3.3.2 Methodology
Pre-deep-learning approaches.

Classical room layout estimation rests on the Manhattan assumption [CoughlanY99]: the scene is built from surfaces aligned with three mutually orthogonal directions, as walls, floors, and ceilings in most built environments are. Hedau et al. [HedauHF09] introduced the task, modeling a cluttered indoor image jointly as a 3D box layout (the room as if empty) and per-pixel surface labels (visible walls, floor, ceiling, and objects). Three mutually orthogonal vanishing points are first estimated with a robustified variant of Rother’s method [Rother02], in which a line segment ll votes for a candidate vanishing point pp with

v⁢(l,p)=|l|⋅exp⁡(−α⁢(l,p)22⁢σ2),v(l,p)=|l|\cdot\exp\!\left(-\frac{\alpha(l,p)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right), (6.37)

where α⁢(l,p)\alpha(l,p) is the angle between ll and the line from the midpoint of ll to pp, |l||l| is the segment length, and σ\sigma is a fixed bandwidth; candidates are selected greedily, removing the lines that supported each selected point. The vanishing points fix the orientation of the box; sampling pairs of rays through two of them generates box-layout hypotheses, whose remaining edges follow from the third vanishing point, and a learned structured regressor scores the hypotheses and selects the layout.

Deep learning approaches.

Mallya and Lazebnik [MallyaL15] first used a fully convolutional network to predict informative edge maps, then kept the classical hypothesis-generation-and-ranking step, scoring hypotheses with features from the learned edges together with line membership and geometric context. Later deep estimators are best organized by input modality and geometric representation, which vary independently: panorama input does not imply a cuboid output, and non-cuboid geometry need not break the Manhattan assumption. Figure 6.16 groups the representative methods of 2015–2021 along these lines.

(i) Perspective-image corner and edge predictors. RoomNet [lee2017roomnet] regresses an ordered set of room corners with a recurrent encoder–decoder conditioned on one of 11 predefined cuboid topologies, and LayoutNet [ZouCSH18] predicts corner and boundary probability maps and fits a cuboid to them. The topology constraint simplifies reconstruction, but a single perspective view often leaves part of the room outside the frame.

(ii) Panorama-based methods. A 360∘360^{\circ} equirectangular panorama removes the field-of-view truncation of a perspective image, though not occlusion. LayoutNet [ZouCSH18] predicts 2D corner and boundary maps from a gravity-aligned panorama; HorizonNet [sun2019horizonnet] compresses the layout into three 1D per-column signals (floor-wall boundary, ceiling-wall boundary, and wall-wall corner indicator), adds Pano Stretch augmentation, and reconstructs general Manhattan layouts as well as cuboids; HoHoNet [sun2021hohonet] learns latent horizontal features decodable into layout, depth, and semantics; and LED2-Net [wang2021led2net] supervises the layout through differentiable depth rendering, comparing depth rendered from the predicted layout with the target geometry.

(iii) Beyond-cuboid and Atlanta-world methods. Floor-plan prediction separates the number of walls from the constraints on their orientation. DuLa-Net [yang2019dulanet] combines equirectangular and ceiling–floor projections to estimate a floor plan under a Manhattan prior, which admits non-rectangular rooms with orthogonal walls. AtlantaNet [pintore2020atlantanet] projects a gravity-aligned panorama onto horizontal planes above and below the camera and predicts a room footprint and height under the Atlanta-world model, which keeps walls vertical but allows arbitrary horizontal orientation, including curved footprints. Both still assume vertical walls, so slanted walls and ceilings remain out of reach.

(iv) Plane-based indoor geometry and outdoor cross-view prediction. GeoLayout [0005ZZ20] predicts pixel-level plane parameters, infers the depth map of each dominant plane, and reads layout boundaries off the intersections of those depth maps, a geometric alternative to regressing polygon vertices; the accompanying Matterport3D-Layout dataset covers cuboid and non-cuboid rooms. For outdoor scenes, Yang et al. [YangLLYMHP21] use a cross-view transformation with cycle-consistency constraints to predict road layout and vehicle occupancy in bird’s-eye view from a monocular front-facing image.

6.3.3.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.20 summarizes the benchmarks. Perspective-image evaluation grew from Hedau [HedauHF09] (308 web and LabelMe images with box layouts and surface labels) through its augmented successor Hedau+ and the more cluttered SUNbox drawn from SUN2012 [XiaoHEOT10], both built by Mallya and Lazebnik [MallyaL15] to train FCN edge predictors, to LSUN Room Layout [yu2015lsun], the standard perspective benchmark with corner positions and cuboid topologies on over 5K images. Corridor and video data serve navigation: Yang [YangMS16] labels ground versus wall in corridor images, FreeYourCamera [FurlanMSLS13] records six-degree-of-freedom smartphone walks that frequently violate box and Manhattan assumptions, and MichiganIndoorCorridor [TsaiXLK11] provides non-Manhattan corridors with glass and reflections. Panoramic and 3D evaluation rests on PanoContext [zhang2014panocontext] (cuboid layouts and furniture for about 500 SUN360 panoramas, the standard testbed for LayoutNet, HorizonNet, and LED2-Net), Stanford 2D-3D-S [armeni2017joint] (70,496 perspective RGB images and 1,413 RGB panoramas, with aligned depth, normals, semantics, and 3D meshes over 270 rooms), and Matterport3D-Layout [0005ZZ20], derived from Matterport3D [chang2017matterport3d] with RANSAC-fitted plane ground truth for cuboid and non-cuboid rooms.

Metrics follow the output representation. Perspective benchmarks (Hedau, LSUN) report pixel error, the fraction of pixels whose predicted surface label differs from the ground truth, and corner error, the mean distance between predicted and true corners normalized by image size; the edge-map methods additionally report the contour-detection F-scores at the optimal dataset scale (ODS, one threshold for the whole set) and optimal image scale (OIS, the best threshold per image). Panoramic and 3D benchmarks (PanoContext and panoramic layout subsets of Stanford 2D-3D-S and Matterport3D) report 3D and 2D room IoU between the predicted and ground-truth layout volumes or floor plans, with frequency-weighted IoU and pixel accuracy as segmentation-style complements. A method trained for one input type rarely transfers to the other without re-training, so perspective and panoramic results are not compared directly, and the outdoor road-layout protocol [YangLLYMHP21] is separate again.

Table 6.21 compares the panorama methods under one protocol. The 1D column representation of HorizonNet gained about eight IoU points over LayoutNet’s 2D maps on PanoContext, and the geometric supervision of LED2-Net adds a further point or two on every benchmark; AtlantaNet exceeds HorizonNet on the Matterport3D subset, whereas DuLa-Net remains below it, so these results do not show a uniform advantage for beyond-cuboid methods.

6.3.3.4 Challenges

The geometric priors that make layout estimation tractable also bound it. Cuboid models cannot express alcoves or L-shaped plans; Manhattan models keep orthogonal walls even when the footprint is free-form; the Atlanta-world model of AtlantaNet [pintore2020atlantanet] frees wall orientation but not wall tilt; and plane-based methods such as GeoLayout [0005ZZ20] approximate curved geometry only with many planes. Slanted enclosures, split levels, and the outdoor bird’s-eye-view target of [YangLLYMHP21], which is a different output space altogether, all sit outside the standard formulations. Clutter and occlusion are the second obstacle: furniture hides the corners, boundaries, and vanishing lines that both classical and learned methods read, so estimators must hallucinate hidden structure from layout priors, and confidently wrong boundaries without uncertainty are the typical failure. Generalization follows from the data: benchmarks are indoor, mostly rooms and corridors, and models trained on one set degrade on another’s appearance, architecture, and lighting, while sparse, unposed multi-view capture breaks the pose assumptions of classical pipelines; the feed-forward geometry models of §6.2.4 are the natural starting point for layout from such input.

6.3.4 Action Detection

Action detection (AD) finds human actions in untrimmed video: for each action instance it returns the time interval [ts,te][t_{s},t_{e}] in which it occurs and its category cc. Where action recognition classifies a clip that has already been trimmed to one action, detection must also decide when actions start and end, in streams that contain many of them. It belongs to spatial structure construction because it organizes the entities and relations of a scene along the time axis into events, the temporal counterpart of the scene graphs above and the basis of video SGG and human–object interaction. Figure 6.17 illustrates the task.

6.3.4.1 Task Definition

Given an untrimmed video (or a continuous multi-sensor stream), AD outputs a set of tuples (ts,te,c)(t_{s},t_{e},c) with start time, end time, and category for every action instance. The following terms emphasize different aspects of the task. Action classification (AC) takes a trimmed clip and predicts one category, with no localization. Temporal action localization (TAL) predicts start and end times in untrimmed video, and may include multiple instances; the term is often used interchangeably with TAD. Temporal action detection (TAD) emphasizes joint localization and classification of multiple instances per video, possibly overlapping or concurrent, across temporal scales, each to be localized and classified.

6.3.4.2 Methodology

Figure 6.18 organizes the methods by the three settings; each builds on the previous one’s representations.

Action Classification.

Two-stream CNNs [simonyan2014two] model appearance from RGB frames in one stream and motion from dense optical flow in another, fusing the two at the output. 3D CNNs [diba2017temporal] convolve over space and time jointly, C3D [tran2015learning] and I3D [carreira2017quo] being the standard examples, at the cost of a large parameter count that R(2+1)D [tran2018closer] and P3D [qiu2017learning] reduce by factoring 3D convolution into 2D spatial and 1D temporal steps. TSN [wang2016temporal] samples a few snippets sparsely across a long video and supervises at video level, which scales long-range temporal modeling cheaply, and Transformers [girdhar2019video, yang2022recurring] model global spatio-temporal dependencies among sampled tokens beyond the local reach of convolution.

Temporal Action Localization.

Early TAL ran a classifier over dense, fixed-size sliding windows, which was both slow and blind to the wide range of action durations. Structured segment networks [zhao2017temporal] instead model a proposal’s starting, ongoing, and ending stages and score its completeness, which refines boundary regression. Boundary-sensitive methods [lin2018bsn] go further and predict start and end probabilities at every snippet, then pair high-confidence boundary points into proposals; this flexible boundary generation is the component on which later detection systems rest.

Because precise boundary annotation is expensive, weakly supervised TAL (WSTAL) [shou2018autoloc, zhang2021cola, paul2018w] learns from video-level labels alone. The task becomes multiple-instance learning: a video is positive if at least one segment contains the action, class activation sequences are derived from video features, and foreground segments are thresholded into proposals. Trained only with a classification loss, such models fire on the most discriminative moments rather than the whole action, so proposals are incomplete and high confidence does not imply accurate boundaries. Point-level supervision (P-TAL) [xia2024realigning, lee2021learning, fu2022compact] adds one labeled frame per instance, which tends to fall near the temporally most salient, roughly central moment, and uses it to realign confidence and infer complete boundaries from that single anchor.

Temporal Action Detection.

TAD methods differ in how they generate and score temporal proposals. Anchor-based detection [gao2017turn] transplants Faster R-CNN and SSD to the time axis: a dense set of multi-scale temporal anchors is classified and regressed, first in two stages (S-CNN [shou2016temporal]) and then in one (SSAD [lin2017single]); fixed anchors produce many redundant proposals and limit boundary precision, which anchor-free variants such as AFSD [lin2021learning] address by regressing boundaries from a temporal center representation. Boundary-based detection [xiong2017pursuit, lin2018bsn] is bottom-up: start and end probabilities are predicted over the whole timeline and boundary matching scores every candidate pairing, which gives flexible, precise boundaries; TSA-Net [gong2019scale] adds multi-dilation temporal convolution for multi-scale context and BGCN [chen2021boundary] graph convolution over co-occurring proposals. Query-based detection [wu2021towards, shi2022react, kim2023self, zhu2024dual] follows DETR: a small set of learned queries attends to global video features in a Transformer encoder–decoder and decodes the action set in parallel, removing anchors, NMS, and hand-designed matching at the cost of heavier computation. Across the three, anchors give dense parallel scoring but coarse boundaries, boundary methods give precise boundaries but complex matching, and query methods give the simplest end-to-end pipeline; all three keep moving toward longer-range context, continuous temporal representations, and less frame-level annotation.

6.3.4.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.22 lists the benchmarks by role. UCF101 [soomro2012ucf101] and HMDB51 [kuehne2011hmdb] are trimmed-clip classification sets; AVA [gu2018ava] adds spatio-temporal boxes on movie footage. THUMOS’14 [jiang2014thumos], whose 20 classes carry dense temporal boundaries, and ActivityNet [caba2015activitynet], with 200 classes over 20K untrimmed videos, are the standard TAL and TAD benchmarks, extended in scale and granularity by HACS Segment [zhao2019hacs] and FineAction [liu2022fineaction]. MultiTHUMOS [yeung2018every], Charades [sigurdsson2016hollywood], and TVSeries [de2016online] supply dense, multi-label, overlapping actions in sports, homes, and television; Breakfast [kuehne2014language], 50Salads [stein2013combining], MPII Cooking 2 [rohrbach2016recognizing], and COIN [tang2019coin] cover procedural cooking and instructional activity for segmentation and step detection; and MEVA [corona2021meva] (thousands of hours of surveillance) and MoVi [ghorbani2021movi] (motion-captured actors) sit at the large-scale and controlled extremes.

Each setting has its own metric. Action classification reports Top-1 accuracy, AccTop⁢-⁢1=1N⁢∑i=1N𝕀⁢(y^i=yi)\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{Top}\text{-}1}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(\hat{% y}_{i}=y_{i}), with Top-kk on large label sets; temporal boundaries are given, so localization is not assessed. Localization quality is measured by the temporal intersection over union of predicted and ground-truth intervals,

tIoU⁢(Ip,Ig)=|Ip∩Ig||Ip∪Ig|,\mathrm{tIoU}(I_{p},I_{g})=\frac{|I_{p}\cap I_{g}|}{|I_{p}\cup I_{g}|}, (6.38)

a prediction counting as correct above a threshold τ\tau; TAL reports average precision at one or several thresholds. TAD scores detections (Ip,y^,s)(I_{p},\hat{y},s) with confidence ss by mean average precision over classes and thresholds,

mAP=1|𝒞|⁢∑c∈𝒞1|{τm}|⁢∑τmAPc⁢(τm),\mathrm{mAP}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\frac{1}{|\{\tau_{m}% \}|}\sum_{\tau_{m}}\mathrm{AP}_{c}(\tau_{m}), (6.39)

which penalizes misclassification, loose boundaries, and duplicates together; THUMOS’14 uses τ∈{0.3,…,0.7}\tau\in\{0.3,\dots,0.7\} and ActivityNet {0.5,…,0.95}\{0.5,\dots,0.95\}, and proposal methods also report average recall at a fixed proposal budget. Weakly supervised methods are often evaluated on ActivityNet-1.2 rather than 1.3, so their numbers are not interchangeable with fully supervised ones.

Table 6.23 shows how far the two settings have diverged. Trimmed-clip classification on UCF101 was effectively solved once Kinetics-pretrained 3D networks arrived, with I3D and R(2+1)D within a point of each other near 98%. Detection on THUMOS’14 tells a different story: mAP@0.5 moved from 19.0 (S-CNN) to 36.9 (BSN) over the anchor-to-boundary transition, jumped to 55.5 with anchor-free salient-boundary features (AFSD), and reached 70.4 with query-based decoding (DualDETR), while the best weakly supervised method (CoLA, 32.2) matches fully supervised accuracy of only a few years earlier, which quantifies what video-level labels still cost.

6.3.4.4 Challenges

Fully supervised TAD depends on densely annotated boundaries, which scale poorly to long, loosely structured real-world video; weakly and semi-supervised methods relax this with video-level labels or sparse temporal cues [zhao2025pose, ghoddoosian2023weakly], at the accuracy cost the table above makes visible. Actions are also still detected in isolation. Coupling TAD with structured temporal representations such as scene graphs or event schemas [wu2025universal, lu2025benchmarking] would let a system infer boundaries, temporal relations, and higher-level activity structure jointly, which matters most in instructional video, driving, and human–robot interaction. Finally, benchmarks and detectors remain visual and closed-set, whereas real action understanding draws on audio, language, gaze, and context and must handle actions outside a fixed vocabulary [zhou2024learning, bao2025exploiting, liu2026synergistic]; multimodal temporal detection, where audio or language sharpens boundaries and disambiguates semantics, and open-vocabulary formulations that loosen the classification-centric setup are the directions large multimodal video corpora now make feasible.

6.3.5 Mapping and SLAM

Mapping builds a spatial representation of an unknown environment from streaming sensor observations, together with an estimate of the agent’s trajectory through it. Doing so from on-board sensors requires the agent to localize itself inside the partial map it is still building: the chicken-and-egg problem known as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). SLAM resolves it by estimating trajectory and map jointly from the same sensor stream, and observations of previously visited places supply the external references that bound the drift of purely proprioceptive odometry (IMU, wheel encoders). The result is a globally consistent spatial model that supports localization, path planning, obstacle avoidance, and exploration. Figure 6.20 depicts the pipeline from sensors through front-end odometry and back-end optimization to the final map.

6.3.5.1 Task Definition

The input is a stream of exteroceptive observations (camera images, RGB-D frames, LiDAR, or radar), optionally fused with proprioceptive readings (IMU, wheel odometry, velocity and steering commands) and priors such as a coarse map, an initial pose, or GPS. The output is a map plus the estimated trajectory. Maps lie on an abstraction–detail spectrum: a topological map is a graph of distinctive places and their traversable connections, with no metric layout; a sparse metric map stores registered keypoints or landmarks and the camera-pose graph that observes them, enough for accurate localization but not for geometry; and a dense metric map reconstructs a complete surface or volume (point cloud, mesh, TSDF, or occupancy grid) for obstacle avoidance and 3D reconstruction. Two dense representations have become prominent in the past three years: neural implicit maps that store geometry and appearance in network weights (an MLP in iMAP [Sucar2021iMAP], a voxel-grid encoder in NICE-SLAM [Zhu2022NICESLAM]) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) maps that represent the scene as explicit, differentiable 3D Gaussians [Keetha2024SplaTAM, Yan2024GSSLAM, Matsuki2024MonoGS].

6.3.5.2 Methodology

SLAM systems are classified by the exteroceptive sensor and by the density of the map they build. LiDAR SLAM measures range directly with a stable error model; KISS-ICP [Vizzo2023KISSICP] and KISS-SLAM [Guadagnino2025KISSSLAM] show that a minimal pipeline delivers robust real-time 3D LiDAR odometry and mapping at city scale. Visual SLAM uses monocular, stereo, or RGB-D cameras, exploiting texture for place recognition, with PTAM [KleinMurray2007PTAM] and the ORB-SLAM family [mur2015orb, Campos2021ORBSLAM3] as the foundational systems. Multi-sensor SLAM tightly fuses cameras, IMUs, and/or LiDAR (VINS-Mono, OKVIS, FAST-LIO2), and event-camera SLAM uses asynchronous per-pixel brightness changes for high-speed and high-dynamic-range operation [Huang2026EventSLAMSurvey]. By map density, sparse keypoint-and-pose-graph systems (ORB-SLAM) sit next to direct methods that minimize photometric error over semi-dense (LSD-SLAM [engel2014lsd]) or sparse (DSO [engel2017direct]) image samples, dense geometric systems that fuse point clouds, meshes, or TSDFs (KinectFusion, ElasticFusion), neural implicit systems (iMAP [Sucar2021iMAP], NICE-SLAM [Zhu2022NICESLAM], Co-SLAM, NICER-SLAM), and 3DGS systems that render and optimize Gaussians jointly with poses (SplaTAM [Keetha2024SplaTAM], MonoGS [Matsuki2024MonoGS], SplatSLAM). Read historically, the field moved from feature-based geometry (PTAM, ORB-SLAM) to direct methods (LSD-SLAM, DSO), to tightly coupled multi-sensor systems (OKVIS, VINS-Mono, ORB-SLAM3), to learning-augmented pipelines (DROID-SLAM [teed2021droid], SuperPoint and SuperGlue matching [detone2018superpoint, sarlin2020superglue]), to neural implicit and then 3DGS maps, and most recently to 3D geometry foundation models (DUSt3R [wang2024dust3r], MASt3R [mast3r], MASt3R-SLAM [Murai2025MASt3RSLAM]).

Whatever the sensor or map, a SLAM system runs the four modules of Figure 6.20 in a loop. The front end is visual (or LiDAR) odometry, the incremental motion estimate between consecutive readings treated as a stand-alone task in §6.2.4; because each pose is estimated relative to the last, its errors accumulate as drift. Back-end optimization corrects that drift globally. Modern back ends pose the problem as factor-graph optimization: robot poses and landmarks are nodes, and measurements between them (visual reprojection, IMU pre-integration, GPS, loop-closure relative poses) are factors; solving for all nodes at once yields a consistent trajectory and map, factor graphs absorb heterogeneous sensors naturally, and incremental solvers such as iSAM2 update the estimate in real time, with GTSAM, g2o, and OKVIS as representative libraries. Loop closing supplies the back end with its strongest constraints by recognizing that the agent has returned to a previously visited place, comparing current observations against the history and, on a match, adding a constraint between two temporally distant poses that pulls the accumulated drift of the intervening trajectory back into alignment. Mapping finally places the sensor data in the global frame using the optimized trajectory, in whatever representation the application needs; for neural implicit and 3DGS maps it also minimizes a rendering loss (photometric or perceptual such as LPIPS) between observed images and views rendered from the current map, optimizing geometry, appearance, and poses jointly [Keetha2024SplaTAM].

6.3.5.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.24 groups the benchmarks by what they stress. The classical trajectory sets are TUM RGB-D [Sturm2012TUMRGBD] (handheld indoor RGB-D with motion-capture ground truth), KITTI [KITTI-GeigerLU12] (stereo and LiDAR driving), and the synthetic ICL-NUIM [HandaWMD14] with exact ground truth, while COLD [PronobisC09] targets topological localization under changing conditions. Visual-inertial systems are tested on EuRoC [Burri2016EuRoC] (micro-aerial vehicle), TUM VI [Schubert2018TUMVI], and OpenLORIS-Scene [ShiLZTTLZSQSGW020], the last built for lifelong SLAM in changing indoor scenes, and Bonn RGB-D [PalazzoloBLGS19] isolates dynamic objects. Large synthetic corpora (SceneNet [McCormacHLD17], InteriorNet [LiSMCTYHTL18], Replica [straub2019replica], TartanAir [TartanAir]) supply photorealistic training and controlled evaluation, with Replica the standard testbed for neural implicit and 3DGS SLAM; ScanNet++ [yeshwanth2023scannet++] and ETH3D SLAM [ETH3DSLAM] add laser-scanned geometry for dense reconstruction quality; and DSEC [gehrig2021dsec] and CU-Multi [albin2025cu] extend evaluation to event cameras and multi-robot data association. AirSwarm [li2025airswarm] is a multi-UAV research platform rather than a benchmark dataset.

Evaluation covers trajectory, map, rendering, and system cost. Trajectory accuracy uses the absolute trajectory error and relative pose error defined in §6.2.4, after aligning the estimated trajectory to the ground truth by a rigid or, for monocular systems, similarity transform; RMSE is the usual summary, with mean, median, and standard deviation also reported. Dense maps are scored by accuracy (mean distance from reconstructed points to the nearest ground-truth point) and completeness (the reverse), summarized by an F-score at a distance threshold, with Chamfer distance common for neural and 3DGS maps. Neural implicit and 3DGS maps add novel-view-synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) on held-out views of the same trajectory. Memory footprint, tracking and mapping frame rates, and end-to-end latency decide embedded deployment [Guadagnino2025KISSSLAM]. Mature evaluation tools such as EVO22 2 https://github.com/MichaelGrupp/evo and the RPG Trajectory Evaluation toolbox33 3 https://github.com/uzh-rpg/rpg_trajectory_evaluation implement these protocols.

6.3.5.4 Challenges

Deployment often violates common SLAM assumptions of static scenes, stable illumination, abundant texture, and ample computation. Dynamic objects induce correspondences that drift with their own motion; illumination change, reflective and transparent surfaces, and repetitive texture create perceptual aliasing that confuses data association and place recognition alike; and resource-constrained platforms must run ever heavier front and back ends. Current work answers each directly. Moving features are detected and excluded through semantic segmentation, motion-consistency checks, or learned masks; learned matchers (SuperPoint [detone2018superpoint], SuperGlue [sarlin2020superglue], LoFTR [Sun2021LoFTR]) replace hand-crafted descriptors and tolerate larger viewpoint and illumination changes; neural implicit and 3DGS maps are optimized jointly with poses and yield photorealistic reconstructions usable for inspection, telepresence, and policy learning; and the two-view geometry priors of DUSt3R [wang2024dust3r] and MASt3R [mast3r] remove the fragile hand-engineered front end, already enabling real-time dense monocular SLAM at the robustness of MASt3R-SLAM [Murai2025MASt3RSLAM].

Two broader shifts follow. Lifelong SLAM aims at months of continuous operation by combining relocalization, map update, and place re-identification against changing environments, and is now an evaluation track of its own; collaborative multi-agent SLAM fuses observations across robots for faster coverage and graceful degradation, increasingly together with event cameras and heterogeneous sensors for high-speed, low-light, and high-dynamic-range conditions. What remains open is concrete: 3DGS maps still do not scale to city-level memory and rendering budgets, learned components carry a sim-to-real gap, and incorrect loop closures under strong perceptual aliasing are still the failure that breaks every back end.

6.4 Spatio-Temporal Perception

Most of what precedes has described a single instant. Spatio-temporal perception adds the missing axis, asking not only where entities are but how they move, when events happen, and which identities persist. Its three concerns rise from the pixel through the object to the event: scene flow recovers dense, per-point motion between frames; object tracking maintains the identity of an entity as it moves through space and time; and temporal localization fixes when an action or event occurs along a sequence. Together they give the largely static perception of the preceding sections a temporal thread, the continuity on which motion understanding and long-horizon perception depend.

6.4.1 Scene Flow Estimation

Scene flow is the dense three-dimensional motion of every visible surface point between two instants: optical flow lifted out of the image plane and joined to the change in depth. The image-based pipelines surveyed here take stereo video, monocular video, or a multi-view sequence and produce per-pixel 3D motion; some refinement modules additionally consume estimated or measured depth. Dynamic scene reconstruction [park2021nerfies], motion-aware rendering [li2021neural], physical interaction modeling [Bear2021Physion], and egocentric world understanding [grauman2022ego4d] all consume it.

6.4.1.1 Task Definition

Given consecutive frames ItI_{t} and It+1I_{t+1} (optionally with a stereo partner or several views, and with intrinsics and relative poses when known), scene flow estimation returns a field 𝐯⁢(𝐱)∈ℝ3\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{3} that displaces the surface point imaged at pixel 𝐱\mathbf{x} in frame tt to its position at t+1t+1, in camera or world coordinates. In the stereo setting this is equivalently a triple (dt,dt+1,𝐟)(d_{t},d_{t+1},\mathbf{f}) of disparity in both frames plus optical flow, which is how the KITTI benchmark represents and scores it. In image-only pipelines, structure and motion are inferred from appearance, parallax, and temporal correspondence. Geometry-aware refinement modules may instead take depth estimated upstream or measured by RGB-D sensors; point-cloud-only methods are outside the scope here.

6.4.1.2 Methodology

Methods differ along two axes: what they observe (stereo, the classical and still dominant setting; monocular video, the self-supervised frontier; multi-view rigs) and what supervises them (synthetic ground truth, photometric and geometric consistency, or view synthesis). Figure 6.21 groups them into five families along these axes.

Variational and energy-based methods.

vedula1999three introduced the term and the problem: recover 3D structure and 3D motion jointly from a calibrated camera array. huguet2007variational formulated it using stereo image pairs at two consecutive times, solving disparity and flow jointly in one variational energy; wedel2011stereoscopic decoupled the two into a stereo stage and a flow stage, which made real-time estimation feasible; and basha2013multi returned to multi-view input under a view-centered energy. The strongest classical formulation is the piecewise-rigid scene model of vogel20153d (PRSF/PRSM), which segments the scene into rigidly moving planar patches and was the leading entry on KITTI Scene Flow at the benchmark’s release.

End-to-end stereo and temporal CNNs.

mayer2016large recast disparity and flow as supervised regression (DispNet, FlowNet) and released FlyingThings3D, Monkaa, and Driving, the synthetic corpora that made this training regime possible. SENSE [jiang2019sense] shares one encoder across disparity, optical flow, occlusion, and semantic heads; DRISF [ma2019deep] keeps the piecewise-rigid prior of Vogel et al. but implements it as an instance-level decoder over learned features. DRISF surpassed both listed variational baselines on KITTI Scene Flow, while SENSE improved on OSF but not PRSM (Table 6.26), shifting the bottleneck from optimization to supervised data.

Recurrent geometric refinement.

RAFT [teed2020raft] introduced all-pairs correlation volumes with GRU-based iterative updates for 2D optical flow; RAFT-3D [teed2021raft] uses image and depth pairs to iteratively refine a per-pixel SE(3) field with rigid-motion embeddings. Depth can be obtained from stereo or RGB-D input; it is an input to the refinement rather than necessarily inferred jointly from appearance. Its scene-flow results are included in Table 6.26.

Monocular and self-supervised methods.

Mono-SF [brickwedde2019mono] was the first monocular entry on KITTI Scene Flow, resolving scale with a learned single-view depth prior. Self-Mono-SF [hur2020self] jointly predicts disparity and scene flow with a single decoder, using unlabeled stereo video during training and monocular image pairs at test time; stereo geometry provides the scale cue, while photometric and 3D consistency losses provide self-supervision. A separate test-time optimization approach for LiDAR point clouds (Neural Scene Flow Prior [li2021neuralsfp]) lies outside the image-based scope of this subsection.

Implicit-field and view-synthesis-coupled methods.

A parallel line never targets scene flow as output but obtains a dense 4D motion field as a byproduct of dynamic view synthesis. Neural Scene Flow Fields [li2021neural] trains a dynamic NeRF together with an explicit scene-flow MLP; D-NeRF [pumarola2021d] represents motion as a deformation field into a canonical frame; Nerfies [park2021nerfies] extends this to casually captured monocular video; and 4D Gaussian Splatting [wu20244d] attaches time-parameterized motion to explicit Gaussian primitives. These methods are evaluated by rendering quality rather than by motion error, a split returned to under Challenges below.

6.4.1.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.25 lists the image-based benchmarks. Synthetic sets provide dense, exact ground truth at scale (FlyingThings3D as the standard pretraining corpus; Sintel and Spring for film-grade motion, with Spring at HD resolution and super-resolved ground truth; TartanAir for environment diversity), while KITTI Scene Flow 2015 [menze2015object], built on the KITTI suite [KITTI-GeigerLU12], is the only real-world benchmark and carries sparse LiDAR-derived labels on 200 training and 200 test scenes. LiDAR-based scene-flow splits of nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes], Waymo Open [WaymoOpen-SunKDCPTGZCCVHN20], and Argoverse 2 [wilson2023argoverse], and the event-camera flow of DSEC [gehrig2021dsec], serve the point-cloud and event communities and are not image-based benchmarks in the sense used here.

KITTI scores scene flow in image space. A pixel’s disparity in frame tt (D1), its disparity in frame t+1t{+}1 (D2), and its optical flow (Fl) are each counted as outliers when the error exceeds both 3 px and 5% of the ground-truth value, and a scene-flow outlier (SF) is any pixel that fails at least one of the three; the benchmark reports outlier percentages over all pixels and separately over background and foreground. Point-level evaluation on synthetic data instead uses the 3D end-point error

EPE3⁢D=1N⁢∑i=1N‖𝐯^i−𝐯i‖2,\mathrm{EPE}_{3D}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{i}-\mathbf{v}_{% i}\|_{2}, (6.40)

with 𝐯^i\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{i} and 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i} the predicted and true motion of point ii, together with accuracy ratios at fixed thresholds (the fraction of points with error below 0.05 m or 5%, and below 0.1 m or 10%) and an outlier ratio (error above 0.3 m or 10%), conventions inherited from point-cloud scene flow.

Table 6.26 collects KITTI Scene Flow 2015 test results for the explicit-output families. RAFT-3D reduces SF-all error from 8.97% (PRSM) to 5.77%; the table does not separate foreground and background results. The monocular rows are a different regime: Mono-SF, with a learned depth prior, sits at 23% SF-all, and Self-Mono-SF without any ground truth at 49.5% (33.9% after fine-tuning), the price of giving up stereo. The implicit-field family has no row because it reports rendering quality (PSNR, LPIPS) on its own scene sets rather than motion error.

6.4.1.4 Challenges

The supervision landscape is lopsided. Every dense-ground-truth benchmark in Table 6.25 is synthetic and stereo, so monocular methods are scored only against KITTI’s sparse labels, and models pretrained on FlyingThings3D or Sintel still lose accuracy on real driving footage after fine-tuning, most visibly on foreground motion where synthetic random-object trajectories differ from vehicle kinematics. All current benchmarks also emphasize rigid or random-object motion; dense ground truth for non-rigid humans, hands, and animals does not exist at scale, which leaves the family of implicit-field methods that handle such motion best without a quantitative yardstick.

That yardstick problem is the second challenge. Explicit-output methods [vogel20153d, jiang2019sense, teed2021raft] are scored by KITTI’s outlier rates; implicit-field methods [li2021neural, pumarola2021d, wu20244d] by PSNR and LPIPS of rendered views. No protocol evaluates both on the same input, so the two paradigms are compared only qualitatively, and whether a motion field is good depends on whether scene flow is the end (the KITTI leaderboard) or a means (reconstruction, novel-view synthesis, physical reasoning). The cost profiles diverge as well: RAFT-3D needs several GRU iterations per frame, variational methods minutes per frame, and implicit fields minutes to hours per scene.

Foundation priors are reshaping the monocular line. Depth Anything [DepthAnything] and DINOv2 [dinov2] supply the per-pixel depth and semantic features that Self-Mono-SF had to learn from scratch, and SAM 2 [ravi2024sam2] segmentation together with the object-pose estimators of Section 6.2.5 makes an object-centric formulation (a per-object SE(3) trajectory plus residual non-rigid motion) practical, a bridge to the tracking problem of Section 6.4.2. As implicit-field scene flow merges into 4D reconstruction, with 4D Gaussian Splatting [wu20244d] the early example, evaluation is likely to follow the downstream task rather than the KITTI leaderboard.

6.4.2 Object Tracking

Tracking localizes entities in every frame and associates the detections across frames so that each entity keeps one identity through the sequence. Where detection and segmentation describe a single instant, tracking yields trajectories, the representation that autonomous driving [luo2021exploring, chiu2021probabilistic], surveillance [ojha2015imageobjectsurveillance], AR/VR [chen2021hightracking], and robotics [Deitke2020RoboTHOR] build on.

6.4.2.1 Task Definition

Given a frame sequence {It}t=1T\{I_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} (a video, or RGB-D, LiDAR, or multi-view streams), a tracker returns a set of trajectories {𝒯k}\{\mathcal{T}_{k}\}, each 𝒯k={(t,btk)}\mathcal{T}_{k}=\{(t,b_{t}^{k})\} a time-indexed series of states btkb_{t}^{k} with one identity kk held fixed over the sequence. The state is a bounding box in the basic setting and a segmentation mask, a 3D box, or a set of keypoints in the variants.

The variants, illustrated in Figure 6.22, differ in how the targets are specified and what state is tracked. Single object tracking (SOT) [fan2019lasot, muller2018trackingnet] follows one target given its first-frame box; multiple object tracking (MOT) [milan2016mot16, dendorfer2020mot20, yu2020bdd100k] tracks every instance of given categories, typically pedestrians and vehicles, under identity constraints; MOTS [voigtlaender2019mots] and video object segmentation replace boxes with masks; 3D-MOT [AB3DMOT, yin2021center, caesar2020nuscenes, WaymoOpen-SunKDCPTGZCCVHN20] outputs world-coordinate 3D boxes from LiDAR, RGB-D, or multi-view input; pose tracking [andriluka2018posetrack, iqbal2017posetrack, samanta2016data] and landmark tracking [zafeiriou20173d] follow skeletal joints or facial keypoints; and panoptic tracking combines pixel-level semantic classes for stuff with temporally consistent instance identities for things. Category-specific trackers for pedestrians [stadler2021improving], vehicles [van2001real], or animals [zhang2023animaltrack] specialize any of these.

6.4.2.2 Methodology

Figure 6.23 organizes the methods into four families around image-plane box and mask tracking (SOT, MOT, MOTS, VOS). Pose, landmark, and panoptic tracking reuse the same propagate-or-associate machinery with a different state representation and are covered at the benchmark level in Table 6.27.

Propagation-based methods.

Because a target moves little between consecutive frames, its previous state is a strong prior for the current one, and the oldest tracking paradigm exploits this by predicting the next state from the current one and correcting it against the new frame. Correlation filters realize this in the frequency domain: MOSSE [bolme2010visual] learns a minimum-output-sum-of-squared-error filter from a single frame and updates it online at hundreds of frames per second; KCF [henriques2014high] and MKCF [tang2015multi] add kernelization and multiple-kernel learning, respectively; ECO [DanelljanBKF17] adds factorized convolution operators, a compact generative sample model, and conservative updates. These trackers are fast enough for embedded use but drift under large appearance change and clutter. MDNet [NamH16] answered with online discriminative learning, a shared CNN with per-sequence domain branches that separate target from background, at a high per-frame cost. Siamese trackers moved the representation learning offline: SiamFC [BertinettoVHVT16] correlates a template embedding with the search-region embedding in one forward pass, and SiamRPN [LiYWZH18], ATOM [DanelljanBKF19], and DiMP [BhatDGT19] add region-proposal regression, IoU-prediction refinement, and a discriminatively learned prediction head. Transformer trackers then replaced correlation with attention: TransT [ChenYZ0YL21] fuses template and search features with self- and cross-attention, STARK [0002PF0L21] predicts the box with an encoder–decoder that also carries temporal state, and OSTrack [YeCMSC22] joins feature extraction and relation modeling in a single stream over concatenated template and search tokens, the current baseline design.

Mask propagation applies the same idea at the pixel level for video object segmentation [pont20172017, xu2018youtube], with memory of past frames replacing a single template. XMem [ChengS22XMem] keeps multi-scale spatiotemporal memories that remain stable over videos of more than 10,000 frames; AOT [YangWY21aot] and DeAOT [YangY22adeaot] encode object identities as tokens so that many objects propagate in one pass; and SAM 2 [ravi2024sam2] adds a streaming memory to the Segment Anything Model [kirillov2023sam], giving promptable tracking that transfers across VOS benchmarks.

Detect-then-associate methods.

The MOT standard pipeline detects objects in every frame and then solves an assignment problem between detections and existing tracks. SORT [bewley2016sort] predicts track positions with a Kalman filter [welch1995kalman] and matches by IoU with the Hungarian algorithm [Kuhn10]; DeepSORT [WojkeBP17] adds an appearance embedding so that tracks survive occlusion. Track-RCNN [voigtlaender2019mots], JDE [WangZLLW20jde], and FairMOT [ZhangWWZL21FairMOT] train the re-identification embedding jointly with the detector; association remains a separate step, which keeps them in this family. All of these discard low-confidence detections, and since occluded targets are exactly those with low scores, trajectories fragment where they are hardest to keep. ByteTrack [ZhangSJYWYLLW22] associates nearly every detection and uses motion similarity to the existing tracks to reject the false positives among the low-score boxes, a change in association alone that raised MOT17 HOTA by several points (Table 6.28). In 3D, the same pipeline reappears: AB3DMOT [AB3DMOT] runs a 3D Kalman filter with Hungarian matching on LiDAR detections, and CenterPoint [yin2021center] tracks 3D object centers through predicted velocities, with nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes] using AMOTA/AMOTP and Waymo [WaymoOpen-SunKDCPTGZCCVHN20] using MOTA/MOTP.

Joint detection–association methods.

End-to-end trackers fold association into the detector. CenterTrack [ZhouKK20] represents objects as center points and regresses their offset to the previous frame, so that association is a local lookup; TrackFormer [MeinhardtKLF22] introduces tracking-by-attention, in which track queries carried from the previous frame and new object queries are decoded jointly by a Transformer; MOTR [zeng2022motr] extends DETR [carion2020end] with track queries that persist across the whole sequence and are supervised with a sequence-level loss, which is what gives it its advantage on DanceTrack [SunCJYBKL22], where appearance is uninformative and motion is non-linear. The price is training cost and data: these models need long annotated sequences and remain behind detect-then-associate trackers on MOT17 (Table 6.28).

Universal models.

A single model for SOT, MOT, VOS, and MOTS is the most recent direction. UniTrack [wang2021different] showed that one self-supervised appearance representation serves propagation and association tasks alike; Unicorn [yan2022unicorn] trains one network end to end for all four tasks; UTT [MaSZ0XYY22] unifies SOT and MOT in a Transformer; UniVS [li2024univs] casts every video-segmentation task as prompt-driven segmentation; and OneTracker [HongYZLZGJCLCZ24] adapts a foundation tracker to RGB, depth, thermal, and event inputs with light adapters. In practice, SAM [kirillov2023sam] combined with a memory tracker (XMem, DeAOT) already provides promptable multi-object segmentation and tracking from points, boxes, scribbles, or text, and methods such as UASTrack [UASTrack] and Un-Track [WuZRV0PGT24UNTrack] extend unified tracking to RGB paired with depth, thermal, or event inputs. Language enters as a specification signal as well: LaSOT [fan2019lasot] pairs every sequence with a sentence, TNL2K [wang2021tnl2k] is built for text-initialized tracking, and LaMOT [li2025lamot] brings language-guided specification to the multi-object setting.

6.4.2.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.27 groups the benchmarks by what is tracked. The SOT line runs from short, category-agnostic clips (OTB100, TC128, the VOT challenges) to large, long-term, category-diverse training sets (TrackingNet, LaSOT, GOT-10k, whose test classes are disjoint from training) and to condition-specific tests for aerial footage (UAV123), high frame rate (NFS), and language initialization (TNL2K). MOT benchmarks are pedestrian-only in MOT16/17 and MOT20 and multi-class driving footage in BDD100K; the 3D-MOT counterparts are the nuScenes and Waymo tracking tasks. DAVIS and YouTube-VOS supply mask-level ground truth, the latter with categories unseen at training time; the RGB-D sets add depth and have grown from tens of sequences (PTB, STC) to over a thousand (RGBD1K); and pose tracking moved from single-person upper-body clips (VideoPose2.0, Poses in the Wild, ICDPose) to multi-person full-body sequences with person identities (PoseTrack18, CMU Panoptic).

Each line has its own metrics. SOT uses the success plot: with SR⁢(τ)\mathrm{SR}(\tau) the fraction of frames whose predicted-box IoU exceeds τ\tau, the headline number is its area under the curve,

AUC=∫01SR⁢(τ)⁢𝑑τ,\mathrm{AUC}=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm{SR}(\tau)\,d\tau, (6.41)

reported with normalized precision (the fraction of frames whose center error, divided by the target size, is below a threshold) on LaSOT and TrackingNet, and with average overlap (mean IoU over frames) and SR0.5\mathrm{SR}_{0.5}, SR0.75\mathrm{SR}_{0.75} on GOT-10k; the VOT challenges use expected average overlap (EAO), which folds accuracy and failure rate into one expectation [roffo2016visual]. MOT scores detection and identity jointly. MOTA [bernardin2008evaluating] charges false negatives, false positives, and identity switches against the number of ground-truth objects,

MOTA=1−FN+FP+IDSGT,\mathrm{MOTA}=1-\frac{\mathrm{FN}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{IDS}}{\mathrm{GT}}, (6.42)

and so is dominated by detection; IDF1 is the F1 score of identity-level true positives, IDF1=2⁢IDTP/(2⁢IDTP+IDFP+IDFN)\mathrm{IDF1}=2\,\mathrm{IDTP}/(2\,\mathrm{IDTP}+\mathrm{IDFP}+\mathrm{IDFN}), and emphasizes identity preservation; HOTA [luiten2021hota], DetA⋅AssA\sqrt{\mathrm{DetA}\cdot\mathrm{AssA}} averaged over localization thresholds, balances the two and has become the primary MOT metric. VOS reports the Jaccard index 𝒥=|M∩G|/|M∪G|\mathcal{J}=|M\cap G|/|M\cup G| of predicted and true masks and the contour F-measure ℱ\mathcal{F} from boundary precision and recall [perazzi2016benchmark], averaged as 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}.

Table 6.28 reports the methods of the Methodology above on the benchmarks each line treats as standard. Within SOT the step from a discriminative head over correlation features (DiMP) to attention-based fusion (TransT, STARK) is worth about ten points of LaSOT AUC, and the one-stream design of OSTrack adds six more over TransT. On MOT17 the detect-then-associate trackers lead, and ByteTrack’s gain over FairMOT comes from association alone; the end-to-end trackers (CenterTrack, TrackFormer, MOTR) trail on MOT17 but MOTR leads ByteTrack by 6.5 HOTA on DanceTrack [zeng2022motr], where appearance cues are weak. VOS accuracy on DAVIS-17 has moved from the mid-80s (XMem, DeAOT) to above 90 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} with SAM 2, which is also the first method trained on a corpus far larger than the benchmarks themselves.

6.4.2.4 Challenges

Identity under occlusion remains the central failure. Motion models and appearance embeddings bridge short occlusions, but long occlusions and dense crowds still produce identity switches and fragmented tracks [ZhangSJYWYLLW22, SunCJYBKL22], and memory-based propagation drifts or forgets over long videos even when each step is accurate [ChengS22XMem]. HOTA and IDF1 measure the outcome but not robustness to occlusion length or the calibration of track confidence, so the metrics reward the easy part of the problem.

Trackers are also tuned to a few curated benchmarks and transfer poorly to UAV footage, thermal and event imagery, adverse weather, and multi-camera surveillance; foundation-model trackers such as OneTracker [HongYZLZGJCLCZ24] and the RGB-X methods UASTrack [UASTrack] and Un-Track [WuZRV0PGT24UNTrack] address this directly but inherit the biases of their pretrained backbones. Long streams add memory and compute limits on top of drift.

The accuracy of Transformer trackers comes at a cost that keeps them off embedded hardware, while the lightweight correlation-filter line gives up robustness; and the unified models that would amortize that cost across tasks meet negative transfer between objectives with different demands, mask precision against identity association in particular [yan2022unicorn]. Language and segmentation priors widen what a tracker can be asked to do, at the price of prompt sensitivity that current benchmarks do not measure.

6.4.3 Temporal Localization

Temporal localization answers when something happens in a long, untrimmed video. The condition can be a category from a closed set, which gives temporal action localization (TAL) as treated in Section 6.3.4, or a free-form sentence, which gives temporal sentence grounding (TSG): return the segment that best matches “the person opens the microwave”. This subsection sets the two side by side, with the weight on the text-conditioned problem, which turns localization from exhaustive detection into retrieval and is what video search and interactive navigation [hendricks2017mcn, gao2017tall, krishna2017densecap] rely on.

6.4.3.1 Task Definition

Temporal Action Localization (TAL) takes an untrimmed video V={xt}t=1TV=\{x_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, where xtx_{t} may be a visual, audio, or multimodal feature, and detects all instances of KK predefined action classes, returning 𝒜={ai}i=1N\mathcal{A}=\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} with ai=(tistart,tiend,ci,si)a_{i}=(t_{i}^{\mathrm{start}},\,t_{i}^{\mathrm{end}},\,c_{i},\,s_{i}): start and end times, a class label ci∈{1,…,K}c_{i}\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, and a confidence sis_{i} (the (ts,te,c)(t_{s},t_{e},c) tuples of Section 6.3.4).

Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG), also called natural language video localization or video moment retrieval, pairs VV with a sentence qq and returns a ranked list of moments ℳ⁢(q,V)={mj}j=1M\mathcal{M}(q,V)=\{m_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M}, mj=(τjstart,τjend,rj)m_{j}=(\tau_{j}^{\mathrm{start}},\,\tau_{j}^{\mathrm{end}},\,r_{j}), with boundaries and a relevance score rjr_{j}; usually one segment is the answer. TAL is thus an exhaustive detection task over a closed label set, TSG a targeted retrieval task guided by open-ended language.

Both are studied under several settings, which Figure 6.25 lays side by side. Offline methods see the whole video; online methods infer causally over the streamed prefix and are judged on low-latency detection of action starts [shou2018odas, gao2019startnet]. Supervision ranges from frame-accurate boundaries to video-level labels only (weakly supervised TAL via multiple-instance learning, Section 6.3.4; weakly supervised TSG by aligning the two modalities during training [ma2020vlanet]), with self-supervised video pretraining [tong2022videomae, wang2023videomaev2] and open-vocabulary or zero-shot variants [liberatori2024t3al] reducing the labeled data needed. TSG additionally varies in scope, from a single video [gao2017tall, hendricks2017mcn] to corpus-level retrieval that first finds the video and then the moment (VCMR) [lei2020tvr], and in output, with QVHighlights [lei2021qvhighlights] asking for a saliency ranking of highlight clips alongside the grounded moment.

6.4.3.2 Methodology

Figure 6.24 traces both tasks along the same path from hand-designed pipelines to end-to-end Transformers.

The TAL row is the detection lineage of Section 6.3.4: sliding windows over hand-crafted features such as improved dense trajectories [wang2013idt], then two-stage proposal-plus-classification systems (R-C3D [xu2017rcc3d], SSN [zhao2017temporal], TAL-Net [chao2018talnet]) with dedicated boundary-sensitive proposal generators (BSN [lin2018bsn], BMN [lin2019bmn], G-TAD [xu2020gtad]), then anchor-free dense detectors and query-based set prediction. Three developments go beyond that treatment. Dense single-stage detectors were scaled by ActionFormer [zhang2022actionformer], a multi-scale Transformer encoder over the feature pyramid, and TriDet [shi2023tridet], which replaces self-attention with a convolutional scalable-granularity-perception module and a trident boundary head; both still regress boundaries at every position and rely on non-maximum suppression. DETR-style set prediction removes anchors and suppression: RTD-Net [tan2021rtdnet] applies a relaxed Transformer decoder to proposal generation and TadTR [liu2022tadtr] decodes the full action set end to end [liu2022e2etad, kim2024tetad]. And masked video pretraining [tong2022videomae, wang2023videomaev2] now supplies the backbones that these heads are fine-tuned on.

TSG began with cross-modal matching. CTRL [gao2017tall] embeds the sentence and candidate clips in a shared space and ranks clips, with boundary regression on top; MCN [hendricks2017mcn] does the same for DiDeMo with global video context. Later models reason over the candidates jointly: MAN [zhang2019man] refines moments iteratively through a graph over proposals, 2D-TAN [zhang2020twodtan] scores every (start, end) pair on a two-dimensional temporal-adjacency map so that neighboring candidates inform each other, and VSLNet [zhang2020vslnet] drops proposals altogether and predicts the start and end positions as span extraction, in analogy to reading comprehension. Moment-DETR [lei2021qvhighlights] brought set prediction to grounding, decoding moments and saliency scores directly from an encoder–decoder, while TVR [lei2020tvr] extended grounding to corpus scale with a coarse-to-fine search over subtitles and frames.

6.4.3.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.29 lists the benchmarks; the TAL rows are those of Section 6.3.4, retained for comparison. The TSG benchmarks move from a closed domain (TACoS [tacos2013], cooking) to open-domain sentences over indoor activity (Charades-STA [gao2017tall]), Flickr videos with multiple references per query (DiDeMo [hendricks2017mcn]), and dense paragraph-level captions (ActivityNet Captions [krishna2017densecap]); YouCook2 [zhou2017youcook2] adds procedural structure, TVR [lei2020tvr] multimodal (subtitle) context and corpus-level retrieval, and QVHighlights [lei2021qvhighlights] saliency labels for joint highlight detection.

Temporal IoU between a predicted and a ground-truth segment is the primitive for both tasks, and TAL is scored by mAP at fixed tIoU thresholds (per-threshold on THUMOS14, averaged over [0.5:0.95][0.5{:}0.95] on ActivityNet) and by AR@AN for proposal quality [anet2019proposals], as defined in Section 6.3.4. TSG uses retrieval metrics instead. For queries 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, ranked predictions m^j\hat{m}_{j}, and reference segments G⁢(q)G(q),

R⁢@⁢n,IoU=θ=1|𝒬|⁢∑q∈𝒬𝟏⁢(max1≤j≤n⁡maxg∈G⁢(q)⁡tIoU⁢(m^j,g)≥θ)\mathrm{R}@n,\mathrm{IoU}{=}\theta\,=\,\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in% \mathcal{Q}}\mathbf{1}\!\left(\max_{1\leq j\leq n}\;\max_{g\in G(q)}\mathrm{% tIoU}(\hat{m}_{j},g)\geq\theta\right) (6.43)

is the fraction of queries for which some top-nn prediction overlaps a reference by at least θ\theta (commonly n∈{1,5}n\in\{1,5\}, θ∈{0.3,0.5,0.7}\theta\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}), and mIoU=1|𝒬|⁢∑qmaxg∈G⁢(q)⁡tIoU⁢(m^1,g)\mathrm{mIoU}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q}\max_{g\in G(q)}\mathrm{tIoU}(% \hat{m}_{1},g) scores the top prediction alone; QVHighlights adds mAP over tIoU thresholds [lei2021qvhighlights]. Recall at a threshold binarizes overlap and ignores the quality of the ranking, which motivated ranking-sensitive alternatives such as AxIoU [togashi2022axiou], and annotator disagreement about where a described moment begins and ends puts a ceiling on how precisely any of these can be measured.

Table 6.30 gives R@1 results for the TSG methods above; TAL numbers are in the table of Section 6.3.4. Relational reasoning over candidates (2D-TAN) and span prediction (VSLNet) improved the listed Charades-STA R@1 from CTRL’s 23.6/8.9 to 39.7/23.3 and 54.2/35.2, respectively, and Moment-DETR adds a further step on Charades-STA without proposals or suppression; its QVHighlights numbers are the reference point for joint grounding and highlight detection.

6.4.3.4 Challenges

Boundaries are soft. Actions span sub-second gestures to multi-minute activities, which no single temporal resolution serves, and annotators disagree about where an instance starts and ends; a sentence adds its own ambiguity about which part of an activity it describes. The tIoU-thresholded metrics treat these fuzzy boundaries as exact, so part of the measured error is irreducible [togashi2022axiou], and probabilistic boundary modeling with calibrated confidences is the natural response.

The two tasks are converging. A closed label set limits TAL, while TSG is bounded by the vocabulary of its query sets; text prompts in place of class labels [liberatori2024t3al] and set prediction for moments [lei2021qvhighlights] point to a single architecture that grounds both categories and sentences. Doing this over minutes of video, across camera viewpoints (egocentric footage in particular), with audio, narration, or noisy subtitles as further evidence [lei2020tvr, lei2021qvhighlights], and causally for streaming use [shou2018odas] is where the current systems fall short: memory-efficient long-context encoders and corpus-scale coarse-to-fine retrieval are the two ingredients most actively developed.

6.5 Multimodal Spatial Perception

The preceding sections perceive space largely through vision. Yet vision alone is often incomplete: it is blind past occluders, silent about what lies outside the frame, and mute on which entity a person actually means. Multimodal spatial perception closes these gaps by grounding spatial understanding in signals beyond the image. The section takes two complementary couplings: audio-visual spatial localization, which uses sound to place events that vision may miss, and vision-language grounding, which ties linguistic reference to the specific entity or region it denotes. Neither adds a new spatial primitive; each supplies a channel of evidence that makes perception more complete where a single modality falls short.

6.5.1 Audio-Visual Spatial Localization

Humans localize a sound by combining auditory cues (interaural level and time differences, spectral shaping) with visual context (lip motion, object dynamics) [blauert1997spatial]. Audio-visual spatial localization (AV-SL) asks a machine to do the same: find the pixel region, object, or 3D point that a sound comes from, under reverberation, noise, occlusion, and several simultaneous sources [arandjelovic2017look, owens2018audio]. The two modalities are complementary. Binaural or array audio supplies directional cues, while distance requires additional geometric, near-field, or learned evidence; vision says which entities are plausible sounders and separates acoustically confusable ones (two similar instruments, only one playing). Spatial audio for AR/VR [morgado2018self], teleconferencing [tao2021talknet], and audio-guided navigation [chen2020soundspaces] are the main consumers.

6.5.1.1 Task Definition
