The input is an audio stream AA (mono, binaural, or multichannel, optionally ambisonic [zotter2019ambisonics]) time-aligned with a video VV (RGB, depth, or multi-view) of the same interval; the audio may contain zero, one, or several sources, and the video may show silent objects that look like sounders. The output localizes the sounding entity in a form that depends on the variant: a 2D heatmap or mask, a face or body box with a speaking state, an event class with its temporal extent and direction of arrival (DOA, azimuth and elevation) and optionally distance [politis2023dataset], a 2D location with depth, or a 3D point or trajectory in camera or world coordinates. For visible-region localization, off-screen sources or audio with no visible source should yield a null prediction; 3D acoustic localization may still estimate an off-screen source.

Five variants are in common use. Visual sound source localization (VSSL) highlights the sounding region of a frame or clip as a class-agnostic heatmap, in single- and multi-source settings and increasingly with negative or off-screen audio as a robustness test. Active speaker detection (ASD) decides who is speaking and localizes the talker as a face track, often under streaming constraints [tao2021talknet]. Audio-visual sound event localization and detection (AV-SELD) couples what and when with where: event class, temporal extent, DOA, and in recent benchmarks distance [politis2023dataset]. The 2.5D variant adds depth or range to a 2D localization from monocular depth [DepthAnything], stereo, or echoes [gao2020visualechoes]; and 3D DOA estimation returns a spatial bearing, whereas source-position or trajectory estimation additionally uses range or triangulation constraints from calibrated cameras, arrays, or egocentric rigs [grauman2022ego4d].

6.5.1.2 Methodology

Figure 6.26 maps the five variants onto four method families.

Cross-Modal Correspondence (VSSL).

VSSL is learned almost entirely without location labels, from the co-occurrence of sound and image. An audio encoder maps the clip to an embedding 𝐚\mathbf{a}, a visual encoder maps the frame to a feature map 𝐯⁢(𝐱)\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}), and the localization map is the per-position similarity

S⁢(𝐱)=𝐚⊤⁢𝐯⁢(𝐱)‖𝐚‖⁢‖𝐯⁢(𝐱)‖,S(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x})}{\|\mathbf{a}\|\,% \|\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x})\|}, (6.44)

trained so that matching audio-image pairs score higher than mismatched ones [senocak2018learning, owens2018audio]; Sound of Pixels [zhao2018sound] instead mixes two clips and asks the network to separate them conditioned on pixel features, which forces the same alignment. Later work targets the failure modes of co-occurrence. LVS [chen2021localizing] mines hard negatives inside the same image (regions that look like sounders but do not match the audio) and introduces the VGG-SS localization benchmark; deep multimodal clustering [hu2019deep] and coarse-to-fine mixture objectives [qian2020multiple] handle several sources at once; and SLAVC [mo2022closer] shows that earlier methods depend on early stopping and adds momentum encoders and extreme visual dropout so that the alignment does not collapse onto background.

Audio–Lip Alignment (ASD).

ASD runs a face detector and tracker and then decides, per track and per frame, whether the visible mouth produced the audio. The decision rests on audio-visual synchrony: a visual encoder over the lip region and an audio encoder over the spectrogram are compared across time [afouras2020self], and TalkNet [tao2021talknet] adds long-term temporal modeling of both streams with cross-attention, which is what separates a brief pause from a non-speaker. Active Speakers in Context [alcazar2020active] scores each candidate jointly with the other faces in the frame, and ASDNet [kopuklu2021how] makes the three stages explicit (per-frame audio-visual encoding, inter-speaker relation modeling, temporal modeling), with each stage trained for its role.

Joint Event and DOA Prediction (AV-SELD).

SELDnet [adavanne2018sound] set the template: a convolutional recurrent network over multichannel spectrogram features with two heads, one classifying active events per frame and one regressing their DOA. ACCDOA [shimada2021accdoa] folds the two into one output, a vector per class whose direction is the DOA and whose length is the activity, which removes the need to balance two losses; the DCASE challenge tracks [politis2020overview] standardized the protocol, and STARSS23 [politis2023dataset] added video and source distance.

Geometric Lifting (2.5D and 3D).

Lifting a 2D localization to metric space uses geometry rather than learned correspondence alone. VisualEchoes [gao2020visualechoes] shows that echoes of an emitted chirp carry depth: the time and spectrum of the return, fused with the image, improve monocular depth estimation and give the 2.5D variant its range. Audio-visual spatial alignment [morgado2020learning] learns representations by predicting whether 360∘ video and ambisonic audio are spatially consistent, a pretext that encodes direction, and self-supervised spatial audio generation [morgado2018self] learns the inverse mapping from 360∘ video to ambisonics. Full 3D systems combine classical array processing (time differences of arrival from GCC-PHAT [knapp1976generalized], steered-response-power beamforming [dibiase2001robust]) with calibrated cameras and triangulation, and in simulation (SoundSpaces [chen2020soundspaces, chen2022soundspaces]) with the agent’s own motion.

6.5.1.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.31 pairs each variant with its benchmarks and metrics; there is no shared benchmark across variants because their outputs differ.

VSSL is scored by thresholding the localization map and computing consensus intersection over union (cIoU) against the annotations; reported metrics include the fraction of test images with cIoU above 0.5 (localization accuracy) and the area under the IoU-threshold curve (AUC) [senocak2018learning]; the extended VGG-SS and Flickr protocols add clips whose audio has no visible source and report detection-style average precision requiring both visible-source presence and correct localization [chen2021localizing, mo2022closer]. ASD uses detection-style mAP over face tracks with speaking labels [roth2020ava]. SELD combines detection (F-score, error rate) with localization (DOA error, localization recall) [politis2020overview], while STARSS23 additionally provides source-distance annotations [politis2023dataset]; 2.5D inherits the depth metrics of Section 6.2.1, and 3D settings report angular and positional error.

Table 6.32 collects the two variants with a stable leaderboard. On VSSL the negative-audio protocol changes the ranking: LVS leads the earlier methods on the standard Flickr test but drops to 9.8 AP when silent clips are mixed in, whereas SLAVC holds both. ASD on AVA-ActiveSpeaker has moved from 79.2 mAP for the dataset baseline to above 93 with explicit temporal and inter-speaker modeling, and the remaining differences among top systems are about latency and streaming rather than accuracy. AV-SELD has no such table: each DCASE edition changes the data and the metric, and distance-aware evaluation is not directly comparable to the DOA-only tracks that SELDnet and ACCDOA were evaluated on.

6.5.1.4 Challenges

Co-occurrence is not causation. A model that has learned which objects usually make which sounds will localize a guitar whether or not it is playing, and the negative-audio protocols [chen2021localizing, mo2022closer] exist because the standard tests rewarded exactly this; the open problem is grounding on the acoustic evidence itself, which matters most for off-screen and silent cases where the right answer is no localization.

Going from 2D saliency to metric 3D requires semantics and geometry together. Depth foundation models [DepthAnything] (Section 6.2.1) and self-supervised visual features [dinov2] now supply priors that AV-SL pipelines previously learned from scratch, and STARSS23 [politis2023dataset] provides joint event, time, DOA, and distance annotations, supporting distance-aware extensions; multi-object objectives for overlapping events are the current frontier there.

Multiple simultaneous sources, identity through occlusion, and on-screen/off-screen transitions over long videos [qian2020multiple, tian2018audio] are the AV-SL form of the identity problem of Section 6.4.2 and the pose-continuity problem of Section 6.2.5. Streaming use adds causal encoders, low-latency fusion, calibration drift, and graceful fallback when one modality is missing [tao2021talknet, kopuklu2021how].

6.5.2 Vision-Language Grounding

Vision-language grounding ties a linguistic reference to the element of a scene it denotes. Given “Put your hand on the small mug on the right side of the table behind the blue book”, a grounded system must resolve the noun phrase, its attributes, and its spatial relations to one particular mug in the image; this referential link is what instruction following, multimodal dialogue, and human-robot interaction build on.

6.5.2.1 Task Definition

The input is a scene SS (an image, a video, or a 3D environment) and a query QQ, from a bare noun phrase (“the red cup”) to a sentence with attributes, relations, actions, or an implicit goal (“the person who is waving”, “something to open the box with”). The output ℛ⁢(Q,S)\mathcal{R}(Q,S) is the referred region in the form the variant requires: a box, a mask, a set of regions (possibly empty), a per-frame mask track, or a 3D box. Two formulations recur through the methods below: ranking a set of candidate regions rr by a cross-modal score, or regressing the region directly,

r^=arg⁡maxr∈𝒞⁢(S)⁡s⁢(ϕ⁢(Q),ψ⁢(S,r))orr^=fθ⁢(S,Q),\hat{r}=\arg\max_{r\in\mathcal{C}(S)}s\big{(}\phi(Q),\psi(S,r)\big{)}\qquad% \text{or}\qquad\hat{r}=f_{\theta}(S,Q), (6.45)

with ϕ\phi and ψ\psi the text and region encoders and 𝒞⁢(S)\mathcal{C}(S) a proposal set.

Figure 6.27 lays out the five variants, which differ in scene modality, output granularity, and query complexity.

Referring expression comprehension and segmentation (REC / RES). One image, one expression, one target, returned as a box (REC) or a mask (RES). RefCOCO and RefCOCO+ [yu2016modeling] (short phrases, the latter without location words) and RefCOCOg [mao2016generation] (longer descriptions), all using MS COCO [lin2014microsoft] images, with expressions collected through ReferItGame [kazemzadeh2014referitgame] or Mechanical Turk, have been the standard benchmarks for a decade; Flickr30k Entities [plummer2015flickr30k, young2014image] grounds every entity mention of a caption at once.

Generalized REC / RES (GREC / GRES). An expression may match zero, one, or several objects (“the red carrots” versus “the unicorn”), which single-target methods cannot represent. gRefCOCO [liu2023gres], Ref-ZOM [hu2023beyond], PhraseCut [wu2020phrasecut], and OmniLabel [schulter2023omnilabel] evaluate this setting, and MaskGroups-HQ [cao2025refer] generalizes the prompt itself to arbitrary groups of masks specified by text and reference masks. The output is a set, so the metric must be as well (see Datasets and Metrics below).

Reasoning grounding. Some queries require inference beyond noun matching: “the loser” needs a judgment about the people shown, “turn on the TV” needs the remote. CLEVR-Ref+ [liu2019clevr] diagnoses this on rendered scenes with ground-truth reasoning programs; ReasonSeg [lai2024lisa] poses implicit, multi-step queries on real images with mask output, extended by MMR [jang2025mmr] (194K implicit queries, multi-target and part-level), ReasonSeg-Inst [yang2023lisa++] (instance level), and MC-Bench [xu2024mcbench] (instances across image pairs). Ref-Adv [dong2026ref] keeps the classic REC format but makes expressions minimally sufficient, negation-heavy, and paired with same-category distractors.

Video referring and reasoning grounding. The referent must be found in every frame through motion, appearance change, and occlusion, and the query may name it by what it does (“the man waving his hand”). Refer-Youtube-VOS [seo2020urvos], Refer-DAVIS17 [khoreva2018video], A2D- and JHMDB-Sentences [gavrilyuk2018actor], MeViS [ding2023mevis], ReVOS [yan2024visa], and ReasonVOS [bai2024one] add language to existing segmentation and actor-action datasets; Ref-VPS [bagchi2025refereverything] extends the referent from objects to processes such as smoke spreading or waves breaking, which have no object boundary at all. Tracking machinery is usually folded in to carry identity across frames [fang2025decoupled].

3D and embodied grounding. The scene is a point cloud or a set of views, and the query refers to an object in 3D (“the chair next to the window”). ScanRefer [chen2020scanrefer] requires detecting the referent as a 3D box and Multi3DRefer [zhang2023multi3drefer] allows zero to many targets; ReferIt3D [achlioptas2020referit3d] provides the object instances and scores selection among them; Instruct3D [he2024segpoint] and Multi3DRes [wu20243d] ask for point-level masks from instruction-style queries. Embodied grounding makes the output an action: an agent told “go pick up the red cup on the right” must identify the cup and reach it [zhen20243d].

6.5.2.2 Methodology

The methods below fall into eight families, (A) to (H); Figure 6.28 illustrates (A) through (G). They are trajectories rather than eras: the oldest paradigm has resurfaced at foundation-model scale.

(A) Proposal Ranking.

The first grounding models instantiate the ranking form of Eq. (6.45): detect region proposals, embed them and the query in a joint space, and pick the best-scoring region. Deep Fragment Embeddings [karpathy2014deep] aligned sentence fragments with detected regions, and scene-graph CRFs [johnson2015image] grounded structured queries to regions for retrieval. Proposal quality bounded these methods and context-dependent expressions defeated them. The same two-stage shape has returned with far stronger proposals: RAS [cao2025refer] has a segmentation foundation model propose candidate masks and a mask-centric multimodal LLM select the group that satisfies the prompt, and this non-autoregressive selection beats mask generation in both accuracy and latency.

(B) Compositional Reasoning.

Modular networks parse the expression and route its parts to dedicated modules. CMN [hu2017modeling] decomposes an expression into a subject–relationship–object triplet handled by localization and relationship modules; MAttNet [yu2018mattnet] soft-parses phrases into appearance, location, and relationship attention modules; dynamic graph attention [yang2019dynamic] reasons over the linguistic structure on a scene graph. These models disambiguate compositional queries (“the man behind the woman in red”) but inherit every parsing error.

(C) End-to-End Grounding.

The regression form of Eq. (6.45) removes proposals: a single network fuses the sentence embedding with the image feature map and predicts the box. One-Stage Grounding [yang2019fast] did this with a detector head, TransVG [deng2021transvg] with a pure Transformer in which a learnable token attends over visual and textual tokens and regresses coordinates. On the segmentation side, CRIS [wang2022cris] transfers CLIP’s image-text alignment to the pixel level with text-to-pixel contrastive learning and made end-to-end RES the standard formulation.

(D) Grounded Pre-Training.

Phrase-region alignment learned at scale turned grounding into an open-vocabulary capability. MDETR [kamath2021mdetr] trains a DETR-style set predictor on text-aligned detection corpora so that every box is tied to a span of the caption; GLIP [li2022grounded] reformulates detection as phrase grounding and scales to 27M region-caption pairs, giving zero-shot transfer; RegionCLIP [zhong2022regionclip] adds region-level contrastive alignment, and Grounding DINO [liu2024grounding] deep language fusion at every stage of a DINO detector, which made it the default open-vocabulary detector of later tool chains (family (G)). The residual weakness is the entity shortcut: models latch onto object names and ignore the description. DesCo [li2023desco] counters it in the data, pre-training on LLM-generated rich descriptions with context-sensitive negative queries, which raises description-conditioned detection on LVIS and OmniLabel.

(E) Grounding MLLMs.

The first multimodal LLMs built for grounding gave the language backbone a region interface. Kosmos-2 [peng2023kosmos] emits location tokens that hyperlink phrases to boxes inside the generated text; Ferret [you2023ferret] and Ferret-v2 [zhang2024ferret] encode boxes, points, and free-form regions as inputs at any resolution. Mask output comes from attaching a decoder: LISA [lai2024lisa] decodes a dedicated segmentation token’s embedding into a mask, which is what makes reasoning segmentation possible, and LISA++ [yang2023lisa++] extends it to instances within a dialogue; GLaMM [rasheed2024glamm] unifies phrase grounding, referring segmentation, and free-form conversation under a grounded-conversation objective; Sa2VA [yuan2025sa2va] couples a LLaVA-style backbone to SAM 2 [ravi2024sam2] and carries dense grounding from images to video referring segmentation. Moondream 3’s segmentation extension [reid2026moondream] dispenses with the decoder and writes the mask autoregressively as a vector path, refined by a lightweight head and trained with reinforcement learning on mask overlap.

(F) Generalist MLLMs.

A parallel line keeps no grounding component at all: the model writes coordinates as plain text, and grounding is one capability among many. Florence-2 [xiao2024florence] is the compact case, a sequence-to-sequence model trained on the 5.4B-annotation FLD-5B corpus that casts captioning, detection, grounding, and polygon-vertex segmentation into one text interface, with mask accuracy below the decoder-based models of family (E). The frontier generalists, Gemini [reid2024gemini], Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL [bai2025qwen2.5vl], InternVL 2.5 and InternVL 3 [chen2024expanding, zhu2025internvl3], and Seed1.5-VL [guo2025seed1.5vl], now match or exceed the specialists on the RefCOCO family from prompting alone (Table 6.34); Llama 3 [grattafiori2024llama] folds phrase-to-box and phrase-to-mask annotations into its multimodal pre-training but reports no REC numbers.

(G) Tool-Augmented Agents.

A third line delegates localization to specialist models under an outer control loop, which has moved from fixed pipelines to generated programs to learned tool use. Grounded SAM [ren2024grounded] chains Grounding DINO boxes into SAM [kirillov2023sam] masks without training; ViperGPT [suris2023vipergpt] has a code LLM write a Python program that calls perception APIs, so that logic and arithmetic are symbolic and perception is delegated, with interpretable intermediate steps. SegAgent [zhu2025segagent] treats mask annotation as a sequential decision process, imitating the click sequences of human annotators on an interactive segmenter; DeepEyes [zheng2025deepeyes] internalizes the tool, using reinforcement learning to make the model emit coordinates that trigger zoom-in crops inside its own chain of thought. SAM 3 Agent [carion2025sam] wraps SAM 3, whose concept prompts return every instance matching a noun phrase, with an MLLM that proposes phrases, inspects the returned masks, and selects those satisfying the full expression, which gives zero-shot referring and reasoning segmentation without grounding-specific training.

(H) Generation for Grounding.

The newest family treats a large text-to-image or text-to-video generator as a grounding model, on the premise that generative pre-training already induces a fine-grained map from language to spatial and temporal structure. VD-IT [zhu2024exploring] uses a frozen text-to-video diffusion model as the feature extractor for referring video segmentation and finds its features more temporally consistent and better aligned with language than discriminative video backbones; ReferEverything [bagchi2025refereverything] keeps the generator intact and fine-tunes it to predict mask latents decoded by the frozen VAE, which transfers zero-shot to rare objects, “stuff”, and the amorphous processes of Ref-VPS. Vision Banana [gabeur2026image] instruction-tunes a state-of-the-art image generator to render the task output as an image, segmentation as painting the referred region a prescribed color, and matches specialist systems zero-shot while keeping its generative ability. Grounding quality in this family rises with the underlying generator.

6.5.2.3 Datasets and Metrics

Table 6.33 lists the benchmarks by variant. Annotation cost rises steeply from a 2D box to a per-frame mask to a 3D box, so image-level REC/RES corpora dominate in size and maturity, video referring sets are an order of magnitude smaller, and 3D corpora smaller still. Within the image benchmarks a generational split has opened. RefCOCO/+/g now serve mainly as training corpora: specialists and generalist MLLMs report Acc@0.5 above 90% on them, an audit found label errors in 14%, 24%, and 5% of RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg [chen2025revisiting], and much of the score survives shuffling the word order of the expression [dong2026ref]. The evaluation-oriented replacements are built to expose what saturation hides: Ref-L4 [chen2025revisiting] (cleaned labels, long expressions, a 365-category vocabulary), Ref-Adv [dong2026ref] (shortcut-suppressed, where the same models fall to roughly 60%), HC-RefLoCo [wei2024hcrefloco], GigaGrounding [ma2024gigaground], and GroundingME [li2026groundingme], which scores discrimination, spatial reasoning, limited visibility, and the rejection of ungroundable queries, and on which the best model resolves 45% of samples while most score zero on rejection.

Every metric here is built on the IoU of predicted and reference regions (Section 6.4.2 gives the mask form). REC reports Accuracy@0.5, the fraction of expressions whose box reaches IoU ≥0.5\geq 0.5, with stricter thresholds and the threshold-averaged mAcc [chen2025revisiting] increasingly added; phrase grounding, where several proposals may be returned, reports Recall@kk. For set-valued outputs (GREC / GRES) the prediction is compared with the ground-truth set through per-expression F1 over boxes or masks [hu2023beyond] and a no-target accuracy for expressions with no referent [liu2023gres], and OmniLabel’s APdescr{}_{\text{descr}} computes average precision over free-form descriptions including negative ones [schulter2023omnilabel]. Segmentation reports two aggregates that differ in weighting: gIoU (also called mIoU) averages per-sample IoU and so weights every expression equally, whereas cIoU accumulates intersection and union over the whole set before dividing and so weights large objects more; reasoning and referring segmentation papers report both [lai2024lisa], often with Precision@XX for the distribution of mask quality and a boundary IoU for edge accuracy [reid2026moondream]. Video referring segmentation uses the 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} composite of Section 6.4.2.

Table 6.34 reports the two variants on which the families can be compared. On REC the step from proposal ranking and modular reasoning (MAttNet) to end-to-end regression (TransVG) and then to grounded pre-training (MDETR, Grounding DINO) is about 14 points of RefCOCO Acc@0.5, and the generalist MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL 2.5) sit at or above the best specialist without benchmark-specific training. On RES the grounding MLLMs with a mask decoder have passed the end-to-end specialists (CRIS to Sa2VA is eleven cIoU points on RefCOCO), and Sa2VA’s video columns show the same model carrying over to referring video segmentation; on ReasonSeg, LISA-7B reaches 52.9 gIoU after fine-tuning where open-vocabulary segmenters stay below 30 [lai2024lisa]. The tool-augmented and generative families are evaluated zero-shot on subsets of these benchmarks and are not directly comparable here. What the table cannot show is cross-variant breadth: methods strong on image REC routinely degrade on video, reasoning, and 3D grounding, and no single architecture leads all five variants.

6.5.2.4 Challenges

Ambiguity and interaction. “The guy on the right” depends on the viewpoint, and “the red cup” presumes one salient red cup. People resolve this through shared context or a follow-up question; grounding models make an arbitrary choice or fall back on a dataset bias such as the largest instance. Recognizing that an expression matches several entities, abstaining under uncertainty, and asking for clarification are outside almost every current benchmark, which is one-shot (one query, one image), while real use is a dialogue with memory of what was grounded before.

Reasoning and commonsense. “The tool needed to open the box” cannot be resolved from the image alone, and adversarial evaluation shows that much of current REC accuracy rests on shortcut matching rather than reasoning [dong2026ref]. LLM-based models carry the knowledge but may answer “a key” when none is visible, and vision-only models lack it entirely; reasoning-driven segmentation [lai2024lisa] and agentic active perception [zheng2025deepeyes] are the two bridges. Video adds temporal and causal structure (“the man who picks up the phone and then leaves”, “the car that caused the accident”) that current video grounding, which attends mostly to appearance and simple motion, does not capture.

Open world and 3D. Open-vocabulary detectors and CLIP-based models have blind spots on rare objects, fine-grained distinctions (viola versus violin), proper nouns, and figurative references (“the blue crown” for a cap), and per-category analyses of large multimodal models show a strong bias toward common training categories [chen2025revisiting]. Description-conditioned pre-training [li2023desco] and generative pre-training [bagchi2025refereverything, gabeur2026image] are the routes to long-tail coverage that do not require labeling it. Functional references (“the driver’s seat”) also imply spatial context that only 3D understanding resolves, and the 3D-language work surveyed above [hong20233d, zhen20243d] will grow with augmented reality and robotics.

Efficiency and evaluation. The strongest systems are multi-model tool chains or LLMs with vision adapters and do not fit AR glasses or robots; compact models [xiao2024florence, reid2026moondream] and non-autoregressive selection [cao2025refer] show that accuracy does not require scale, but the accuracy-efficiency frontier is unmapped. Evaluation has the saturation problem described under Datasets and Metrics above, and the new benchmarks, each with its own protocol, risk a cycle of leaderboard chasing; a single protocol spanning image, video, 3D, and dialogue, scoring rejection and clarification as well as localization, does not yet exist.

6.6 Summary and Outlook

This chapter followed spatial perception from the elemental to the structured: recognizing the entities in a scene, fixing them in metric geometry, binding them into relations, layouts, and maps, carrying that structure through time, and supplementing vision with sound and language. Three observations recur across these tasks.

Priors fill gaps that observation leaves open. Monocular depth, surface normals, and camera motion are underdetermined by a single image: scale, reflectance, and the geometry behind an occluder are not fixed by the pixels (§6.2.1, §6.2.4). Learned models increasingly resolve this ambiguity with strong priors, which makes them confident on familiar scenes and fragile on transparent or reflective materials, moving objects, adverse conditions, and domains their training data under-represent. Distinguishing what a percept observes from what a prior supplies is a requirement the later chapters inherit, and Chapter 15 returns to it as a question of observability.

Foundation models move the bottleneck rather than remove it. Open-vocabulary detectors and segmenters, zero-shot scene classifiers, and 3D geometry foundation models have widened what perception covers without task-specific training, yet the hardest cases persist at the long tail: small and rare objects, unseen instances in clutter, and metric judgments of distance, size, and angle, on which multimodal models remain weak even when their semantic predictions are strong (§6.3.1). The accuracy–efficiency tension noted for detection recurs in every task of the chapter.

Evaluation rewards the easier part of each problem. Many benchmarks are synthetic, saturated, or confined to a few curated scenes; tracking metrics do not measure robustness to occlusion length (§6.4.2), temporal-localization metrics treat fuzzy boundaries as exact, and grounding benchmarks pose a single query against a single image rather than an interaction (§6.5.2).

What the chapter delivers is structured spatial evidence: entities with positions, relations, trajectories, and maps. Chapter 7 takes that evidence as input and asks what can be inferred and planned from it, and Chapter 8 runs the mapping in the opposite direction.

Chapter 7 Spatial Reasoning

Spatial reasoning is the step that turns perceived structure into decisions: given detections, depths, poses, and a task, it works out the relations, the causes, and the actions that follow, the why and how of spatial interaction rather than merely the what and where. It is where perception becomes goal-directed, supporting inference, planning, and problem-solving in physical and virtual environments.

The chapter is organized along the spectrum by which spatial reasoning has actually developed, from explicit symbolic models to learned and foundation-model-driven ones. At one end, reasoning runs over hand-built representations of geometry, physics, and logic, whose structure is inspectable and whose conclusions can be certified. In the middle, it emerges from data, as neural models acquire spatial competence directly rather than being told the rules. More recently, large pre-trained models supply reasoning as a general capability to be elicited and steered. Hybrid approaches recombine these, pairing the semantic reach of foundation models with the precision and verifiability of symbolic and learned components; a closing survey of benchmarks then records how the field measures spatial reasoning as it shifts from passive observation toward active, situated interaction.

7.1 Rule-based Symbolic Spatial Reasoning

Rule-based symbolic spatial reasoning covers the methods that operate over explicit, model-based representations of space (geometric primitives, physical laws, graph connectivity, formal constraints, action rules, or causal mechanisms) rather than over learned latent representations alone. What sets this family apart is that reasoning happens inside a model that can be inspected: its state and transitions are legible, so claims about feasibility, optimality, or safety can be backed by certificates rather than empirical averages, and when a plan fails it fails legibly, as an infeasible inverse kinematics, a violated constraint, a missing precondition, or an inconsistent causal attribution, not as an opaque correlation.

The section surveys six kinds of explicit structure, ordered from the most concrete to the most abstract: geometric and algebraic models of position, orientation, motion, and feasibility; physical models of contact, friction, and stability; topological and graph abstractions of space that turn planning into search; formal constraint systems whose solvers return certified plans or proofs of infeasibility; rule-based and programmatic logic that sequences and supervises actions; and causal models that explain, predict counterfactually, and prescribe interventions.

These paradigms are not isolated alternatives. Modern robotic systems routinely compose them: geometric solvers serve as feasibility oracles inside constraint-based search; behavior trees wrap symbolic plans for fault tolerance; causal action languages compile to SAT; topological maps anchor both classical and learning-based navigation policies. The unifying thread is that each paradigm carries explicit structure (a state, an operator, a constraint, a rule, or a mechanism) that can be inspected, composed, and reasoned about.

7.1.1 Geometric and Algebraic Reasoning

Geometric and algebraic reasoning uses explicit mathematical models of position, orientation, shape, and motion to turn local measurements (image points, depths, joint angles, odometry) into quantities that can be analyzed and verified: where things are in a common frame, what a sensor can see, what a mechanism can reach, and whether a grasp will hold. The same models extend to time-varying settings, where relationships evolve under kinematic and differential constraints and the question becomes not only where entities can be but how they can move. Precision, interpretability, and domain independence have made this the common substrate of robotics [Murray1994RoboticManipulation, Lynch2017ModernRobotics, siciliano2010robotics], AR/VR [hartley2003multiple, azuma1997survey], and autonomous systems [Thrun2005Probabilistic, sola2018micro, LaValle2006Planning], and the source of the hard constraints that learned components are checked against. Figure 7.1 gives the abstract formulation.

7.1.1.1 Task Definition

Given measurements {𝐳k}\{\mathbf{z}_{k}\} expressed in local frames (pixels, ranges, joint readings, pose increments) and a system model Θ\Theta (sensor calibration, kinematic parameters, environment geometry), geometric reasoning computes a world-frame quantity and a feasibility verdict,

𝐱=g⁢({𝐳k};Θ),ψ⁢(𝐱;Θ)∈{true,false},\mathbf{x}=g(\{\mathbf{z}_{k}\};\,\Theta),\qquad\psi(\mathbf{x};\,\Theta)\in\{% \mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}, (7.1)

where 𝐱\mathbf{x} may be a pose, a reconstructed surface, a workspace or visibility region, or a trajectory, and ψ\psi is a chosen predicate, such as reachability, visibility, or force closure, checked against the model. In the time-varying case the inputs are indexed over time and 𝐱\mathbf{x} becomes a trajectory with reachable sets and feasibility certificates along it.

7.1.1.2 Methodology
Transformation and Pose Representation.

Rigid-body relationships between sensors, objects, and mechanisms are elements of the special Euclidean group

𝐓=[𝐑𝐭𝟎⊤1]∈S⁢E⁢(3),\mathbf{T}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{R}&\mathbf{t}\\ \mathbf{0}^{\top}&1\end{bmatrix}\in SE(3), (7.2)

where 𝐑∈S⁢O⁢(3)\mathbf{R}\in SO(3) is a rotation and 𝐭∈ℝ3\mathbf{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} a translation; composing them moves measurements across frames. Early robotics parameterized serial chains through the Denavit–Hartenberg convention [Denavit1955Kinematic, Paul1981Robot], which gives forward kinematics from a minimal set of link parameters. Lie-group formulations instead write motion as exponentials of screw axes, the product-of-exponentials representation [Murray1994RoboticManipulation, Lynch2017ModernRobotics], which is coordinate-free and behaves well where the DH parameterization has discontinuities. Quaternions [Shoemake1985QuaternionCurves, Horn1987Orientation] and dual quaternions [Daniilidis1999DualQuat, horn2021online] give compact, numerically stable encodings of rotation and screw motion for calibration and sensor fusion.

Projective and Multi-View Geometry.

Reasoning from images must recover 3D structure and camera motion from 2D measurements under perspective distortion and scale ambiguity. The constraint between corresponding points in two views is the epipolar condition

𝐱′⁣⊤⁢𝐅𝐱=0,\mathbf{x}^{\prime\top}\mathbf{F}\mathbf{x}=0, (7.3)

with 𝐅\mathbf{F} the fundamental matrix. The eight-point algorithm [LonguetHiggins1981Scene] solves for 𝐅\mathbf{F} linearly, Hartley’s normalization [Hartley1997EightPoint] made it numerically stable, and Nistér’s five-point solver [Nister2004FivePoint] reaches the minimal case for calibrated cameras. Zhang’s homography-based calibration [zhang2000flexible] removed the need for special rigs; the field is consolidated in [hartley2003multiple], and structure-from-motion systems such as COLMAP [schonberger2016structure] scale it to thousands of images, with RANSAC [Fischler1981RANSAC] enforcing the algebraic constraints against outliers throughout.

Jacobian and Differential Formulations.

For motion rather than static configuration, the map from configuration to task space,

𝐱=f⁢(𝐪),\mathbf{x}=f(\mathbf{q}), (7.4)

is differentiated to relate velocities,

𝐱˙=𝐉⁢(𝐪)⁢𝐪˙,\dot{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})\dot{\mathbf{q}}, (7.5)

and the Jacobian 𝐉⁢(𝐪)\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q}) carries the information about feasibility, singularities, and controllability along a motion. Whitney’s resolved motion rate control [Whitney1969ResolvedMotion] used it to command Cartesian velocities without closed-form inverse kinematics; Nakamura’s damped least squares [Nakamura1986IKSingularity] trades exactness for stability near singularities; redundancy resolution [Liegeois1977Redundancy, Siciliano1991Redundancy] uses null-space motion for secondary objectives; and Khatib’s operational-space formulation [Khatib1987OperationalSpace] separates task and null-space dynamics so that objectives are written directly in task space.

Visibility and Coverage Geometry.

What a sensor at pose pp can observe is the set

𝒱⁢(p)={x∈ℰ∣line⁢(p,x)∩𝒪=∅},\mathcal{V}(p)=\{x\in\mathcal{E}\mid\text{line}(p,x)\cap\mathcal{O}=\emptyset\}, (7.6)

with ℰ\mathcal{E} the environment and 𝒪\mathcal{O} the obstacles. The Art Gallery theorem [Chvatal1975ArtGallery, ORourke1987ArtGallery] bounds the number of viewpoints needed for full coverage; polygon visibility [Lee1983Visibility] and shortest-path queries [Guibas1987ShortestPath] made the computations algorithmic; and Tarabanis et al. [Tarabanis1995SensorPlanning] cast sensor planning as geometric optimization over fields of view modeled as cones, frusta, or polygons.

Workspace and Reachability Analysis.

The reachable workspace of a mechanism is

ℛ={𝐱∣∃𝐪∈𝒞free⁢ such that ⁢𝐱=f⁢(𝐪)},\mathcal{R}=\{\mathbf{x}\mid\exists\,\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}}% \text{ such that }\mathbf{x}=f(\mathbf{q})\}, (7.7)

with 𝒞free\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}} the feasible configuration space. Roth [Roth1975Performance] and Gosselin [Gosselin1990Singularity] added performance and dexterity measures so that manipulability is characterized along with reachability; Merlet [Merlet1998Workspace] classified workspace types; Zlatanov et al. [Zlatanov1994Constraints] analyzed constraint-induced singularities; and sampling-based reachability maps [lu2026richmap] trade closed-form guarantees for empirical coverage in high-dimensional systems.

Contact and Grasp Geometry.

Whether a set of contacts can hold an object is decided in wrench space. Ferrari and Canny [Ferrari1992Grasp] model the forces each contact can apply as a convex set of wrenches 𝒲\mathcal{W}; the grasp is force-closed if

𝟎∈int⁢conv⁢(𝒲),\mathbf{0}\in\text{int}\,\text{conv}(\mathcal{W}), (7.8)

so that any external wrench can be resisted. GraspIt! [Miller2004GraspIt] made these metrics computable for arbitrary hands and objects; task-oriented measures [Lin2015TaskGrasp] weight the wrench space by what the task requires; and Dex-Net [Mahler2017DexNet] samples analytic grasps at scale to train data-driven grasp predictors that keep the geometric criterion as their label.

7.1.1.3 Benchmarks

Geometric reasoning is evaluated against geometrically grounded ground truth: camera poses and intrinsics, depth maps and meshes, object models, grasp annotations. The pose, odometry, SLAM, and multi-view reconstruction benchmarks (TUM RGB-D [Sturm2012TUMRGBD], EuRoC [Burri2016EuRoC], TUM-VI [Schubert2018TUMVI], KITTI [KITTI-GeigerLU12], ETH3D [Schoeps2017ETH3D], Tanks and Temples [knapitsch2017tanks], DTU [Aanaes2016DTU], Middlebury [Seitz2006Middlebury, Scharstein2002Stereo], HPatches [Balntas2017HPatches]) and the long-term localization suites under seasonal and day-night change (Aachen, RobotCar Seasons, CMU Seasons [Sattler2018Benchmarking], InLoc [Taira2018InLoc], 4Seasons [wenzel2021seasons]) are those of Section 6.2.4 and Section 6.3.5, where their protocols and headline results are tabulated. Specific to the reasoning problems above are BAL [agarwal2010bundle], which standardizes large bundle-adjustment problems for solver evaluation; the Active Vision Dataset [Johns2016AVD], ScanNet [dai2017scannet], and HM3D [Ramakrishnan2021HM3D] for next-best-view, coverage, and exploration protocols; Cornell [Jiang2011Cornell], Jacquard [Depierre2018Jacquard], and GraspNet-1Billion [Fang2020GraspNet] for grasp quality (rectangle labels, simulated grasp trials, and dense 6-DoF annotations with seen / unseen / novel splits respectively), with the YCB object set [Calli2015YCB] as the shared physical test set; and MoveIt [Cohen2012MoveIt], whose reachability tooling is the de facto harness for inverse kinematics and motion-planning evaluation.

7.1.1.4 Challenges and Trends

The formulations above assume exact geometry, and real sensing is noisy, incomplete, and subject to calibration drift [Sturm2012TUMRGBD, Burri2016EuRoC]; bundle adjustment [agarwal2010bundle] and reachability analysis scale poorly with problem size; many methods fail near singularities or degenerate feature configurations [Nakamura1986IKSingularity, Hartley1997EightPoint]; the frameworks are strongest for static rigid bodies and approximate deformable and human-centric geometry [SicilianoKhatib2016]; and evaluation is concentrated on a few canonical datasets and manipulators, which limits cross-domain comparison.

The response has been to keep the geometry and wrap it in probabilistic or learned machinery: factor-graph SLAM and robust bundle adjustment attach uncertainty to the symbolic model (Section 6.3.5); learned correspondence priors are refined by RANSAC [Fischler1981RANSAC]; and the long-term benchmarks [wenzel2021seasons, Sattler2018Benchmarking] push the same pipelines toward continual adaptation under changing conditions.

7.1.2 Physical Reasoning

Physically-aware spatial reasoning predicts how a spatial configuration evolves under physical law: rigid-body dynamics, contact and friction, and the conditions for static stability. Will a grasp hold? How will an object move when pushed? Will a stack of blocks stand or fall? Answering these from a model of mechanics, rather than from observed correlations, is what lets a robot anticipate the outcome of an interaction before committing to it; Figure 7.2 shows the three canonical cases.

7.1.2.1 Task Definition

Let the environment at time tt be the state

𝐬t=(𝐪t,𝐯t,θ),\mathbf{s}_{t}=(\mathbf{q}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t},\theta), (7.9)

with generalized coordinates 𝐪t∈ℝn\mathbf{q}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, velocities 𝐯t=𝐪˙t\mathbf{v}_{t}=\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{t}, and physical parameters θ\theta (masses and inertias in the mass matrix M⁢(𝐪)M(\mathbf{q}), friction coefficients {μk}\{\mu_{k}\}, restitution, geometry). An action 𝐮t\mathbf{u}_{t} (a push, a grasp) enters as a generalized force 𝝉ext,t+1\bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{ext},t+1}, and the next state follows from a contact-implicit time-stepping update:

M⁢(𝐪t)⁢𝐯t+1−𝐯tΔ⁢t+𝐡⁢(𝐪t,𝐯t+1)\displaystyle M(\mathbf{q}_{t})\,\frac{\mathbf{v}_{t+1}-\mathbf{v}_{t}}{\Delta t% }+\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q}_{t},\mathbf{v}_{t+1}) =𝝉ext,t+1+∑k=1K(Jn,k⊤⁢λn,k+Jt,k⊤⁢𝝀t,k),\displaystyle=\bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{ext},t+1}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big{(}J_{n,k}^{\top}% \lambda_{n,k}+J_{t,k}^{\top}\bm{\lambda}_{t,k}\Big{)}, (7.10)
𝐪t+1\displaystyle\mathbf{q}_{t+1} =𝐪t+Δ⁢t⁢𝐯t+1,\displaystyle=\mathbf{q}_{t}+\Delta t\,\mathbf{v}_{t+1},

where 𝐡\mathbf{h} collects Coriolis, centrifugal, and gravitational terms, and for each potential contact kk with gap function ϕk⁢(𝐪)\phi_{k}(\mathbf{q}) and Jacobians Jn,k,Jt,kJ_{n,k},J_{t,k} the normal and tangential contact forces satisfy non-penetration, complementarity, and Coulomb friction:

ϕk⁢(𝐪t+1)≥0,λn,k\displaystyle\phi_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{t+1})\geq 0,\quad\lambda_{n,k} ≥0,λn,k⁢ϕk⁢(𝐪t+1)=0,\displaystyle\geq 0,\quad\lambda_{n,k}\,\phi_{k}(\mathbf{q}_{t+1})=0, (7.11)
‖𝝀t,k‖\displaystyle\|\bm{\lambda}_{t,k}\| ≤μk⁢λn,k.\displaystyle\leq\mu_{k}\,\lambda_{n,k}.

Physical reasoning is the computation, or approximation, of this transition 𝐬t+1=𝒯⁢(𝐬t,𝐮t)\mathbf{s}_{t+1}=\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{s}_{t},\mathbf{u}_{t}) and of the queries derived from it (stability, collision, reachability). When motion is slow enough that inertial terms vanish, the quasi-static form

∑k=1K(Jn,k⊤⁢λn,k+Jt,k⊤⁢𝝀t,k)+𝝉ext−𝐡⁢(𝐪,𝟎)≈𝟎,‖𝝀t,k‖≤μk⁢λn,k,\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big{(}J_{n,k}^{\top}\lambda_{n,k}+J_{t,k}^{\top}\bm{\lambda}_{t% ,k}\Big{)}+\bm{\tau}_{\mathrm{ext}}-\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{0})\approx% \mathbf{0},\qquad\|\bm{\lambda}_{t,k}\|\leq\mu_{k}\,\lambda_{n,k}, (7.12)

reduces reasoning to an equilibrium feasibility test, which is the setting of the classical analytic models of grasping, pushing, and stacking.

7.1.2.2 Methodology

Model-based physical reasoning is carried out either numerically, in a physics engine that integrates the dynamics above, or analytically, with closed-form criteria for the quasi-static cases. Both rest on the same Newtonian foundation and differ in whether fidelity or interpretability is the priority.

Physics Engines.

MuJoCo [todorov2012mujoco], Bullet [coumans2021], ODE, and DART [DART2023] integrate rigid-body dynamics with contact by time stepping, and they resolve contact in one of two ways. Penalty methods treat a contact as a compliant spring-damper that resists interpenetration,

fn,k=max⁡(0,kp⁢δk+kd⁢δ˙k),f_{n,k}=\max\!\left(0,k_{p}\,\delta_{k}+k_{d}\,\dot{\delta}_{k}\right), (7.13)

with penetration depth δk\delta_{k}, stiffness kpk_{p}, and damping kdk_{d}, and regularize friction similarly; they are cheap and simple, but stiff parameters destabilize the integration and soft ones introduce artificial compliance, which is acceptable in graphics and approximate planning but not in control. Constraint-based methods enforce Eq. (7.11) directly as complementarity constraints [trinkle1997dynamic], solved per step as a linear or nonlinear complementarity problem [cottle2009linear], a convex quadratic program [lin1987iterative], or a second-order cone program for exact friction cones [alizadeh2003second] (projected Gauss–Seidel and sequential-impulse schemes are the usual implementations). They give physically consistent, nearly penetration-free contact forces at higher cost and with harder scaling in the number of contacts, so engines in practice hybridize: hard constraints on normal forces, regularized tangential friction, warm starting, contact aggregation, and stabilization terms.

Analytic Quasi-Static Models.

For the three settings of Figure 7.2, closed-form criteria replace simulation. At a point contact the admissible forces form the friction cone

ℱk={(fn,k,𝐟t,k)∣fn,k≥0,‖𝐟t,k‖≤μk⁢fn,k},\mathcal{F}_{k}=\{(f_{n,k},\mathbf{f}_{t,k})\mid f_{n,k}\geq 0,\ \|\mathbf{f}_% {t,k}\|\leq\mu_{k}f_{n,k}\}, (7.14)

which a polyhedral approximation turns into linear constraints. Mapping each contact’s cone through its moment arm into wrench space and taking the convex hull gives the grasp wrench space, and the grasp is force-closed when the origin lies strictly inside it, Eq. (7.8) [bicchi2000robotic]; form closure is the stronger, purely geometric condition in which contact geometry alone prevents motion, and the Ferrari–Canny ϵ\epsilon-metric (the distance from the origin to the hull boundary) grades grasp quality. For planar pushing the limit surface relates the applied wrench to the resulting slip, and its ellipsoidal approximation yields a motion cone of object velocities reachable from a given push, the basis of stable pushing and closed-loop push planning. For stacking, stability under gravity requires that the gravitational wrench be balanced by the supporting contacts [groth2018shapestacks]: without friction, the center of mass must project into the support polygon; with friction, the contacts’ friction cones must generate a wrench cone containing the negative of the gravitational wrench.

7.1.2.3 Benchmarks

PHYRE [bakhtin2019phyre] poses 2D physics puzzles in which an object must be placed so that simulated physics reaches a goal, scored by the log-weighted area under the success-rate curve as the attempt budget increases (AUCCESS) within and across puzzle templates; ShapeStacks [groth2018shapestacks] labels 3D stacks as stable or unstable; PlasticineLab [huang2021plasticinelab] is a differentiable-physics suite for deformable manipulation; and the video suites IntPhys [riochet2018intphys], CLEVRER [Yi2020CLEVRER], and Physion [Bear2021Physion] test prediction and counterfactual judgment of physical outcomes, with ComPhy [chen2022comphy] asking for hidden properties such as mass to be inferred from motion. Grasp quality under quasi-static analysis is evaluated on the grasping benchmarks of §7.1.1 (Cornell, YCB, GraspNet-1Billion). Metrics are predictive: position or trajectory error against the simulated outcome, success rate (stable stack, successful push or grasp), binary stability accuracy, and physical-plausibility terms such as momentum conservation and constraint violation.

7.1.2.4 Challenges and Trends

The parameters that matter most, mass, friction, elasticity, internal stability, are rarely observable. They must be inferred from interaction, from how far an object moves when pushed or how it responds to a collision; ComPhy [chen2022comphy] tests exactly this, and most methods still either assume the parameters known, as classical simulation does, or approximate them in ways that fail outside the lab. Latent-dynamics learning [battaglia2016interaction] and system identification [an1985estimation, muralidhar2020phynet] are the two established routes.

The simulation-to-reality gap is the second limit. Small errors in restitution, micro-contact behavior, or unmodeled environmental factors compound once a policy leaves the engine, and fidelity trades against speed: high-fidelity simulation is too slow for large-scale training or real-time control, lightweight approximation too inaccurate. Hybrid physics-plus-learning models, domain adaptation between simulated and real dynamics, and uncertainty-aware transfer each address one side of this trade-off; none closes it.

Perception is the third. Geometry, material, and object state come from noisy, incomplete sensing, and a small error in shape, pose, or contact location propagates into a large error in predicted force or stability. Systems that couple vision to a physics engine, Galileo [wu2015galileo] and PhyNet [muralidhar2020phynet] among them, show that physical priors improve perception and that physical consistency can constrain it in return, but end-to-end pipelines in which the two regularize each other remain the exception.

7.1.3 Topological and Graph-based Reasoning

Topological and graph-based reasoning replaces continuous geometry with discrete connectivity, so that path planning, exploration, and coordination become combinatorial search over nodes and edges: places, corridors, and routes rather than metric trajectories. The abstraction is what makes large-scale, dynamic, or partially known environments tractable, where maintaining globally consistent geometry is hard but connectivity and reachability are stable. Figure 7.3 gives the abstract formulation.

7.1.3.1 Task Definition

Given a configuration space 𝒞\mathcal{C} with free subset 𝒞free⊆𝒞\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{free}}\subseteq\mathcal{C} (known a priori or inferred online from sensor streams), robot constraints, and optional priors such as floor plans or road networks, most methods build a planning graph G=(V,E,𝐰)G=(V,E,\mathbf{w}) in which vertices VV are places, sampled configurations, or abstract states, edges EE are feasible transitions, and 𝐰:E→ℝ≥0\mathbf{w}:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} assigns metric or semantic costs (distance, time, energy, risk); in some methods the graph is implicit and expanded locally during search. The output is a collision-free path π=⟨v0=s,…,vk=g⟩\pi=\langle v_{0}=s,\dots,v_{k}=g\rangle of minimal accumulated cost, a topological map of place connectivity (often linked to local metric submaps), or, with several agents, conflict-free trajectories {πi⁢(t)}i=1N\{\pi_{i}(t)\}_{i=1}^{N} that minimize makespan or total cost under vertex and edge conflict constraints.

7.1.3.2 Methodology
Visibility and Line-of-Sight Graphs.

Connecting configurations that can see each other reduces shortest-path planning to graph search with interpretable waypoints. The visibility graph of Lozano-Pérez and Wesley [LozanoPerez1979Visibility] links obstacle, start, and goal vertices and recovers exact Euclidean shortest paths in polygonal environments by Dijkstra or A*; the configuration-space construction via Minkowski sums [LozanoPerez1983Cspace] extends it to robots of finite size by growing the obstacles instead of shrinking the robot; continuous-Dijkstra algorithms settle the complexity at O⁢(n⁢log⁡n)O(n\log n) [Hershberger1999EuclideanShortest, Mitchell2000Handbook]. Grid planners bring line-of-sight into the search itself: Field D* interpolates across cell faces for smooth, replannable paths [Ferguson2006FieldD], Theta* updates parents by visibility to produce near-Euclidean paths on the fly [Nash2007Theta], and Jump Point Search prunes symmetric grid paths by jumping to points where successor choices change [Harabor2011JPS].

Clearance-Oriented Skeletons.

Where safety matters more than length, free space is retracted to a skeleton that keeps connectivity and maximizes distance to obstacles. Voronoi diagrams and medial axes give maximal-clearance paths, with Fortune’s sweepline [Fortune1987Voronoi] for efficient planar construction; the generalized and hierarchical Voronoi graphs [Choset2000HGVG, Choset2000GVGExploration] let a robot follow ridges with its sensors and build the clearance roadmap incrementally while detecting junctions and loops; and distance-transform updates [Felzenszwalb2012EDT, Lau2013DynamicEDT] maintain the skeleton in dynamic environments for real-time replanning.

Decomposition Graphs and Coverage.

Discretizing space into cells trades geometric fidelity for simplicity and completeness. Occupancy grids [Moravec1985SonarMaps, Elfes1989Occupancy] are probabilistic cell maps updated from range data on which planning is grid search; exact decompositions serve coverage, with boustrophedon decomposition [Choset1998Boustro] partitioning free space into monotone cells and ordering them through an adjacency graph for complete, low-redundancy sweeps; and the coverage literature is systematized in [Galceran2013CoverageSurvey].

Sampling-Based Roadmaps and Trees.

In high-dimensional configuration spaces, the graph is discovered by sampling. Probabilistic roadmaps [Kavraki1996PRM] sample and connect configurations in a preprocessing phase amortized over many queries and are probabilistically complete; RRT and RRT-Connect [LaValle1998RRT, Kuffner2000RRTConnect] grow trees toward unexplored regions for single-query planning under kinematic and kinodynamic constraints; PRM* and RRT* [Karaman2011RRTStar] add connection-radius and rewiring rules that make them asymptotically optimal; and FMT* [Janson2015FMT] performs lazy dynamic programming over a batch of samples, while BIT* [Gammell2015BIT] combines heuristic search with progressively denser sample batches for anytime improvement.

Optimal, Any-Angle, and Incremental Graph Search.

On a given graph, Dijkstra’s algorithm and A* [Dijkstra1959, Hart1968Astar] are the optimal single-source and heuristic searches; LPA* [Koenig2004LPA] and D* Lite [Koenig2002DstarLite] repair a shortest path incrementally as edge costs change; and the any-angle planners above (Field D*, Theta*) improve path quality, while JPS accelerates optimal search on its underlying grid.

Multi-Agent and Hierarchical Graph Reasoning.

With several agents on one graph, coordination is search over a time-expanded network. Conflict-Based Search [Sharon2015CBS] splits the problem into a high-level search over conflict constraints and low-level single-agent planning and is complete and optimal; ICTS [Sharon2013ICTS] searches joint cost allocations backed by individual searches; ECBS and EECBS [Barer2014ECBS, Li2021EECBS] are bounded-suboptimal with focal heuristics and better conflict handling; and SAT or ILP compilations [Surynek2016SATMAPF, Yu2016OptimalMAPF] reach global optimality on moderate fleets at the cost of solver scalability. Hierarchical and multi-resolution planning [Botea2004HPA] and contraction hierarchies [Geisberger2008CH] precompute abstraction layers that answer shortest-path queries on continental road networks in well under a millisecond, with standardized maps and instances [Sturtevant2012Benchmarks, MovingAI2025] for comparison.

7.1.3.3 Benchmarks

The MovingAI suite [Sturtevant2012Benchmarks, MovingAI2025] supplies standardized 2D maps from games, cities, and synthetic generators for single-agent search (path cost, runtime, memory, node expansions) and the MAPF instances on which CBS, ICTS, ECBS, and compilation-based solvers are compared by makespan, sum of costs, and success under time and memory limits, with the ICAPS MAPF tracker [Stern2019MAPFsurvey] as the community leaderboard. OMPL’s Planner Arena [OMPL2025] compares PRM, RRT, FMT, and BIT variants on success rate, planning time, path quality, and anytime behavior, and the DIMACS shortest-path challenge [DIMACS2025] evaluates query latency, preprocessing cost, and optimality on continental road graphs. Topological mapping and pose-graph SLAM are stressed by place recognition under appearance change: RADISH [radish2003] provides classic multi-sensor logs, and Oxford RobotCar [Maddern2017RobotCar], NCLT [Carlevaris2016NCLT], and Nordland [olid2018singleviewplace] span seasons and weather, with KITTI and EuRoC (Section 6.2.4) for urban and indoor pose graphs.

7.1.3.4 Challenges and Trends

Graph density sets the trade-off: sparse graphs lose connectivity or optimality, dense ones lose real-time response, and the problem sharpens in high-dimensional and lifelong settings [Karaman2011RRTStar, Koenig2002DstarLite]. Perceptual aliasing, drifting pose graphs, and dynamic obstacles complicate planning under partial information [Thrun2005Probabilistic, Stachniss2006Mapping], and on the topological SLAM benchmarks the binding difficulty is not search but appearance robustness, with cross-season and cross-weather queries far harder than same-condition retrieval. Multi-agent coordination strains conflict resolution and time-expanded representations as fleets grow, while fairness and deadlock avoidance must be kept [Sharon2015CBS, Yu2016OptimalMAPF, Stern2019MAPFsurvey].

The directions are structured rather than end-to-end: hierarchical and multi-resolution planning that abstracts and refines [Botea2004HPA, Geisberger2008CH], risk-aware and formally verified planning under uncertainty [Luders2010ChanceConstraints, zhang2023safety], bounded-suboptimal and distributed coordination for responsiveness [Barer2014ECBS, Li2021EECBS], and neuro-symbolic methods that enrich the graph with learned perception, heuristics, and semantics [kimura-etal-2021-neuro].

7.1.4 Constraint-based Spatial Solving

Many robotics problems are not about finding a plan but one that must satisfy strict requirements: no collisions, no joint-limit violations, stable contacts, correct timing, sometimes guaranteed dynamics or safety margins. Constraint-based spatial solving states the problem as a collection of constraints, what must hold and what must not, and hands it to a solver that either returns a satisfying solution or proves that none exists. Compared with sampling- and heuristic-driven planning, this buys certificates of feasibility, an explanation of why a candidate fails, and, under an explicit model, optimality or bounded-suboptimality guarantees, which is what manipulation in clutter, multi-robot coordination in shared space, and assembly demand. Figure 7.4 gives the abstract formulation.

7.1.4.1 Task Definition

Let x=(𝐪1:T,𝐮1:T,𝐳)x=(\mathbf{q}_{1:T},\mathbf{u}_{1:T},\mathbf{z}) collect continuous states and controls together with discrete mode and logic variables 𝐳\mathbf{z}. Constraint-based solving seeks

find ⁢x∈𝒳s.t.gi⁢(x)≤0,hj⁢(x)=0,ϕ⁢(𝐳,x)=⊤,\text{find }x\in\mathcal{X}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad g_{i}(x)\leq 0,\ \ h_{j}(x)=0% ,\ \ \phi(\mathbf{z},x)=\top, (7.15)

where the inequalities gig_{i} encode geometric and dynamic feasibility (collision, joint, and dynamics limits), the equalities hjh_{j} encode kinematics and contact conditions, and ϕ\phi encodes task logic such as preconditions and effects. The optimization variant minimizes an objective f⁢(x)f(x) as well. The output is a feasible xx (a collision-free and dynamically admissible trajectory, a task-robot schedule, an assembly sequence), with an objective value or optimality gap when optimizing, or a certificate that no such xx exists.

7.1.4.2 Methodology

The solver families differ in the variables and constraints they handle and the guarantees they return; practical systems are rarely pure, combining discrete reasoning over actions and modes with continuous optimization over motions and contacts, and calling fast geometric oracles (collision checking, inverse kinematics) inside the solver loop.

Constraint Programming (CSP/CP).

When the decisions are combinatorial (which object, which placement, which grasp) but each must pass a geometric test, constraint programming encodes the choices as variables under constraints and interleaves symbolic branching with propagation, pruning, and geometric checks. Lozano-Pérez and Kaelbling [LozanoPerez2014ConstraintTAMP] cast task-and-motion planning as constraint satisfaction over action skeletons, pruning symbolic branches as soon as a geometric feasibility test fails; Lagriffoul et al. [Lagriffoul2012ConstraintPropagation] propagate and filter continuous domains before any expensive collision or IK call, so that many failures become cheap inconsistencies; and Dantam et al. [Dantam2018IncrementalTAMP] interleave discrete search with incremental feasibility queries that reuse information across related constraints.

SAT/SMT Compilations.

Compiling planning and feasibility into Boolean formulas, or into formulas over richer theories such as real arithmetic, puts clause learning, incremental solving, and conflict-driven pruning to work. dReal [Gao2013dReal] decides nonlinear real arithmetic up to a numerical tolerance (δ\delta-completeness), which gives certified answers where exact decidability is impossible; SMT-based planning for hybrid systems [Shoukry2016SMTPlanning] reasons first over an abstraction and adds constraints as counterexamples appear; SAT encodings of multi-agent pathfinding [Surynek2016SATMAPF] obtain optimal schedules on time-expanded graphs (the MAPF problem itself is treated in §7.1.3); and SMT over linear real arithmetic extends the encodings to continuous time and to robustness against execution delays [Kolarik2023MAPFSMT, Tan2024RobustMAPF].

Mixed-Integer Formulations (MICP/MILP).

When discrete mode choices (which region, which contact mode, which precondition) interact with continuous geometry and dynamics, binary variables encode the nonconvex choice and convex constraints capture feasibility within a mode. IRIS [Deits2014IRIS] inflates large convex obstacle-free regions that serve as certified safe sets, turning collision avoidance into membership constraints with explicit margins; Graphs of Convex Sets [Marcucci2024GCSShortest] compile motion planning through clutter into a shortest-path problem over convex nodes and edges that convex optimization, with mixed-integer selection where needed, solves with certificates; and later work constructs convex sets directly in configuration space and in space-time [Marcucci2023SciRobotics, Dai2024CIRIS]. In each case a globally nonconvex feasibility problem is replaced by a sequence of convex ones without giving up the guarantee.

Trajectory Optimization.

Even with the task fixed, an executable motion must satisfy kinematic limits, collision avoidance, smoothness, and often dynamics, which is a continuous, usually nonconvex, constrained optimization whose local optimum comes with optimality conditions and sensitivities. CHOMP [Zucker2013CHOMP] deforms an initial path by functional gradient descent on a signed-distance field; STOMP [Kalakrishnan2011STOMP] replaces the gradient with stochastic perturbations to handle non-smooth costs and local minima; TrajOpt [Schulman2014TrajOpt] solves a sequence of convex programs with hinge-loss collision penalties; and GPMP2 [Mukadam2018GPMP2] writes planning as inference on a sparse factor graph with Gaussian-process priors, which gives scalability and incremental replanning. Increasingly these optimizers run inside the safe sets of IRIS and GCS, which supply initialization, constrain the search, or verify the result.

Inverse Kinematics as a Constraint Subproblem.

“Is there a joint configuration that reaches this pose under limits and collisions?” is the most frequent feasibility query in any hybrid planner, so IK solvers are built as fast oracles. IKFast [Diankov2010IKFast] derives closed-form solutions and generates optimized code for repeated real-time queries; TRAC-IK [Beeson2015TRACIK] combines complementary numerical strategies to raise the solve rate and avoid stalling the planner above it; and global IK by mixed-integer programming [Dai2019GlobalIK] returns certifiable solutions for full chains when a feasibility proof is needed.

Hybrid Logic–Geometric Planning.

In long-horizon problems the discrete decision (what to do next) and the continuous one (how to do it) cannot be separated, and task-and-motion planners close the loop between them. Logic-Geometric Programming [toussaint2015lgp, Toussaint2017LGPcoop] couples symbolic action sequences to bound-constrained nonlinear programs through a multi-bound tree search, so that continuous feasibility and cost decide which symbolic branches are worth expanding; PDDLStream [garrett2020pddlstream] integrates black-box geometric generators (grasps, placements, motions) into symbolic planning by optimistic refinement, requesting continuous witnesses only when needed while remaining complete under suitable stream assumptions; R-LGP [Ly2023RLGP] biases the search with reachability guidance; and COAST [Vu2024COAST] uses constraints to communicate between task planner and stream generators, cutting wasted geometric proposals by an order of magnitude in planning time.

7.1.4.3 Benchmarks

Evaluation asks whether a method returns solutions that satisfy strict feasibility conditions and, increasingly, whether it can show that it did (margins, certificates, optimality gaps) under a comparable oracle budget of collision checks and IK calls. OMPL’s benchmark suite and Planner Arena [Sucan2012OMPL] score planners on standardized problems with feasibility diagnostics and solution cost; the platform-independent TAMP benchmarks of Lagriffoul et al. [Lagriffoul2018TAMPBench] specify symbolic operators together with IK and collision feasibility so that a jointly feasible task-motion plan is required; and the assembly benchmarks RAMP [Collins2023RAMP] (real-world assemblies requiring geometric fit, stability under gravity, and grasp or fixture feasibility), ASAP [Tian2024ASAP] (large-scale 3D assembly sequences validated by physics-based feasibility checks), and FurnitureBench [Heo2023FurnitureBench] (long-horizon real-world furniture assembly scored by success rate and completion time) stress feasibility across geometry, stability, and sequencing at once. Multi-robot coordination under space-time collision constraints uses the MAPF benchmarks of §7.1.3.

7.1.4.4 Challenges and Trends

The central difficulty is integrating a discrete task structure with continuous, highly nonconvex feasibility at scale and with certificates. Task-level choices (modes, grasps, placements, contact sets, schedules) interact combinatorially with geometric and dynamic constraints and fragment the feasible set; mixed-integer formulations grow expensive with the number of binary decisions [Deits2014IRIS, Marcucci2023SciRobotics], trajectory optimizers return locally feasible motions that may violate a symbolic assumption such as the intended contact mode [Zucker2013CHOMP, Schulman2014TrajOpt], and symbolic planners propose sequences that are geometrically unrealizable. Information flows poorly in both directions: continuous solvers rarely return explanations (active sets, separating hyperplanes, unsatisfiable cores) that the symbolic layer could use to prune, and symbolic abstractions are often too coarse to keep the continuous subproblems tractable [garrett2020pddlstream, toussaint2015lgp]. On the hybrid and assembly benchmarks this coupling, not raw search speed, is what separates planners: those that interleave symbolic branching with continuous oracles waste fewer feasibility checks and degrade more gracefully across domains.

Assurance under uncertainty is the second difficulty. Real systems need machine-checkable feasibility and fast infeasibility proofs, but nonlinear dynamics, contact, and hybrid interactions make strong certificates hard; convex surrogates and bounded-horizon relaxations buy speed at the price of completeness or tightness; execution requires real-time replanning with expensive oracles in the loop; and robustness to noise and model error calls for explicit risk and temporal-logic constraints [Blackmore2011ChanceConstraints, Raman2014STL, Ames2019CBF]. Evaluations still under-report certificate quality, oracle counts, and failure explanations.

The trend is toward structure with certificates: graphs of convex or geodesically convex safe sets that reduce global nonconvex feasibility to sequences of convex subproblems with explicit proofs [Marcucci2024GCSShortest, Dai2024CIRIS], coupled to trajectory-optimization and MPC back-ends that return sensitivities and constraint activations for the search above them; chance constraints, temporal logic, and control barrier functions for persistent safety [Blackmore2011ChanceConstraints, Ames2019CBF]; GPU acceleration for real-time replanning; and learning that guides branching, cutting, or warm starts without discarding the guarantee [Ly2023RLGP, Vu2024COAST].

7.1.5 Rule-based and Programmatic Reasoning

Rule-based and programmatic reasoning is the explicit, human-auditable layer that decides when an action is allowed, in what order actions happen, and what to do next when conditions change, using symbolic operators, transition rules, or program-like control structures. In a robot it is the supervisory layer that sequences reusable skills (navigate, grasp, insert) and invokes geometric solvers or learned policies only when their preconditions hold, which is what makes a decision explainable (why the detour when the corridor was blocked), verifiable, and able to carry commonsense and safety constraints through a long task. Figure 7.5 gives the abstract formulation.

7.1.5.1 Task Definition

A symbolic planning problem is a tuple Π=⟨𝒮,𝒜,s0,G⟩\Pi=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},s_{0},G\rangle with symbolic states 𝒮\mathcal{S}, an operator library 𝒜\mathcal{A}, an initial state s0s_{0}, and a goal GG; each operator a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} carries a precondition and effects,

a=(pre⁢(a),eff+⁢(a),eff−⁢(a)),s′=(s∖eff−⁢(a))∪eff+⁢(a),a=\big{(}\mathrm{pre}(a),\ \mathrm{eff}^{+}(a),\ \mathrm{eff}^{-}(a)\big{)},% \qquad s^{\prime}=\big{(}s\setminus\mathrm{eff}^{-}(a)\big{)}\cup\mathrm{eff}^% {+}(a), (7.16)

and is applicable in ss iff pre⁢(a)⊆s\mathrm{pre}(a)\subseteq s. The planning output is a sequence π=⟨a1,…,ak⟩\pi=\langle a_{1},\dots,a_{k}\rangle whose successive application to s0s_{0} reaches a state satisfying GG; the reactive variant instead returns a policy μ\mu that maps the current observation and symbolic state to a behavior. Depending on the formalism, the inputs also carry resources, temporal constraints, and exogenous events.

7.1.5.2 Methodology

The formalisms split by whether they plan (search for a correct sequence before acting) or react (choose a behavior continually at run time); deployed systems usually do both, with a planner proposing the sequence and an execution structure (FSM, behavior tree, rule engine) monitoring conditions and triggering recovery.

Classical Symbolic Planning (STRIPS/PDDL and Heuristic Search).

STRIPS [Fikes1971STRIPS] fixed the representation: planning as search over symbolic states with action schemas, so that a plan can be checked against the model and the continuous motion layer sits behind a clean abstraction boundary. PDDL [McDermott1998PDDL] standardized domain and problem specification so that planners could be compared across navigation, logistics, and assembly, with extensions (ADL, numeric fluents, temporal constructs) that capture robotic requirements without abandoning explicit semantics. Graphplan [Blum1997PlanningGraph] builds a planning graph whose mutual-exclusion constraints prune incompatible action combinations early, and FF [Hoffmann2001FF] made forward search fast with relaxed-plan heuristics that ignore delete effects, which capture ordering constraints such as unstacking before stacking in object-rich domains. Task-and-motion planning (§7.1.4) extends these planners with geometric feasibility checks [Kaelbling2011HierarchicalNow, Garrett2021TAMPReview, Zhao2024TAMPsurvey]; the common pattern is to keep the symbolic reasoning explicit, delegate feasibility to motion and IK solvers, and wrap the plan in an execution structure with monitors and recovery.

Finite-State Machines and Reactive Mode Switching.

An FSM switches among a few well-defined behaviors (navigate, align, grasp) with explicit transition guards, which makes it transparent and fast but prone to state explosion as contingencies multiply. Statecharts [Harel1987Statecharts] add hierarchy and concurrency, so that complex controllers are nested reusable submachines with precise semantics; Brooks’ subsumption architecture [Brooks1986Subsumption] layers behaviors so that higher ones override lower ones, a blueprint for composing navigation and avoidance without global planning, systematized as behavior-based robotics [Arkin1998BehaviorBased]; teleo-reactive programs [Nilsson1994TeleoReactive] evaluate conditions continuously and fire the highest-priority satisfied rule; and ROS tooling such as FlexBE [conner2023flexbe] provides hierarchical, event-driven state machines at deployment scale.

Behavior Trees.

A behavior tree re-evaluates its conditions on every tick and chooses among structured alternatives (sequence, fallback, parallel), so that long-horizon execution survives disturbances without committing to one fixed sequence; subtrees encapsulate reusable routines, guards and fallbacks trigger immediate recovery, and the composition semantics fit perception and motion skills. BTs originated in game AI [Isla2005Halo2]; Marzinotto et al. [Marzinotto2014BT] formalized their semantics and their relation to other switching structures, and Colledanchise and Ögren [Colledanchise2017BT, Colledanchise2018BTbook] showed which compositions preserve safety and robustness and consolidated the design principles. Compiling or wrapping a symbolic plan into a BT keeps the nominal task structure while exposing runtime guards and recovery branches [mart2021behaviourtree]; ARIAC systems pair PDDL planning with BT execution monitors to handle failures, occlusions, and defective parts [liu2024autonomous]; and event-driven BTs [Agis2020EDBT] react to non-periodic stimuli rather than waiting for the next tick.

Logic-based Execution and Production Rule Systems.

A production system keeps a working memory of facts and fires forward-chaining rules when their conditions hold, which suits event-condition-action policies, mode switching, and safety enforcement (no-go zones, mutual exclusions, priorities) and depends on fast incremental matching. OPS5 [Forgy1981OPS5] set the model; the Rete algorithm [Forgy1982Rete] caches partial matches so that large rule sets update in milliseconds as facts change; CLIPS [Riley1991CLIPS] made the toolchain portable; and Soar [Laird1987Soar] integrated large rule bases with planning and execution in one architecture. In robotics, KnowRob [tenorth2013knowrob] and CRAM [beetz2010cram, beetz2023cram] join symbolic knowledge to rule-driven execution for reasoning about actions, effects, and everyday manipulation, and LTLMoP [finucane2010ltlmop] compiles temporal-logic specifications into correct-by-construction reactive controllers whose safety and sequencing constraints are explicit at the program level.

7.1.5.3 Benchmarks

The International Planning Competition supplies the canonical PDDL domains and problems across classical, temporal and numeric, probabilistic, and HTN tracks, compared by plan quality, makespan, and runtime [McDermott1998PDDL], with planning.domains [PlanningDomains] mirroring and extending the sets for reproducible evaluation. Long-horizon embodied suites test execution under partial observability and variation: BEHAVIOR-100 in iGibson and BEHAVIOR-1K in OmniGibson [Srivastava2022BEHAVIOR, li2024behavior1k] specify household activities at the predicate level, ALFRED [shridhar2020alfred] and TEACh [Padmakumar2022TEACh] score instruction-conditioned action sequences, and RoboTHOR [Deitke2020RoboTHOR] and the Habitat challenge [szot2021habitat2] pair high-level decision logic with navigation policies under SPL. ARIAC [liu2024autonomous] injects faulty parts, occlusions, and failures into kitting and assembly, and FurnitureBench [Heo2023FurnitureBench] and RoboCup@Home [Wisspeintner2009RoboCupHome] stress recovery and explainability on real tasks; qualitative solvers over RCC-8 [Randell1992RCC] and Allen relations [janhunen2019allen] are tested on consistency problems, and composite pipelines reuse the TAMP and OMPL harnesses of §7.1.4.

7.1.5.4 Challenges and Trends

The results on these benchmarks divide along the closed-world boundary. On IPC-style domains with fully specified preconditions and effects, classical planners remain strong; on long-horizon embodied tasks the limit is perception noise and grounding ambiguity rather than search, and a logically applicable action may be geometrically unrealizable because of a collision, an IK failure, or a missing grasp. Hand-authored operators, rules, and recovery logic also grow combinatorially with object count and contingency. Integrated task-and-motion planning (§7.1.4) answers the coupling problem by interleaving symbolic search with feasibility checks or compiling symbolic commitments into optimization back-ends [LozanoPerez2014ConstraintTAMP, garrett2020pddlstream, toussaint2015lgp], and hierarchical abstraction and compositional skill models contain the search while keeping it auditable [Garrett2021TAMPReview, Zhao2024TAMPsurvey].

Robustness to noise and nonstationarity is why the industrial and instruction-conditioned benchmarks reward compositions rather than single formalisms: a behavior tree around a symbolic plan makes disturbances and recoveries explicit through runtime guards, fallbacks, and safety-preserving composition [Marzinotto2014BT, Colledanchise2017BT, Colledanchise2018BTbook], and Rete-style engines [Forgy1982Rete] supply fast event-condition-action policies over streaming facts, the pattern ARIAC entries converge on [liu2024autonomous].
