Generative Feedback via Future Observations.

The most direct use of a world model is to synthesize future or counterfactual pixels and read spatial evidence off them, an analysis-by-synthesis strategy in which the reasoning outcome oo (a spatial relationship, structure, or physical property) is whatever best reproduces the observed or imagined imagery under ℙ\mathbb{P}. Predating deep generative models, Galileo [wu2015galileo] instantiates this idea with a physics engine in place of a neural simulator: it tracks object velocities across raw videos and recovers 3D shape, mass, and friction as the parameters that best reproduce the observed motion, so that the projected state proj⁡(st)\operatorname{proj}(s_{t}) is the object velocity vtv_{t} and the videos themselves define the transition distribution ℙ⁢(v0,…,vT∣c)\mathbb{P}(v_{0},\dots,v_{T}\mid c). Modern instances replace the engine with an Internet-scale image or video diffusion prior: DragAPart [li2024dragapart], Puppet-Master [li2024puppetmaster], ATOP [vora2025articulate], and DreamArt [lu2025dreamart] fine-tune such priors into articulation simulators ℙ⁢(I0,…,IT∣c)\mathbb{P}(I_{0},\dots,I_{T}\mid c) whose frames It=proj⁡(st)I_{t}=\operatorname{proj}(s_{t}) render an articulated object under a hypothesized configuration, and recover the 3D articulation (e.g., , its motion axes) by aligning the rendered hypothesis with the synthesized video. A second, inference-time use synthesizes unobserved viewpoints to resolve spatial questions that a single view underdetermines: MindJourney [yang2026mindjourney] lets a vision-language model “imagine” the scene from a new camera pose with a view-conditioned world model before answering, turning the world model into a test-time reasoning aid rather than a training-time simulator. Because such imagination is expensive and not always helpful, AVIC [yu2026avic] learns when and how much to imagine, gating world-model invocation on the sufficiency of the current visual evidence and matching or exceeding fixed-imagination strategies at a fraction of the world-model calls. Pushing imagination from a fixed sweep to an active policy, SpatialDreamer [cao2025spatialdreamer] closes the loop: a reinforcement-learned agent chooses which viewpoints to imagine through the world model and then grounds its answer in the imagined evidence, under a geometric policy-optimization objective that rewards geometrically consistent rollouts.

Generative Feedback via Future States.

Rather than decode pixels, a second line rolls the world model out in a structured or higher-dimensional state space, trading photorealism for geometric consistency. TesserAct [zhen2025tesseract] learns a 4D (3D-plus-time) world model whose rollouts stay spatially coherent enough to support robotic manipulation, and persistent-3D world models [zhou2025learning] maintain an explicit 3D memory so that revisited regions remain consistent across long horizons. State-space feedback is attractive when the downstream query is itself geometric, since it sidesteps the appearance-modeling burden that pixel rollouts carry.

Generative Feedback via Action-Conditioned Trajectories.

When the goal is to act, the world model is queried as a simulator: candidate action sequences are rolled out and scored by the favorability of the resulting states, yielding a policy π:(s≤t,a<t)↦at\pi:(s_{\leq t},a_{<t})\mapsto a_{t} that steers the episode toward a preferred terminal state sT∈Sgoods_{T}\in S_{\text{good}} (the model-based-RL view; the broader treatment of RL with spatial inductive biases is §7.2.5). The paradigm originates with Ha and Schmidhuber [ha2018world], who introduced the term “world model” in its current sense, training a generative recurrent model of future observations and using it as an internal simulator for policy search, and with Dreamer [hafner2019dreamer], which learned the simulator in a compact latent space and optimized the policy purely on imagined rollouts. Scaling this recipe, UniSim [yang2023learning] builds a video-diffusion simulator from which real-world manipulation policies can be extracted, and DreamGen [jang2025dreamgen] uses video world models as trajectory generators, pseudo-labeling the synthesized rollouts with an inverse-dynamics model to train policies that generalize to new behaviors and environments. Most recently, VAGEN [wang2025vagen] turns this feedback back onto the reasoner itself, using reinforcement learning to supervise a vision-language agent’s internal world-model reasoning: it decomposes that reasoning into state estimation (“what is the current state?”) and transition modeling (“what comes next?”) and rewards accurate latent prediction.

Latent-Representation Feedback.

A final family dispenses with generation entirely and consumes the world model’s predictive latent as the spatial signal. Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn to predict the representation of a future or masked observation rather than its pixels: I-JEPA [assran2023jepa] establishes the recipe for images, and V-JEPA 2 [assran2025vjepa] extends it to video, yielding dynamics-aware embeddings that support understanding, prediction, and planning without ever rendering a frame, while VL-JEPA [chen2025vl] ports the idea to vision-language inputs. A related line keeps the latent explicitly geometric: 3DThinker [chen20253dthinker] performs 3D mental imagery during reasoning by generating a 3D latent and aligning it with that of a 3D foundation model, letting a vision-language model reason about spatial relations from only a few views without any 3D input or explicit rendering. Because the feedback is an embedding rather than an image, latent world models avoid the appearance-synthesis cost and the pixel-space memory drift that limit generative rollouts, at the price of a signal that is harder to inspect directly; they are an increasingly prominent, query-efficient alternative for spatial reasoning.

7.3.8.3 Benchmarks

Evaluation follows the usage mode. Planning-oriented use is scored on the embodied suites of §7.3.2 and on long-horizon household environments such as ALFWorld [shridhar2020alfworld] and VirtualHome [puig2018virtualhome], where the question is whether policies extracted from imagined rollouts transfer to the real environment. Understanding-oriented use is scored on the static spatial probes that single views underdetermine, VSI-Bench [yang2025vsibench] and MindCube [yin2025spatial] among them, under test-time-scaling protocols that vary how many imagined views the reasoner is allowed and whether a verifier selects among them [jha2025probing, yu2026avic]. The world model itself is assessed on video-generation quality (FVD, FID) together with task-specific physics-consistency probes, and surveys of general world models track the field’s shift from 2D toward 3D-consistent simulation [xie2025worldsurvey], while recent analyses argue that advancing MLLM spatial reasoning demands purpose-built recipes and data rather than scale alone [zhang2025scaling]. No single benchmark currently exercises a world model along perception fidelity, action conditioning, and long-horizon spatial memory at once, a gap the challenges below make explicit.

7.3.8.4 Challenges and Trends

Reading the world model as a tool clarifies where the difficulties lie: some are inherited from the instrument itself, and are properly the concern of §8.6, while others are specific to how a reasoner queries it. The most active questions of 2025–2026 are no longer whether a world model can imagine, but whether its imagined evidence can be trusted and whether consulting it is worth the cost.

Imagination is not a free lunch. Systematic probes report that world-model imagination improves spatial reasoning in only a minority of cases, and that adding imagined views yields non-monotonic, sometimes negative accuracy gains at steep token and latency cost [yu2026avic, jha2025probing]; the sheer amount of imagination is an unreliable proxy for accuracy [zhang2025scaling], which recasts “when and how much to imagine” as a first-class test-time-scaling problem, with adaptive gating [yu2026avic] an early answer and a predictive account of which queries need the world model still missing. Faithfulness is the companion problem: a world model can render fluent futures that are physically or relationally wrong, so likelihood under ℙ\mathbb{P} is necessary but not sufficient, and when the imagined evidence lacks fidelity verification buys little, since heuristic verifiers give limited calibration gains and an information bottleneck sets in, as a reasoner cannot recover a signal the imagination never contained [jha2025probing]. Grounding imagined evidence to the actual scene and calibrating trust in it remain open; physics-consistency objectives and geometry-grounded latents [chen20253dthinker] are partial responses.

The reasoner can be no more reliable than the simulator it queries. Even state-of-the-art models such as Genie 3 [genie3], despite markedly longer-horizon consistency, still drift in spatial memory, and consistency mechanisms [zhou2025learning, li2025vmem] narrow but do not close this gap, with hallucination and long-horizon error compounding over rollout length; raising this ceiling is the province of world-model construction (§8.6), and the reasoning methods surveyed here can only mitigate its symptoms.

The feedback forms also trade off along different axes, with no principled account of which a given query should use: pixel rollouts are inspectable but expensive and prone to appearance drift; state or 4D rollouts are geometrically consistent but require structured simulators; latent feedback is cheap but opaque; action rollouts commit early to a policy; and most systems commit to one form a priori. Extending world-model-based reasoning beyond pixels (e.g., , to forces [gillman2025force], tactile, or audio modalities) is gated by the absence of internet-scale pre-training data in those modalities.

Two shifts define the current frontier. From external tool to trained-in reasoning: rather than invoking a frozen simulator at inference time, recent work trains the reasoner’s use of the world model, whether by reinforcement learning that supervises an internal state-estimation and transition-modeling loop [wang2025vagen] or that rewards geometrically consistent active imagination [cao2025spatialdreamer], or by distilling the world model’s imagined dynamics directly into a vision-language model so that no simulator need be queried at test time [zhang2026world2vlm]. From pixels to predictive latents: the imagined branch is increasingly consumed as a latent process whose hidden states guide reasoning, rather than as a faithfully rendered video [assran2023jepa, assran2025vjepa, chen20253dthinker]. Both shifts move the field away from ever-larger, faithfully-rendered pixel simulators and toward cheaper, more trustworthy, query-efficient feedback that a reasoner can afford to consult, and can be trained to consult well.

7.4 Hybrid Spatial Reasoning

Conventional approaches to spatial reasoning exhibit fundamental limitations. Systems that rely solely on linguistic or symbolic reasoning typically lack perceptual grounding in real-world visual and physical structures (e.g., , geometry, physics, spatial continuity), making them inadequate for handling cross-view transformations, temporal evolution, or physically coherent scenarios. Conversely, purely perceptual or vision-based systems, such as those combining visual recognition with rule-based geometric reasoning, often fall short in performing high-level abstract reasoning, multi-step planning, long-term memory integration, or interactive decision-making. These limitations have motivated a growing body of work advocating for a hybrid paradigm of spatial reasoning: integrating heterogeneous modules with distinct capabilities (perception, world modeling, memory, and action) so as to jointly leverage low-level spatial and physical cues together with high-level cognitive reasoning capabilities. A perceptual or physics-informed module supplies geometry, relations, affordances, and dynamics; a symbolic or neural module plans, infers, and abstracts over them; memory and history extend the pipeline to multi-step, multi-view, and temporally extended tasks; and because no single modality, task, or dataset carries the whole system, the composition transfers across vision-only, language-only, embodied, and multimodal settings.

7.4.1 Task Definition

A hybrid spatial reasoning system is a pair ({Mi}i=1k,π)(\{M_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k},\pi): a set of kk heterogeneous modules Mi∈{Mpercept,Mworld,Msymb,Mmem,Mplan,Mact}M_{i}\in\{M_{\text{percept}},M_{\text{world}},M_{\text{symb}},M_{\text{mem}},M% _{\text{plan}},M_{\text{act}}\}, each contributing a distinct inductive bias (perception, world model, symbolic constraints, memory, planning, or action), and an orchestration function π:𝒮→{1,…,k}\pi:\mathcal{S}\to\{1,\dots,k\} that selects which module acts on the current system state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} (perception, internal map, history). Starting from the input s0=xs_{0}=x, the system evolves as

st+1=Mπ⁢(st)⁢(st),y=Read⁢(sT),s_{t+1}=M_{\pi(s_{t})}(s_{t}),\qquad y=\mathrm{Read}(s_{T}), (7.45)

and the three composition styles found in practice are special cases of Eq. (7.45): a pipeline fixes π\pi to a constant module order, an iterative system lets π\pi revisit modules until a verifier accepts, and an end-to-end system makes every MiM_{i} differentiable so that the whole trajectory is trained jointly. Hybrid spatial reasoning is the paradigm in which π\pi and the module set {Mi}\{M_{i}\} are designed together to minimize the precision-grounding asymmetry: the foundation models of §7.3 supply semantic competence, and the symbolic and learning-based components of §7.1–§7.2 supply metric precision and verifiable structure. Existing systems therefore differ along three axes: which modules they compose, how they compose them (pipeline, iterative, or end-to-end), and how the orchestration function is realized (hand-coded rules or a learned policy).

7.4.2 Methodology

Five hybridization patterns recur in the literature, distinguished by which module the foundation model is paired with and by what supplies the truth signal.

Foundation Models with Reinforcement Learning.

A prominent hybrid couples a foundation model’s semantic competence with reinforcement learning’s long-horizon decision-making, often closed by a verifier that supplies executable structure (Figure 7.29). The foundation model proposes hypotheses, sub-goals, or candidate action sequences; an RL policy πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}} commits to and executes them over extended horizons; and the resulting reward, optionally augmented by a physics engine or symbolic checker, updates both the policy and the orchestration. Embodied-R [zhao2025embodied] instantiates this division of labor: a large vision–language model handles perception, while a small language model trained by RL, with a reward that scores the logical consistency between its reasoning trace and its answer, performs the slow, deliberative spatial reasoning, evaluated on UrbanVideo-Bench and VSI-Bench. The group-relative fine-tuning recipes of §7.2.5 (Reason-RFT, OctoNav, SpaceR [tan2025reasonrft, gao2026octonav, ouyang2025spacer]) are the same hybrid with the verifier folded into a verifiable reward and are not repeated here. The foundation model contributes broad priors and RL supplies credit assignment and exploration; the cost is the sample inefficiency and reward-specification difficulty inherited from RL (§7.2.5).

Foundation Models with Explicit Physical Simulation.

A second pattern pairs the foundation model with a physics engine, so that the truth signal is a simulated trajectory rather than a learned score; the engine side is the physical reasoning of §7.1.2. The LLM proposes hypotheses, structural descriptions, or programs, the simulator executes them under conservation laws, kinematic constraints, contact dynamics, and reachability limits, and the discrepancy between simulation and observation is fed back for another round. LLMPhy [cherian2024llmphy] is the clearest instance: the LLM writes Python programs that embed estimates of latent physical parameters (friction, stiffness, mass) and of the scene layout, a physics engine executes them, and the reconstruction error against the observed video is returned as feedback, so that building the digital twin becomes a black-box optimization driven by the LLM. DiffGen [jin2024diffgen] makes the loop differentiable, generating robot demonstrations by descending gradients through a differentiable simulator, a differentiable renderer, and a vision–language model until the rendered outcome matches the language instruction in embedding space. PhysVLM [zhou2025physvlm] moves the physics into the input instead: a robot’s reachable workspace is abstracted into a robot-agnostic space-physical reachability map that the VLM consumes alongside the image, trained on Phys100K and evaluated on the EQA-phys benchmark. At the far end, ChronoLLM [wang2025chronollm] fine-tunes LLMs to write PyChrono multibody-simulation scripts, from a single pendulum to a full vehicle on deformable terrain; here the model authors the simulation rather than reasoning inside it, which places it at the boundary with the code-generation paradigm of §7.3.4. What the simulator contributes is an inductive bias that stays valid for unseen objects and configurations, so the hybrid extrapolates where a purely statistical model would not.

Foundation Models with Symbolic Reasoning.

A third pattern inserts an explicit symbolic layer (logical constraints, relational predicates, or formal planning specifications) between natural-language reasoning and executable spatial inference, replacing the hand-crafted parsers of §7.1 with foundation-model-generated symbolic structure. Two sub-patterns differ in when the symbolic machinery is used. In the first it is called at inference time: NS3D [hsu2023ns3d] has an LLM translate a 3D referring expression into a first-order logic program that a neural executor grounds against the scene’s objects and relations on ReferIt3D, and LEFT [hsu2023s] (§7.3.4) makes the same programs differentiable so that concept grounding is learned rather than hand-specified. In the second, symbolic knowledge enters only at training time as a constraint on a neural model: premsri2024neurosymbolic train language models for reasoning over spatial language with spatial logic rules as auxiliary losses, and RelateSeg [lin2025neuro] extracts relations such as ⟨cat,to-right-of,person⟩\langle\text{cat},\text{to-right-of},\text{person}\rangle from open-vocabulary segmentation outputs, writes them as first-order logic, and relaxes them with fuzzy logic into a single auxiliary loss that improves mIoU on four benchmarks without adding parameters. The Scene Language [zhang2025scenelanguage] (§8.2.5) is the representation such hybrids increasingly target: programs for structure, words for semantics, embeddings for appearance. The symbolic layer buys consistency and compositional guarantees; its price is a closed predicate vocabulary that the neural side constantly exceeds, a point taken up under Challenges and Trends below.

Foundation Models with Spatial Memory and World Models.

A fourth pattern gives the foundation model a persistent spatial state that it does not have to carry in its context window: an explicit memory (episodic trajectories, topological maps, 3D layouts) or a learned world model that predicts how the scene changes under action. The hybrid question is the interface between the two. MSNav [liu2025msnav] splits zero-shot vision-and-language navigation into a memory module, a spatial module, and a decision module, with a small fine-tuned LLM extracting the landmarks and relations the spatial module needs, and reaches state-of-the-art zero-shot results on R2R and REVERIE. MindExplore [li2025towardsvla] stacks a reasoning layer (task-specific chains of thought that emit meta-actions) over an acting layer (a mixture of policy experts with a multimodal diffusion policy) and uses a memory mechanism as the feedback channel between the two, running at 30 FPS in dynamic sand environments. The 3D spatial memories of §7.3.6 (3DSPMR [cai2025vision], Embodied-RAG [xie2024embodiedrag], Meta-Memory [mao2025meta]) and the world-model coupling of §7.3.8 are the memory- and simulator-side components these hybrids draw on; MindJourney’s test-time gain on SAT [yang2026mindjourney] (about eight points of top-1 accuracy from imagined viewpoints alone, with the VLM untouched) is the cleanest quantitative evidence that a world model used as a tool closes part of the gap. In each case the foundation model keeps high-level inference, instruction following, and semantic grounding, and offloads persistence, geometry, and dynamics to the dedicated module.

Agentic Orchestration of Hybrid Components.

The fifth pattern makes the orchestration function itself the object of design: a foundation model acts as a deliberative controller that decides, at each step, which of the perception, world-model, symbolic, memory, and action modules to invoke, within a closed perceive–reason–act–reflect loop (Figure 7.30). It differs from the agentic reasoning of §7.3.7 in what is being scheduled: there, tools and memory; here, additionally symbolic engines and physics simulators, with the scheduler π\pi of Eq. (7.45) itself a candidate for learning. VADAR [marsili2025visual] (§7.3.4) is the program-synthesis version of such a controller, generating the API it then calls. “See it. Say it. Sorted” [zhang2025seeitsayit] is a training-free version for sketch-to-diagram generation: a critic VLM proposes a few qualitative relational edits, several LLMs synthesize candidate SVG programs, and a judge VLM selects among them, which keeps global constraints such as alignment and connectivity intact where numerical estimation would drift. manh2025mindmeetspace arrive at the same module inventory from neuroscience, arguing that such a controller should sit over multimodal sensing, multisensory integration, egocentric–allocentric conversion, a cognitive map, spatial memory, and spatial reasoning. The gain is compositionality and long-horizon consistency that no static architecture provides; the cost is the latency and attribution problems discussed below.

7.4.3 Benchmarks

Hybrid systems are evaluated end to end on the benchmark of their target task rather than module by module, and the benchmark is often one the paper introduces. Among the systems above, Embodied-R reports on UrbanVideo-Bench and VSI-Bench, MindJourney on SAT, NS3D on ReferIt3D, MSNav on R2R and REVERIE, and PhysVLM on RoboVQA and OpenEQA alongside its own EQA-phys; LLMPhy ships TraySim, CLEVRER-LLMPhy, and Real-TraySim, MindExplore ships SandGo-1k and SandThink-21k, and DrawingBench [kim2025drawingbench] is built specifically for agentic hybrids, scoring an LLM’s sequence of low-level mouse actions against eight rule-based criteria for the spatial configuration it was asked to draw. Physics-side components are still checked against PHYRE and ShapeStacks (§7.1.2) and symbolic components against the constraint- and rule-based suites of §7.1.4–§7.1.5, but no current benchmark attributes an end-to-end score to the modules that produced it; that gap is taken up under Challenges and Trends below and in the cross-paradigm survey of §7.5 (Table 7.6, whose 15-row agentic subset is Table 7.5 of §7.3.7).

7.4.4 Challenges and Trends

Hybrid spatial reasoning has produced architectures that combine complementary inductive biases in principled ways, but several recurring limitations originate in the module-composition framework itself rather than in any individual module.

Frame, Scale, and Geometric Consistency. Unlike generic modular systems, spatial hybrids must reconcile heterogeneous spatial representations across modules: perception emits camera or egocentric frames, map and memory modules operate in world or allocentric coordinates, symbolic reasoners abstract to topological relations, and physics engines expect metric units. Misaligned reference frames, scales, or conventions silently corrupt downstream reasoning, and because each module reports confidence in its own terms, small upstream pose, depth, or scale errors propagate and compound across the pipeline without a coherent notion of uncertainty. Maintaining frame, scale, and geometric consistency is thus a first-order obstacle with no analogue in non-spatial hybrid systems.

Interfaces, Latency, and Attribution. The strength of a hybrid system is bounded by its worst module interface. Symbolic-to-neural translation is particularly brittle when the symbolic side uses closed-vocabulary predicates while the neural side proposes open-vocabulary ones, and the interface design becomes a hidden first-class hyperparameter that current literature seldom isolates. Each module invocation also adds wall-clock latency that compounds across a perceive–reason–act–reflect loop, so high-frequency manipulation and navigation may not be reachable through orchestration alone. And when a hybrid fails, attributing the failure to a specific module is non-trivial; this complicates iteration and is often cited as a practical reason why end-to-end models can outperform hybrid stacks on aggregate benchmarks despite offering weaker per-module guarantees.

The orchestration function π\pi is migrating from hand-coded rules to learnable orchestration policies trained with reinforcement or imitation learning, which blurs the boundary with §7.3.7. Differentiable hybrid stacks, built from differentiable physics simulators, differentiable optimization layers (§7.2.4), and differentiable retrieval, make end-to-end training of a hybrid viable and remove the historical interface penalty, offering a path through the precision–grounding asymmetry that motivates this section. Evaluation is changing too, toward the holistic and diagnostic: in response to the attribution problem, emerging practice pairs aggregate task metrics with per-module diagnostic probes and counterfactual module-swap ablations that isolate where a hybrid system succeeds or fails, a direction consolidated in the cross-paradigm benchmark survey of §7.5. z

7.5 Spatial Reasoning Benchmarks

Early spatial-reasoning benchmarks positioned the model as a detached observer. CLEVR [johnson2017clevr] and VSR [liu2023visual] ask for relative geometric relations from a static third-person viewpoint, and their 2D inputs leave depth ambiguous, a weakness that 3DSRBench [ma20253dsrbench], MMSI-Bench [yang2025mmsi], DSI-Bench [zhang2025dsi], and STI-Bench [li2025sti] now probe directly. SQA3D [ma2022sqa3d], OpenEQA [majumdar2024openeqa], and EmbSpatial-Bench [du2024embspatial] instead place the model inside the scene, so that it must self-localize before it can answer, and ScanQA [azuma2022scanqa], ScanRefer [chen2020scanrefer], and Multi3DRefer [zhang2023multi3drefer] ground queries in point clouds and RGB-D data, where the answer is a coordinate rather than a relation. The reasoning demanded has deepened in parallel: IntPhys [riochet2018intphys] and Physion [Bear2021Physion] test whether a model expects gravity, collision, and friction to hold over time, and OpenEQA and RealWorldQA [xai2024grok15v] ask functional questions (“Can I navigate through this gap?”, “Where would I find a cloth to clean a spill?”) in which geometry matters only through what it affords.

Data provenance splits the field. Simulators, the sources behind SpatialVLM [chen2024spatialvlm], AI2-THOR [kolve2017ai2thor], and Habitat [szot2021habitat2], yield unlimited, perfectly annotated data; real-world collections such as ScanNet [dai2017scannet] and OpenEQA supply the clutter, occlusion, and sensor noise that simulation does not reproduce. The resulting practice is sim-to-real: pre-train on large synthetic corpora for general spatial logic, then fine-tune on the scarcer real data. Annotated 3D data remain scarce and fine-grained metric estimation remains hard for large models; both limits recur throughout the table below.

7.5.1 Comparative Analysis

Table 7.6 compiles 61 spatial-reasoning benchmarks across four categories (physical-focused, rooted in §7.1.2; vision-based, overlapping with §7.3.1; 3D-focused, rooted in §7.3.6 and §7.3.8; and robot-environment, rooted in §7.3.7 and §7.4). A narrower 15-row subset focused specifically on agentic spatial reasoning is provided in Table 7.5 of §7.3.7; this subset filters Table 7.6 to image-and-video benchmarks that exercise agentic deployments.

A modality migration runs from the top of the table to the bottom: the physical-focused benchmarks rely on synthetic 3D renderings, the vision-based block is image- and video-heavy with growing 3D extensions, the 3D-focused block is built on point clouds and RGB-D scans, and the robot block has moved largely to 3D environments. The Perspective axis is imbalanced: a large fraction of vision-based benchmarks carry Undeclared ego/exo annotations, the physical-focused benchmarks lean exo (a third-person observer judging physical plausibility), and the robot block is entirely ego; the field is migrating from spectator-style observation to situated cognition faster than benchmark annotations record it. The Data-Source spectrum is bifurcated between predominantly synthetic or simulated (top block and robot block) and predominantly real (middle blocks), with the Real/Sim benchmarks (SpaRE, 3DSRBench, RoboSpatial, SpatialVLM, SITE) as the bridge that the sim-to-real training practice of the opening relies on.

7.5.2 Future Directions
Unified Spatial-Cognition Benchmark.

No single benchmark in Table 7.6 exercises a model along all of perception fidelity, symbolic precision, memory persistence, and long-horizon action conditioning simultaneously. A unified benchmark covering all four §7 paradigms (§7.1 rule-based, §7.2 learning-based, §7.3 foundation-model-driven, §7.4 hybrid) would close the evaluation-attribution challenge flagged under Challenges and Trends in §7.4.

Cross-Modal Evaluation.

The current axes (Modality, View, Perspective, Data Source, Task Type) under-specify the cross-modal demand of contemporary spatial reasoning. Future benchmarks should explicitly probe modality-to-modality transfer (e.g., , 2D-trained models evaluated on 3D queries; text-conditioned policies evaluated on video-grounded tasks), so that the modality-mismatch challenge flagged in §7.3.6 (text-vs.-image-vs.-3D retrieval) becomes a first-class evaluation axis rather than a per-paper case study.

Embodied Long-Horizon Coverage.

The Robot block in Table 7.6 covers navigation thoroughly but under-represents long-horizon manipulation and multi-room interactive tasks. The §7.3.7 15-row subset (Table 7.5) further restricts attention to image-and-video benchmarks; the embodied long-horizon suites ALFWorld and VirtualHome (§7.3.4) and cross-embodiment evaluation on Open X-Embodiment (§7.3.2) are the nearest existing coverage, and standardizing on them would close the long-horizon-spatiotemporal-coherence challenge flagged under Challenges and Trends in §7.3.7.

From Descriptive to Interactive Spatial Reasoning.

The Task Type column of Table 7.6 is dominated by visual question answering: the overwhelming majority of benchmarks ask a model to describe static spatial relations (“where is the object”), and only the small Robot block evaluates reasoning that is conditioned on the agent’s own actions. Yet the trajectory traced in this chapter, from passive observation to situated interaction, calls for benchmarks that test interactive spatial reasoning: predicting how an action changes the spatial state, judging affordances and reachability (“can I fit, reach, or grasp this”), and reasoning counterfactually about manipulation outcomes. Such evaluation couples the action-conditioned reasoning of §7.2.5 with the embodied hybrid pipelines of §7.4, extending the descriptive benchmarks surveyed here toward the manipulation- and affordance-grounded settings that embodied deployment ultimately demands.

7.6 Summary and Outlook

This chapter followed spatial reasoning along the spectrum on which it developed: inference over explicit geometric, physical, topological, logical, and causal models (§7.1); reasoning acquired from data (§7.2); reasoning elicited from large pre-trained models (§7.3); hybrids that combine these components (§7.4); and the benchmarks that measure them (§7.5).

Precision and grounding sit at opposite ends of the spectrum. Rule-based methods are inspectable and can certify feasibility or safety, but they assume exact, fully specified inputs and a closed vocabulary of predicates, and they break down where perception is noisy or a task falls outside the authored rules. Learning-based methods acquire spatial competence from data, yet often reach high benchmark accuracy through dataset-specific shortcuts that do not survive novel compositions (§7.2.1), and they need far more interaction than classical planners. Foundation models bring broad semantic competence, but their visual encoders retain only coarse geometry, textual reasoning mistracks coordinates over multi-step chains (§7.3.3), and vision-language-action models often interpret an instruction correctly and execute it incorrectly (§7.3.2). Hybrid systems aim to pair the semantic reach of the last family with the metric precision and verifiability of the first two.

The failures concentrate at interfaces. Across tool-augmented, memory-augmented, and hybrid reasoning, the recurring limitations arise less within any single component than where components meet: in forming a query that a memory or tool can answer, in translating between closed and open vocabularies, and in keeping coordinate frames and scales consistent across modules (§7.4).

Evaluation lags the shift toward situated reasoning. The field is moving from questions posed to a detached observer toward agents that must localize themselves, gather evidence, and act, yet no current benchmark exercises perception fidelity, symbolic precision, memory persistence, and long-horizon action together, and few attribute an end-to-end score to the components that produced it (§7.5).

Reasoning in this chapter takes the evidence of Chapter 6 as given. Chapter 8 turns to the inverse problem of producing spatial content, and its world models (§8.6) supply the simulators that world-model-based reasoning (§7.3.8) consults.

Chapter 8 Spatial Reconstruction and Generation

Spatial reconstruction and generation is the productive counterpart to spatial perception and reasoning: rather than analyzing a scene that is given, it synthesizes spatial content, recovering or creating the geometry, appearance, and dynamics of objects, scenes, and worlds from conditions such as text, images, partial observations, or explicit constraints. Where perception (Chapter 6) maps observations into structured spatial representations and reasoning (Chapter 7) draws inferences over them, generation closes the loop by mapping intent back into concrete spatial artifacts, a capability central to embodied agents, content creation, simulation, and world modeling.

The chapter is organized along an axis of increasing output structure and dimensionality, from flat images to volumetric objects and scenes, to video, embodied motion, and full four-dimensional space-time content, and finally to world models and to programmatic generation that emits interpretable, executable structure. What holds this range together is a single recurring backbone: an encoder maps conditions into a latent, a generator samples structure, and a decoder or renderer produces the final artifact, specialized to each output domain. Read this way, the subfields are less seven separate problems than one conditional-generation abstraction instantiated against progressively richer codomains.

8.1 2D Spatial Generation

The 2D spatial generation encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks that require synthesizing or editing images under explicit spatial constraints. These constraints may be user-specified (bounding boxes, masks, sketches, keypoints, depth maps) or derived from scene understanding (layout graphs, semantic maps, relational structures), and the overarching goal is to produce images that are not only visually realistic but also faithful to the specified spatial configuration: objects appearing in the correct locations, at the correct scales and orientations, while remaining globally coherent in lighting, perspective, and style. 2D generation is where the most mature semantic-to-pixel prior in contemporary AI is taught to honor spatial structure: it is the proving ground on which large pre-trained visual priors are forced to localize objects, follow geometric scaffolds, respect occlusion ordering, and obey region- or instruction-level edits, all without falling out of the implicit grammar of natural images.

The section follows the 2D pipeline in three steps that share one latent-generator framework. §8.1.1 reviews foundational text-to-image generation, the semantic-to-pixel prior on which everything else here is built, and the three paradigms (adversarial, autoregressive, and diffusion with its flow-matching generalization) that parameterize it. §8.1.2 adds a structural condition (layouts, masks, edges, depth, pose, scene graphs, region phrases) and asks how it is injected into a frozen or co-trained generator. §8.1.3 replaces the empty canvas with an existing image and a mask, so that the generator must change what lies inside the mask while preserving what lies outside it.

8.1.1 Text-to-image Generation

Text-to-image (T2I) generation synthesizes an image from a natural-language description. For the rest of this chapter its importance lies less in the images themselves than in the prior it provides: a high-capacity mapping from compositional language to the visual space of objects, surfaces, layouts, and viewpoints, learned once at web scale and then reused. The spatial controllers of §8.1.2 and the editors of §8.1.3 impose constraints on this prior rather than replacing it, and the text-to-3D pipelines of §8.2 distill it through score distillation or multi-view consistency objectives; whatever relational competence the prior has, or lacks, therefore propagates downstream. The field has passed through three architectural paradigms, from adversarial training to autoregressive token modeling to iterative denoising, with diffusion and its flow-matching generalization now setting the standard for quality and prompt fidelity [rombach2022ldm, peebles2023dit].

8.1.1.1 Task Definition

We formulate text-to-image generation in a paradigm-agnostic form that exposes the structural choices shared by modern systems. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} denote the space of tokenized text prompts and 𝒴=[0,1]H×W×3\mathcal{Y}=[0,1]^{H\times W\times 3} the pixel-space image domain. Almost all modern T2I systems operate not directly on 𝒴\mathcal{Y} but on a compressed latent space 𝒵⊂ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} provided by an autoencoder pair

E:𝒴→𝒵,D:𝒵→𝒴,D∘E≈id𝒴,E:\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z},\qquad D:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y}% ,\qquad D\!\circ\!E\approx\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{Y}}, (8.1)

where EE encodes a training image into a low-dimensional code and DD decodes a code back into a pixel image. A text encoder ϕ:𝒳→ℰ\phi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{E} maps the prompt into a conditioning embedding ϕ⁢(𝐱)∈ℰ\phi(\mathbf{x})\in\mathcal{E}. The core learning problem is then to train a conditional latent sampler

Gθ:ℰ→𝒵,𝐳^∼pθ⁢(𝐳|ϕ⁢(𝐱)),G_{\theta}:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{z}}\sim p_{% \theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}\,\big{|}\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\big{)}, (8.2)

so that, after decoding, the resulting image 𝐲^=D⁢(𝐳^)\hat{\mathbf{y}}=D(\hat{\mathbf{z}}) is both photorealistic and semantically aligned with the prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The three paradigms covered below differ chiefly in how the conditional distribution pθ⁢(𝐳∣ϕ⁢(𝐱))p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid\phi(\mathbf{x})) is parameterized and optimized; the autoencoder pair (E,D)(E,D) and the text encoder ϕ\phi are largely shared design choices across paradigms. Figure 8.1 schematizes this paradigm-agnostic pipeline and the substrate that the three paradigms share.

8.1.1.2 Methodology

Three generative paradigms, taken in the order in which each dominated T2I, parameterize the sampler GθG_{\theta} of Eq. (8.2) differently; the bottom row of Figure 8.1 draws them against the common pipeline. A second set of advances refines the sampler without redefining it: backbone evolution, sampling acceleration, and the migration of leading systems to proprietary stacks. Structural conditioning interfaces, the fourth such refinement, are the subject of §8.1.2 and are not repeated here.

Generative Adversarial Networks.

GAN-based T2I models instantiate GθG_{\theta} as a feed-forward generator Gθ⁢(𝐧,ϕ⁢(𝐱))→𝐳^G_{\theta}(\mathbf{n},\phi(\mathbf{x}))\!\to\!\hat{\mathbf{z}} driven by an auxiliary noise vector 𝐧∼𝒩⁢(0,I)\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I); the conditional distribution pθ⁢(𝐳∣ϕ⁢(𝐱))p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}\mid\phi(\mathbf{x})) is defined only implicitly, as the pushforward of 𝐧\mathbf{n} through GθG_{\theta}. Training follows the two-player game of goodfellow2014gan, pitting the generator against a discriminator DψD_{\psi},

minθ⁡maxψ⁡𝔼𝐲∼pdata⁢[log⁡Dψ⁢(𝐲,ϕ⁢(𝐱))]+𝔼𝐧⁢[log⁡(1−Dψ⁢(D⁢(Gθ⁢(𝐧,ϕ⁢(𝐱))),ϕ⁢(𝐱)))],\min_{\theta}\max_{\psi}\ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}\sim p_{\text{data}}}\!\big{[}% \log D_{\psi}(\mathbf{y},\phi(\mathbf{x}))\big{]}+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{n}}\!% \big{[}\log\!\big{(}1-D_{\psi}(D(G_{\theta}(\mathbf{n},\phi(\mathbf{x}))),\phi% (\mathbf{x}))\big{)}\big{]}, (8.3)

in which DψD_{\psi} scores both photorealism and text-image consistency. The result is sharp high-frequency detail and single-pass inference, bought at the price of unstable training and mode collapse. Within this framework, StackGAN [stackgan2017] generated a low-resolution image first and refined it with a second GAN conditioned on both the text and the coarse image; AttnGAN [attngan2018] let the generator attend to individual words while rendering different regions, with an auxiliary image-text matching loss (DAMSM) that reduced attribute errors such as wrongly colored objects; XMC-GAN [xmcgan2021] replaced that loss with cross-modal contrastive learning and improved multi-object prompts. By 2021 diffusion models had overtaken these systems on COCO, chiefly because they train stably and cover more of the image distribution, and research attention moved on; the GAN emphasis on high-frequency detail survives in hybrid and adversarially fine-tuned samplers.

Autoregressive Models.

Autoregressive (AR) models discretize the latent space: the autoencoder EE is realized as a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) whose output is a sequence of discrete tokens 𝐳=(z1,…,zN)∈𝒱N\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\dots,z_{N})\in\mathcal{V}^{N} over a learned codebook 𝒱\mathcal{V}, and GθG_{\theta} is factorized in causal raster order,

pθ⁢(𝐳|ϕ⁢(𝐱))=∏n=1Npθ⁢(zn|z<n,ϕ⁢(𝐱)),p_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}\,\big{|}\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\big{)}\;=\;\prod_{n=1% }^{N}p_{\theta}\!\big{(}z_{n}\,\big{|}\,z_{<n},\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\big{)}, (8.4)

trained by maximum likelihood on the next-token cross-entropy. T2I thus becomes sequence-to-sequence translation, and the transformer that performs it inherits the compositional competence of language models: DALL-E [dalle2021] modeled text and image tokens as a single sequence and showed zero-shot generalization across prompt types. The cost is decoding latency, one forward pass per token, which grows with resolution. Parti [parti2022] scaled the transformer to 20B parameters, generated at 256×256256\times 256, and reached 1024×10241024\times 1024 with a convolutional super-resolution stage; Muse [chang2023muse] abandoned strict sequential order for masked token prediction, filling in many tokens per step over a handful of rounds, and matched diffusion quality on several benchmarks at a fraction of the sampling time. AR generation remains attractive where images are produced jointly with text (interleaved documents, storyboards) and a single sequence model handles both.

Diffusion Models.

Diffusion models realize GθG_{\theta} as iterative denoising rather than a single feed-forward pass. A fixed forward process corrupts the clean latent 𝐳0=E⁢(𝐲)\mathbf{z}_{0}=E(\mathbf{y}) along a schedule (αt,σt)t=0T(\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t})_{t=0}^{T}, 𝐳t=αt⁢𝐳0+σt⁢ϵ\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{z}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon with ϵ∼𝒩⁢(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and 𝐳T≈𝒩⁢(0,I)\mathbf{z}_{T}\!\approx\!\mathcal{N}(0,I); a noise-prediction network ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} learns to invert it under the denoising score-matching objective

minθ⁡𝔼t,𝐳0,ϵ⁢[‖ϵ−ϵθ⁢(𝐳t,t,ϕ⁢(𝐱))‖22],\min_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{z}_{0},\epsilon}\!\left[\left\|\epsilon-% \epsilon_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}_{t},\,t,\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\big{)}\right\|% _{2}^{2}\right], (8.5)

which is the diffusion-specific realization of the training objective implicit in Eq. (8.2). At inference the model starts from 𝐳T∼𝒩⁢(0,I)\mathbf{z}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), applies ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} for t=T,…,1t=T,\dots,1, and decodes 𝐲^=D⁢(𝐳^0)\hat{\mathbf{y}}=D(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{0}); each step corrects a small error, which is why the final samples are both detailed and faithful. Running this process in the latent space of Eq. (8.1) rather than in pixels, as Latent Diffusion Models [rombach2022ldm] did (e.g., , 4×64×644\times 64\times 64 instead of 3×512×5123\times 512\times 512 for a 512px image), cut memory and compute enough to train on commodity hardware and to release Stable Diffusion openly. Conditioning the denoiser on embeddings from a pretrained language-image model, as in GLIDE [glide2022] and DALL⋅\cdotE 2 [dalle2_2022], improved prompt alignment, and classifier-free guidance [ho2022classifierfree] supplied a single knob that trades diversity against fidelity by extrapolating the conditional prediction away from the unconditional one. The remaining weakness is sampling cost, dozens of sequential network evaluations per image; higher-order ODE samplers and the distillation methods below address it. Diffusion or flow-matching cores now underlie most leading systems, with the native multimodal autoregressive stacks discussed under proprietary systems the main exception.

Flow Matching and Rectified Flow.

Rather than a fourth paradigm, flow matching is diffusion reformulated in continuous time. It parameterizes GθG_{\theta} as a learned velocity field vθ⁢(𝐳t,t,ϕ⁢(𝐱))v_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi(\mathbf{x})) instead of a noise predictor: training picks the straight interpolation 𝐳t=(1−t)⁢𝐳0+t⁢𝐳1\mathbf{z}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{z}_{0}+t\mathbf{z}_{1} between a clean latent 𝐳0=E⁢(𝐲)\mathbf{z}_{0}=E(\mathbf{y}) and a Gaussian sample 𝐳1∼𝒩⁢(0,I)\mathbf{z}_{1}\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,I) and regresses the velocity,

minθ⁡𝔼t,(𝐳0,𝐳1)⁢[‖vθ⁢(𝐳t,t,ϕ⁢(𝐱))−(𝐳1−𝐳0)‖22],\min_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{t,(\mathbf{z}_{0},\mathbf{z}_{1})}\!\left[\left\|v_% {\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi(\mathbf{x}))-(\mathbf{z}_{1}-\mathbf{z}_{0})% \right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (8.6)

and inference integrates the probability-flow ODE d⁢𝐳t/d⁢t=vθ⁢(𝐳t,t,ϕ⁢(𝐱))\mathrm{d}\mathbf{z}_{t}/\mathrm{d}t=v_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\phi(\mathbf{% x})) from t=1t=1 back to t=0t=0. The formulation was introduced concurrently by lipman2023flow (Flow Matching) and liu2023rectifiedflow (Rectified Flow); albergo2023building gave the unifying stochastic-interpolant view in which diffusion is the special case of a noisier interpolation schedule. Three consequences matter in practice. Straight-line interpolations yield nearly straight ODE trajectories, so matched quality is reached in noticeably fewer steps (genuine one-step generation still needs a reflow or distillation stage); the objective is a single regression with no noise-schedule design and no per-schedule guidance recalibration; and the loss scales smoothly with model size and resolution. Stable Diffusion 3 [sd3rft2024] scaled the recipe to T2I on a DiT-style transformer backbone and reported the best GenEval scores among open models together with favorable human preference on Parti-prompts; the Flux family followed the same recipe. Flow matching composes with every refinement below as readily as a noise-predictor core does and has become the default continuous-time formulation in 2024-onwards systems.

Backbone Evolution: From U-Net to Diffusion Transformers.

Early diffusion models used the U-Net for its multiscale feature fusion and locality bias. The Diffusion Transformer (DiT) of peebles2023dit replaced it with a stack of transformer layers over latent patch tokens, giving every denoising step a global receptive field, and showed that FID improves monotonically with depth, width, and token count along predictable scaling laws, reaching FID 2.27 on class-conditional ImageNet at 2562256^{2}. Attention cost grows quadratically with resolution, so hybrid CNN-transformer designs and efficient attention remain active; the DiT lineage nonetheless underlies SD3 and most 2024-onwards systems, and it points toward a single transformer that generates several modalities, differing only in tokenization and training data.

Sampling Acceleration and Distillation.

Fifty or more denoising steps rule out interactive use and low-power deployment. salimans2022progressive distilled a TT-step teacher into a T/2T/2-step student and iterated the halving to reach 11–44 steps. Consistency Models [song2023consistency] train a network to map a noisy latent at any timestep directly to the clean image, either from scratch with a consistency loss or by distilling a pretrained diffusion model, and Latent Consistency Models [lcm2023] applied the idea to Stable Diffusion’s latent space, matching 5050-step quality in 22–44 steps. All of these are post-training procedures that leave the architecture untouched, so any strong backbone can be made fast after the fact.

Proprietary and Commercial Systems.

Leading systems have migrated to proprietary, industrially scaled stacks of three kinds. Native multimodal models such as OpenAI’s GPT Image 1.5 [openai2025images] and Google’s Gemini 3 Pro Image (Nano Banana Pro) run a unified transformer over interleaved text and image tokens and emphasize semantic reasoning and multi-turn editing; latent-diffusion iterations such as Imagen 4 scale the LDM recipe with stronger text encoders and curated data; preference-tuned systems such as Midjourney v7 [midjourney_v7_alpha] and FLUX.2 [max] [bfl_flux2_max] fine-tune strong priors on human-preference data (FLUX.2 on the rectified-flow recipe of §8.1.1.2; Midjourney’s architecture is undisclosed). Each reduces to one of the three paradigms plus some of the refinements just listed; because architectural and training detail is withheld, public benchmarking and reproduction still rest on the open SD / DiT stack.

8.1.1.3 Benchmarks

Three independent things are usually conflated under “benchmark”: the training corpora on which models are fit, the evaluation suites of prompts that probe particular capabilities, and the metrics that score the resulting images. A model trained on LAION-5B can be evaluated on GenEval prompts and scored by FID, CLIPScore, or an LLM judge, and disagreement between those scores is itself informative.

Training Corpora.

Corpus scale has driven much of T2I progress. Early work fit fine-grained sets with ten captions per image, CUB-200-2011 (11,788 bird images) [wah2011cub] and Oxford-102 Flowers (8,189 images) [nilsback2008flowers]; MS-COCO Captions [lin2014microsoft] (123,287 images, five captions each) became the standard general-scene corpus and, for years, the evaluation set as well, a conflation that the suites below were designed to end. Current models train on web-scale image-text pairs: LAION-5B [schuhmann2022laion5b] releases 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered pairs, and proprietary corpora of similar scale, less documented, underlie DALL-E 2 and Parti. Scale brought duplication, demographic bias, unsafe content, and licensing disputes with it, and filtered subsets such as LAION-Aesthetics and curation pipelines are now part of every training recipe.

Evaluation Benchmark Suites.

An evaluation suite is a curated prompt set plus a verification protocol: prompts are adversarial or capability-stratified, reference images are usually absent, and scoring is automatic (an object detector, a VQA model, or an LLM/MLLM judge) rather than reconstruction-based. Table 8.1 lists the main suites since 2022. The earliest, DrawBench [saharia2022photorealistic] and PartiPrompts [parti2022], are human-pairwise prompt sets released with Imagen and Parti; HRS-Bench [bakr2023hrsbench] and HEIM [lee2023heim] are holistic, scoring 13 and 12 axes respectively; TIFA [hu2023tifa], GenEval [ghosh2023geneval], and T2I-CompBench [huang2023t2icompbench] introduced automatic verification by VQA, object detection, and BLIP-VQA plus UniDet, and the latter two are now reported alongside FID and CLIPScore in most papers. For spatial intelligence the salient suite is VISOR [gokhale2022visor], which isolates two-object relations (left/right, above/below) over 25,28025{,}280 prompts and finds that otherwise strong models frequently render the wrong configuration. DPG-Bench [hu2024ella] targets dense, long compositional prompts, GenAI-Bench [li2024genaibench] pairs compositional prompts with VQAScore judging, and WISE [niu2025wise] asks whether generated images agree with real-world facts (flag colors, landmarks, anatomy), a knowledge axis orthogonal to compositional binding.

Evaluation Metrics.

Metrics fall into four tiers. Distributional metrics compare the generated and real image populations and say nothing about any individual prompt: the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [heusel2017gans] is the Wasserstein-2 distance between Gaussian fits of Inception-V3 features of generated and real images, the Inception Score rewards images that are individually confidently classified yet collectively diverse, and generative precision/recall [sajjadi2018assessing, kynkaanniemi2019improved] separate quality from coverage through neighborhood tests in feature space. Alignment metrics score one image against its prompt; CLIPScore [hessel2021clipscore], the cosine similarity between the CLIP embeddings of 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}} and 𝐱\mathbf{x}, is cheap and reference-free but inherits CLIP’s insensitivity to attribute binding, counting, and spatial relations. Learned preference models, HPSv2 [wu2023hpsv2], ImageReward [xu2023imagereward] (fit to 137137K human comparisons), and PickScore [kirstain2023pickapic] (fit to the ∼500{\sim}500K real-user comparisons of Pick-a-Pic), regress a scalar that correlates with average user preference, bundling realism, alignment, and aesthetics; they have become the default automatic ranking while inheriting their raters’ biases and degrading out of distribution.

The newest tier uses a vision-language model as judge. TIFA [hu2023tifa] has a language model write verification questions from the prompt and a VQA model answer them against the image, the score being the fraction answered correctly; VQAScore [lin2024evaluating] collapses this to a single yes/no probability under a fine-tuned CLIP-FlanT5 model and reports the best human correlation on compositional suites; VIEScore [ku2023viescore] and LLMScore [lu2023llmscore] prompt a multimodal LLM with a structured rubric and return per-axis scores with brief rationales, and direct prompting of frontier VLMs with custom rubrics has become routine for ad-hoc capability probes. Judge metrics track human preference on compositional and spatial prompts far better than CLIPScore, at the cost of a frontier-model call per image, sensitivity to rubric wording, and drift across judge-model versions that makes numbers from different papers hard to compare. No single tier suffices, and current papers report a tuple (FID or IS, CLIPScore, one or two preference scores, one judge score) on several suites plus a small human study; cross-metric disagreement is read as a warning rather than averaged away.

8.1.1.4 Challenges and Trends

The weakness that matters most for this handbook is spatial-relation faithfulness, a sub-problem of compositionality. Models frequently misplace objects relative to one another: a prompt that puts a cup to the left of a laptop is often rendered with the two swapped or stacked, and VISOR [gokhale2022visor] shows that language-specified relations are frequently ignored outright. Data-centric remedies help; SPRIGHT [chatterjee2024spright] re-captions training images with explicit spatial descriptions and measurably improves consistency, but reliable control over where objects appear remains open. Because layout-conditioned generation (§8.1.2) and text-to-3D (§8.2) inherit whatever relational competence this prior provides, the limitation is foundational rather than cosmetic. Fine structure is a second gap: legible text, hands, and faces still fail in otherwise strong models and appear to need architectural or data-specific fixes rather than scale alone.

Evaluation reliability is the third. Automatic scores correlate imperfectly with human judgment precisely on the compositional, counting, and spatial-relation prompts that matter here; judge-based metrics close part of the gap but add rubric sensitivity and judge-version drift, so headline numbers across papers are not directly comparable. As GenEval and T2I-CompBench become standard, their prompts risk leaking into web-scraped training corpora, in which case high scores increasingly measure memorization rather than capability; periodic refresh of held-out prompts, blinded judges, and explicit train/test decontamination are the obvious countermeasures and are not yet routine.

Societal concerns follow the data. Models inherit demographic bias from their corpora and will produce unsafe content on request; prompt classifiers, safety filters, and fine-tuning on curated subsets reduce but do not remove the problem, and photorealistic synthesis raises misinformation and intellectual-property questions that watermarking and data curation address only in part. The extension of these priors along the time axis, where identity and motion must stay consistent across frames, is the subject of §8.3; the next two subsections stay in the image plane and ask how the prior can be made to obey spatial constraints and local edits.

8.1.2 2D Spatial-aware Image Generation

2D spatial-aware image generation synthesizes images that are faithful not only to a text prompt but to explicit spatial constraints in the image plane: where objects appear, how large they are, what shape they take, and how they relate to one another (left of, on, behind). The constraint may be a set of boxes or a scene layout, an instance or semantic mask, an edge or sketch map, a depth or normal map, 2D keypoints, a scene graph, or a phrase bound to a region, and the pipelines that honor it are almost all diffusion models augmented with a conditioning pathway or a guidance term. The tension that organizes the subfield is three-way: adherence to hard constraints against perceptual realism and diversity, and both against compositionality when many small or occluding objects carry discrete relations. Depth and normal maps enter here as structural guides for occlusion ordering and surface orientation, not as metric measurements; recovering true distance belongs to reconstruction (§8.2).

8.1.2.1 Task Definition

We inherit the latent-generator framework of §8.1.1. Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} denote tokenized prompts, 𝒵\mathcal{Z} the latent space induced by the autoencoder pair (E,D)(E,D) of Eq. (8.1), and ϕ:𝒳→ℰ\phi:\mathcal{X}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{E} the text encoder. Spatial-aware generation augments this framework with a structural condition 𝐜∈𝒞\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C} drawn from one or more conditioning channels (boxes, masks, edges, depth, pose, scene graphs, region phrases, reference images), encoded by a condition encoder κ:𝒞→𝒞′\kappa:\mathcal{C}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{C}^{\prime}. The conditional latent sampler of Eq. (8.2) is extended to a joint conditional

Gθ:ℰ×𝒞′→𝒵,𝐳^∼pθ⁢(𝐳|ϕ⁢(𝐱),κ⁢(𝐜)),G_{\theta}:\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z},\qquad% \hat{\mathbf{z}}\sim p_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}\,\big{|}\,\phi(\mathbf{x}),% \,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.7)

and the generated image 𝐲^=D⁢(𝐳^)\hat{\mathbf{y}}=D(\hat{\mathbf{z}}) is required to be (i) photorealistic, (ii) semantically aligned with 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and (iii) faithful to the structural condition 𝐜\mathbf{c} in placement, scale, shape, and pairwise relation. The unconditional limit 𝐜=∅\mathbf{c}=\varnothing recovers pure T2I generation as in §8.1.1; the substance of the present subsection lies in how κ\kappa is realized for each conditioning channel and how its output is injected into GθG_{\theta}. Which channel populates 𝐜\mathbf{c}, and how densely, ranges from pixel-level maps (masks, edges, depth) through coordinate-level scaffolds (boxes, keypoints) to discrete symbols (scene graphs, region phrases); the modality survey below follows that ordering. Interactive constraints supplied by dragging handles during generation belong to the editing regime of §8.1.3.

8.1.2.2 Methodology

Two axes organize the methods: the conditioning modality (what kind of structural input 𝐜\mathbf{c} is consumed) and the injection mechanism (how κ⁢(𝐜)\kappa(\mathbf{c}) enters the latent sampler GθG_{\theta}). They are nearly independent. One mechanism, a ControlNet-style side branch, serves canny edges, pose skeletons, depth, and segmentation alike, and one modality, bounding boxes, is served by side branches, grounded cross-attention, or inference-time attention shaping, so the design space is a matrix of (modality ×\times mechanism) cells rather than a list of monolithic methods. Figure 8.2 draws the five mechanisms on one backbone silhouette.

Conditioning Modalities.

Dense pixel-level scaffolds supply a value at every location, which makes them the easiest channels to follow and the most restrictive on creativity. Instance and semantic masks drive region-conditioned synthesis, with MultiDiffusion [multidiffusion] offering a training-free protocol that samples jointly over overlapping mask windows; edges, sketches, and line art, popularized by the canny and soft-edge variants of ControlNet [zhang2023adding] and the edge head of T2I-Adapter [t2iadapter2023], fix only the location of intensity discontinuities and leave texture and appearance to the prompt; depth and normal maps, served by ControlNet’s depth variant, impose coarse occlusion ordering and surface orientation without requiring a metric reconstruction. Coordinate-level scaffolds drop to per-region or per-point supervision. Boxes with labels are the most studied channel, a set of (box,label)(\text{box},\text{label}) tuples fixing location and rough scale, with LayoutDiffusion [zheng2023layoutdiffusion], LayoutLLM [qu2023layoutllm], and the open-set GLIGEN [li2023gligen] as representatives; 2D keypoints (typically human pose) are sparser still, a handful of joint coordinates, injected through ControlNet or handled by GLIGEN as a special case of grounding. Discrete symbolic structure carries no pixel- or coordinate-level information at all, and the model must map it onto the image plane itself. Scene graphs reach back to the sg2im line of johnson2018image and re-emerged in the diffusion era through LLM-emitted layouts, as in LayoutLLM, where the graph is first decoded into a coordinate-level layout; region phrases and referring expressions bind a text span to a box, mask, or free-form polygon and are served by GLIGEN’s grounded cross-attention and by phrase-grounding heads attached to SD and SDXL [sdxl2023].

Injection Mechanisms.

Five mechanism families cover the literature; production pipelines routinely stack a side branch for dense geometric channels, an adapter for style or a reference image, and inference-time guidance to sharpen adherence on adversarial prompts.

Side-branch controllers. The backbone weights stay frozen and an auxiliary branch mirroring the encoder half of the base U-Net is trained, connected through zero-convolution layers whose weights are initialized to zero so that the augmented model reproduces the base model exactly at the start of training and degrades gracefully if the branch is poorly tuned. ControlNet [zhang2023adding] is the prototype and the first widely adopted retrofit pathway for non-text structural control: the condition (a canny edge map, an OpenPose skeleton, a depth or normal map, a segmentation mask, or a scribble) is encoded by the side branch in parallel with the noisy latent and injected into the base U-Net through additive residual connections at each scale. One branch is trained per modality on labeled image–condition pairs, which produced a library of plug-in controllers for SD 1.5 and SDXL [sdxl2023] that compose with prompt conditioning at inference time without retraining the backbone; most later designs either shrink this recipe or fold it into a unified adapter library.

Lightweight adapters. Where the side branch spends capacity (half a U-Net per modality), T2I-Adapter [t2iadapter2023], developed concurrently with the same goal of plug-in control over a frozen backbone, spends as little as possible: a few residual blocks per modality whose multi-scale features are added directly into the corresponding encoder stages. Several adapters can be combined at inference, an image conditioned simultaneously on an OpenPose skeleton, a depth map, and a color palette with a scalar weight on each, so the adapter is preferred for multi-channel fusion and fast iteration, and the side branch where maximum single-channel fidelity matters.

Grounded cross-attention. Side branches and adapters run an external pathway alongside the backbone; the next two families intervene inside its attention stack. GLIGEN [li2023gligen] inserts a new gated self-attention layer between the existing self-attention and cross-attention of each U-Net transformer block; the layer attends jointly over the visual tokens and a set of grounding tokens that encode each (phrase,box)(\text{phrase},\text{box}) pair, a learned scalar gate controls how strongly the grounding signal enters the residual stream, and only the new layer is trained, so the network falls back to ungrounded behavior when no constraint is supplied. The problem it solves is complementary to the side branch: not how to inject a dense pixel-level scaffold, but how to introduce open-set symbolic grounding (any category named in text, localized by a box, keypoints, or a reference image) into a frozen T2I backbone, with several grounding channels interleaved within one mechanism.

Layout-aware cross-attention. LayoutDiffusion [zheng2023layoutdiffusion] is the dense-supervised cousin of grounded attention: rather than gating a new layer onto a frozen backbone, it co-trains a layout-aware cross-attention block end to end for layout-to-image (L2I) generation specifically. A structured layout, a set of (box,class label)(\text{box},\text{class label}) tuples, becomes a sequence of region tokens fused with the noisy latent at every denoising step, and an explicit object–scene factorization models global scene context separately from per-object features so that object identity, scale, and pairwise relations survive in cluttered scenes. It reports stronger layout IoU and relation satisfaction than ControlNet or T2I-Adapter on multi-object COCO benchmarks, at the cost of being specialized to box-and-label input rather than the broader modality library.

Inference-time guidance. The fifth family adds no parameters and modifies only sampling. BoxDiff [xie2023boxdiff] is the canonical training-free spatial controller: it shapes the cross-attention maps so that activations of box-localized prompt tokens concentrate inside their boxes while the backbone stays untouched. MultiDiffusion [multidiffusion] fuses overlapping mask windows at sampling time, and composing scores from several conditional models or tuning the classifier-free guidance scale per region are related strategies. Because nothing is retrained, these methods suit rapid prototyping, backbones whose weights are unavailable for fine-tuning, and per-prompt sharpening on top of the trained mechanisms above.

8.1.2.3 Benchmarks

Two things change relative to §8.1.1. The ground truth is a structural annotation (a layout, a mask, a keypoint set) rather than a reference image, so reconstruction-style metrics give way to adherence metrics that score how closely the generated image honors 𝐜\mathbf{c}; and every channel admits its own adherence metric, so a meaningful report combines a channel-specific score with the realism and alignment scores inherited from the previous subsection.

Training Corpora.

Spatial-aware models are typically trained on corpora that pair images with rich structural annotations: COCO Captions [lin2014microsoft] for layouts and captions; ADE20K [zhou2017ade20k] (2020K images, 150150 classes) for semantic and instance masks; Visual Genome [krishna2017visual] for object boxes, attributes, and pairwise relations supporting scene-graph conditioning; RefCOCO / RefCOCO+ / RefCOCOg [yu2016modeling] for phrase grounding; and PhraseCut [wu2020phrasecut] for region-prompt mask supervision. Additional structure (canny edges, depth, normals, OpenPose skeletons) is typically derived on the fly from these base corpora by running pretrained predictors over each image, producing the paired image–condition data on which ControlNet-style and adapter-style pipelines are trained.

Evaluation Benchmark Suites.

Most of the suites surveyed in §8.1.1 (Table 8.1) include axes that probe spatial-aware generation directly and serve as its primary out-of-the-box benchmarks. GenEval [ghosh2023geneval] exposes a position subset that scores whether two objects appear in a specified relation (left of, above); T2I-CompBench [huang2023t2icompbench] provides explicit spatial and non-spatial relationship categories with BLIP-VQA and UniDet scoring; HRS-Bench [bakr2023hrsbench] includes a spatial skill among its thirteen; GenAI-Bench [li2024genaibench] offers compositional prompts on which spatial relations are a frequent failure of CLIP-based scoring; and WISE [niu2025wise] measures knowledge-grounded location accuracy. Beyond these, the L2I literature reports task-specific evaluations on COCO layouts: detection-based AP for box-localized objects alongside FID and CLIPScore.

Constraint-specific Metrics.

Layout adherence is box IoU between the conditioning layout and the boxes recovered by a frozen detector on 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}}, often with per-object center distance; mask adherence uses mask IoU and boundary FF-score against the conditioning mask; edge and sketch adherence report recall (sometimes precision) of edges re-extracted from 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}}; geometry adherence reports depth RMSE and normal angular error where ground-truth geometry exists; pose adherence reports keypoint reprojection error or PCK; and relational adherence reports relation-satisfaction accuracy and per-entity object AP for scene-graph and phrase-grounded settings. These numbers do not aggregate: averaging layout IoU with mask IoU has no operational meaning, since the two live on different scales and reward different shape regimes, and most papers report a different subset of them, which is the main obstacle to cross-paper comparison in this subfield.

8.1.2.4 Challenges and Trends

Spatial-aware T2I inherits the compositionality and evaluation problems of §8.1.1 and sharpens them.

Faithful multi-object composition. Crowded scenes with many small or partially occluded objects and hard relations (support, containment, depth ordering) fail in three recognizable ways: attention dilution, in which a prompt token’s cross-attention spreads across the canvas and no object is well localized; attribute leakage, in which color, material, or count attaches to the wrong object (the canonical “red cube on a blue sphere” confusion); and object dropping, in which small or rare entities in a multi-object layout are simply omitted. On GenEval the position and counting subsets remain the weakest axes across SD 1.5, SDXL, and SD 3 [sd3rft2024]. Remedies work at three levels: Attend-and-Excite [chefer2023attend] reweights cross-attention at inference so that every subject token is strongly activated somewhere in the canvas; StructureDiffusion [feng2023training] uses prompt syntax to constrain attention structure without training; and LLM-emitted layouts, LayoutGPT [feng2023layoutgpt] and the multimodal-LLM-driven RPG of yang2024mastering, plan a structured layout from the free-form prompt and hand it to an L2I renderer. Whether the gap closes through a stronger compositional prior in the backbone or through planning as a separate stage is unresolved, and the two are not exclusive.

Constraint satisfaction against creativity and diversity. Turning guidance up tightens adherence until, past a model-dependent threshold, edges oversharpen, textures flatten, and variation across seeds collapses; the same curve appears for the ControlNet conditioning weight, GLIGEN’s gating strength, and the classifier-free guidance scale, leaving practitioners to tune two or three knobs at once. Annealing the control weight along the denoising trajectory, per-region or per-token guidance scales, and down-weighting guidance where the base model is already confident are the current responses; how to expose such schedules to end users without overwhelming the interface is open. Chaining spatial-aware generation with repeated local edits adds a drift problem of its own, treated in §8.1.3.

Geometry-aware realism in 2D. Depth and normal conditioning fix coarse occlusion but introduce their own artifacts: boundary banding where a sharp depth discontinuity meets a smooth gradient in the generated image, scale ambiguity because a monocular depth map carries no absolute scale and two objects at the same depth value can be rendered at incompatible physical sizes, and lighting incoherence because the map fixes geometry but not the light field, so shadows disagree with the implied surface orientations. Better estimators are the first lever, with the diffusion-prior Marigold [ke2024repurposing] producing sharper and more globally consistent depth than CNN baselines and Depth Anything [DepthAnything] staying robust on out-of-distribution conditioning images; differentiable geometry proxies that translate depth into shading constraints are the second, explored at the boundary with full 3D synthesis (§8.2) but not yet integrated into general T2I backbones. Region grounding also changes the safety picture, since a harmful edit can be confined to a footprint that whole-image forensics miss; that concern belongs to editing and is taken up in §8.1.3.

8.1.3 2D Spatial Inpainting & Editing

2D spatial inpainting & editing modifies an image inside a specified region while leaving the rest intact: filling holes and occlusions, removing or inserting objects, changing attributes (color, material, texture, text), adjusting layout, or harmonizing pasted content with its new background. The intent arrives as a mask, a structural hint (edges, sketches), a geometry proxy (depth, normals), or a natural-language instruction, and the tensions are between local editability and global consistency of lighting, perspective, and shadow, between constraint adherence and realism, and between semantic plausibility and identity preservation for person- or product-centric edits. Editing holds the model to its strongest geometric account: the unedited region of II supplies ground-truth pixels that any plausible edit must respect, exposing failure modes that pure synthesis can hide, among them color drift, lighting reflow, identity loss, and attribute leakage across the mask boundary.

8.1.3.1 Task Definition

We inherit the latent-generator framework of §8.1.1. Let (E,D)(E,D) denote the autoencoder pair of Eq. (8.1), ϕ:𝒳→ℰ\phi:\mathcal{X}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{E} the text encoder, and GθG_{\theta} the conditional latent sampler of Eq. (8.2). Inpainting and editing depart from de-novo generation in one crucial respect: the input is no longer the empty set but an existing image I∈𝒴I\in\mathcal{Y}, encoded into 𝐳in=E⁢(I)\mathbf{z}^{\text{in}}=E(I). A mask ℳ∈{0,1}H×W\mathcal{M}\in\{0,1\}^{H\times W} designates the editable region, and an editing control set 𝐜∈𝒞\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C} (text prompts, structural cues, exemplar patches, or drag-style handles) populates the conditioning channel, encoded by κ:𝒞→𝒞′\kappa:\mathcal{C}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{C}^{\prime}. The conditional latent sampler is extended to

Gθ:𝒵×{0,1}H×W×ℰ×𝒞′→𝒵,𝐳^∼pθ⁢(𝐳|𝐳in,ℳ,ϕ⁢(𝐱),κ⁢(𝐜)),G_{\theta}:\mathcal{Z}\times\{0,1\}^{H\times W}\times\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal% {C}^{\prime}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{Z},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{z}}\sim p_{\theta}\!% \big{(}\mathbf{z}\,\big{|}\,\mathbf{z}^{\text{in}},\,\mathcal{M},\,\phi(% \mathbf{x}),\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.8)

and the edited image I^=D⁢(𝐳^)\hat{I}=D(\hat{\mathbf{z}}) is required to (i) realize the requested change inside ℳ\mathcal{M}, (ii) preserve II outside ℳ\mathcal{M} up to imperceptible deviations, and (iii) remain globally coherent in color, lighting, geometry, and semantics. Setting 𝐳in=∅\mathbf{z}^{\text{in}}=\varnothing and ℳ=𝟏\mathcal{M}=\mathbf{1} recovers the spatial-aware synthesis of §8.1.2 (Eq. (8.7)); the distinctive substance of editing therefore lies in the interplay between the preservation constraint outside ℳ\mathcal{M} and the change constraint inside it. The mask may be hard, soft, inferred from a referring expression, or implicit (whole-image instruction editing with ℳ=𝟏\mathcal{M}=\mathbf{1}).

Variants by Task Type.

The tasks differ in what populates 𝐜\mathbf{c} and ℳ\mathcal{M} and in whether ground-truth pixels exist for evaluation. Reconstruction-style completion carries no semantic intent: hole filling repairs scratches and occlusions from (I,ℳ)(I,\mathcal{M}) alone, and object removal reconstructs the background behind a specified instance. Constraint-driven local synthesis adds intent inside ℳ\mathcal{M}: text-guided local editing follows an instruction scoped to a region (“make the left cup red”), structure-guided inpainting takes edges, sketches, or semantic maps as a scaffold for shape and boundary, and geometry-guided inpainting conditions on depth or normals to respect occlusion ordering. Object-level edits treat the region as an object whose identity or embedding in the scene is the unit of change: insertion with harmonization of color, grain, lighting, shadows, and reflections; attribute and appearance editing that changes material or style while preserving identity (garments, products, logos); and exemplar-guided transfer that drives content or style from a reference patch. Interactive workflows replace declarative constraints with actions taken at edit time: point- or handle-based reshaping, and multi-round, multi-region sessions in which stability across rounds is itself the requirement. The metrics appropriate to each are collected in Benchmarks below.

8.1.3.2 Methodology

Methods are organized by editing mechanism, that is, by how GθG_{\theta} of Eq. (8.8) is realized so that change is confined to ℳ\mathcal{M} and preservation is enforced outside it.
