The mechanism is largely independent of the task type above, since text-guided local editing can be served by masked denoising, by inversion and rewrite, or by an instruction-tuned editor, and one mechanism such as inversion serves both attribute edits and structure-guided ones. Figure 8.3 sets the five mechanisms against a single example edit.

Editing Mechanisms.

Masked latent denoising. The most direct realization of Eq. (8.8) runs the diffusion sampler only inside ℳ\mathcal{M} while clamping the latent outside ℳ\mathcal{M} to a noise-perturbed copy of 𝐳in\mathbf{z}^{\text{in}} at every step. RePaint [lugmayr2022repaint] does this with a pretrained, unconditional DDPM and no retraining, replacing the known-region pixels with a forward-noised sample of the input at each reverse step and adding a resampling schedule that re-injects noise periodically so the in-fill can re-harmonize with its context over several rounds. Blended Diffusion [avrahami2022blended] made the same scheme text-driven by interleaving a CLIP-guided gradient step that steers the content inside ℳ\mathcal{M} toward a target prompt with the context-clamping step outside it, the first widely cited text-guided local editor. LaMa [suvorov2022lama] predates the diffusion line and is instead a feed-forward inpainter whose fast Fourier convolutions give every layer an image-wide receptive field, a Fourier-domain inductive bias that stays robust on the very large holes that defeat purely local CNN backbones. Region-aware noise schedules and classifier-free guidance are standard add-ons, and ControlNet-inpaint and the inpainting variants of T2I-Adapter (§8.1.2.2) compose with masked denoising by supplying the inside-ℳ\mathcal{M} condition.

Inversion + rewrite. A complementary strategy first recovers the noise trajectory that the model would have used to generate II (inversion) and then re-runs the reverse process under an edited prompt while reusing or swapping the attention maps of the original (rewrite). Prompt-to-Prompt [prompt-to-prompt] reuses or reweights source cross-attention maps during generation under the edited prompt, which preserves spatial structure while changing selected semantic content; for a real image an inversion step first supplies a suitable noise trajectory. Imagic [kawar2023imagic] jointly optimizes the text embedding and lightly fine-tunes the model to reconstruct II, then interpolates the embedding toward the target prompt, preserving identity-level features (faces, garments) under non-rigid edits. Null-Text Inversion [mokady2023nulltext] fixes the practical failure that plain DDIM inversion drifts away from II under classifier-free guidance, by optimizing the null-text embeddings used in the inverse pass so that exact reconstruction holds at ordinary guidance scales. The family needs no full backbone fine-tune for Prompt-to-Prompt or Null-Text and dominates attribute, style, and structure-preserving real-image edits.

Instruction-tuned editing. A third family avoids inversion entirely by retraining a diffusion editor on paired (before, instruction, after) triplets, mapping II directly to I^\hat{I} from a natural-language instruction with no explicit mask. InstructPix2Pix [brooks2023instructpix2pixlearningfollowimage] built its corpus by pairing GPT-3-generated edit instructions with Prompt-to-Prompt edits of Stable Diffusion samples and fine-tuned Stable Diffusion on the triplets, so that at inference the user supplies only (I,instruction)(I,\text{instruction}) and the editor localizes the change itself. MagicBrush [zhang2024magicbrush] replaced the synthetic data with about 10K manually annotated real-image edits across multi-turn sessions, yielding both a stronger supervised editor and the standard instruction-editing test set. Emu Edit [sheynin2024emu] trained a single model on a heterogeneous mixture of recognition (segmentation, detection) and generation (insertion, removal, style change) tasks with learned task embeddings that route each input, and leads its own benchmark on precision and instruction following. Instruction editors are the most user-friendly mechanism, no mask and no inversion, at the cost of large supervised retraining.

Exemplar / reference-guided editing. A visual exemplar, an example image or patch encoding the desired content or style, replaces the textual instruction and enters through an auxiliary cross-attention pathway beside the standard text conditioning. Paint-by-Example [yang2023paintbyexample] fine-tunes Stable Diffusion to fill ℳ\mathcal{M} with the content of an exemplar whose identity is encoded by a CLIP image encoder, with strong exemplar augmentation (cropping, color jitter) at training time to prevent copy-paste behavior and force semantic rather than pixel-level transfer. IP-Adapter [ye2023ipadapter] generalizes this into a plug-in reference channel: a lightweight decoupled cross-attention head consumes a CLIP image embedding of the exemplar and is inserted into a frozen SD or SDXL backbone, so that any number of reference images can be combined with text prompts and with structural adapters such as ControlNet at inference time. It is the standard route for subject personalization and style transfer when the desired content is hard to describe in words.

Drag-based latent optimization. The most interactive family takes user-supplied (source point, target point) pairs and iteratively optimizes the latent so that the features at each source point migrate to the corresponding target while a locality regularizer pins the latent outside the user-marked region. DragGAN [pan2023draggan] introduced the recipe on a StyleGAN backbone: a motion-supervision loss tracks the source feature and pulls it toward the target by gradient descent in the 𝒲+\mathcal{W}^{+} latent space, and a point-tracking step re-localizes the moved feature at each iteration to prevent drift. DragDiffusion [shi2023dragdiffusion] ported the recipe to the LDM latent space, running a per-timestep latent-update loop together with an identity-preserving LoRA fine-tune of the U-Net so that both the dragged subject and the unmarked context survive. Both are inference-time optimizers with latency proportional to the number of drag iterations, and no other family yet offers the same directness of spatial control.

Read across the five families, the mechanisms track the generative substrate: feed-forward inpainters such as LaMa gave way to inversion-based diffusion editors (Prompt-to-Prompt, Imagic), which in turn yielded to supervised instruction-tuned editors (InstructPix2Pix, Emu Edit) as paired data became available at scale. Orthogonal to that migration, the structural conditioning interfaces of §8.1.2 compose with every mechanism here, so a production pipeline pairs a mechanism with a structural channel rather than choosing one: Blended Diffusion with ControlNet-depth for geometry-aware text-guided edits, or IP-Adapter with DragDiffusion for exemplar-driven drag edits.

8.1.3.3 Benchmarks

Editing is evaluated in two regimes: reference-based, where a held-out ground-truth region exists (holes synthesized over real images), and reference-free, where only constraint satisfaction and human preference are available (instruction editing). No single suite covers both, so the field keeps a small library of task-specific benchmarks next to the holistic T2I suites of §8.1.1.

Training Corpora.

Inpainting draws on Places2 [zhou2017places] and Paris StreetView for scene-level masks, DIV2K for high-resolution patches, and the COCO / ADE20K mask supervision of §8.1.2 [lin2014microsoft, zhou2017ade20k]. Constraint-driven local synthesis reuses the structural channels of the previous subsection, RefCOCO / RefCOCO+ / RefCOCOg [yu2016modeling] and PhraseCut [wu2020phrasecut] for referring-expression masks, SA-1B masks [kirillov2023sam], and COCO edge and depth predictions, with the convention that the mask is supplied or derived from the expression; geometry-guided editing adds depth and normal supervision from NYUv2 [silberman2012nyudv2], Replica [straub2019replica], and synthetic corpora, and insertion with harmonization uses composite datasets such as iHarmony4. Instruction editing has its own data ecology: the synthetic InstructPix2Pix corpus of Prompt-to-Prompt-generated triplets, the manually annotated MagicBrush triplets [zhang2024magicbrush], and the multi-task Emu Edit training mixture [sheynin2024emu].

Evaluation Benchmark Suites.

The holistic suites of §8.1.1 (Table 8.1) carry over in part: T2I-CompBench [huang2023t2icompbench] and GenAI-Bench [li2024genaibench] score the attribute and compositional fidelity that edited images must also satisfy, and HEIM [lee2023heim] includes alignment and quality axes that apply to edits. The dedicated suites are EditBench [wang2023editbench], released with Imagen Editor, a curated set of text-guided inpainting prompts over object, attribute, and scene categories that serves as the standard evaluation for text-driven mask inpainting; the MagicBrush test set [zhang2024magicbrush], 1,0531{,}053 manually annotated single- and multi-turn triplets, which is the standard for instruction-tuned editors; and the Emu Edit benchmark [sheynin2024emu], which extends instruction editing to per-task subsets (insertion, removal, style change, color change, global change). Drag-based methods evaluate on small custom test sets curated by pan2023draggan and shi2023dragdiffusion; a community-wide drag-editing benchmark has not yet emerged.

Constraint-specific Metrics.

Reconstruction quality (PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS against ground truth, with FID / KID for diverse-completion settings) is defined only where held-out content exists. Region adherence uses mask-restricted CLIPScore or region-level VQAScore to ask whether the edit honors the prompt inside ℳ\mathcal{M}; edit locality measures ℓ1\ell_{1} or LPIPS outside ℳ\mathcal{M} against II, lower being better; harmonization is scored by color-statistic divergence, shadow-direction consistency, and the rate at which an off-the-shelf forgery detector flags the composite; identity preservation uses feature-cosine similarity over face or landmark regions for people and CLIP-image similarity for products and characters; and instruction following is paired accuracy, whether I^\hat{I} honors the instruction better than II, judged by human raters or by a VLM over a structured rubric, as is now standard on MagicBrush and Emu Edit. Change inside ℳ\mathcal{M} and preservation outside it are reported together; a method that wins on one and loses on the other has not solved the task.

8.1.3.4 Challenges and Trends

Several problems are specific to editing an existing image.

Structure-faithful hallucination in large holes. Large irregular holes and rare structures remain the hardest case: inpainters tile a salient local texture across the hole instead of synthesizing appropriate content, straight lines, perspective cues, and silhouettes break at the mask seam, and in-fills that are locally plausible contradict the global scene (a patch of grass inside a room). Quality degrades sharply with hole size. LaMa’s image-wide Fourier convolutions and RePaint’s resampling schedule (§8.1.3.2) are the established responses; retrieval-augmented priors, which search a paired corpus for candidate completions and use them as soft conditioning, are an emerging one at the intersection of editing and retrieval.

Edit locality against drift across rounds. A single well-calibrated edit does not guarantee a stable session. Across rounds the unedited background shifts in white balance or saturation (color drift), shadows and highlights migrate as if the edit had changed the global illumination (lighting reflow), and salient textures from the edited region reappear in nearby unedited regions through attention leakage (texture replication); the errors compound even when each round individually meets its locality budget. Hard attention masking that confines non-edit tokens to ℳ\mathcal{M}, mask-aware noise schedules that anneal noise inside ℳ\mathcal{M} only, and edit-history-aware sampling that conditions on the trajectory of prior edits are the active mitigations. Inversion-based editors (Null-Text Inversion [mokady2023nulltext], Imagic [kawar2023imagic]) carry a variant of the problem: any residual reconstruction error in the inverted trajectory leaks into the edit and accumulates.

Harmonization under complex illumination. Inserted content betrays itself when the host scene has structured light: its shadow disagrees with the dominant light direction recoverable from the scene, there is no interreflection between the object and adjacent surfaces, and its albedo is tone-mapped inconsistently with the host, producing the cut-and-paste look that off-the-shelf forgery detectors flag. Differentiable rendering proxies that turn depth and normals into shading constraints and back-propagate harmonization losses into the editor, illumination maps as an additional conditioning channel, and explicit shadow-synthesis modules are being explored; integration with the 3D-aware methods of §8.2 is the natural next step and remains nascent.

Language grounding and safety. Region-level instructions must be grounded reliably: an edit aimed at one object spills onto neighbors with similar attributes, spatial referring expressions are misparsed (“the left cup” lands on the right one), and mildly perturbed instructions produce large deviations in the edit trajectory. Borrowing GLIGEN’s gated grounding [li2023gligen] (§8.1.2.2) to confine edit attention, and using LLM-emitted layouts to harden the grounding before the edit is applied, are the current responses. The same precision cuts the other way for safety. A harmful edit (an identity swap inside one bounding box, watermark removal inside one mask) can be confined to a footprint that whole-image forensic detectors miss; large generative models reproduce individual training images under targeted prompting [somepalli2023diffusion], which becomes acute when the training set contains copyrighted artwork or identifiable faces and motivates artist-side defenses such as Glaze [shan2023glaze], which perturbs source artworks so that downstream fine-tunes mimic a different style; and most pipelines still lack robust per-image watermarking, so a photograph with a small synthesized region cannot be told from a wholly synthetic one. Watermarking, region-aware safety filters, and licensing frameworks for the underlying corpora are all needed, and none is settled.

Evaluation under plausibility ambiguity. Ground-truth pixels are often not the only plausible completion: a removed pedestrian leaves a hole that could contain road, curb, or shadow, and any reconstruction metric that compares against one ground truth over-penalizes good alternatives, while PSNR and SSIM rate sharp but contextually wrong in-fills highly. The field is converging on paired evaluation, asking whether I^\hat{I} honors the instruction better than II under a held-out judge, now standard on MagicBrush [zhang2024magicbrush] and Emu Edit [sheynin2024emu]; the judge-prompt sensitivity and benchmark-contamination caveats of §8.1.1 apply here as well.

Scalability and interactive latency. Inversion-based methods store cross-attention activations at every timestep, multi-step sampling at 44K and above scales with image area for standard U-Net backbones, and drag editors run an inner optimization loop per operation, so interactive editing lags behind the user’s hand by hundreds of milliseconds. Consistency-style distillation [song2023consistency, lcm2023] (§8.1.1) compresses the reverse trajectory to a handful of steps, memory-efficient adaptive patching runs the denoiser only in a window around ℳ\mathcal{M}, and progressive-refinement schedules return a coarse preview within a perceptual-latency budget and refine in the background. Closing the gap to the responsiveness of a photo editor is increasingly a systems problem shared with production T2I inference stacks.

8.2 3D Spatial Reconstruction and Generation

The 3D spatial reconstruction and generation encompasses the tasks that turn images, video, sensor readings, or high-level prompts into an explicit 3D representation (a textured mesh, a signed-distance or occupancy field, a neural radiance field, or a 3D Gaussian field) of an object, a scene, or a complete navigable environment. Whereas §8.1 taught a 2D semantic-to-pixel before honor spatial structure on the image plane, this section lifts that prior off the plane and into the volumetric substrate on which embodied perception, simulation, and interaction ultimately operate. This is where appearance and geometry are forced into a single, view-consistent representation: a model must not only produce plausible pixels but place matter correctly in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} so that the result can be rendered from arbitrary viewpoints, physically simulated, navigated, and edited. It is the bridge between the flat generative priors of §8.1 and the embodied world models, simulators, and digital twins that consume 3D structure downstream.

The five subsections are organized by the direction and source of the map into a shared 3D-representation space ℛ\mathcal{R}. §8.2.1 starts with a single asset: 3D object synthesis turns the 2D prior of §8.1 into a volumetric generator through 3D-native training, score distillation, multi-view lifting, or feed-forward reconstruction. §8.2.2 scales that generator to a structured scene of placed objects and a room envelope. §8.2.3 reverses the direction: reconstruction recovers a representation faithful to sensor observations, and meets synthesis exactly where the observations run out. §8.2.4 routes through a 360-degree panorama as a structured 2D intermediate that is then lifted to 3D, and §8.2.5 closes the loop by editing an existing representation under user control.

8.2.1 3D Object Synthesis

3D object synthesis generates a complete, usable 3D asset (geometry and, optionally, appearance) from text, a single image, or a sparse set of views. Where reconstruction recovers an object consistent with given observations, synthesis additionally asks for plausible completion of what was never observed, for generative diversity, and for usability in downstream graphics and embodied pipelines (e.g., , game engines, simulators, manipulation); the output is a textured mesh, a radiance field, or a set of 3D Gaussians depending on which of fidelity, editability, rendering speed, and toolchain compatibility matters most. It is also the point at which the semantic-to-pixel prior of §8.1 (the conditional latent sampler GθG_{\theta} of Eq. (8.2)) becomes a semantic-to-3D prior Gθ3DG_{\theta}^{\text{3D}}: 3D-native generators train on 3D corpora directly, score-distillation pipelines invert the frozen 2D prior under rendering supervision, multi-view pipelines fine-tune it to emit consistent views and lift them, and feed-forward reconstructors and 3D-native latent diffusion exploit the recent object-scale 3D corpora to learn one-shot text- or image-to-3D maps. Figure 8.4 illustrates the text- or single-image-conditioned setting.

8.2.1.1 Task Definition

We cast 3D object synthesis as a paradigm-agnostic extension of the latent-generator framework of §8.1.1. Let ℛ\mathcal{R} denote a 3D-representation space taken from {mesh,SDF,voxel,triplane,NeRF,3DGS,structured latent}\{\,\textit{mesh},\,\textit{SDF},\,\textit{voxel},\,\textit{triplane},\,% \textit{NeRF},\,\text{{3DGS}},\,\textit{structured latent}\,\}, and let 𝒞\mathcal{C} denote the conditioning-input space comprising a text prompt 𝐱∈𝒳\mathbf{x}\!\in\!\mathcal{X} embedded via ϕ\phi (as in Eq. (8.2)), a single image I∈𝒴I\!\in\!\mathcal{Y}, or a multi-view set {(Iv,πv)}v=1V\{(I_{v},\pi_{v})\}_{v=1}^{V} pairing images with camera poses πv\pi_{v}. A condition encoder κ:𝒞→𝒞′\kappa:\mathcal{C}\!\to\!\mathcal{C}^{\prime} maps each input into a shared conditioning embedding. The core learning problem is to train a conditional 3D generator

Gθ3D:𝒞′→ℛ,𝐫^∼pθ3D⁢(𝐫|κ⁢(𝐜)),G_{\theta}^{\text{3D}}:\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{R},\qquad\hat{% \mathbf{r}}\sim p_{\theta}^{\text{3D}}\!\big{(}\mathbf{r}\,\big{|}\,\kappa(% \mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.9)

so that the sampled asset 𝐫^∈ℛ\hat{\mathbf{r}}\in\mathcal{R} admits high-fidelity geometry, plausibly completes unobserved regions, and renders consistently across viewpoints. Two limiting cases locate Eq. (8.9) in the literature. When κ⁢(𝐜)=∅\kappa(\mathbf{c})=\varnothing the sampler degenerates to unconditional 3D generation, the regime of early GAN- and diffusion-based 3D generators trained on category-specific corpora. At the other extreme, when 𝐜\mathbf{c} is text-only and Gθ3DG_{\theta}^{\text{3D}} is realized by distilling the 2D sampler GθG_{\theta} of Eq. (8.2) (via score-distillation sampling, multi-view consistency objectives, or volume-rendering supervision), one recovers the DreamFusion-style text-to-3D pipeline that has dominated open-vocabulary 3D synthesis since 2022.

8.2.1.2 Methodology

The four paradigms below are four ways of parameterizing and optimizing the sampler Gθ3DG_{\theta}^{\text{3D}} of Eq. (8.9), taken in the order in which each became prominent. Figure 8.5 contrasts them, making explicit which components are trained versus frozen and where the 3D representation ℛ\mathcal{R} is instantiated.

3D-Native Generators.

The earliest 3D generators instantiate Gθ3DG_{\theta}^{\text{3D}} as a sampler trained directly on a 3D representation, by denoising score matching on voxels, SDFs, or triplanes or, in earlier work, by an adversarial fit to a category-specific 3D corpus pdata3D⁢(𝐫)p_{\text{data}}^{\text{3D}}(\mathbf{r}),

ℒnative⁢(θ)=𝔼𝐫0∼pdata3D,t,ϵ⁢[‖ϵ−ϵθ3D⁢(𝐫t,t,κ⁢(𝐜))‖2],𝐫t=αt⁢𝐫0+σt⁢ϵ,\mathcal{L}_{\text{native}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r}_{0}\sim p_{\text{% data}}^{\text{3D}},\,t,\,\epsilon}\Big{[}\big{\|}\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}^{% \text{3D}}\!\big{(}\mathbf{r}_{t},\,t,\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}\big{\|}^{2}% \Big{]},\quad\mathbf{r}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{r}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\,\epsilon, (8.10)

where the noise predictor ϵθ3D\epsilon_{\theta}^{\text{3D}} operates directly on 𝐫∈ℛ\mathbf{r}\!\in\!\mathcal{R} with no 2D intermediary, so the supervision signal scales with the size of the 3D corpus rather than with 2D image–text pairs. Because 3D data is heterogeneous, these generators are themselves diverse, having been instantiated on signed distance fields [gao2022get3d], voxel grids [wu2016learning, yang20173d, zhu2018visual], point clouds [lin2018learning, huang2020pf], view sets [park2017transformation, nguyen2019hologan], neural radiance fields [chan2022efficient, chan2021pi, deng2022gram, niemeyer2021giraffe, schwarz2020graf], triplanes [chen2023singlestage, shue20233dtriplanetriplane, wang2023rodin], and 3D Gaussian Splatting [wewer2024latentsplat, roessle2024l3dg, zou2024triplane]. The scarcity and monotony of 3D corpora remain the bottleneck: even with sophisticated architectures, generated geometry and texture lack fidelity and stay confined to a handful of canonical categories, which is what pushed the field, around 2022–2023, toward paradigms that use the much larger 2D corpora as an indirect supervision signal for 3D structure.

2D-Prior Distillation (SDS Family).

The second paradigm sidesteps the 3D-data bottleneck by realizing Gθ3DG_{\theta}^{\text{3D}} as a per-shape optimization that distills gradients from a pretrained 2D generator (a CLIP model [radford2021learning] or a 2D diffusion model [rombach2022ldm]) trained on web-scale image data [schuhmann2022laion5b]. Given the frozen 2D noise predictor ϵϕ\epsilon_{\phi} of Eq. (8.2) and a differentiable renderer Render⁢(𝐫θ,π)\mathrm{Render}(\mathbf{r}_{\theta},\pi) that images a 3D representation 𝐫θ∈ℛ\mathbf{r}_{\theta}\!\in\!\mathcal{R} under camera pose π\pi, score distillation updates only the per-shape 3D parameters θ\theta via the gradient

∇θℒSDS=𝔼t,ϵ,π⁢[w⁢(t)⁢(ϵϕ⁢(𝐲tπ,t,ϕ⁢(𝐱))−ϵ)⁢∂𝐲π∂θ],𝐲π=Render⁢(𝐫θ,π),\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SDS}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\,\epsilon,\,\pi}\Big{[}% \,w(t)\,\big{(}\epsilon_{\phi}(\mathbf{y}_{t}^{\pi},\,t,\,\phi(\mathbf{x}))-% \epsilon\big{)}\,\tfrac{\partial\mathbf{y}^{\pi}}{\partial\theta}\,\Big{]},% \quad\mathbf{y}^{\pi}=\mathrm{Render}(\mathbf{r}_{\theta},\pi), (8.11)

where w⁢(t)w(t) is a step-dependent weighting and 𝐲tπ\mathbf{y}_{t}^{\pi} is the rendered view perturbed by the diffusion forward process. The contrast with Eq. (8.10) is sharp: the 2D prior of §8.1 is held fixed and no 3D corpus is consumed, while the trainable parameters live in the representation of a single asset, hence the per-shape optimization cost paid at inference. A line of work [jain2022zerodreamfields, poole2022dreamfusion, lin2023magic3d, wang2023score] applies score-distillation sampling (SDS) or its variants to a NeRF or mesh; DreamFusion [poole2022dreamfusion] obtains zero-shot text-to-3D by optimizing a NeRF whose multi-view renderings the 2D diffusion prior scores, and GaussianDreamer [yi2024gaussiandreamer] moves the same recipe onto a 3DGS representation. These methods need no 3D training data, but because the optimization is rerun for every prompt they are slow, prone to over-saturated color, and subject to the “multi-face” (Janus) artifact in which the 2D prior fails to disambiguate the front and back of an object; variational score distillation [wang2023prolificdreamer] mitigates the over-saturation but not the per-prompt cost.

Multi-View Generation and Lifting.

The third paradigm realizes Gθ3DG_{\theta}^{\text{3D}} as a two-stage pipeline: a fine-tuned 2D diffusion model generates a small set of geometrically consistent views, and a separate reconstructor lifts them to a 3D asset, so that Eq. (8.9) factorizes as

𝐫^=ℱψ⁢({𝐲^v,πv}v=1V),𝐲^v∼pθ⁢(𝐲v|𝐲ref,πv,ϕ⁢(𝐱)),\hat{\mathbf{r}}=\mathcal{F}_{\psi}\Big{(}\big{\{}\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{v},\,\pi_{% v}\big{\}}_{v=1}^{V}\Big{)},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{v}\sim p_{\theta}\big{(}% \mathbf{y}_{v}\,\big{|}\,\mathbf{y}_{\text{ref}},\,\pi_{v},\,\phi(\mathbf{x})% \big{)}, (8.12)

where the view-conditional 2D sampler pθ(⋅∣⋅)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\cdot) is a fine-tuned variant of Eq. (8.2) that additionally consumes a reference image or text 𝐲ref\mathbf{y}_{\text{ref}} and a target camera pose πv\pi_{v}, and ℱψ\mathcal{F}_{\psi} is a (typically feed-forward) multi-view-to-3D reconstructor. Two differences from Eq. (8.11) follow: the 2D prior is fine-tuned rather than frozen, and the 3D representation appears only inside the deterministic lift ℱψ\mathcal{F}_{\psi}, with no per-shape inner loop at inference, which is what lets this paradigm run one to two orders of magnitude faster than SDS at the price of depending on the view-consistency of the synthesized 𝐲^v\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{v}. The first step was to make a pretrained diffusion model pose-aware. Following fine-tuning recipes such as ControlNet [zhang2023adding] and LoRA [hu2022lora], several works [raj2023dreambooth3d, seo2023let3DFuse] fine-tune for cross-view consistency; Zero-1-to-3 [liu2023zero] opened the open-world single-image setting by training a diffusion model to synthesize a novel view conditioned on an input view and a relative camera pose; MVDream [shi2023mvdream] and ImageDream [wang2023imagedream] fix a world-camera coordinate convention from which geometry can be recovered; Magic123 [qian2023magic123] combines the Zero-1-to-3 prior with the 2D prior of Stable Diffusion; One-2-3-45 [liu2023one2345] lifts Zero-1-to-3 views to a mesh; and Consistent123 [lin2024consistent123] and MVD-Fusion [hu2024mvdfusion] add boundary and depth priors. Attention then turned to consistency across the generated views: SyncDreamer [liu2023syncdreamer] correlates features across views with a 3D-aware attention, CAT3D and Free3D [gao2024cat3d, zheng2024free3d] model the multi-view distribution jointly, and Zero123++ [shi2023zero123++] tiles six surrounding views into a single grid image, a trick inherited by One-2-3-45++ [liu2024one2345++], Instant3D [li2023instant3d], InstantMesh [xu2024instantmesh], and AR-1-to-3 [zhang2025ar123].

Feed-Forward Reconstruction and 3D-Native Latent Diffusion.

The fourth group amortizes generation across object-scale 3D corpora rather than optimizing each asset against a frozen 2D prior, in two instantiations. A feed-forward reconstructor trains Gθ3DG_{\theta}^{\text{3D}} end-to-end to map the conditioning embedding κ⁢(𝐜)\kappa(\mathbf{c}) directly to a 3D representation 𝐫^∈ℛ\hat{\mathbf{r}}\!\in\!\mathcal{R}, supervised by differentiable rendering against VV ground-truth views {𝐲v,πv}\{\mathbf{y}_{v},\pi_{v}\} drawn from the corpus,

ℒLRM⁢(θ)=𝔼(𝐜,{𝐲v,πv}v)∼pdata3D⁢∑v=1V‖Render⁢(Gθ3D⁢(κ⁢(𝐜)),πv)−𝐲v‖2.\mathcal{L}_{\text{LRM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{c},\,\{\mathbf{y}_{v},% \pi_{v}\}_{v})\sim p_{\text{data}}^{\text{3D}}}\,\sum_{v=1}^{V}\big{\|}\mathrm% {Render}\big{(}G_{\theta}^{\text{3D}}(\kappa(\mathbf{c})),\,\pi_{v}\big{)}-% \mathbf{y}_{v}\big{\|}^{2}. (8.13)

A 3D-native latent diffusion model instead learns a 3D autoencoder pair (E3D,D3D)(E^{\text{3D}},D^{\text{3D}}) with 𝐳3D=E3D⁢(𝐫)\mathbf{z}^{\text{3D}}\!=\!E^{\text{3D}}(\mathbf{r}), trains a denoising model on the compact latent, and decodes via 𝐫^=D3D⁢(𝐳^3D)\hat{\mathbf{r}}=D^{\text{3D}}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{\text{3D}}),

ℒ3DL⁢(θ)=𝔼𝐳03D,t,ϵ⁢[‖ϵ−ϵθ⁢(𝐳t3D,t,κ⁢(𝐜))‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{3DL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}^{\text{3D}}_{0},\,t,\,% \epsilon}\Big{[}\big{\|}\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{\text{3D}% }_{t},\,t,\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}\big{\|}^{2}\Big{]}, (8.14)

which is the 2D LDM objective Eq. (8.5) of §8.1.1 with the autoencoder moved from pixels to ℛ\mathcal{R}. Both variants avoid the per-shape optimization of Eq. (8.11), but only the reconstructor uses a single prediction pass; latent diffusion still samples iteratively. The unlocking factor was the arrival of Objaverse and Objaverse-XL [deitke2023objaverse, deitke2023objaversexl]. LRM [hong2023lrm] and its follow-ups [tang2024lgm, wang2024crm, wang2025moving] show that large transformers trained purely with rendering losses capture object geometry and texture in detail and generalize to unseen images, and a parallel line introduces compact 3D-native latent codes [chen20253dtopia, zhang20233dshape2vecset, ye2022structured, yang2025prometheus] whose distribution a latent diffusion model can learn; TRELLIS [xiang2025trellis], CLAY [zhang2024clay], HiGS-RGBN [shen2025highGSRGBN], and Hunyuan3D [yang2024hunyuan3d] build on this to bring generated assets close to production grade while keeping the open-vocabulary reach that the SDS family pioneered.

Two design choices cut across the four paradigms. The representation ℛ\mathcal{R} (mesh, SDF, voxel, triplane, NeRF, 3DGS, or structured latent) is largely independent of the paradigm: SDS has been run on NeRFs and on 3DGS, feed-forward reconstructors output triplanes, meshes, or Gaussians, and latent-diffusion stacks decode to almost any explicit representation through a learned VAE. So is the conditioning modality: the same backbone takes text, a single image, or sparse views by changing only the encoder κ\kappa and the camera-pose embedding, and production systems chain them (image-to-3D conditioned on a text-to-image preview). The succession of paradigms itself tracks the accumulation of supervision at each level, from 3D-native corpora to 2D image–text pairs to Zero-1-to-3-style multi-view priors to Objaverse-XL-scale 3D, with the most recent industrial systems sitting in the fourth paradigm while inheriting the multi-view-consistency tricks of the third.

8.2.1.3 Benchmarks

Evaluation draws on object-scale training corpora, on dedicated benchmark suites that curate prompts and human ratings, and on metrics that probe alignment, geometry, and appearance separately.

Training Corpora.

Object-scale 3D corpora drive the feed-forward and latent-diffusion paradigms; Table 8.2 lists the ones most commonly used, and Figure 8.6 shows representative Objaverse-XL assets. They span the classical CAD repository ShapeNet [shapenet2015], category-bounded real-world scans with accurate geometry and PBR textures (Google Scanned Objects [downs2022googleGSO], OmniObject3D [wu2023omniobject3d] with dense multi-view imagery), the open-vocabulary web-scraped Objaverse and Objaverse-XL [deitke2023objaverse, deitke2023objaversexl] that unlocked the fourth paradigm, and G-Objaverse [zuo2024gobjavers], which adds text-driven synthesized assets between the two.

Evaluation Benchmark Suites.

Recent benchmarks have moved to multi-dimensional assessment beyond plain text–image alignment. GT23D-Bench [cai2024gt23d] curates a high-fidelity dataset and a suite of 3D-aware metrics spanning alignment and visual quality; MATE-3D [zhang2025mate3d] provides designed prompt categories with large-scale human annotations across several perceptual dimensions and introduces HyperScore as a learned evaluator; T23D-QA [li2025t23d] adopts a question-answer protocol that scores geometry, texture, and alignment independently; and Gen3DEval [maiti2025gen3deval] fine-tunes a vision-language model for 3D quality assessment, scoring text fidelity, appearance, and surface quality from rendered surface normals. Together with the 3D-relevant subsets of the 2D suites collected in §8.1.1 (Table 8.1), they form the de facto evaluation protocol for 3D object synthesis.

Constraint-specific Metrics.

Because an asset is judged from many viewpoints and under different downstream uses, evaluation reports complementary metrics along three axes. Text-3D alignment renders multi-view images from the asset and measures text–image similarity with CLIP-like encoders, aggregated across views (mean, worst-case, or view-consistency variants); pure CLIP alignment can be misled by texture “shortcuts” and does not guarantee geometric correctness, which motivates the 3D-aware alignment scores of GT23D-Bench [cai2024gt23d] and learned evaluators such as HyperScore [zhang2025mate3d]. Geometry quality is measured against ground-truth shapes, where they exist, by Chamfer Distance (CD) [huang2025spar3d], F-score at varying thresholds, normal consistency, and volumetric IoU for watertight meshes; for text-to-3D without ground truth it falls back on multi-view depth and normal consistency, silhouette consistency, and learned 3D-quality predictors. Appearance and multi-view consistency are measured by perceptual distances (LPIPS) between rendered views and references where available, by view-consistency measures (variance across views under fixed lighting and camera trajectories), and by human studies, which recent benchmarks collect as multi-dimensional ratings to calibrate the automatic metrics [zhang2025mate3d, li2025t23d].

The paradigm succession of §8.2.1.2 shows up in two measurable quantities. Generation time has fallen by about three orders of magnitude: DreamFusion [poole2022dreamfusion] needs roughly 1.5 hours per asset and Magic3D [lin2023magic3d] about 40 minutes, whereas LRM [hong2023lrm] reconstructs a shape in about 5 seconds and InstantMesh [xu2024instantmesh] completes image-to-3D in around 10 seconds. Image-to-3D geometry is now routinely scored on Google Scanned Objects [downs2022googleGSO] with Chamfer Distance (lower is better) and F-score at τ=0.2\tau{=}0.2 (higher is better), where InstantMesh [xu2024instantmesh] reaches CD ≈0.18\approx 0.18 and FS ≈0.88\approx 0.88, ahead of TripoSR [tochilkin2024triposr] (0.2170.217 / 0.8430.843), CRM [wang2024crm] (0.2520.252 / 0.7870.787), and LGM [tang2024lgm] (0.3450.345 / 0.6710.671). Coarse text-to-3D alignment, by contrast, is saturated: CLIP-style scores no longer separate the strongest systems, so Hunyuan3D 2.0 [hunyuan3d22025tencent] reports ULIP- and Uni3D-based image- and text-to-shape similarity backed by a study in which 50 participants rated 300 unselected results, and learned evaluators (HyperScore on MATE-3D [zhang2025mate3d], T23D-QA [li2025t23d]) score geometry and texture on separate axes. The reconstruction metrics carry their own caveat: CD and F-score saturate on coarse geometry and can reward visually plausible but physically thin assets, so reported gains are credible mainly where geometric, perceptual, and human ratings agree. Commercial text- and image-to-3D services now ship these capabilities with PBR export to game engines, alongside research systems such as Meta 3D Gen [bensadoun2024meta3dgen] and the open-vocabulary 3D-native-latent systems CLAY [zhang2024clay], TRELLIS [xiang2025trellis], and Hunyuan3D [yang2024hunyuan3d, hunyuan3d22025tencent].

8.2.1.4 Challenges and Trends

Four problems remain open, and they depend on one another: the multi-view consistency of the asset, the representation it lands in, whether progress on either can be measured reliably, and the data that ultimately drives all three.

Multi-View and 3D Consistency under Open-Vocabulary Prompts.

Enforcing consistent geometry and texture across viewpoints while preserving fine detail remains difficult in all four paradigms, and the failures have names. The Janus artifact renders both the front and the back of an object as a frontal face, most acutely in SDS pipelines, where the 2D prior cannot disambiguate camera direction; view drift makes adjacent views of a multi-view stack disagree on geometry, a residual concern in Zero-1-to-3-style cascades that SyncDreamer’s cross-view attention and Zero123++’s tiled six-view trick only partly remove; and texture seams appear where neighboring views’ color and lighting cannot be merged into a globally coherent UV map, a persistent weakness of feed-forward reconstructors. These failures motivate 3D-native backbones with structured latents [xiang2025trellis] that share parameters across views by construction, and benchmarks that score multi-view consistency rather than a single rendered view [zhang2025mate3d].

Representation Trade-offs between Fidelity, Editability, and Deployability.

Even a consistent asset must land somewhere a downstream tool can consume, and the choice of representation is not neutral. Meshes with UV/PBR textures are what game engines and simulators want but lose detail to discretization; radiance fields and Gaussians give high visual fidelity and fast rendering but require conversion, which introduces its own failures: topology breakage during marching-cubes-style meshing, baked illumination that fuses lighting into albedo when converting from a NeRF or 3DGS, and texture bleeding across UV seams. The response is unified latent representations that decode to several formats [xiang2025trellis], so that a single generator serves diverse downstream requirements and the choice of ℛ\mathcal{R} is deferred to inference.

Scalable, Reliable Evaluation and Human-Aligned Metrics.

These representation choices complicate evaluation, because the metric panel a paper reports tends to depend on which format its generator targets, and the automatic metrics remain imperfect for geometry plausibility and asset usability. CLIP-style alignment is fooled by texture shortcuts that ignore the underlying shape; Chamfer Distance saturates on coarse geometry while penalizing semantically irrelevant fine detail; and LPIPS on rendered views cannot distinguish a physically plausible asset from a visually plausible cardboard cut-out. Multi-dimensional evaluators trained on large human-annotation sets (e.g., , HyperScore on MATE-3D [zhang2025mate3d]) and diagnostic benchmarks (e.g., , GT23D-Bench [cai2024gt23d], T23D-QA [li2025t23d]) that score alignment, geometry, and texture on independent axes are the current answer, so that progress on one axis is no longer masked by averaging.

Data Scaling and Asset Readiness.

Underlying consistency, representation, and evaluation alike is the supply of training data and the industrial scale at which it can be exploited. Large-scale corpora such as Objaverse-XL [deitke2023objaversexl] and industrial-scale systems such as Hunyuan3D [hunyuan3d22025tencent, hunyuan3d2025hunyuan3domni] and Meta 3D Gen [bensadoun2024meta3dgen] point toward high-resolution, engine-ready assets with controllable materials, relightable textures, and post-processing for watertightness and topology. The question has shifted from whether a paradigm can be trained at scale, which the fourth paradigm has settled, to which slice of the 3D-asset distribution the available corpora still under-represent: articulated objects, semi-transparent or refractive materials, and topologically non-trivial assemblies are visibly thinner in current open corpora than in production pipelines, and closing this gap is the explicit target of recent industrial releases.

8.2.2 3D Scene Synthesis

Scene-level synthesis extends 3D generation from a single asset 𝐫∈ℛ\mathbf{r}\!\in\!\mathcal{R} to an entire environment: a clutter of objects whose positions, orientations, and pairwise relations together compose a navigable room or open-world scene. Where §8.2.1 models the conditional distribution of one object given a prompt, scene synthesis must jointly model (i) a variable number of objects, (ii) their global SE⁢(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) placements, (iii) their pairwise spatial and functional relations, and (iv) the envelope geometry (floor, walls, ceiling) that closes the scene; the output is a structured set rather than a vector in ℛ\mathcal{R}, and the conditioning broadens from text to layouts, scene graphs, sparse calibrated views, and full camera trajectories. The result must be navigable, not only renderable, which makes the problem harder than object synthesis along three axes at once: geometric coherence across the clutter, semantic consistency between related objects, and view generalization along an SE⁢(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) trajectory rather than a fixed look-at orbit. Four families answer it: layout- and scene-graph-conditioned generators that produce the structured set from a symbolic prior; view-to-3D synthesizers that regress or sample a continuous radiance or Gaussian field from sparse calibrated views; view-to-view synthesizers that skip the explicit 3D representation and learn a conditional map from observed to novel views; and video-model-based synthesizers that treat a pretrained video diffusion model as an implicit 3D prior with the camera trajectory as an additional conditioning channel.

8.2.2.1 Task Definition

We cast 3D scene synthesis as a scene-level extension of the object-synthesis framework of §8.2.1. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the scene-output space whose elements 𝐬=({𝐫i}i=1N,{𝐓i}i=1N,𝐆,ℰroom)\mathbf{s}=\big{(}\{\mathbf{r}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},\,\{\mathbf{T}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},% \,\mathbf{G},\,\mathcal{E}_{\text{room}}\big{)} package NN object representations 𝐫i∈ℛ\mathbf{r}_{i}\!\in\!\mathcal{R} (with ℛ\mathcal{R} the per-object space of §8.2.1), their global poses 𝐓i∈SE⁢(3)\mathbf{T}_{i}\!\in\!\mathrm{SE}(3), a relational graph 𝐆\mathbf{G} over the object set, and an envelope geometry ℰroom\mathcal{E}_{\text{room}} encoding the room shell (walls, floor, ceiling). The conditioning space broadens to 𝒞scene⊇{text ⁢𝐱,layout ⁢𝐋,scene graph ⁢𝐆in,sparse views ⁢{(Iv,πv)}v,camera trajectory ⁢{πv}v}\mathcal{C}^{\text{scene}}\supseteq\{\,\text{text }\mathbf{x},\,\text{layout }% \mathbf{L},\,\text{scene graph }\mathbf{G}_{\text{in}},\,\text{sparse views }% \{(I_{v},\pi_{v})\}_{v},\,\text{camera trajectory }\{\pi_{v}\}_{v}\,\}, with a condition encoder κscene:𝒞scene→𝒞scene⁣′\kappa^{\text{scene}}:\mathcal{C}^{\text{scene}}\!\to\!\mathcal{C}^{\text{% scene}\prime} mapping each input mode into a shared embedding. The core learning problem is to train a conditional scene generator

Gθscene:𝒞scene⁣′→𝒮,𝐬^∼pθscene⁢(𝐬|κscene⁢(𝐜)),G_{\theta}^{\text{scene}}:\mathcal{C}^{\text{scene}\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{% S},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{s}}\sim p_{\theta}^{\text{scene}}\!\big{(}\mathbf{s}\,% \big{|}\,\kappa^{\text{scene}}(\mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.15)

so that the sampled scene 𝐬^∈𝒮\hat{\mathbf{s}}\!\in\!\mathcal{S} admits coherent inter-object geometry, semantically plausible relations, and view-consistent renderings under arbitrary SE⁢(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) trajectories. Two limiting cases fix the scope of Eq. (8.15). When N=1N\!=\!1, 𝐆=∅\mathbf{G}\!=\!\varnothing, and ℰroom=∅\mathcal{E}_{\text{room}}\!=\!\varnothing, the scene degenerates to a single asset and the sampler recovers Eq. (8.9): scene synthesis is a strict generalization of object synthesis. At the opposite extreme, when 𝒮\mathcal{S} is instantiated as an ordered sequence of views {Iv}v=1V\{I_{v}\}_{v=1}^{V} without an explicit 3D substrate, the sampler reduces to a camera-trajectory-conditioned video generator (the regime of §8.2.2.2 below), so that “scene synthesis” and “consistent video generation” are two boundary regimes of the same problem.

8.2.2.2 Methodology

Each of the four paradigms is a different factorization of GθsceneG_{\theta}^{\text{scene}} in Eq. (8.15), from sparse structural controls (layouts and scene graphs) through continuous 3D representations to video-based synthesis; Figure 8.7 previews them against a common scene.

Layout and Scene-graph Conditioned Methods.

A major line of research generates 3D environments from high-level structural priors such as layouts 𝐋\mathbf{L} or scene graphs 𝐆in\mathbf{G}_{\text{in}}, instantiating Eq. (8.15) by materializing the structured tuple as an explicit object set,

𝐬^={(𝐫^i,𝐓^i)}i=1N,𝐬^∼pθ⁢({(𝐫i,𝐓i)}i|κ⁢(𝐋⁢ or ⁢𝐆in),ϕ⁢(𝐱)),\hat{\mathbf{s}}=\big{\{}(\hat{\mathbf{r}}_{i},\,\hat{\mathbf{T}}_{i})\big{\}}% _{i=1}^{N},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{s}}\sim p_{\theta}\!\Big{(}\{(\mathbf{r}_{i},% \mathbf{T}_{i})\}_{i}\,\Big{|}\,\kappa(\mathbf{L}\text{ or }\mathbf{G}_{\text{% in}}),\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\Big{)}, (8.16)

where the joint over the NN slots and their poses is factorized autoregressively (a transformer over object slots) or as a denoising diffusion over the slot tensor. SceneFormer [wang2021sceneformer] explored autoregressive modeling of room layouts and furniture placement, and DiffuScene [tang2024diffuscene] introduced diffusion over object arrangements, improving realism and diversity. Recent work adds language and visual reasoning for compositional control: LayoutGPT [feng2023layoutgpt] plans the layout with an LLM before neural scene construction, and LayoutVLM [sun2025layoutvlm] optimizes layout consistency under multimodal alignment. Scene-graph approaches (GraphDreamer [gao2024graphdreamer], CommonScenes [zhai2023commonscenes], EchoScene [zhai2024echoscene]) use relational reasoning to keep placements plausible, and InstructScene [lin2024instructscene] adds natural-language conditions for controllable scene creation. Beyond indoor settings, CityCraft [deng2024citycraft] scales layout synthesis to the city level, and GALA3D [zhou2024gala3d] couples layout-guided diffusion with Gaussian-based rendering for photorealistic multi-object environments.

View-to-3D Representation Synthesis.

The second paradigm trades the explicit structured set for a continuous 3D representation, recovering the scene as a radiance field or 3D Gaussian collection from sparse calibrated views; the scene tuple collapses into a single field,

ℛ^scene=ℱψ⁢({(Iv,πv)}v=1V),𝐬^≡ℛ^scene,\hat{\mathcal{R}}^{\text{scene}}=\mathcal{F}_{\psi}\!\Big{(}\big{\{}(I_{v},\pi% _{v})\big{\}}_{v=1}^{V}\Big{)},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{s}}\equiv\hat{\mathcal{R}}^{% \text{scene}}, (8.17)

where ℱψ\mathcal{F}_{\psi} is either a deterministic feed-forward regressor or a generative sampler over the field. This scales the multi-view-and-lift recipe of §8.2.1.2 from one asset to a full scene by replacing the per-object reconstructor with a scene-scale one. Deterministic regressors such as PixelNeRF [yu2021pixelnerf], PixelSplat [charatan2024pixelsplat], DepthSplat [xu2024depthsplat], and MVSplat [chen2024mvsplat] / MVSplat360 [chen2024mvsplat360] stay strictly faithful to the input views and are reconstruction methods, treated in §8.2.3.2. The generative variant samples the field instead: DreamScene [li2024dreamscene] introduces a diffusion prior over Gaussian fields for text-conditioned scene creation, and Generative 3DGS [Schwarz2025ggs] generates 3D Gaussians for scenes with video priors.

View-to-View Synthesis (Regression and Generative).

The third paradigm skips the explicit 3D representation altogether and formulates novel view synthesis as a direct conditional 2D-to-2D map from observed to target views,

I^π∗∼pθ⁢(Iπ∗|{(Iv,πv)}v=1V,π∗),\hat{I}_{\pi^{*}}\sim p_{\theta}\!\Big{(}I_{\pi^{*}}\,\Big{|}\,\big{\{}(I_{v},% \pi_{v})\big{\}}_{v=1}^{V},\,\pi^{*}\Big{)}, (8.18)

where π∗\pi^{*} is the target camera pose and no intermediate 3D representation is materialized. Regression-based approaches learn a deterministic map: SRT [sajjadi2022scene] encodes the scene into latent tokens that support interpolation and extrapolation across viewpoints, and LVSM [jin2025lvsm] predicts novel views with a large feed-forward transformer and minimal 3D inductive bias. Generative approaches model the conditional distribution over unseen views, which permits stochastic synthesis under ambiguity and large viewpoint changes: Photoconsistent-NVS [yu2023long] and SEVA [zhou2025stable] use diffusion to improve diversity and robustness along extended camera trajectories, and CausNVS [kong2025causnvs] generates views autoregressively and causally, modeling inter-view dependencies explicitly to stay coherent across complex viewpoint transitions.

Video-model Based Scene Synthesis.

The fourth paradigm adds temporal coherence to the viewpoint variety of the view-to-view family by exploiting large video generation models as spatiotemporal priors; the scene tuple is materialized as a frame sequence,

{I^v}v=1V∼pθvideo⁢({Iv}v=1V|{πv}v=1V,ϕ⁢(𝐱)),\{\hat{I}_{v}\}_{v=1}^{V}\sim p_{\theta}^{\text{video}}\!\Big{(}\{I_{v}\}_{v=1% }^{V}\,\Big{|}\,\{\pi_{v}\}_{v=1}^{V},\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\Big{)}, (8.19)

treating the scene as the implicit 3D structure of a coherent video and the camera trajectory {πv}\{\pi_{v}\} as an explicit conditioning channel. Where the feed-forward reconstructors of §8.2.1.2 output a static asset in one pass, the video paradigm trades static 3D for temporally coherent multi-frame output that mirrors the navigability requirement of a scene more directly. CameraCtrl [he2024cameractrl] and MotionCtrl [wang2024motionctrl] condition video generation on camera trajectories directly; ViewCrafter [yu2024viewcrafter] and Gen3C [ren2025gen3c] add geometric guidance by unprojecting observed views into an intermediate 3D representation and reprojecting it to the target viewpoints, which improves pose fidelity; and CAT4D [wu2025cat4d] and 4DiM [watson2024controlling] train jointly on posed static multi-view data and on temporal video data, so that viewpoint variation and temporal dynamics are modeled together for 4D scene synthesis.

8.2.2.3 Benchmarks

The four paradigms draw on different training corpora and report on different metric panels, each inherited from a precursor task.

Training Corpora.

Table 8.3 lists the corpora in use. Layout-conditioned methods rely overwhelmingly on 3D-FRONT [fu20213dfront], usually combined with its companion 3D-FUTURE [fu20213dfuture] furniture library for instance-level geometry. View-based methods (P2 / P3) draw on real-world scans of residential interiors (ScanNet [dai2017scannet], Matterport3D [chang2017matterport3d]), on photorealistic synthetic corpora with ground-truth depth and normals (Hypersim [roberts2021hypersim]), and on Replica [straub2019replica] for compact high-fidelity indoor benchmarks. Video-model-based methods (P4) inherit the web-scale supervision of their underlying video prior, far larger than any 3D corpus but without explicit 3D supervision, supplemented by camera-pose-annotated subsets distilled from ScanNet, RealEstate10K [zhou2018stereo], or hand-labeled trajectories.

Evaluation Benchmark Suites.

Layout-conditioned methods report the metrics introduced with ATISS on 3D-FRONT (object-category frequency, pairwise-relation accuracy, and FID on rendered top-down or perspective views). View-to-3D and view-to-view methods adopt the NeRF-era panel of PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS on held-out views of ScanNet, RealEstate10K [zhou2018stereo], or DL3DV-10K [ling2024dl3dv]. Video-model-based methods add FVD and a camera-trajectory-adherence metric, the mean translation and rotation error between requested and recovered camera poses.

Constraint-specific Metrics.

Four axes mirror the scene tuple of Eq. (8.15): layout adherence (object-count agreement, pairwise-relation accuracy on 𝐆\mathbf{G}, and bounding-box IoU between requested and synthesized placements); geometric fidelity where ground truth exists (Chamfer Distance, F-score, and depth and normal consistency against held-out views); photometric quality (PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS against ground-truth views, FID / KID against held-out scene distributions, and FVD for video outputs); and camera-pose adherence, most relevant for P4 (translation and rotation error of poses recovered by structure-from-motion or a learned pose regressor). A paper reports the subset of axes its paradigm can be scored on, which is why comparison across paradigms remains difficult.

8.2.2.4 Challenges and Trends

Scene synthesis meets the problems of object synthesis on a structured set: more conditioning variables, more output components, and longer trajectories enter the cost at once.

Cross-Paradigm Inconsistency.

The four paradigms solve subtly different problems, and each leaves a gap when used alone: a layout-conditioned generator can satisfy the symbolic prior 𝐆in\mathbf{G}_{\text{in}} yet produce a non-traversable static scene, and a view-to-3D generator can produce a navigable Gaussian field that ignores the requested object semantics. The gaps surface as layout-adherence drift, where the generated NeRF or 3DGS no longer satisfies the input layout once the user roams outside the trained view envelope; object drop, where small or thin objects from 𝐋\mathbf{L} are silently omitted during continuous-field synthesis; and geometry flattening, where a multi-object composition collapses into a single textured slab when the 2D or video prior dominates. Hybrids such as GALA3D [zhou2024gala3d] and ViewCrafter [yu2024viewcrafter] chain a layout or geometry prior with a Gaussian or video renderer to keep both halves honest, and future systems will more likely compose the four paradigms than choose among them.

Scaling Beyond Indoor Rooms.

Almost all paradigms remain anchored to furnished indoor rooms because that is where the training corpora live: 3D-FRONT [fu20213dfront] alone supplies the layout supervision for the dominant P1 methods, and ScanNet, Matterport3D, and Hypersim dominate P2 / P3. The result is an outdoor and urban scale gap that CityCraft [deng2024citycraft] is among the few systems to address, a category imbalance with many furniture classes but few terrain, vegetation, or industrial ones, and an open-world domain shift under which methods trained on residential interiors fail on industrial sites, excavations, or invented environments. Web-scraped open-vocabulary scene corpora and hybrid synthetic-real pipelines that blend procedurally generated environments with captured scans are the active responses, both for breadth and to control the long tail of the scene-class distribution.

Camera-Trajectory Coherence under Long-Horizon Synthesis.

The video paradigm (§8.2.2.2) excels at short camera moves but degrades on long, unbounded trajectories that require persistent world memory. Long trajectories expose temporal blur, where textures shimmer or drift between frames; scene amnesia, where objects reappear with different geometry when the camera revisits a location; and pose-conditioning collapse, where the model learns to ignore the camera signal in favor of the marginal video distribution. ViewCrafter [yu2024viewcrafter]’s unprojection and reprojection scaffold, Gen3C [ren2025gen3c]’s 3D cache, and CAT4D [wu2025cat4d]’s joint multi-view and video training all inject an explicit 3D inductive bias back into the video prior, but the trade-off between the video prior’s perceptual quality and the geometric prior’s rigidity remains an open design tension.

Evaluation.

A P1 layout-adherence score and a P3 PSNR cannot be ranked against each other, no single dataset evaluates layout faithfulness, geometric fidelity, photometric quality, and pose adherence jointly, and no human-aligned evaluator analogous to HyperScore [zhang2025mate3d] has been validated on scene outputs.

Trends: Toward 4D and World Models.

Scene synthesis targets static geometry conditioned on camera poses, but the same formulation is being extended toward 4D synthesis and action-conditioned world modeling: Dreamer [hafner2019dreamer], GameNGen [valevski2024diffusion], Diamond [alonso2024diffusionworldmodelingvisual], RTFM [worldlabs_rtfm], and Genie3 [genie3] move from static view or video synthesis toward open-ended environment generation in which spatial structure, temporal evolution, and interaction are modeled together. From the standpoint of this subsection, scalable, temporally coherent video generation with explicit viewpoint control is the foundation those systems build on; they are treated as world models in §8.6.

8.2.3 3D Scene Reconstruction

3D reconstruction recovers a digital 3D representation of a scene or object from sensor observations such as RGB images, video, depth maps, or point clouds, and has long been a foundational problem in computer vision, graphics, and immersive systems such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and digital twins. Its difference from the synthesis tasks of §8.2.1 and §8.2.2 is one of intent: synthesis is open-ended generation in which plausibility and diversity dominate, whereas reconstruction must explain the input views faithfully before any inference about unobserved regions is attempted. Reconstruction is where perception becomes geometry: it turns raw sensor streams into an explicit, metric 3D substrate that simulators, AR / VR systems, digital twins, and embodied agents can reason over, manipulate, and render, and it supplies the ground-truth geometry against which the generative tasks of §8.2 are ultimately measured. Three families follow: iterative reconstruction, which solves a per-scene optimization against the input views; feed-forward reconstruction, which amortizes that cost into a learned map from observations to a 3D representation; and complete reconstruction, which generatively fills the occluded regions and so makes the boundary with synthesis explicit. Figure 8.8 previews representative reconstruction tasks.

8.2.3.1 Task Definition

We cast 3D scene reconstruction as the observation-conditioned counterpart of the generative frameworks of §8.2.1 and §8.2.2. Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} denote the space of multi-sensor observations. Each observation 𝐎∈𝒪\mathbf{O}\in\mathcal{O} is represented as a finite collection of sensor measurements. Depending on the sensing setup, 𝐎\mathbf{O} may consist of multi-view RGB images {Iv}v=1V\{I_{v}\}_{v=1}^{V}, posed images {(Iv,πv)}v=1V\{(I_{v},\pi_{v})\}_{v=1}^{V}, RGB-D or RGB-normal observations {(Iv,dv)}v=1V\{(I_{v},d_{v})\}_{v=1}^{V}, point clouds, LiDAR scans, or their combinations. Here, IvI_{v} denotes the RGB image from view vv, πv\pi_{v} denotes the corresponding calibrated camera pose, and dvd_{v} denotes an associated depth or normal map. Let ℛrec\mathcal{R}^{\text{rec}} denote the output 3D-representation space, taken from the same ℛ\mathcal{R} as in §8.2.1, including mesh, SDF, voxel, triplane, NeRF, 3DGS, point map, structured latent. The core learning problem is to obtain a reconstruction operator

Gθrec:𝒪→ℛrec,𝐫^rec=Gθrec⁢(𝐎)(deterministic)or𝐫^rec∼pθrec⁢(𝐫rec|𝐎)(generative),G_{\theta}^{\text{rec}}:\mathcal{O}\rightarrow\mathcal{R}^{\text{rec}},\qquad% \hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}=G_{\theta}^{\text{rec}}(\mathbf{O})\quad\text{(% deterministic)}\quad\text{or}\quad\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}\sim p_{\theta}% ^{\text{rec}}\!\big{(}\mathbf{r}^{\text{rec}}\,\big{|}\,\mathbf{O}\big{)}\quad% \text{(generative)}, (8.20)

that minimizes a reconstruction loss against the input views,

ℒrec⁢(𝐫^rec,𝐎)=∑(Iv,πv)∈𝐎‖Render⁢(𝐫^rec,πv)−Iv‖2+λ⁢Ω⁢(𝐫^rec),\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}\big{(}\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}},\mathbf{O}\big{)}% \;=\;\sum_{(I_{v},\pi_{v})\in\mathbf{O}}\big{\|}\mathrm{Render}(\hat{\mathbf{r% }}^{\text{rec}},\pi_{v})-I_{v}\big{\|}^{2}\;+\;\lambda\,\Omega(\hat{\mathbf{r}% }^{\text{rec}}), (8.21)

where Ω\Omega is an optional geometric or smoothness regularizer and Render\mathrm{Render} is a differentiable renderer of ℛrec\mathcal{R}^{\text{rec}}. The structural contrast with §8.2.1 is sharp: there, the conditioning κ⁢(𝐜)\kappa(\mathbf{c}) is a high-level prior (text, single image, multi-view) and the objective is a generative likelihood; here, the conditioning 𝐎\mathbf{O} is sensor data and the objective is an observation-fidelity loss.

8.2.3.2 Methodology

The three paradigms are three parameterizations of the reconstruction operator GθrecG_{\theta}^{\text{rec}} of Eq. (8.20), taken in the order in which each became dominant. Figure 8.9 contrasts them, making explicit whether the 3D representation is optimized per scene, regressed in a single forward pass, or sampled from a generative posterior over the unobserved regions.

Iterative 3D Reconstruction.

The classical paradigm casts reconstruction as a per-scene optimization: there is no learned θ\theta shared across scenes; the 3D representation 𝐫\mathbf{r} itself is the optimization variable, and Eq. (8.21) is minimized from scratch for each new input,

𝐫^=arg⁡min𝐫∈ℛrec⁢∑(Iv,πv)∈𝐎‖Render⁢(𝐫,πv)−Iv‖2+λ⁢Ω⁢(𝐫).\hat{\mathbf{r}}\;=\;\arg\min_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{R}^{\text{rec}}}\;\sum_{(% I_{v},\pi_{v})\in\mathbf{O}}\big{\|}\mathrm{Render}(\mathbf{r},\pi_{v})-I_{v}% \big{\|}^{2}\;+\;\lambda\,\Omega(\mathbf{r}). (8.22)

Classical image-based reconstruction is rooted in Structure-from-Motion (SfM) [bolles1987epipolar, tomasi1992shape, fitzgibbon1998automatic, schonberger2016structure], which estimates camera poses from unposed images, followed by Multi-View Stereo (MVS) [ullman1979interpretation, hartley2003multiple, Agarwal2010BAL, snavely2006photo, furukawa2015multi, schonberger2016pixelwise], which recovers dense geometry. Decades of refinement have made SfM + MVS a mature and widely used pipeline (see [hartley2003multiple] for a comprehensive treatment), yet it still struggles with textureless surfaces, reflective objects, and large illumination changes.

A more recent line represents the scene as a continuous function parameterized by a neural network: signed distance functions [park2019deepsdf, chibane2020neural, wang2021neus, yu2022monosdf], occupancy fields [mescheder2019occupancy, peng2020convolutional], and neural radiance fields [mildenhall2021nerf, barron2021mip, wang2021nerf, barron2022mip]. The original formulations were expensive to train and render and limited in quality; PlenOctrees [yu2021plenoctrees], Plenoxels [fridovich2022plenoxels], Instant-NGP [muller2022instant], RefNeRF [verbin2022ref], TensoRF [chen2022tensorf], and ZipNeRF [barron2023zip] are among the many follow-ups that improved efficiency and fidelity, but all of them still require a large number of input images per scene. Sparse-view variants add auxiliary information such as regularization [niemeyer2022regnerf], depth priors [roessle2022dense, deng2022depth], point clouds [xu2022point], and surface priors [oechsle2021unisurf], or distill a 2D diffusion prior into the per-scene representation, the SDS recipe of §8.2.1.2 applied to reconstruction from one or a few images [melas2023realfusion, metzer2023latent, tang2023make]. 3D Gaussian Splatting [kerbl20233d] then made per-scene optimization fast, training within minutes and rendering in real time, with subsequent work adding depth regularization, anti-aliasing, mesh extraction, and surface alignment [chung2024depth, yu2024mip, huang20242d, guedon2024sugar]. All of these systems, however, work well only over nearby views or a small scene and must be re-optimized from scratch for every new input, which motivates the amortized paradigm.

Feed-forward 3D Reconstruction.

The feed-forward paradigm amortizes the per-scene optimization of Eq. (8.22) across a learned prior: a network GθrecG_{\theta}^{\text{rec}} is trained once on a large multi-view corpus, then deployed in a single forward pass on unseen inputs, minimizing

ℒFF⁢(θ)=𝔼(𝐎,𝐫gt)∼pdata⁢[𝒟⁢(Gθrec⁢(𝐎),𝐫gt)],\mathcal{L}_{\text{FF}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{O},\,\mathbf{r}_{% \text{gt}})\sim p_{\text{data}}}\Big{[}\mathcal{D}\big{(}G_{\theta}^{\text{rec% }}(\mathbf{O}),\,\mathbf{r}_{\text{gt}}\big{)}\Big{]}, (8.23)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} is a representation-specific distance (Chamfer Distance for point maps, a rendering loss for radiance fields) and (𝐎,𝐫gt)(\mathbf{O},\mathbf{r}_{\text{gt}}) are observation–asset pairs drawn from a 3D corpus. This is the reconstruction-side analogue of the view-to-3D paradigm of §8.2.2.2: sparse calibrated views are mapped feed-forward to a continuous scene representation, but the supervision is a reconstruction loss against ground-truth 3D rather than a rendering loss against held-out views alone.

Early feed-forward work applied 2D networks to individual 3D representations, for depth estimation [eigen2014depth, liu2015learning], voxel reconstruction [choy20163d, wu20153d], point-cloud reconstruction [fan2017point, qi2017pointnet], and mesh deformation [wang2018pixel2mesh, gkioxari2019mesh], but remained limited to single objects or small datasets. Learned components then replaced individual stages of the SfM + MVS pipeline, keypoint detection and description [detone2018superpoint, dusmanu2019d2, tyszkiewicz2020disk], image matching [sarlin2020superglue, lindenberger2023lightglue], pose estimation [kendall2015posenet, yin2018geonet, kendall2017geometric], and depth prediction [zhou2017unsupervised, yin2018geonet], proving more robust and accurate than their hand-designed counterparts and being integrated into the classical pipeline [vzbontar2016stereo, yao2018mvsnet, yao2019recurrent]. DUSt3R [wang2024dust3r] and MASt3R [mast3r] then reconstructed large scenes from unposed images end to end: similar in spirit to MVS but without explicit keypoint detection, matching, and pose estimation, the model predicts point maps in the reference view directly and recovers camera poses in post-processing, and follow-ups [tang2025mv, wang2025Cut3R, yang2025fast3r, zhang2025FLARE, wang2025vggt] have improved quality and efficiency at scale.

Beyond geometry alone, a parallel line recovers geometry and appearance together through differentiable rendering. Scene Representation Networks [sitzmann2019scene] and Light Field Networks [sitzmann2021light] introduced ray-based querying for novel-view synthesis and were followed by epipolar attention [suhail2022light, suhail2022generalizable], large transformers [jin2025lvsm, jiang2025rayzer], and integration with pretrained generative models [zheng2024free3d, gao2024cat3d]; PixelNeRF [yu2021pixelnerf] pioneered pixel-aligned features for NeRF-based reconstruction and inspired 3D volume representations [chen2021mvsnerf, xu2024murf], feature-matching fusion [chen2025explicit], and large transformers [du2023learning, hong2023lrm]. 3D Gaussian Splatting [kerbl20233d] has since become the representation of choice for feed-forward reconstruction, in PixelSplat [charatan2024pixelsplat], Splatter Image [szymanowicz2024splatter], MVSplat [chen2024mvsplat], Flash3D [szymanowicz2024flash3d], LatentSplat [wewer2024latentsplat], Splatt3R [smart2024splatt3r], GS-LRM [zhang2024gs], NoPoSplat [ye2024no], and DepthSplat [xu2024depthsplat]. These methods synthesize novel views with high appearance fidelity, but the views remain confined to small camera changes within the observed envelope, which motivates the generative paradigm below.

Complete 3D Reconstruction.

A harder regime is to reconstruct a complete scene from an observation 𝐎\mathbf{O} that covers only part of it, which requires inferring both visible and occluded regions; the operator shifts from a deterministic map to a generative posterior over the unobserved regions,

𝐫^rec∼pθrec(𝐫rec|𝐎),𝐫rec|visible≈observation-consistent,𝐫rec|occluded∼pθ(⋅|𝐎),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}\sim p_{\theta}^{\text{rec}}\!\big{(}\mathbf{r}^{% \text{rec}}\,\big{|}\,\mathbf{O}\big{)},\qquad\mathbf{r}^{\text{rec}}\big{|}_{% \text{visible}}\approx\text{observation-consistent},\quad\mathbf{r}^{\text{rec% }}\big{|}_{\text{occluded}}\sim p_{\theta}(\,\cdot\,\big{|}\,\mathbf{O}), (8.24)

which shares the formal structure of the synthesis sampler of Eq. (8.9) with the conditioning replaced by a strong observation constraint 𝐎\mathbf{O}.

Complete reconstruction has been studied extensively for single objects [vahdat2022lion, zhang20233dshape2vecset, zhao2023michelangelo, zhang2024clay, ren2024xcube, xiang2025trellis, tochilkin2024triposr, yang2024hunyuan3d, hunyuan3d22025tencent, li2025triposg] but remains under-explored for large scenes. Classical scene-scale methods fuse depth maps from multiple views into a volumetric representation [curless1996volumetric, newcombe2011kinectfusion, whelan2015elasticfusion, dai2017bundlefusion, niessner2013real], but they are sensitive to depth errors and produce noisy, incomplete reconstructions. A newer line fine-tunes large pretrained diffusion models [rombach2022ldm, blattmann2023stable] for the task, conditioning on controlled camera trajectories [wang2024motionctrl, sargent2024zeronvs, wu2024reconfusion, gao2024cat3d, wallingford2024image, zhou2025stable] or on auxiliary signals [liu2024reconx, yu2024viewcrafter, chen2024mvsplat360, yu2025wonderworld]; these methods synthesize observation-consistent views but leave the underlying geometry implicit. A small but growing body of work addresses geometry directly: WVD [zhang2024world] and Bolt3D [szymanowicz2025bolt3d] generate a hybrid RGB + point-map output that recovers geometry and appearance rather than novel views alone, and LaRI [li2025lari] reconstructs a complete scene from a single image, still limited to small indoor scenes.

Two design choices cut across the three paradigms. The density of the observation decides which paradigm applies: a dense calibrated multi-view set calls for per-scene optimization, a sparse uncalibrated capture for a feed-forward map, and a single image for a generative posterior, since progressively more of the scene must be inferred rather than observed. The output representation ℛrec\mathcal{R}^{\text{rec}}, by contrast, is largely independent of the paradigm and driven by the downstream consumer: a point map (DUSt3R), a mesh (classical MVS post-processing), a NeRF (per-scene optimization, PixelNeRF), a 3DGS field (3DGS, PixelSplat), or a hybrid RGB + point map (Bolt3D, WVD).

8.2.3.3 Benchmarks

Datasets span object-centric collections, indoor scenes, and outdoor environments, and partition further by acquisition (synthetic or real-world) and dynamics (static or dynamic); Table 8.4 summarizes those most commonly used.

Training Corpora.

Synthetic corpora such as Objaverse [deitke2023objaverse] supply large and diverse 3D assets, and MegaSynth [jiang2025megasynth] and Zeroverse [xie2024lrmzero] explore procedurally generated data for scalable supervision. Real-world static corpora include ARKitScenes [baruch2021arkitscenes] and ScanNet++ [yeshwanth2023scannet++] for indoor capture, dynamic corpora such as KITTI-360 [liao2022kitti360] capture outdoor scenes with temporal variation, and TartanAir [TartanAir] contains both static and dynamic scenes, which permits evaluation across both settings.

Evaluation Benchmark Suites.

Iterative methods (P1) are evaluated on DTU [Aanaes2016DTU] and Tanks-and-Temples [knapitsch2017tanks] for geometric fidelity and on the NeRF-era benchmarks LLFF [mildenhall2019llff], MipNeRF360 [barron2022mip], and RealEstate10K [zhou2018stereo] for novel-view quality. Feed-forward methods (P2) adopt the same panel together with ScanNet [dai2017scannet] subsets that supply ground-truth point maps for direct geometry supervision. Complete-reconstruction methods (P3) have no standardized suite and typically report on the precursor benchmark of their underlying 2D or video prior.

Constraint-specific Metrics.

Four axes mirror the rendering-versus-geometry decomposition of Eq. (8.21). Photometric quality is measured by PSNR, SSIM [wang2004image], and LPIPS [zhang2018unreasonable], covering pixel-level fidelity, structural similarity, and perceptual consistency of novel views. Camera-pose adherence uses Relative Translation Accuracy (RTA), Relative Rotation Accuracy (RRA), and the Area Under the Curve (AUC) that summarizes pose accuracy across angular thresholds. Geometric fidelity of point maps and point clouds is measured by Accuracy (precision), Completeness (recall), and Chamfer Distance, where Accuracy reflects geometric precision, Completeness measures surface coverage, and Chamfer Distance aggregates both. Depth quality for monocular estimation uses the absolute relative error |y−y^|/y|y-\hat{y}|/y and the inlier ratio δ<T\delta\!<\!T (the fraction of predictions within a multiplicative threshold of the ground truth), with median scaling or least-squares fitting applied beforehand because monocular depth is scale-ambiguous; multi-view depth reports Accuracy, Completeness, and Overall, the mean of the first two and equivalent to Chamfer Distance.

The paradigm succession of §8.2.3.2 is visible in two quantities. Per-scene optimization has moved from NeRF [mildenhall2021nerf], which trains for hours and renders at a few frames per second, to 3D Gaussian Splatting [kerbl20233d], which trains a scene in minutes and renders in real time (≥30{\geq}30 fps at 1080p); the feed-forward paradigm removes per-scene optimization altogether, with DUSt3R / MASt3R [wang2024dust3r, mast3r] and VGGT [wang2025vggt] recovering point maps, depth, and camera poses in a single sub-second forward pass and Fast3R [yang2025fast3r] processing over a thousand images at once. On pose, learned reconstructors now rival classical pipelines: VGGT [wang2025vggt] reports a camera-pose AUC@30 of 85.3 on RealEstate10K in pure feed-forward mode and 93.5 with bundle-adjustment refinement. Two caveats apply. There is no cross-paradigm leaderboard, since P1 is scored on novel-view PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS, P2 adds geometric Accuracy / Completeness / Chamfer Distance and pose AUC, and P3 inherits whichever protocol its 2D or video prior used; and on raw depth-map accuracy feed-forward models still trail tuned MVS pipelines, with quality degrading under free-viewpoint extrapolation (§8.2.3.4), so the strongest numbers hold inside the observed view envelope. Phone-based NeRF and Gaussian-Splatting capture apps and the open-source Nerfstudio stack have brought per-scene reconstruction to commodity devices, while classical photogrammetry suites remain the production baseline for metric accuracy.

8.2.3.4 Challenges and Trends

Four problems span the pipeline end to end: the data the model trains on, the accuracy it can deliver, the quality of the views it renders, and the compute envelope that constrains all three at long input lengths; reconstruction shares the first and third with its synthesis counterparts but sharpens the other two because it commits to recovering ground truth from raw sensor data.

Limited Modality in Datasets.

Most reconstruction and view-synthesis datasets cover a narrow band of modalities. Widely used benchmarks such as RealEstate10K [zhou2018stereo] and MipNeRF360 [barron2022mip] are RGB-only, without depth, LiDAR, or semantic annotation, and even Objaverse-XL [deitke2023objaversexl], with 10.2M objects, is primarily synthetic mesh data without real-world sensor modalities. Merging datasets of different modalities is the usual workaround, at the cost of domain shift and annotation inconsistency, and the gap is widest for dynamic scenes: datasets with synchronized RGB, depth, optical flow, and 3D motion remain far fewer than static ones, and most dynamic datasets record either camera motion or object motion rather than both with a full sensor suite. The open problem is a scalable, modality-rich corpus that combines the diversity of Objaverse [deitke2023objaverse] with the multi-sensor completeness of ScanNet++ [yeshwanth2023scannet++], collected under one protocol so that aligned RGB, depth, and semantic signals supervise the same model.

Reconstruction Accuracy.

Feed-forward models still trail traditional MVS pipelines [zhang2023geomvsnet, zhang2025advances] on raw depth-map accuracy, because MVS exploits known camera parameters and a hypothesized depth set to build cost volumes from which depth is predicted. Whether feed-forward reconstructors [yang2025fast3r, wang2025vggt] learn an approximation of such cost volumes implicitly in their attention layers is an open question; injecting explicit camera parameters or other priors into the backbone, for instance through Diffusion Transformers [peebles2023dit], is one route to closing the gap.

Free-viewpoint Rendering.

The accuracy gap is most visible at free-viewpoint rendering, where the model must produce novel views far from the input camera distribution. Disocclusions, geometric uncertainty, and limited generalization conspire: regions never observed come out blurred, ghosted, or geometrically wrong, because current methods rely on local consistency and cannot infer plausible content for occluded areas, and view-dependent effects and complex light transport demand reasoning beyond interpolation. Hallucinating missing detail while keeping novel views consistent is exactly the generative regime of §8.2.3.2.

Long Context Input.

Reconstruction from many views meets a hard computational ceiling: methods for geometry reasoning and novel-view synthesis rely on full attention, whose compute grows quadratically with the number of tokens; exact-attention kernels such as FlashAttention-2 [dao2023flashattention2] remove the quadratic memory of the attention matrix but not the quadratic compute. VGGT [wang2025vggt], for example, needs about 21 GB of GPU memory for 100 input frames and about 41 GB for 200, so inference over long sequences and training on many views quickly exceed a single GPU. Recurrent alternatives such as CUT3R [wang2025Cut3R] integrate new views incrementally while maintaining a memory state, which keeps inference memory near constant, but they forget earlier views and degrade as the number of inputs grows. Reasoning efficiently over hundreds or thousands of views while keeping memory and compute manageable remains open, with recurrent and sparse-attention architectures the main candidates.

8.2.4 3D Panorama Synthesis

3D panorama synthesis occupies a distinctive position in spatial generation: rather than producing a 3D representation directly, it generates a complete 360-degree omnidirectional image as a structured intermediate from which a full 3D environment can then be lifted. The panorama gives embodied agents, AR / VR pipelines, and world models a holistic spatial context with minimal occlusion anchored at one observation point, and it bridges the mature 2D generative prior of §8.1 with the 3D substrate on which the rest of §8.2 operates. Four method families trace the path from a single omnidirectional snapshot to an explorable world: panoramic image synthesis, panoramic video generation, panoramic 3D reconstruction, and panorama-based 3D scene generation.

8.2.4.1 Task Definition
