Panorama synthesis generates a complete 360-degree environment conditioned on text, a reference panorama or NFoV image, a spatial layout, or a specified viewpoint; unlike object-centric or narrow-field-of-view (NFoV) generation, it covers the whole environment around the observer at once rather than a fragment of it. Formally, we cast it as the omnidirectional-intermediate counterpart of the generative frameworks of §8.2.1 and §8.2.2. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the space of panoramic images (functions defined on the sphere 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} and encoded through a projection operator Π∈{ERP,cubemap,tangent,fisheye}\Pi\in\{\text{ERP},\text{cubemap},\text{tangent},\text{fisheye}\} onto a processable 2D array) and let 𝐜∈𝒞⊇{text,reference panorama / NFoV image,layout,viewpoint / camera trajectory}\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}\supseteq\{\text{text},\text{reference panorama / NFoV% image},\text{layout},\text{viewpoint / camera trajectory}\} be the conditioning. Panorama synthesis first learns a panoramic generator and then optionally lifts its output into 3D,

Gθpano:𝒞′→𝒫,P^∼pθpano⁢(P|κ⁢(𝐜)),𝐫^rec=Λ⁢(P^),G_{\theta}^{\text{pano}}:\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{P},\qquad\hat% {P}\sim p_{\theta}^{\text{pano}}\!\big{(}P\,\big{|}\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}% ,\qquad\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}=\Lambda\big{(}\hat{P}\big{)}, (8.25)

where κ\kappa is the condition encoder of §8.2.1, P^∈𝒫\hat{P}\in\mathcal{P} is the synthesized omnidirectional image, and Λ:𝒫→ℛrec\Lambda:\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathcal{R}^{\text{rec}} is an optional lifting operator mapping the panorama into the 3D-representation space ℛrec\mathcal{R}^{\text{rec}} of §8.2.3 (drawn from ℛ\mathcal{R} of §8.2.1, e.g., NeRF, 3DGS, mesh, point map). Equation (8.25) makes the role of the panorama as a structured intermediate explicit: the hard generative work is performed on the sphere by GθpanoG_{\theta}^{\text{pano}} (inheriting the 2D generator GθG_{\theta} of Eq. (8.2) with its outputs defined on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} rather than the plane), while Λ\Lambda reuses the reconstruction machinery of §8.2.3. This is also what separates panorama synthesis from the scene synthesis of §8.2.2, which produces 3D representations directly from arbitrary viewpoints distributed over SE⁢(3)\mathrm{SE}(3): here every direction around one observation point is represented coherently first, and 3D structure is recovered from that complete view. Two limiting cases locate Eq. (8.25) within §8.2. When Λ=id\Lambda=\mathrm{id} (no lifting), the task collapses to omnidirectional 2D image generation, a spatially aware variant of the text-to-image sampler of §8.1 defined on the sphere rather than the plane. When 𝐜\mathbf{c} is a set of sparse posed panoramas and Λ\Lambda is a per-scene optimization, Eq. (8.25) reduces to panoramic reconstruction, recovering the observation-conditioned operator of Eq. (8.20).

Panoramic Image Formats.

The projection Π\Pi fixes how the sphere is laid out for a 2D network and which distortions the generator must absorb. Equirectangular projection (ERP) maps the sphere onto a rectangle in latitude–longitude coordinates; it stretches content near the poles but is continuous and directly compatible with standard 2D pipelines and convolutional networks, which has made it the dominant format for learning-based synthesis. Cubemap projection represents the sphere as six perspective faces (front, back, left, right, top, bottom), removing polar distortion at the cost of discontinuities along face boundaries, and is the native format of real-time rendering and VR / AR systems, where each face is processed as an ordinary perspective image. Tangent images and perspective patches decompose the panorama into overlapping tangent-plane projections so that models trained on ordinary perspective images can be reused. Fisheye and dual-fisheye projections capture 180–220 degrees per lens with radial distortion; most consumer 360-degree cameras capture two hemispheres this way and stitch them, so dual-fisheye is the native acquisition format even when methods operate on ERP.

8.2.4.2 Methodology

The four families are four instantiations of the panoramic generator GθpanoG_{\theta}^{\text{pano}} and lifting operator Λ\Lambda of Eq. (8.25): image synthesis stops at a static panorama, video generation extends it over time, panoramic reconstruction applies Λ\Lambda to observed panoramas, and panorama-based scene generation composes the two. Figure 8.10 schematizes them and the panorama-as-intermediate pipeline that connects them.

Panoramic Image Synthesis.

Two task formulations differ in their conditioning: text-to-panorama generation, which leans on the prior of a pretrained generator and is judged on semantic alignment and diversity, and image-conditioned panorama generation, which expands an NFoV image or an incomplete panorama by inpainting or outpainting and must preserve the content, style, and panoramic distortion of its input. Formally, this family is the base case of Eq. (8.25) with the lifting operator disabled: it samples a single static omnidirectional image and stops,

P^∼pθpano⁢(P∣κ⁢(𝐜)),Λ=id,\hat{P}\sim p_{\theta}^{\text{pano}}\!\big{(}P\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)},% \qquad\Lambda=\mathrm{id}, (8.26)

where the generative work is carried out under a chosen projection Π∈{ERP,cubemap,tangent}\Pi\in\{\text{ERP},\text{cubemap},\text{tangent}\} that dictates how spherical distortion is handled; Figure 8.10(a) depicts this static-panorama pathway.

Early approaches [chen2022text2light, may2023cubegan] relied on GANs [goodfellow2014gan] and were constrained by limited training data and mode collapse; diffusion models [ho2020denoising, rombach2022ldm] brought diversity and fidelity, and current methods divide by projection format and architecture. The three strategies below are three realizations of the sampler of Eq. (8.26), differing in how the spherical output is factorized before being mapped onto the sphere,

P^={ΠERP−1⁢(Z^),Z^∼pθ⁢(Z∣κ⁢(𝐜))(direct ERP),Πcube−1⁢({F^i}i=16),{F^i}∼pθ⁢({Fi}∣κ⁢(𝐜))(cubemap),𝒮⁢({I^k}k=1K),I^k∼pθ2D⁢(I∣κ⁢(𝐜))(perspective + stitch),\hat{P}=\begin{cases}\Pi_{\text{ERP}}^{-1}(\hat{Z}),\ \ \hat{Z}\sim p_{\theta}% \big{(}Z\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}&\text{(direct ERP)},\\[3.0pt] \Pi_{\text{cube}}^{-1}\big{(}\{\hat{F}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{6}\big{)},\ \ \{\hat{F}_{i% }\}\sim p_{\theta}\big{(}\{F_{i}\}\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}&\text{(cubemap% )},\\[3.0pt] \mathcal{S}\big{(}\{\hat{I}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\big{)},\ \ \hat{I}_{k}\sim p_{% \theta}^{\text{2D}}\big{(}I\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}&\text{(perspective + % stitch)},\end{cases} (8.27)

where Π−1\Pi^{-1} lifts the generated representation onto the sphere and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a spherical stitch-and-blend operator. The first two cases synthesize the panorama directly (and so require panoramic training data), whereas the third reuses a frozen perspective generator pθ2Dp_{\theta}^{\text{2D}} and pushes the cross-view-consistency burden into 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

▶\blacktriangleright Equirectangular projection (ERP) methods. The direct-ERP case generates on the latitude–longitude grid and must handle polar distortion and the wrap-around seam architecturally. For text-to-panorama generation, DiffPano [ye2024diffpano] fine-tunes a diffusion model with LoRA on ERP, SMGD [sun2025spherical] guides the diffusion process with spherical manifold convolutions that respect geometry across the sphere, and PAR [wang2025conditional] replaces diffusion with autoregressive modeling to avoid the mismatch between ERP and the noise assumptions of standard diffusion. The seam is treated at the denoising or decoding stage: PanoDiff [panodiff] uses geometric augmentation when completing a panorama from unregistered NFoV images, PanoDiffusion [wupanodiffusion] generates depth jointly and rotates the latent circularly to enforce left–right continuity, StitchDiffusion [stitchdiffusion] re-denoises the wrap-around region at every step together with global cropping, and PanFusion [zhang2024taming] pairs an ERP branch with a multi-view perspective branch to draw on both representations. For image-conditioned generation, OmniDreamer [omnidreamer2022] introduced mask-based outpainting from NFoV images with GANs, AOG [aog] and ODIS [odis] explore alternative conditioning for inpainting and outpainting, and PanoDecouple [zheng2025panorama] separates distortion guidance from content completion to counter the “visual cheating” in which a model buys image quality at the cost of geometric accuracy.

▶\blacktriangleright Cubemap-based methods. The second case of Eq. (8.27) generates six perspective faces, which removes polar distortion but moves the problem to the face boundaries. CubeDiff [kalischek2025cubediff] introduced the cubemap representation for text-to-panorama generation, and DreamCube [huang2025dreamcube] synchronizes the six planes to suppress discontinuous seams and inconsistent color tone; overlapping the fields of view of adjacent faces reduces seams further but duplicates generation in the overlap and lowers the effective resolution. JoPano [feng2025jopano] models the faces jointly with a DiT and a Joint-Face Adapter, applies Poisson blending along the boundaries, and introduces the seam metrics (Seam-SSIM, Seam-Sobel) used in §8.2.4.3.

▶\blacktriangleright Perspective image-based methods. The third case leaves a perspective text-to-image model untouched and pushes the consistency burden into the stitch operator 𝒮\mathcal{S}, with or without panorama-specific training. Training-free methods apply a pretrained perspective model directly: MultiDiffusion [multidiffusion] denoises overlapping patches independently and blends them, PanoGen [li2023panogen] outpaints recursively from an initial view until the sphere is covered, DiffCollage [zhang2023diffcollage] casts the panorama as a factor graph whose factor nodes are portions and whose variable nodes are their overlaps so that portions are generated in parallel rather than autoregressively, PanoFree [panofree] iterates warping and inpainting over multi-view images, and SphereDiff [park2025spherediff] moves MultiDiffusion onto a spherical latent with dynamic spherical sampling and distortion-aware weighted averaging so that quality holds up to the poles. These methods ride on advances in perspective generation but struggle with global consistency across the full sphere. Training-based methods fine-tune on panoramic data: MVDiffusion [tang2023MVDiffusion] generates eight perspective views with consistent geometry and reprojects them into a closed-loop panorama, and TanDiT [tandit2025] decomposes the panorama into a structured grid of tangent-plane images that a Diffusion Transformer generates jointly in one denoising pass under spatial attention.

Panoramic Video Generation.

Extending synthesis over time adds temporal coherence to omnidirectional consistency. Formally, this family extends the static generator of Eq. (8.26) over time, sampling a sequence under a joint spatial-and-temporal coherence constraint,

{P^t}t=1T∼pθpano⁢({Pt}t=1T∣κ⁢(𝐜)),s.t.⁢P^t≈𝒲t⁢(P^t−1),\{\hat{P}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\sim p_{\theta}^{\text{pano}}\!\big{(}\{P_{t}\}_{t=1}% ^{T}\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)},\qquad\text{s.t.}\;\;\hat{P}_{t}\approx% \mathcal{W}^{\text{t}}(\hat{P}_{t-1}), (8.28)

where 𝒲t\mathcal{W}^{\text{t}} enforces frame-to-frame motion consistency on top of the per-frame 360-degree wrap-around continuity; Figure 8.10(b) depicts this temporally-extended pathway. The methods share this generator but differ in the conditioning argument 𝐜\mathbf{c} supplied to Eq. (8.28), which separates them into three input modalities,

𝐜={𝐱(text-to-video),P0(image-to-video),{(It,ℳt)}t=1T(perspective-to-video),\mathbf{c}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{x}&\text{(text-to-video)},\\ P_{0}&\text{(image-to-video)},\\ \{(I_{t},\mathcal{M}_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}&\text{(perspective-to-video)},\end{cases} (8.29)

where 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a text prompt, P0P_{0} a static panorama anchor reused as the first frame, and (It,ℳt)(I_{t},\mathcal{M}_{t}) an NFoV frame paired with its visibility mask. The difficulty grows down the list: as the conditioning becomes spatially sparser, the model must hallucinate progressively more of the sphere while preserving the temporal coherence of Eq. (8.28).

▶\blacktriangleright Text-to-panoramic video generation. 360DVD [wang2024360dvd] adapts a pretrained text-to-video model to the ERP domain through adapter modules, keeping wrap-around consistency across frames but struggling to balance text alignment against spherical geometry and to vary style under several control conditions. TiP4GEN [xing2025tip4gen] adopts a dual-branch panoramic-and-perspective architecture in the spirit of PanFusion and lifts the generated video into a geometry-aligned 4D Gaussian scene. PanoWan [xia2025panowan] and PanoDiT [zhang2025panodit] fine-tune large video diffusion transformers on panoramic video data and gain motion quality from scale, and PanoLora [dong2025panolora] treats the task as a projection adaptation from perspective views that LoRA can learn with little data. Training-free alternatives carry the static-panorama machinery into time: SphereDiff [park2025spherediff] extends its spherical latent to video, and DynamicScaler [liu2025dynamicscaler] denoises through a seamless rotating window with an offset-shifting scheme and Global Motion Guidance, which yields arbitrary output resolution at constant memory. Text alone, however, offers little control over layout and motion, which motivates the richer conditioning below.

▶\blacktriangleright Image-to-panoramic video generation. Animating a static panorama anchors the video spatially and asks for plausible omnidirectional motion that respects the input geometry. 4K4DGen [li20244k4dgen] animates user-selected regions with an image-to-video model under overlapping windows, at the cost of fixed-window artifacts and limited motion. ViewPoint [fang2025panoramic] introduces a panorama representation that keeps global spatial continuity while Pano-Perspective attention transfers a perspective video prior, and HoloTime [zhou2025holotime] reconstructs the result as 4D Gaussian Splatting so that the animated scene can be explored under viewpoint changes. GenEx [lu2024genex] generates a 3D-consistent imaginative environment from a single image as a panoramic video stream with loop consistency over long trajectories, which makes it usable for embodied exploration. For explicit control, PanFlow [panflow] conditions on synthetic optical flow as a scene-agnostic motion signal and warps noise spherically so that camera and object motion can be controlled separately while the seam stays consistent; OmniDrag [li2026omnidrag] adds drag-style interaction at scene and object level through a spherical motion estimator; and PanoWorld-X [yin2025panoworld] reprojects ERP features onto the sphere inside a Sphere-Aware Diffusion Transformer to follow diverse camera trajectories.

▶\blacktriangleright Perspective-to-panoramic video generation. Expanding an NFoV video to a full 360-degree video requires coherent hallucination in space and time at once, under visibility masks that change with camera motion. VidPanos [ma2024vidpanos] frames the task as space-time outpainting and uses a generative video model to fill the regions a panning camera never observed; Imagine360 [tan2024imagine360] combines a global panoramic branch with local perspective priors and an elevation-aware design for the moving masks; and Beyond the Frame [beyondtheframe] adds geometry-aware modules and motion-aware conditioning to improve realism and motion consistency in the outpainted regions.

Panoramic 3D Reconstruction and Generation.

Reconstruction bypasses the generator of Eq. (8.25): rather than generating P^\hat{P}, it takes observed posed panoramas and applies the lifting operator directly,

𝐫^rec=Λ⁢({Pv,πv}v=1V),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}=\Lambda\big{(}\{P_{v},\pi_{v}\}_{v=1}^{V}\big{)}, (8.30)

where Λ\Lambda is realized either as a per-scene optimization (iterative) or as an amortized network (feed-forward), mirroring the split of §8.2.3; Figure 8.10(c) depicts this reconstruction pathway. Generation then composes the two directions, feeding a synthesized panorama into the same Λ\Lambda.

▶\blacktriangleright Iterative optimization-based panoramic reconstruction. Realizing Λ\Lambda of Eq. (8.30) as a per-scene optimization,

𝐫^rec=arg⁡min𝐫⁢∑v‖Render⁢(𝐫,πv)−Pv‖2+λ⁢Ω⁢(𝐫),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{r}}\sum_{v}\big{\|}\mathrm{% Render}(\mathbf{r},\pi_{v})-P_{v}\big{\|}^{2}+\lambda\,\Omega(\mathbf{r}), (8.31)

re-solved from scratch for each scene, these methods fit a radiance field or an explicit representation to multi-view panoramas, the panoramic analogue of §8.2.3.2. NeRF-based work includes 360Roam [huang2022360roam] for geometry-aware indoor reconstruction, 360FusionNeRF [kulkarni2023fusion] for novel views from a single panorama under geometric and semantic supervision, EgoNeRF [choi2023egonerf] with spherical grids for egocentric capture, and OmniNeRF [gu2022omninerf], which processes raw dual-fisheye input and its lens distortion. Gaussian-splatting alternatives are faster: 360GS [bai2024360gs] projects Gaussians onto spherical tangent planes, ODGS [lee2024odgs] rasterizes on tangent planes with elevation-aware densification, OP43DGS [wang2024op43dgs] corrects the projection bias of the local affine approximation across camera models, OmniGS [li2024omnigs] exploits omnidirectional optical properties, and Seam360GS [seam360gs] calibrates dual-fisheye input by jointly optimizing translation vectors and learnable angular-distortion embeddings. Scene4U [scene4u] reconstructs from a single panorama in depth layers: an open-vocabulary segmenter and an LLM decompose it semantically, diffusion inpainting restores occluded regions, and 3D Gaussians are fitted per layer.

▶\blacktriangleright Feed-forward generalization-based panoramic reconstruction. Amortizing Λ\Lambda of Eq. (8.30) into a trained network applied in a single forward pass,

𝐫^rec=Λψ⁢({Pv,πv}v=1V),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}=\Lambda_{\psi}\big{(}\{P_{v},\pi_{v}\}_{v=1}^{V}% \big{)}, (8.32)

where Λψ\Lambda_{\psi} is trained once over a panoramic corpus (the analogue of §8.2.3.2), trades the per-scene cost of Eq. (8.31) for a learned prior that reconstructs from sparse panoramas without scene-specific training. PanoGRF [chen2023panogrf] pioneered feed-forward reconstruction of wide-baseline panoramas with depth guidance; PanoSplatt3R [panosplatt3r] extends DUSt3R [wang2024dust3r] to unposed wide-baseline panoramas through RoPE rolling, a rotary positional embedding rolled across attention heads so that ERP periodicity and correspondences across the seam are modeled; and PanSplat [pansplat] builds spherical 3D Gaussian pyramids on a Fibonacci lattice to reach 4K novel views with feed-forward inference and cubemap rendering for memory efficiency.

▶\blacktriangleright Panorama-based 3D generation and world modeling. This family realizes the full composition of Eq. (8.25): it first generates the panorama and then lifts it,

𝐫^rec=Λ⁢(P^),P^∼pθpano⁢(P∣κ⁢(𝐜)),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{rec}}=\Lambda\big{(}\hat{P}\big{)},\qquad\hat{P}\sim p% _{\theta}^{\text{pano}}\!\big{(}P\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.33)

so that the synthesized omnidirectional image of Eq. (8.26) becomes the structured intermediate fed to the reconstruction operator of Eq. (8.30); Figure 8.10(d) depicts this generate-then-lift pathway. Text →\rightarrow panorama →\rightarrow 3D pipelines generate the omnidirectional image with a diffusion model [ye2024diffpano, kalischek2025cubediff] before reconstructing a NeRF, Gaussian, or mesh scene. LayerPano3D [yang2024layerpano3d] parses the panorama into hierarchical depth layers and reconstructs each with 3D Gaussian Splatting, DreamScene360 [zhou2025dreamscene360] fits panoramic Gaussians for free-roaming text-conditioned scenes, Matrix-3D [yang2025matrix] couples trajectory-guided panoramic video generation with a dual-pathway reconstruction that conditions on scene-mesh renders, and HunyuanWorld [team2025hunyuanworld] treats the panorama as a 360-degree world proxy for text- and image-conditioned explorable scenes with mesh export and disentangled object representations. The panoramic video generators GenEx [lu2024genex] and PanoWorld-X [yin2025panoworld] (above) turn the same intermediate into an action- or trajectory-conditioned observation space, which is where panorama synthesis meets the world models of §8.6.

8.2.4.3 Benchmarks

Panoramic datasets must supply geometric consistency over the full sphere, a declared projection format, and, for reconstruction, camera poses and depth; Table 8.5 lists the corpora in use, grouped by modality.

Training Corpora.

For static synthesis, Structured3D [zheng2020structured3d] (synthetic indoor scenes with controlled geometry) and SUN360 [xiao2012recognizing] (real-world indoor and outdoor panoramas) are the standard benchmarks for distortion handling and seam artifacts, in the splits adopted by JoPano, PanoDecouple, and DreamCube [feng2025jopano, zheng2025panorama, huang2025dreamcube]; Matterport3D [chang2017matterport3d], with RGB-D panoramas, camera poses, and mesh geometry across 90 buildings, is the most widely used corpus for both generation and reconstruction [pansplat, yang2024layerpano3d, team2025hunyuanworld, tang2023MVDiffusion, zhang2024taming], and Upright360 [yang2024layerpano3d] filters Matterport3D, web, and Blockade Labs panoramas with GeoCalib [veicht2024geocalib] to near-zero pitch and roll for realistic indoor synthesis. Panoramic video with geometric annotation has been the bottleneck. 360+x [chen2023360plusx] and WEB360 [wang2024360dvd] are small real-world collections (the latter captioned for text conditioning), 360-1M [wallingford2024image] scales to over a million videos for world-model pretraining, PanFlow [panflow] adds optical flow and camera poses on motion-rich sequences, PANOVID [xia2025panowan] aggregates these with Imagine360 [tan2024imagine360] and public VR videos but lacks poses and depth, and Matrix-Pano [yang2025matrix] fills that gap with Unreal Engine 5 renders carrying depth maps and camera trajectories; embodied work renders action-conditioned observations in Unreal Engine directly [lu2024genex, yin2025panoworld]. For reconstruction, Replica [straub2019replica] and Residential [habtegebrial2022somsi] serve as synthetic indoor benchmarks at baselines of about 1.0 m and 0.3 m respectively [pansplat], 360Loc [huang2024360loc] supplies posed panorama sequences used for 4K fine-tuning [pansplat], and the scarcity of posed real panoramic video led PanSplat [pansplat] to capture its own dual-fisheye footage with poses from visual SLAM.

Evaluation Metrics.

Panorama evaluation combines general image and video quality metrics with panorama-specific measures of distortion, seam consistency, and spherical topology.

▶\blacktriangleright Image fidelity and semantic alignment. FID measures distributional similarity between generated and real panoramas [feng2025jopano, yang2024layerpano3d, zheng2025panorama, tandit2025]; PanFusion [zhang2024taming] shows that FAED (Fréchet Auto-Encoder Distance), computed in the latent space of an auto-encoder trained on the target data, tracks panorama quality more closely than Inception features do. Text-to-panorama generation reports CLIP-Score between prompt and output [team2025hunyuanworld, feng2025jopano, yang2024layerpano3d, tandit2025], image-conditioned tasks report CLIP-I between input and output [team2025hunyuanworld], and no-reference quality is scored with BRISQUE and NIQE [team2025hunyuanworld, yang2024layerpano3d, yang2025matrix], complemented by aesthetic scorers and human preference studies, for instance the Average User Ranking protocol of LayerPano3D [yang2024layerpano3d]. Layout-conditioned synthesis measures adherence by 3D and 2D IoU against layouts recovered with HorizonNet [sun2019horizonnet], following PanFusion [zhang2024taming].

▶\blacktriangleright Panorama-specific consistency. Projection-induced distortion and boundary discontinuities call for metrics of their own. JoPano [feng2025jopano] scores cubemap seams with Seam-SSIM (SSIM between adjacent edge pixels of neighboring faces) and Seam-Sobel (gradient discontinuity along the seam); PanoDecouple [zheng2025panorama] introduces Distort-CLIP, a CLIP variant trained to detect panoramic distortion, so that the “visual cheating” of models that improve image quality while degrading geometry becomes measurable; and loop consistency across the 360-degree wrap-around is assessed by PSNR in overlapping regions [tang2023MVDiffusion] or across the left–right boundary [panflow, xia2025panowan].

▶\blacktriangleright Reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. Because pixel density on the sphere is non-uniform, WS-PSNR (Weighted Spherical PSNR) weights pixels by latitude and replaces plain PSNR for equirectangular outputs [pansplat, chen2023panogrf], complemented by SSIM and LPIPS [yang2024layerpano3d, pansplat, yang2025matrix].

▶\blacktriangleright Video quality and spatiotemporal dynamics. Panoramic videos are often projected to several perspective views (e.g., , four views at azimuths {0∘,90∘,180∘,270∘}\{0^{\circ},90^{\circ},180^{\circ},270^{\circ}\} with a 90∘90^{\circ} field of view) so that human raters and perspective-domain tools can be used [team2025hunyuanworld, yang2024layerpano3d, tan2024imagine360]. Q-Align [wu2023qalign], a large multimodal model trained to score visual quality on discrete text-defined levels, is increasingly used for images and videos alike [team2025hunyuanworld, tan2024imagine360]; FVD [unterthiner2018fvd], computed in the feature space of an inflated 3D ConvNet, is the standard distributional metric for video [panflow, xia2025panowan]; VBench [huang2023vbench] adds imaging quality, aesthetic quality, motion smoothness, and subject consistency over projected views; and trajectory-conditioned generation is scored by frame-to-frame consistency and by the range of camera motion it sustains [yin2025panoworld]. Two limits remain. Ground truth is scarce for dynamic panoramic video with depth and camera annotation, so evaluation falls back on projected perspective views or user studies; and world-level properties such as loop consistency over long trajectories and action-conditioned spatial coherence have no dedicated benchmark yet.

8.2.4.4 Challenges and Trends
Unique Challenges in Panoramic Synthesis.

Modeling a complete omnidirectional environment imposes constraints that NFoV synthesis never meets. The first is distortion-aware learning: ERP stretches content near the poles, so visual information is non-uniformly distributed over the image and convolutional kernels designed for translation invariance on the plane struggle with the varying distortion, which motivates spherical manifold convolutions and latitude-aware architectures [sun2025spherical, zheng2025panorama]. The second is seamless boundary consistency: wrap-around coherence across the longitudinal boundary must be preserved to avoid visible seams, typically through circular padding or latent rotation during denoising [panflow, xia2025panowan]. The third is scaling structured generation to 4K and beyond while keeping global geometric and semantic consistency over the whole sphere, which pushes toward memory-efficient attention and hierarchical spherical representations [pansplat, liu2025dynamicscaler].

From Panorama to World Models.

The clearest trend is the move from static spherical snapshots toward interactive 3D world modeling, in which the panorama is the interface through which an embodied agent reasons about a complete environment rather than a fragment of one. The systems that lift a generated panorama into an explorable world (HunyuanWorld [team2025hunyuanworld], Matrix-3D [yang2025matrix]) and World Labs’ Marble [Feifei2025Marble] show what panoramic priors make possible, and temporal panoramic modeling supplies the 4D half: generating temporally coherent panoramic video requires motion dynamics that respect spherical topology and occlusion boundaries [panflow, yin2025panoworld]. Integrated with interactive systems, such panoramic world simulations become a basis for embodied interaction, long-range spatial reasoning, and environment simulation in robotics and immersive media.

Representation Innovations.

Efficiency and fidelity both hinge on the omnidirectional representation. Efficient omnidirectional representations such as the Fibonacci-lattice Gaussian pyramids of PanSplat [pansplat] render at high fidelity without the redundancy of uniform grids, and multi-modal panoramic fusion, which binds 360-degree RGB to depth, semantic labels, and geometric proxies such as surface normals [yang2024layerpano3d, scene4u], makes the synthesized environment both more realistic and more editable, closing part of the gap between 2D generative priors and full 3D scene intelligence.

8.2.5 3D Scene Editing

The preceding subsections build 3D content; 3D scene editing takes an existing asset and modifies it under user control while preserving everything the edit should leave untouched. Such incremental control is exactly what spatial intelligence asks of a 3D world model: an agent that must correct a mistake, personalize an environment, or keep a scene consistent as its task unfolds cannot afford to regenerate the world from scratch every time it changes. Technically, 3D editing lifts the 2D inpainting-and-editing machinery of §8.1.3 from the image plane to a multi-view-consistent 3D representation, adding a cross-view coherence requirement that has no analogue in the 2D case; the five method families below are distinguished by how the edit signal is injected into that representation.

8.2.5.1 Task Definition

3D scene (and object) editing modifies an existing 3D asset or reconstructed scene according to a user intent (typically language or reference images, as in Figure 8.11) while preserving 3D consistency for novel-view rendering. Unlike text-to-3D generation, editing operates on a given representation (e.g., , NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, or meshes) and requires (i) locality and identity preservation for unedited regions, (ii) multi-view (and potentially temporal) coherence, and (iii) controllability over the edited attributes, whether geometry, appearance, material, or semantics.

Formally, 3D editing is the 3D-lifted counterpart of the 2D inpainting-and-editing operator of §8.1.3 (Eq. (8.8)). Given an input 3D representation 𝐫in∈ℛ\mathbf{r}^{\text{in}}\in\mathcal{R} drawn from the same representation space ℛ\mathcal{R} as §8.2.1, an edit intent 𝐜∈𝒞⊇{text instruction,reference image,mask / region,scribble}\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}\supseteq\{\text{text instruction},\text{reference % image},\text{mask / region},\text{scribble}\}, and an optional 3D region of interest ℳ⊆ℝ3\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3}, the goal is an editing operator

Eθ:ℛ×𝒞′→ℛ,𝐫^=Eθ⁢(𝐫in,κ⁢(𝐜)),E_{\theta}:\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{R},\qquad% \hat{\mathbf{r}}=E_{\theta}\big{(}\mathbf{r}^{\text{in}},\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})% \big{)}, (8.34)

trained or optimized to minimize an objective that couples three competing terms,

ℒedit=ℒintent⁢(𝐫^,𝐜;ℳ)⏟edit-region adherence+λp⁢ℒpreserve⁢(𝐫^,𝐫in;ℝ3∖ℳ)⏟identity preservation+λc⁢ℒconsist⁢({Render⁢(𝐫^,πv)}v)⏟multi-view coherence,\mathcal{L}_{\text{edit}}=\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}\big{(}\hat{% \mathbf{r}},\mathbf{c};\mathcal{M}\big{)}}_{\text{edit-region adherence}}\;+\;% \lambda_{\text{p}}\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{preserve}}\big{(}\hat{\mathbf% {r}},\mathbf{r}^{\text{in}};\mathbb{R}^{3}\!\setminus\!\mathcal{M}\big{)}}_{% \text{identity preservation}}\;+\;\lambda_{\text{c}}\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{% \text{consist}}\big{(}\{\mathrm{Render}(\hat{\mathbf{r}},\pi_{v})\}_{v}\big{)}% }_{\text{multi-view coherence}}, (8.35)

where κ\kappa is the condition encoder of §8.2.1, Render\mathrm{Render} is the differentiable renderer of §8.2.3, and λp,λc\lambda_{\text{p}},\lambda_{\text{c}} trade off preservation and consistency against edit strength. The limiting case that anchors Eq. (8.34) to its 2D origin is instructive: when ℛ\mathcal{R} collapses to a single image (V=1V=1, no rendering), EθE_{\theta} reduces exactly to the 2D editing operator of Eq. (8.8) and the multi-view-consistency term vanishes, so 3D editing is 2D editing plus a cross-view coherence constraint.

8.2.5.2 Methodology

Recent 3D object and scene editing methods can be categorized by how the edit signal of Eq. (8.34) is injected into the 3D representation, from lifting 2D edits view by view, through enforcing cross-view consistency, to operating directly on 3D primitives, reasoning with language models, and amortizing the edit into a single feed-forward pass. Figure 8.12 schematizes the five families and how each realizes the operator EθE_{\theta}.

2D-lifted Iterative Editing.

A dominant paradigm inherits from instruction-based NeRF editing [bao2023sine, khalid2024latenteditor, mikaeili2023sked, zhou2023repaintnerf]: the method iterates between rendering views from the current scene, applying a 2D diffusion-based editor to them, and updating the 3D representation to match the edited guidance under geometric regularization. Formally, this family instantiates EθE_{\theta} of Eq. (8.34) as a per-scene optimization that drives the rendered views toward the output of a frozen 2D editor ℰ2D\mathcal{E}_{\text{2D}} (the InstructPix2Pix-style operator of §8.1.3),

𝐫^=arg⁡min𝐫∈ℛ⁢∑v‖Render⁢(𝐫,πv)−ℰ2D⁢(Render⁢(𝐫in,πv),𝐜)‖2+λ⁢Ω⁢(𝐫),\hat{\mathbf{r}}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{r}\in\mathcal{R}}\sum_{v}\big{\|}\mathrm{% Render}(\mathbf{r},\pi_{v})-\mathcal{E}_{\text{2D}}\!\big{(}\mathrm{Render}(% \mathbf{r}^{\text{in}},\pi_{v}),\,\mathbf{c}\big{)}\big{\|}^{2}+\lambda\,% \Omega(\mathbf{r}), (8.36)

so that the 2D edits are lifted into the 3D representation and the arg⁡min\arg\min is re-solved from scratch for every scene; Figure 8.12(a) depicts this render-edit-update loop. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF [haque2023instructnerf2nerf], EditNeRF [liu2021editingnerf], Free-Editor [karim2024freeeditor], and CTRL-D [he2025ctrld] lift instruction-driven 2D edits into the radiance field this way, and with the rise of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [kerbl20233d] the same principle moved to Gaussian primitives: Instruct-GS2GS [vachha2024instructgs2gs] iteratively edits the training images with InstructPix2Pix [brooks2023instructpix2pixlearningfollowimage] and re-optimizes the 3DGS to reflect the instruction while preserving 3D structure [wang2024viewedit, wynn2025morpheus]. The recipe is simple and borrows the full strength of 2D editors, but it is slow, prone to view-dependent artifacts, and only as good as the stability of the 2D editor and the coverage of the rendered guidance views.

Multi-view-consistent Guidance.

Because independently edited views can disagree (inconsistent textures, hallucinated geometry), recent work [chen2024dge] enforces multi-view consistency at the guidance level rather than relying on the 3D update to reconcile conflicting edits. Formally, rather than editing each view independently as in Eq. (8.36), this family makes the guidance images mutually consistent before the lift,

{I^v}=arg⁡min{Iv}⁢∑vℒintent⁢(Iv,𝐜)+β⁢∑(u,v)‖Iu−𝒲u→v⁢(Iv)‖2,\{\hat{I}_{v}\}=\arg\min_{\{I_{v}\}}\sum_{v}\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}(I_{v},% \mathbf{c})\;+\;\beta\!\!\sum_{(u,v)}\big{\|}I_{u}-\mathcal{W}_{u\to v}(I_{v})% \big{\|}^{2}, (8.37)

where 𝒲u→v\mathcal{W}_{u\to v} warps view vv into view uu using geometry or depth derived from the current 3D estimate, penalizing cross-view disagreement; the consolidated {I^v}\{\hat{I}_{v}\} then drive the 3D update of Eq. (8.36), as in Figure 8.12(b). GaussCtrl [wu2024gaussctrl] edits several rendered views in a coupled fashion rather than sequentially, improving multi-view consistency for text-driven 3DGS editing [wang2024viewedit, xia2025towardsConsistent], and VcEdit [wang2024viewedit] integrates the 3DGS into the image-editing process itself with consistency modules that counter cross-view disagreement and mode collapse. A complementary line transfers a single-view edit to other views via geometry: gomel2024diffusionBasedAttention extracts diffusion attention features from a reference edit, warps them across views using depth from the Gaussian splats, and injects the warped features to propagate a coherent edit. These methods preserve 3D coherence more robustly but still struggle with large non-rigid shape changes or severe occlusion, where reliable correspondence and geometry are hard to come by.

3D-native Primitive Editing.

To reduce reliance on unstable 2D guidance and enable interactive use, 3D-native approaches operate directly on explicit scene primitives. Formally, this family bypasses the rendering loop of Eq. (8.36) entirely: a grounding or segmentation operator 𝒢\mathcal{G} selects the target subset of primitives and a direct geometric transform 𝒯\mathcal{T} applies the edit,

𝐫^=𝒯⁢(𝐫in;𝒢⁢(𝐫in,𝐜)),𝒯∈{add,delete,move,recolor,replace},\hat{\mathbf{r}}=\mathcal{T}\!\big{(}\mathbf{r}^{\text{in}};\,\mathcal{G}(% \mathbf{r}^{\text{in}},\mathbf{c})\big{)},\qquad\mathcal{T}\in\{\text{add},\,% \text{delete},\,\text{move},\,\text{recolor},\,\text{replace}\}, (8.38)

acting on explicit Gaussians or mesh facets so that the unedited primitives are preserved by construction: the identity-preservation term of Eq. (8.35) is satisfied structurally rather than by a penalty; Figure 8.12(c) shows this pathway. 3DSceneEditor [yan20243dsceneeditor] runs a fully 3D pipeline, combining instance segmentation and zero-shot grounding to localize the target and then performing Gaussian-level addition, deletion, relocation, recoloring, and replacement with strong controllability in real time, and InterGSEdit [wen2025intergsedit] adds user-in-the-loop key-view selection and a geometry-consistent attention prior for iterative, preference-guided 3DGS editing with control over the edit degree. More broadly, GaussianEditor and 3DSceneEditor [chen2024gaussianeditor, yan20243dsceneeditor] impose higher-level structure on the Gaussians, grouping them by object identity or semantic coherence (typically through zero-shot grounding or segmentation [hu2024semanticanythinggaussians, cen2025segmentany3dgaussians] followed by anchoring) so that an edit can be formulated at the level of an instance rather than of individual primitives, which localizes the target more precisely and protects the background.

LLM-integrated Editing.

Large language models have been integrated into 3D editing pipelines not merely as text encoders but as high-level reasoning and control modules. Formally, the LLM decomposes the instruction into an ordered program of geometry-aware operators applied to the asset,

𝐫^=(oK∘⋯∘o1)⁢(𝐫in),(o1,…,oK)=LLM⁢(𝐜,𝐫in),\hat{\mathbf{r}}=(o_{K}\circ\cdots\circ o_{1})(\mathbf{r}^{\text{in}}),\qquad(% o_{1},\dots,o_{K})=\mathrm{LLM}\big{(}\mathbf{c},\,\mathbf{r}^{\text{in}}\big{% )}, (8.39)

so that high-level reasoning (attribute inference, edit planning, dependency resolution) is separated from the low-level operators oko_{k}, often the primitive transforms of Eq. (8.38), that it dispatches; Figure 8.12(d) depicts this plan-then-execute pathway. ShapeLLM-Omni [ye2025shapellmOmni] casts 3D editing as language-grounded reasoning in which the LLM performs shape understanding, attribute inference, and edit planning before invoking geometry-aware operators, and LL3M [lu2025ll3m] extends this to multimodal 3D manipulation requiring compositional understanding of geometry, appearance, and spatial relations. A complementary line [ma2025feedforward3DEditing] uses the LLM to guide or parameterize image-to-3D or text-to-3D backbones in a feed-forward setting rather than a per-scene optimization, and LLMs also serve as coordination agents for global consistency [huang2024blenderalchemy, zhang2025scenelanguage]: xia2025towardsConsistent shows that reasoning over object identities, relations, and edit dependencies reduces the conflicts that arise in purely diffusion- or optimization-based pipelines when several objects and attributes must be edited at once.

Efficient and Training-free Editing.

A final trend reduces test-time cost through feed-forward reconstruction or reuse of pretrained models [erkocc2025preditor3d, li2025voxhammer]. These strategies are distinct: a training-free editing pipeline can still involve iterative diffusion inference. The amortized feed-forward case evaluates the editing operator of Eq. (8.34) directly,

𝐫^=Eθ⁢(𝐫in,κ⁢(𝐜))(amortized, no per-scene optimization),\hat{\mathbf{r}}=E_{\theta}\big{(}\mathbf{r}^{\text{in}},\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})% \big{)}\quad\text{(amortized, no per-scene optimization)}, (8.40)

eliminating the per-scene arg⁡min\arg\min of Eq. (8.36) by amortizing inference into a trained network. Training-free alternatives instead reuse pretrained components, potentially through single-view guidance, mesh proxies, or iterative native-3D latent editing; Figure 8.12(e) distinguishes these routes from the per-scene optimization loop in panel (a). Free-Editor [karim2024freeeditor] edits a NeRF zero-shot from text without scene-specific retraining, countering multi-view style inconsistency with a “single-view editing” scheme and an Edit Transformer; on the scene-operation side (insert, replace, delete), FreeEdit [madhavaram2025towardsTrainingFree] uses a mesh proxy to perform training-free edits guided by foundation models at near real-time rates in complex indoor scenes. These methods improve usability but typically trade away edit fidelity and coverage, especially for fine-grained geometry, and depend strongly on robust grounding and localization in 3D.

8.2.5.3 Benchmarks

Several benchmarks have recently been introduced for systematic evaluation. 3D-Alpaca-Editing [ye2025shapellmOmni] focuses on instruction-following 3D editing, assessing whether a model interprets natural-language commands correctly while preserving unedited content. CMD [li2025cmd] emphasizes compositional and multi-step instructions, where reasoning and planning matter. Edit3D-Bench [li2025voxhammer] is a general-purpose suite covering geometry, appearance, and object-level operations, with 3D edit regions annotated on 100 source models (300 edits), which allows fair comparison across editing paradigms. 3DEditVerse [xia2025towardsConsistent] is a large-scale paired benchmark built for robustness and generalization across varied objects, scenes, and intents. Together they standardize evaluation in terms of instruction compliance, edit locality, and scalability; Table 8.6 summarizes their scale and the evaluation axes each one annotates.

Evaluation Metrics.

Evaluation considers geometric fidelity, appearance quality, and semantic alignment with the instruction. Geometry is measured by Chamfer Distance (CD) [ma2025feedforward3DEditing], lower being better, and by F-score [xia2025towardsConsistent], which captures surface overlap at a distance threshold. Texture and appearance are assessed by comparing renderings of the edited representation against target or inpainted images with SSIM [wang2004image], LPIPS [zhang2018unreasonable], and DreamSim [fu2023dreamsim] [gao20253dmeshedit]. Visual–text alignment is scored with CLIP- or DINO-based embedding similarity [shu2025gaussedit], and GPTEval3D [wu2024gpt4vt23dgen] uses GPT-4V to compare multi-view renderings of edited shapes on text alignment, 3D plausibility, and texture detail. To measure the edit relative to the input rather than in isolation, directional CLIP (CLIPdir{}_{\text{dir}}) [wynn2025morpheus] checks that the change in image embedding, computed over multi-view renderings of input and output, follows the change in text embedding.

Edit cost is the clearest axis separating the five families. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF [haque2023instructnerf2nerf] takes on the order of 30–90 minutes per edit; GaussianEditor [chen2024gaussianeditor] brings this under 20 minutes by operating on explicit Gaussians; PrEditor3D [erkocc2025preditor3d] edits a shape in a few minutes, and VoxHammer [li2025voxhammer] performs precise local edits training-free in a native 3D latent space. On quality the field reports DINO-I and CLIP-T on Edit3D-Bench [li2025voxhammer], directional CLIP [wynn2025morpheus], and GPT-4V judgment [wu2024gpt4vt23dgen]; the 3D-native and feed-forward families lead on locality and speed, while 2D-lifted methods keep an edge on open-vocabulary appearance edits where a strong 2D editor does the work. The speed of feed-forward editing comes at a cost in fine-grained geometry control and a dependence on robust 3D grounding, taken up below.

8.2.5.4 Challenges and Trends

Several problems remain genuinely open and define the current frontier of 3D editing.

Geometry-level, not merely appearance, editing.

Most current methods edit color and texture well but treat geometry as fixed: precise, instruction-driven changes to shape, including thin, transparent, or high-frequency structures, remain unreliable, and edits that should alter the underlying surface often only repaint it. Closing this gap requires editors that operate on geometry and appearance jointly rather than deferring geometry to a frozen reconstruction.

Large non-rigid and structural edits.

Adding, removing, or substantially deforming structure while preserving the identity of the rest of the asset is still difficult: drag-driven, as-rigid-as-possible Gaussian editors [han2025arapgs] handle moderate deformation, but large non-rigid motion and topology changes frequently lose original detail. Robust structural and compositional editing, including relation-aware multi-object edits, remains an active frontier.

Material–lighting disentanglement and relightable editing.

Because most representations bake illumination into appearance, an edit that changes an object’s material or color is not guaranteed to stay consistent when the scene is relit. Relightable representations that decompose geometry, BRDF, and incident light [gao2024relightable] are a prerequisite for edits that survive relighting and for inserting edited content into new lighting, yet stable material–light decomposition under editing is not solved.

The consistency bottleneck has moved to 3D grounding.

Now that native-3D editing handles appearance coherence, the limiting factor is localization: methods such as VoxHammer [li2025voxhammer] are highly sensitive to 3D mask accuracy and degrade rapidly when the target region is imprecisely grounded. Robust open-vocabulary 3D grounding and segmentation [hu2024semanticanythinggaussians, cen2025segmentany3dgaussians], ideally without user-provided masks [xia2025towardsConsistent], is therefore the new gate on edit quality, and it is most acute in dynamic scenes, where the edited region must be tracked with temporal identity preserved across frames [he2025ctrld].

Two pressures cut across all four. Evaluation remains immature: the benchmarks of §8.2.5.3 are small (Edit3D-Bench annotates 100 source models and 300 edits) and no metric panel is yet standard, so progress on the harder edits above is difficult to measure reliably. And the strongest forward trend is unification, bringing generation, segmentation, grounding, and editing into a single structured pipeline [park2026generative] with interfaces that go beyond text to reference images [shu2025gaussedit], masks [barda2025instant3dit], sketches [mikaeili2023sked], and object-level operations, so that an agent can specify and verify a geometry-, material-, and relighting-consistent edit rather than only a repaint.

8.3 Video Spatial Generation

Video spatial generation is the task of synthesizing a temporally coherent image sequence (a video clip) from a high-level prompt together with optional spatial, temporal, and other conditioning signals. It has advanced substantially in recent years, evolving from early generative adversarial network (GAN)-based approaches [goodfellow2014gan] through autoregressive token models to the diffusion- and diffusion-transformer-based systems that now dominate the field [polyak2024movie, hong2022cogvideo, wan2025wan, sora2024]. This rapid progress has stimulated a wide range of downstream tasks, extending beyond basic text-to-video generation to encompass fine-grained control mechanisms (spatial, e.g., , image, pose, depth, landmark, sketch, and bounding box; temporal, e.g., , optical flow, trajectory, camera, and motion; and other conditional controls, e.g., , style, audio, bird’s-eye view) as well as sophisticated video editing capabilities.

Within the arc of §8, video spatial generation is the temporal extension of the priors built in the preceding two sections. Whereas §8.1 learned a 2D semantic-to-pixel prior on a single image plane and §8.2 lifted that prior into a static volumetric representation, this section adds the time axis: the model must place matter and appearance correctly and make them evolve plausibly as the camera or the scene itself moves through time. Appearance, geometry, and dynamics must now be jointly consistent: a generated clip is judged not only frame by frame but on object permanence, motion plausibility, and multi-view coherence under camera motion, which makes video the natural substrate for the dynamic world models and simulators that consume spatial structure downstream.

Formally, we cast every system in this section as a conditional spatio-temporal sampler that extends the latent-generator framework of §8.1.1. Let 𝒱=[0,1]T×H×W×3\mathcal{V}=[0,1]^{T\times H\times W\times 3} be the space of TT-frame clips and 𝒵vid\mathcal{Z}^{\text{vid}} a compressed spatio-temporal latent space supplied by a video autoencoder that extends the image autoencoder of Eq. (8.1) along the time axis. Writing ϕ\phi for the text encoder of Eq. (8.2) and κ:𝒞→𝒞′\kappa:\mathcal{C}\!\to\!\mathcal{C}^{\prime} for a generic encoder of an auxiliary control signal 𝐜∈𝒞\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}, the core learning problem is to train

Gθvid:ℰ×𝒞′→𝒵vid,𝐳^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐳1:T|ϕ⁢(𝐱),κ⁢(𝐜)),G_{\theta}^{\text{vid}}:\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\rightarrow% \mathcal{Z}^{\text{vid}},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\big{(}% \mathbf{z}^{1:T}\,\big{|}\,\phi(\mathbf{x}),\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.41)

so that the decoded clip 𝐯^=D⁢(𝐳^1:T)\hat{\mathbf{v}}=D(\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}) is photorealistic, temporally coherent, and faithful to both the prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the control 𝐜\mathbf{c}. Two limiting cases anchor the framework: with no auxiliary control (κ=∅\kappa=\varnothing) Eq. (8.41) reduces to text-to-video generation, and with a single frame (T=1T=1) it recovers the image generator of Eq. (8.2) exactly, so video spatial generation is precisely the image prior of §8.1 unrolled in time and equipped with a richer conditioning interface.

The subsections are organized by the axis of control each introduces into Eq. (8.41). Text-to-video generation (§8.3.1) is the base case without auxiliary control; spatial control (§8.3.2) adds a per-frame scaffold such as a pose or depth sequence; temporal control (§8.3.3) adds a motion or camera signal that governs dynamics rather than appearance; §8.3.4 covers the remaining modalities and the frameworks that fuse several at once; and video editing (§8.3.5) modifies an existing clip, lifting the 2D editing of §8.1.3 into time. §8.3.6 compares the five and discusses the challenges they share.

8.3.1 Text-to-Video Generation

Text-to-video (T2V) generation [sora2024, polyak2024movie, hong2022cogvideo, wan2025wan] synthesizes photorealistic, temporally coherent video from a natural-language description. It extends text-to-image (T2I) synthesis along time, so the model must produce plausible motion and state transitions as well as high-fidelity frames, and it does so with no explicit spatial scaffold: object permanence, motion plausibility, and view coherence under camera motion cannot be supplied from outside but must emerge from the generator itself. That is why the unconditional T2V model is the substrate on which the explicit control axes of §8.3.2–§8.3.5 are built. Its architecture has followed the image case, from generative adversarial networks (GANs) through autoregressive models to the diffusion models that dominate today, with progress driven as much by data as by architecture [chen2024panda70mcaptioning70mvideos, NEURIPS2024_57f6683e].

8.3.1.1 Task Definition

Text-to-video generation is the base case of Eq. (8.41) with no auxiliary control (κ=∅\kappa=\varnothing): the generator samples a latent from the prompt embedding alone,

𝐳^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐳1:T|ϕ⁢(𝐱)),\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{1:T}\,\big{|}\,\phi(% \mathbf{x})\big{)}, (8.42)

which is exactly the latent sampler GθG_{\theta} of Eq. (8.2) unrolled over TT frames in the spatio-temporal latent space 𝒵vid\mathcal{Z}^{\text{vid}}.

8.3.1.2 Methodology

The three paradigms factorize the clip distribution pθ⁢(𝐳1:T∣ϕ⁢(𝐱))p_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{1:T}\mid\phi(\mathbf{x})) adversarially, causally over discrete tokens, or by iterative spatio-temporal denoising, and each changes its image counterpart of §8.1.1 in one structural respect; Figure 8.13 contrasts how each handles the temporal dimension.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The first T2V systems extended the image GANs of §8.1.1.2 to clips. The video-specific change is in the discriminator: rather than scoring a single image, it must judge both per-frame realism and the plausibility of motion across the sequence, which is naturally realized as a two-critic objective

minθ⁡maxψs,ψt⁡𝔼𝐯∼pdata⁢[log⁡Dψs⁢(𝐯)+log⁡Dψt⁢(𝐯)]+𝔼𝐧⁢[log⁡(1−Dψs⁢(𝐯^))+log⁡(1−Dψt⁢(𝐯^))],\min_{\theta}\ \max_{\psi_{s},\psi_{t}}\ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{v}\sim p_{\text{% data}}}\!\big{[}\log D_{\psi_{s}}(\mathbf{v})+\log D_{\psi_{t}}(\mathbf{v})% \big{]}+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{n}}\!\big{[}\log\!\big{(}1-D_{\psi_{s}}(\hat{% \mathbf{v}})\big{)}+\log\!\big{(}1-D_{\psi_{t}}(\hat{\mathbf{v}})\big{)}\big{]}, (8.43)

where 𝐯^=D⁢(Gθ⁢(𝐧,ϕ⁢(𝐱)))\hat{\mathbf{v}}=D\big{(}G_{\theta}(\mathbf{n},\phi(\mathbf{x}))\big{)} is the decoded clip, the spatial critic DψsD_{\psi_{s}} scores individual frames, and the temporal critic DψtD_{\psi_{t}} scores motion coherence over the clip, the term absent from the single-discriminator image objective of Eq. (8.3). TGAN [saito2017temporal] and TGAN-v2 [saito2020train] used a temporal generator to produce latent motion vectors from which an image generator rendered frames; MoCoGAN [tulyakov2018mocogan] and MoCoGAN-HD [tian2021good] disentangled content from motion, generating the motion code recurrently; DVD-GAN [clark2019adversarial] instantiated Eq. (8.43) directly with separate spatial and temporal discriminators; and DIGAN [yu2022generating] used implicit neural representations for longer sequences. Even with architectures such as StyleGAN-V [skorokhodov2022stylegan], GANs suffered from flicker, training instability, and mode collapse, which limited the diversity of their motion and pushed the field toward other paradigms.

Autoregressive Models. Autoregressive (AR) models recast T2V as the sequential prediction of §8.1.1.2, tokenizing a clip with a 3D Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (3D VQ-VAE) and predicting each token from its predecessors with a large transformer. The video-specific change is the order of the factorization: where the image model of Eq. (8.4) runs over the spatial tokens of a single frame, the video model factorizes over space and time,

pθ⁢(𝐳1:T|ϕ⁢(𝐱))=∏t=1T∏n=1Npθ⁢(zt,n|𝐳<t,zt,<n,ϕ⁢(𝐱)),p_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{1:T}\,\big{|}\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\big{)}\;=\;% \prod_{t=1}^{T}\prod_{n=1}^{N}p_{\theta}\!\big{(}z_{t,n}\,\big{|}\,\mathbf{z}^% {<t},\,z_{t,<n},\,\phi(\mathbf{x})\big{)}, (8.44)

so that each frame is conditioned on all previously generated frames 𝐳<t\mathbf{z}^{<t}. This inter-frame causal dependency is the source of both the paradigm’s strength (global temporal coherence) and its characteristic failure, the accumulation of per-step error over long roll-outs. VideoGPT [yan2021videogpt] demonstrated the approach for unconditional generation, NÜWA [wu2022nuwa] and CogVideo [hong2022cogvideo] adapted it to text-to-video synthesis, and TATS [ge2022long] addressed quality degradation in long sequences. The paradigm has since resurged in large multimodal backbones: Emu3 [wang2024emu3] generates video inside a language-model backbone by treating frames as discrete visual tokens, and CausVid [yin2025slow] and MAGI-1 [ai2025magi1autoregressivevideogeneration] scale to long-form generation with autoregressive diffusion transformers. Sequential decoding nevertheless remains expensive and prone to the error accumulation that Eq. (8.44) makes explicit.

Diffusion Models. Diffusion models, which now dominate T2V, lift the latent-denoising objective of §8.1.1.2 from a single image to the clip latent 𝐳1:T\mathbf{z}^{1:T}. The forward and reverse processes are those of Eq. (8.5); the video-specific change is that the denoiser ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} operates on a spatio-temporal tensor and is trained to predict the noise added to the whole clip at sampling step ss,

minθ⁡𝔼s,𝐳01:T,ϵ⁢[‖ϵ−ϵθ⁢(𝐳s1:T,s,ϕ⁢(𝐱))‖22],\min_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{s,\,\mathbf{z}_{0}^{1:T},\,\epsilon}\!\left[\big{\|% }\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}_{s}^{1:T},\,s,\,\phi(\mathbf{x}% )\big{)}\big{\|}_{2}^{2}\right], (8.45)

where ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} models dependencies across both space and time, and ss is distinct from the frame index tt. One widely used design factorizes attention into spatial attention within each frame and temporal attention across frames, as illustrated in Figure 8.13(c); other architectures use joint spacetime attention. VDM [ho2022video] applied the idea in pixel space with a 3D U-Net; the breakthrough was moving diffusion into the compressed latent space of a video-specific autoencoder, as in VideoLDM [blattmann2023align], LVDM [he2022latent], and the open-source Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [blattmann2023stable], which cut training and inference cost enough to make high-resolution generation practical.

A second recipe adapts pretrained T2I models. Imagen Video [ho2022imagen] and Make-A-Video [singer2022make] freeze a T2I model and insert trainable temporal modules (e.g., , temporal attention layers or 1D convolutions) between its spatial layers, which are then trained on video to learn motion while the image prior is inherited intact. VideoCrafter [chen2023videocrafter1, chen2024videocrafter2] and LaVie [wang2025lavie] built high-quality generators on this recipe, Tune-A-Video [wu2023tune] adapted it to one-shot tuning on a single clip, and AnimateDiff [guo2023animatediff] turned the temporal modules into plug-and-play motion modules that animate personalized T2I models without further fine-tuning.

Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have since replaced the U-Net backbone, operating on “spacetime patches” (unified tokens representing blocks of video) and scaling well. Sora [sora2024] demonstrated long-duration (up to one minute), high-resolution clips and presented the approach as a step toward world simulation, and a wave of DiT models followed, including Open-Sora [zheng2024open], LATTE [ma2024latte], CogVideoX [yang2024cogvideox], StepVideo [ma2025stepvideot2vtechnicalreportpractice], Movie Gen [polyak2024movie], Wan [wan2025wan], and Veo [DeepMindVeo]. Large open DiT foundation models have substantially narrowed the gap to proprietary systems. HunyuanVideo [kong2024hunyuanvideo], at 1313B parameters the largest open T2V model at release, couples a “dual-stream-to-single-stream” full-attention DiT (text and video tokens processed in separate streams before fusion) with a multimodal-LLM text encoder and a 3D causal VAE, and reports human-evaluated quality competitive with leading closed systems. Mochi 1 [genmo2024mochi] introduces an asymmetric DiT (AsymmDiT) that allocates most capacity to the visual stream, and LTX-Video [hacohen2024ltxvideo] uses a high-compression video VAE to run latent video diffusion in near real time. NVIDIA’s Cosmos [nvidia2025cosmos] reframes the video generator as a world-foundation model for “Physical AI”, trained so that embodied and robotics systems can use it as a learned simulator, which ties video generation to the world models of §8.6. Across these shifts the T2V trajectory has trailed the T2I trajectory of §8.1.1 by roughly a year, each image paradigm being inflated along the time axis once it matured.

8.3.1.3 Benchmarks

Video adds a requirement at every level of evaluation: corpora must pair clips with captions at scale, suites must stratify by temporal phenomena (motion, object permanence, dynamic degree), and metrics must measure cross-frame coherence as well as per-frame quality.

Training Corpora.

Caption–clip scale has been the principal driver of T2V quality, and high-quality paired video–text data is far scarcer than image–text data. Early work repurposed action-recognition corpora such as UCF-101 [soomro2012ucf101] and Kinetics [carreira2017quo], which supply short, class-labeled clips but no captions. WebVid-10M [bain2021frozen], the first web-scale captioned corpus, underpinned most 2022–2023 systems despite noisy alt-text captions and watermarks; later corpora raised caption density and clip length, with Panda-70M [chen2024panda70mcaptioning70mvideos] captioned automatically by cross-modality teachers, MiraData [NEURIPS2024_57f6683e] targeting long clips with dense structured captions, and Koala-36M [wang2025koala36m] explicitly optimizing the consistency between caption and content, the property that most directly limits a generator’s controllability. Table 8.7 gives their scale.

Evaluation Benchmark Suites.

Classical T2V evaluation reported zero-shot distributional scores on the held-out splits of UCF-101 and MSR-VTT [xu2016msrvtt], which probe frame quality and coarse text relevance but say nothing about temporal or compositional faithfulness. Recent suites are purpose-built: VBench [huang2023vbench] decomposes quality into fine-grained dimensions (subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, temporal flicker, per-frame aesthetic and imaging quality), each with an automatic protocol validated against human preference; EvalCrafter [liu2024evalcrafter] aggregates objective metrics over prompts derived from real-world usage; and T2V-CompBench [sun2024t2vcompbench] targets compositional faithfulness over time (attribute binding, spatial relations, motion binding, interactions), the temporal analogue of the T2I-CompBench probe of §8.1.1. Table 8.8 lists them.

Evaluation Metrics.

The metric that defines video evaluation is the Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [unterthiner2018fvd], the spatio-temporal analogue of FID: it compares distributions of features extracted from generated and real clips by a pretrained video backbone (I3D), and is therefore sensitive to motion realism in a way that per-frame FID [heusel2017gans] and Inception Score are not. Text–clip alignment is measured by CLIPSIM, the per-frame CLIPScore [hessel2021clipscore] averaged over the clip, which captures topical relevance but is blind to whether the described motion actually occurs. Because none of these scalars captures coherence or dynamics, papers report several VBench dimensions alongside them, which exposes a trade-off a single number hides: dynamic degree (how much genuine motion a clip contains) against temporal consistency (how stable it stays), since a near-static clip trivially maximizes consistency while failing the prompt. Headline claims are corroborated with human preference.

8.3.1.4 Challenges and Trends

Three problems belong to the unconditional base case. Long-horizon coherence from text alone is the first: with no scaffold, object permanence and motion plausibility must emerge implicitly, and all three paradigms degrade as clips lengthen (GANs flicker, autoregressive roll-outs accumulate the error of Eq. (8.44), diffusion models lose consistency beyond their trained window), so coherence beyond a few seconds remains the binding constraint. Motion realism without a control signal is the second: prompts under-specify dynamics, so the generator must sample from a highly multi-modal motion posterior, and the easy optimum is near-static or physically implausible motion that still scores well on per-frame metrics. The video–text data bottleneck is the third: paired data is scarce relative to images, web captions are short and weakly aligned, and this caps both controllability and the reliability of the automatic captioning used to scale corpora, which is what the dense-caption efforts (Panda-70M, MiraData, Koala-36M) address. The explicit control interfaces of the following subsections relieve the first two by moving structure and dynamics from the prompt into the input.

8.3.2 Spatial Controlled Video Generation

While textual descriptions provide high-level semantic guidance, they often lack the granularity required for precise control over object placement, scene geometry, or character appearance. Spatial-controlled video generation addresses this limitation by augmenting the generation process with explicit spatial conditioning signals, affording users more direct and deterministic influence over the synthesized visual output. The geometry, articulation, and layout that the text-to-video base case of §8.3.1 had to hallucinate from the prompt alone are here externalized into a per-frame scaffold: the spatial structure becomes an input the model must honor rather than an emergent property it must invent, which is precisely what makes the output controllable and verifiable.

8.3.2.1 Task Definition

Spatial control instantiates Eq. (8.41) with a control encoder κs\kappa_{\text{s}} acting on a spatial condition 𝐜s1:T\mathbf{c}_{\text{s}}^{1:T} (a static or sparse reference image, a pose sequence, a depth-map sequence, facial landmarks, a sketch sequence, or a bounding-box track),

𝐳^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐳1:T|ϕ⁢(𝐱),κs⁢(𝐜s1:T)),\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{1:T}\,\big{|}\,\phi(% \mathbf{x}),\,\kappa_{\text{s}}(\mathbf{c}_{\text{s}}^{1:T})\big{)}, (8.46)

so that the scaffold pins down the per-frame spatial layout while the prompt 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the temporal modules supply appearance and motion. The conditioning channels surveyed below differ only in what 𝐜s\mathbf{c}_{\text{s}} encodes (appearance for an image, articulation for pose or landmarks, 3D structure for depth, free-form layout for a sketch, or object location for a bounding box), and recover the text-to-video base case of Eq. (8.42) exactly when 𝐜s=∅\mathbf{c}_{\text{s}}=\varnothing.

8.3.2.2 Methodology

The six channels carry different spatial information, while the injection mechanism depends on the model. A common design is a ControlNet-style adapter [zhang2023adding]: a trainable control branch processes the encoded condition and injects a residual into intermediate features of a video backbone, schematically at layer ℓ\ell

hℓ′=hℓ+Δ⁢hℓ,Δ⁢hℓ=𝒜ψ,ℓ⁢(κs⁢(𝐜s1:T)),h_{\ell}^{\prime}=h_{\ell}+\Delta h_{\ell},\qquad\Delta h_{\ell}=\mathcal{A}_{% \psi,\ell}\!\big{(}\kappa_{\text{s}}(\mathbf{c}_{\text{s}}^{1:T})\big{)}, (8.47)

where hℓh_{\ell} denotes backbone features and 𝒜ψ,ℓ\mathcal{A}_{\psi,\ell} a trainable control branch (dependence on the noisy latent, diffusion step, and other conditioning is omitted, and the backbone may be frozen while the adapter trains); latent concatenation and attention-based conditioning are the other common implementations. Figure 8.14 shows the six channels alongside this adapter pathway: a reference image acts as a static appearance anchor, the other five are usually frame-indexed sequences, and compatible channels can be combined.

Image Control. A reference image (Figure 8.14a) specifies the style, content, or initial state of a video, which is the basis of animating a still and of keeping a subject’s appearance consistent. I2VGen-XL [zhang2023i2vgen], Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [blattmann2023stable], VideoCrafter1 [chen2023videocrafter1], and Lumiere [bar2024lumiere] use the reference image as an initial condition, often by concatenating its latent with the initial noise, and ConsistI2V [ren2024consisti2v] refines this for consistency. The model then generates a plausible motion sequence that evolves from the image, typically under a text prompt, as in DynamiCrafter [xing2024dynamicrafter].

Pose Control. Pose-guided generation (Figure 8.14b) animates articulated subjects, predominantly humans, along a predefined sequence of skeletal poses, the video counterpart of pose-guided image generation [ju2023humansd, zhang2023adding, Ju_2023_CVPR] and the core of avatar animation and character generation. The pose keypoints (e.g., , from MMPose [mmpose2020]) are encoded and injected at each denoising step, frequently through a ControlNet-style adapter [zhang2023adding]. MagicAnimate [xu2024magicanimate], Animate Anyone [hu2024animate], Follow-Your-Pose [ma2024followyourpose], and DreamPose [karras2023dreampose] pair a reference image for appearance with a pose sequence for motion, DisPose [li2024dispose] disentangles the pose guidance, and Champ [zhu2024champ] and MagicPose [chang2023magicpose] target high-fidelity motion, so that the output keeps the subject’s identity while following the target poses.

Depth Control. A sequence of depth maps (Figure 8.14c), estimated from an existing video or rendered from a 3D model, specifies dense 3D structure and so enforces consistent object layout and realistic occlusion. ControlVideo [zhao2025controlvideo], Make-Your-Video [xing2024make], Control-A-Video [chen2023control], and ControlNeXt [peng2024controlnext] adapt the ControlNet framework to video, processing each frame’s depth map with a trainable adapter that guides the denoiser; DreamDance [pang2024dreamdance] and SparseCtrl [guo2024sparsectrl] also use depth for dynamic scene generation.

Landmark Control. Facial landmarks (Figure 8.14d) give fine-grained control over expression and are the standard interface for talking-head animation. EchoMimic [chen2024echomimic], HunyuanPortrait [xu2025hunyuanportrait], and LivePortrait [guo2024liveportrait] animate a static portrait from landmarks, often themselves driven by audio, so that lip movements, blinks, and subtle expressions stay synchronized; TASTE-Rob [zhao2025taste], Takin-ADA [lin2024takin], and Follow-Your-Emoji [ma2024follow] extend landmarks to more expressive control.

Sketch Control. Sketches (Figure 8.14e) let users define compositional layout and motion with simple line drawings, an intuitive interface for animation. ToonCrafter [xing2024tooncrafter], VidSketch [jiang2025vidsketch], AniDoc [meng2025anidoc], and SketchBetween [loftsdottir2022sketchbetween] take a sequence of sketches to guide interpolation or generation, encoding the line art and injecting it as a condition; LayerAnimate [yang2025layeranimate] animates hand-drawn characters and scenes layer by layer, and MagicStick [ma2025magicstick] uses sketch-like structural cues for editing.

Bounding Box (BBox) Control. Bounding-box tracks (Figure 8.14f) specify where objects are and how they move over time, and dominate autonomous-driving simulation: MagicDrive [gao2023magicdrive], DriveDreamer [wang2024drivedreamer], DriveScape [wu2024drivescape], and DreamForge [mei2024dreamforge] use 3D boxes to control the position and motion of vehicles and pedestrians. The box information enters either through cross-attention, as in DiVE [jiang2024dive], or as a spatial feature map, and Boximator [wang2024boximator] and Ctrl-V [luo2025ctrl] generate and control object motion from box sequences.

Nearly every structural channel (pose, depth, sketch, box) is paired with an appearance reference image, since structure alone cannot fix identity or texture, and the channels cluster by application: image and landmark control in portrait and talking-head synthesis, pose and sketch control in character animation, depth and box control in geometry-faithful and driving-simulation settings.

8.3.2.3 Benchmarks

Unlike the text-to-video base case of §8.3.1, spatial control has no single canonical corpus or suite: each channel is trained and evaluated on data specialized to its application. Models are typically built on the general web-scale corpora of §8.3.1 (WebVid-10M [bain2021frozen] and successors) for appearance priors, then specialized on task data: human-animation channels on dance- and fashion-video collections paired with extracted pose keypoints (e.g., , via OpenPose [cao2017realtime] or MMPose [mmpose2020]), talking-head landmark control on portrait-video sets, and bounding-box driving simulation on annotated driving datasets such as nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes], whose 3D box and trajectory labels supply the control signal directly.

Control-fidelity Metrics.

Spatial control is judged on two axes simultaneously: the generic video-quality metrics of §8.3.1 (FVD [unterthiner2018fvd], CLIPSIM, and VBench [huang2023vbench] dimensions) and channel-specific adherence metrics that measure how faithfully the output respects 𝐜s\mathbf{c}_{\text{s}}. The latter are necessarily per-channel: pose and landmark control report keypoint accuracy (re-detected-keypoint distance to the target skeleton or face mesh); depth control reports depth consistency between the re-estimated and the conditioning maps; image control reports identity and appearance preservation (face-/subject-similarity to the reference); and bounding-box control reports detection mAP and trajectory IoU of the generated objects against the conditioning boxes. Neither axis suffices alone, so methods report a quality-plus-adherence tuple: a model can maximize adherence by ignoring the prompt (rigid, texture-collapsed output) or maximize quality by ignoring the control. The same holds for every controlled axis that follows.

8.3.2.4 Challenges and Trends

Single-channel spatial control has three problems of its own; those that arise once several conditions are fused are discussed in §8.3.6. Because the structural scaffold and the appearance reference pass through the same denoiser, strong control leaks structure into texture: pose and depth conditioning induce identity drift or bake the scaffold’s silhouette into the surface, and disentangling what moves from what it looks like (as DisPose [li2024dispose] attempts for pose) remains open. Dense scaffolds (image, depth) over-constrain and suppress plausible motion, whereas sparse ones (boxes, coarse sketches) leave appearance and fine geometry ambiguous, so no channel is uniformly preferable and the right granularity depends on the task. And adapters trained on, say, frontal human dance transfer poorly to unusual viewpoints or non-human subjects, which is the data cost of per-channel specialization and one motivation for the multi-condition frameworks of §8.3.4.

8.3.3 Temporal Controlled Video Generation

Temporal control regulates how motion and timing evolve across frames, the lever behind cinematic camera work, narrative pacing, and believable physical interaction. It is the complement of the spatial scaffold of §8.3.2: where spatial control fixes where things are in each frame, temporal control fixes how they move between frames, externalizing the dynamics (object motion, camera path, timing) that the text-to-video base case of §8.3.1 otherwise had to sample blindly from a highly multi-modal motion posterior.

8.3.3.1 Task Definition

Temporal control instantiates Eq. (8.41) with an encoder κt\kappa_{\text{t}} of a motion or timing signal 𝐦1:T\mathbf{m}^{1:T} (an optical-flow field, an object trajectory, a camera-pose path, or a learned motion embedding),

𝐳^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐳1:T|ϕ⁢(𝐱),κt⁢(𝐦1:T)).\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{1:T}\,\big{|}\,\phi(% \mathbf{x}),\,\kappa_{\text{t}}(\mathbf{m}^{1:T})\big{)}. (8.48)

The contrast with spatial control (Eq. (8.46)) is that 𝐦1:T\mathbf{m}^{1:T} constrains the inter-frame dynamics (how content moves between frames) rather than the per-frame appearance, so κt\kappa_{\text{t}} typically steers the temporal-attention or latent-warping pathway of the denoiser. The channels below differ in how the motion is specified: densely (optical flow), as object paths (trajectory), as virtual-camera parameters (camera), or as a transferable behavioral style (motion).

8.3.3.2 Methodology

The four channels specify inter-frame dynamics through different signals, and no single injection architecture serves them all. One implementation uses a trainable temporal-control branch 𝒯ψ\mathcal{T}_{\psi} to modulate features of a pretrained video backbone,

hℓ′=hℓ+Δ⁢hℓ,Δ⁢hℓ=𝒯ψ,ℓ⁢(κt⁢(𝐦1:T)),h_{\ell}^{\prime}=h_{\ell}+\Delta h_{\ell},\qquad\Delta h_{\ell}=\mathcal{T}_{% \psi,\ell}\!\big{(}\kappa_{\text{t}}(\mathbf{m}^{1:T})\big{)}, (8.49)

with dependence on noisy latents, diffusion step, and text omitted. More broadly, two routes recur: explicit transformations that use the motion to warp noise, latents, or attention features, and encoded conditioning that steers generation through adapters, attention, or learned motion features. They are not tied to particular channels (flow and trajectories can drive learned conditioning, and camera control can use geometry-aware warping), and Figure 8.15 keeps the four input channels separate from the two routes.

Flow Control. The most explicit motion signal (Figure 8.15a) is an optical-flow field, which records the per-pixel displacement between consecutive frames and so specifies dynamics at the finest granularity; conditioning on a sequence of such fields yields specific, coherent motion at the cost of authoring or estimating a dense signal. Motion-I2V [shi2024motion] integrates a motion-field predictor into its diffusion framework so that generation follows the supplied flow, I2VControl [feng2024i2vcontrol] disentangles flow for unified control, and MOFA-Video [niu2024mofa] animates a still image from user-painted motion fields. Go-with-the-Flow [burgert2025gowiththeflow] dispenses with the adapter altogether, warping the diffusion noise prior along the target flow so that the motion constraint lives in the sampling process rather than in an added branch.

Trajectory Control. Sparsifying the dense field into a few object paths (Figure 8.15b) trades pixel-level precision for an interface a user can actually author: a sequence of 2D or 3D coordinates, or a path drawn interactively, directs character movement or object kinematics, entering the denoiser either by modifying the latents or by steering cross-attention maps. MotionCanvas [xing2025motioncanvas], MagicMotion [li2025magicmotion], and Tora [zhang2025tora] consume a predefined curve, FreeTraj [qiu2024freetraj] relaxes this to free-form trajectories, Peekaboo [jain2024peekaboo] also schedules when objects appear and disappear along the path, and DragNUWA [yin2023dragnuwa] and DragAnything [wu2024draganything] let the user drag regions through the frame interactively. MotionCtrl [wang2024motionctrl] handles object trajectory and camera motion in one controller, treating an object path and a camera path as two facets of the same inter-frame displacement.

Camera Control. Moving that displacement from objects to the observer (Figure 8.15c), camera-guided generation manipulates the virtual camera’s extrinsics (translation, rotation) and intrinsics (e.g., , focal length) to produce pans, tilts, zooms, and dolly moves.
