CameraCtrl [he2024cameractrl] and CameraCtrl II [he2025cameractrl] encode the camera trajectory as a conditioning feature; Direct-a-Video [yang2024direct], ViewCrafter [yu2024viewcrafter], and Cavia [xu2024cavia] couple it with novel-view synthesis; and 3DTrajMaster [fu20243dtrajmaster], MotionFlow [meral2024motionflow], and CineMaster [wang2025cinemaster] control camera and objects jointly in 3D. Two directions now lead. ReCamMaster [bai2025recammaster] and TrajectoryCrafter [yu2025trajectorycrafter] re-render an existing monocular clip under a new camera path rather than generating from scratch, and Diffusion-as-Shader [gu2025diffusionshader3dawarevideo] and GS-DiT [bian2025gsditadvancingvideogeneration] route the camera signal through a 3D proxy (a rendered shader pass or a pseudo-4D Gaussian field), which sharpens control by making it geometry-aware.

Motion Control. At the abstract end (Figure 8.15d), the signal is no longer a geometric displacement but a behavioral concept (walking, dancing, jumping) transferred from a reference video as a pose sequence or a learned motion embedding. Unlike the pose control of §8.3.2, it captures the dynamic style and cadence of a behavior rather than a frame-exact skeleton, so the central technical problem is disentanglement: extracting the motion while discarding the reference’s appearance. MotionDirector [zhao2024motiondirector], MotionClone [ling2024motionclone], and VMC [jeong2024vmc] learn this motion–appearance separation; Motion Prompting [geng2025motion], MotionAgent [liao2025motionagent], and MotionMatcher [wu2025motionmatcher] refine its granularity through trajectory- or feature-level motion descriptors; and DreamMotion [jeong2024dreammotion] and Customize-A-Video [ren2024customize] apply a reference clip’s dynamics to a new subject or scene fixed by the text prompt.

The channels trade precision against ease of specification: dense flow gives pixel-accurate control but is laborious to author, a motion embedding is effortless to supply but steers the result only loosely, and the most usable systems therefore pair an abstract signal (a drawn path, a reference clip) with a learned predictor that densifies it into the flow- or latent-level displacement the backbone actually consumes.

8.3.3.3 Benchmarks

As with spatial control (§8.3.2), temporal control has no single canonical suite: each channel is evaluated against data specialized to its signal. Models build on the general corpora of §8.3.1 for appearance and motion priors, then evaluate on task-specific resources: camera control on the posed-video collection RealEstate10K [zhou2018stereo], whose per-frame camera poses supply both the conditioning signal and the evaluation ground truth, increasingly supplemented by the larger and more scene-diverse DL3DV-10K [ling2024dl3dv] to test generalization beyond real-estate walkthroughs; flow control against the MPI-Sintel optical-flow benchmark [sintel] or flow re-estimated from generated clips with RAFT [teed2020raft]; and motion- and trajectory-control quality through the motion-smoothness and dynamic-degree dimensions of VBench [huang2023vbench].

Control-fidelity Metrics.

Alongside the generic video-quality metrics of §8.3.1, each channel measures adherence by re-extracting the control signal from the generated clip and comparing it with the conditioning input; the estimator and the error differ per channel.

Flow adherence. The optical flow of the generated clip is re-estimated with RAFT [teed2020raft] and compared to the conditioning flow by the end-point error (EPE), the per-pixel L2L_{2} displacement difference averaged over pixels and frames. A complementary flow-warping error warps each generated frame onto the next with the target flow and reports the photometric residual, which tests whether the rendered motion realizes the commanded displacement rather than merely correlating with it.

Trajectory adherence. The controlled object is re-localized in the output with a dense point tracker such as CoTracker [karaev2024cotracker] or a detector, and its tracked center is compared to the target path by the mean L2L_{2} distance, normalized by frame size and averaged over time and instances; this is the object motion-control error reported by Tora [zhang2025tora] and DragNUWA [yin2023dragnuwa], and it penalizes both spatial deviation and mistimed arrival.

Camera adherence. The camera trajectory of the generated clip is recovered by structure-from-motion (COLMAP [schonberger2016structure]) and aligned to the target up to a similarity transform, since pose is recoverable only up to scale. Following CameraCtrl [he2024cameractrl], a rotation error (the geodesic angle between estimated and target rotations, summed over frames) and a translation error (the L2L_{2} distance between scale-normalized camera centers) are reported; failure to reconstruct a stable trajectory at all is itself diagnostic of an incoherent output.

Motion-transfer fidelity. With no ground-truth video, fidelity is measured from two sides: a motion-similarity term compares the dynamics of output and reference (the correlation of tracked point trajectories or temporal feature statistics), and an appearance-divergence term (CLIP similarity to the new prompt together with low feature similarity to the reference’s appearance) confirms that the subject was re-synthesized rather than copied.

As for spatial control, these adherence errors are reported together with generic quality, since a near-static clip trivially minimizes EPE and pose error while ignoring the prompt.

8.3.3.4 Challenges and Trends

Three problems are specific to temporal control; fusing it with other conditions is discussed in §8.3.6. Because the motion signal passes through the same backbone that renders appearance, a transferred motion often drags the source clip’s identity or texture with it, the leakage that MotionDirector [zhao2024motiondirector] and VMC [jeong2024vmc] try to disentangle and that remains unsolved for large appearance gaps between reference and target. Dense flow over-constrains and suppresses generative freedom, whereas a single trajectory or a short reference clip under-specifies the global dynamics, which is why methods increasingly interpose a learned predictor that densifies an abstract signal into a flow- or latent-level field. And a commanded camera path or object trajectory can demand views or dynamics inconsistent with the scene geometry, producing parallax errors and object distortion; 3D-aware camera control (ViewCrafter [yu2024viewcrafter], CineMaster [wang2025cinemaster]) routes the control through an explicit geometric proxy for exactly this reason, which links temporal control back to the volumetric representations of §8.2.

8.3.4 Other Controlled Video Generation

Beyond the spatial scaffolds of §8.3.2 and the motion signals of §8.3.3, a video can be steered by further, application-specific conditions: an artistic style reference, a handful of draggable points, a bird’s-eye-view road layout, a target text string to render, or a synchronizing audio track. Each externalizes an attribute that text specifies only loosely, extending controllable generation to creative, interactive, and domain-specific settings; together they raise the question the single-axis interfaces leave open, how to honor several conditions at once, which the universal frameworks at the end of this subsection try to answer.

8.3.4.1 Task Definition

Taken one at a time, each “other” modality instantiates the generic conditional sampler of Eq. (8.41) with an encoder κo\kappa_{\text{o}} of a heterogeneous control signal 𝐜\mathbf{c} (a style reference, a set of draggable points, a BEV layout, a target text string, or an audio track). The distinctive task of this subsection, however, is to honor several such conditions simultaneously: universal and multi-task frameworks fuse KK encoded signals into a single sequence,

𝐳^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐳1:T|ϕ⁢(𝐱),κ1⁢(𝐜1),…,κK⁢(𝐜K)),\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{1:T}\,\big{|}\,\phi(% \mathbf{x}),\,\kappa_{1}(\mathbf{c}_{1}),\dots,\kappa_{K}(\mathbf{c}_{K})\big{% )}, (8.50)

so that the KK encoded conditions are processed jointly rather than one axis at a time, with K=1K=1 recovering the single-modality case and κk=∅\kappa_{k}=\varnothing for all kk recovering the text-to-video base case of §8.3.1.

8.3.4.2 Methodology

The methods fall into single-modality channels (style, points, BEV, text rendering, audio) and multi-task frameworks that combine compatible conditions. Writing uk=κk⁢(𝐜k)u_{k}=\kappa_{k}(\mathbf{c}_{k}), the common interface is

𝐳^1:T=Gθ⁢(𝐧,ϕ⁢(𝐱);ℱψ⁢(u1,…,uK)),\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}=G_{\theta}\!\big{(}\mathbf{n},\phi(\mathbf{x});\mathcal% {F}_{\psi}(u_{1},\dots,u_{K})\big{)}, (8.51)

where ℱψ\mathcal{F}_{\psi} is a model-specific conditioning interface that may act at several layers rather than produce one fixed-size embedding. Three implementations are representative and can be combined: summed adapter residuals ∑kΔ⁢hk\sum_{k}\Delta h_{k}, concatenation of the encoded channels with the model input or features, and unified attention over condition tokens. Figure 8.16 shows the five input modalities and these three fusion designs; K=1K=1 denotes one selected modality and K>1K>1 a supported combination.

Style Control. Style-guided generation transfers the artistic style of a reference image or video to a target video. Per-frame style transfer flickers; diffusion-based approaches such as Rerender A Video [yang2023rerender], StyleCrafter [liu2023stylecrafter], FRESCO [yang2024fresco], and StyleMaster [ye2025stylemaster] instead integrate the style into generation, often by guiding it with the CLIP embedding of the style reference so that the style holds across frames, and UniVST [song2024univst] generalizes this into a universal framework. FrameGuidance [jang2025frameguidancetrainingfreeguidance] and OmniVDiff [xi2025omnivdiffomnicontrollablevideo] add training-free frame-level guidance and omni-controllable diffusion, respectively.

Point Control. Point control fixes motion through a sparse, interactive interface: the user drags a few points on an object from an initial frame to a new position in a later frame, and the model infers a plausible motion for the whole object. Drag-A-Video [teng2023drag] introduced the approach by optimizing latent codes to satisfy the point constraints, Track4Gen [jeong2025track4genteachingvideodiffusion] focuses on tracking the user-specified points robustly, and the 3D-aware camera controllers of §8.3.3 [gu2025diffusionshader3dawarevideo, bian2025gsditadvancingvideogeneration] also accept sparse point input for non-rigid manipulation.

Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) Control. BEV-guided generation serves autonomous-driving simulation: a sequence of top-down semantic maps dictates the road layout, the positions of other vehicles, and the movements of pedestrians. DriveDreamer-2 [zhao2024drivedreamer2llmenhancedworldmodels], MagicDrive-V2 [gao2025magicdrivev2highresolutionlongvideo], DiVE [jiang2024dive], DreamForge [mei2024dreamforge], and Panacea [wen2023panaceapanoramiccontrollablevideo] take these maps as input and generate first-person driving video consistent with the specified layout and dynamics.

Text Rendering. Many generators cannot render coherent, legible text inside a scene, so a dedicated channel treats the target string itself as the control signal. Text-Animator [liu2024textanimatorcontrollablevisualtext] adds text-embedding injection and refinement modules that improve the structure and temporal stability of rendered text, and Wan [wan2025wan] reports being the first video foundation model able to render legible Chinese and English text.

Audio Control. Audio-controlled generation synthesizes video synchronized with an input audio signal, in two sub-domains. Voice-guided generation produces talking heads: EMO [tian2024emoemoteportraitalive], VASA-1 [xu2024vasa1lifelikeaudiodriventalking], DreamTalk [ma2023dreamtalk], and AniPortrait [wei2024aniportrait] take a reference image and a speech clip, extract audio features with a pretrained encoder, and drive facial motion with accurate lip-sync and expression; Say Anything [ma2025sayanythingaudiodrivenlipsynchronization], MuseTalk [zhang2025musetalkrealtimehighfidelityvideo], and CAFE-TALK [chen2025cafetalkgenerating3dtalking] focus on high-fidelity lip synchronization, and V-Express [wang2024vexpressconditionaldropoutprogressive] and MegActor [yang2024megactorharnesspowerraw] balance audio against other control signals. Sound-guided generation follows more general audio such as music or ambient sound, using its rhythm, pitch, and emotional tone to drive visual elements, motion, and scene transitions: TA2V [10420468], MotionCraft [aira2024motioncraftphysicsbasedzeroshotvideo], AV-Link [hajiali2025avlinktemporallyaligneddiffusionfeatures], and ASVA [linz2024asva] generate music visualizations or scenes that follow the energy and structure of a track, and MagicInfinite [yi2025magicinfinitegeneratinginfinitetalking] and Sound2Sight [cherian2020sound2sightgeneratingvisualdynamics] explore more open-ended audio-driven generation.

Universal and Multi-Task Control. The single-modality channels each add one encoder; universal frameworks realize the fusion of Eq. (8.50) in a single model, along two lines. Autoregressive models built on multimodal large language models generate video from discrete visual tokens, as in VideoPoet [kondratyuk2024videopoetlargelanguagemodel] and Emu3 [wang2024emu3]. Diffusion models are being adapted to many conditions at once: VideoComposer [wang2023videocomposercompositionalvideosynthesis] integrates depth, pose, motion, and other conditions by channel concatenation, OmniHuman [lin2025omnihuman1rethinkingscalinguponestage] generates human video under multiple controls by mixing cross-attention and concatenation, and FullDiT [ju2025fullditmultitaskvideogenerative] processes all conditions with unified attention, the third realization of ℱψ\mathcal{F}_{\psi}.

8.3.4.3 Benchmarks

Being heterogeneous, the “other” modalities share no single suite: each is evaluated against data and metrics specialized to its signal, with the general corpora of §8.3.1 supplying the appearance and motion priors. BEV control is evaluated on driving collections such as nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes], whose paired BEV layouts and front-camera footage furnish both the conditioning signal and the ground truth. Voice-guided talking-head generation is evaluated on portrait-video collections (HDTF [zhang2021hdtf] and VFHQ [xie2022vfhq] are standard) and sound-guided generation on audio–video corpora with aligned music or ambient tracks. Style and point control, having no canonical benchmark, are assessed on the general corpora plus qualitative and user studies.

Control-fidelity Metrics.

Beyond the generic video-quality metrics of §8.3.1 (FVD [unterthiner2018fvd], CLIPSIM, and VBench [huang2023vbench] dimensions), each modality adds an adherence metric tailored to its signal, reported together with generic quality as in §8.3.2. Style adherence combines a CLIP style-similarity to the reference with a temporal-consistency term that penalizes flicker. Point adherence re-localizes the dragged keypoints in the output and reports their L2L_{2} deviation from the target path, as in the trajectory metric of §8.3.3. BEV adherence renders or detects objects in the generated clip and reports detection-mAP and layout-IoU against the input map. Text adherence runs OCR on the rendered frames and reports recognition accuracy and legibility. Audio adherence measures lip-sync quality with SyncNet-style confidence and landmark error for voice, and audio–visual synchrony for sound.

8.3.4.4 Challenges and Trends

The central difficulty here, fusing conditions of incommensurate dimensionality and strength without one washing out or dominating the others, is shared with the spatial and temporal axes and discussed in §8.3.6. Two problems are specific to these modalities. Text rendering must keep glyphs legible and stable at once, and per-frame legibility and temporal coherence pull against each other as the camera or the text moves. BEV control covers a narrow domain: models trained on a handful of driving datasets inherit their sensor rigs, cities, and traffic statistics, and generalize poorly beyond them.

8.3.5 Video Editing

Video editing takes an existing clip and modifies it under user instruction, rather than generating one from scratch (§8.3.1) or steering that generation with controls (§8.3.2–§8.3.4). It is the temporal lift of the image editing of §8.1.3, and its defining demand is selective preservation: the operator must change only the targeted content while holding the source’s geometry, layout, and motion fixed across every frame, so the central technical problem is to balance editability against spatio-temporal consistency without artifacts or unintended drift.

8.3.5.1 Task Definition

Given a source clip encoded as 𝐳in,1:T=E⁢(𝐯in)\mathbf{z}^{\text{in},1:T}=E(\mathbf{v}^{\text{in}}) and an edit instruction 𝐜\mathbf{c}, an editing operator

𝐳^1:T=Eθvid⁢(𝐳in,1:T,ϕ⁢(𝐱),κ⁢(𝐜))\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}=E_{\theta}^{\text{vid}}\!\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{\text{in},1% :T},\,\phi(\mathbf{x}),\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)} (8.52)

returns an edited clip that applies the requested change while preserving unedited content and the source motion, recovering the image editing operator of Eq. (8.8) exactly at T=1T=1. Eq. (8.52) encodes two competing objectives: editability (the output must realize the instruction 𝐜\mathbf{c}) and preservation (the unedited regions and the source dynamics must survive untouched).

8.3.5.2 Methodology

The five paradigms are overlapping choices of training strategy and preservation mechanism: training-free editing keeps the weights fixed, one-shot tuning updates selected parameters on the source clip, trained instruction editors learn across editing data, attention-based editing reuses or modifies source attention, and structural guidance conditions the edit on source-derived depth, edges, or poses. Many of them share a diffusion recipe that inverts the source clip and re-denoises it under the instruction; writing Inv\mathrm{Inv} for DDIM inversion of the pretrained or adapted backbone ϵθ0\epsilon_{\theta}^{0} of §8.3.1,

𝐳S1:T=Inv⁢(𝐳in,1:T;ϕ⁢(𝐱src)),𝐳^1:T=Denoise⁢(𝐳S1:T;ϕ⁢(𝐱),κ⁢(𝐜)),\mathbf{z}_{S}^{1:T}=\mathrm{Inv}\big{(}\mathbf{z}^{\text{in},1:T};\,\phi(% \mathbf{x}^{\text{src}})\big{)},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{1:T}=\mathrm{Denoise}% \big{(}\mathbf{z}_{S}^{1:T};\,\phi(\mathbf{x}),\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.53)

where SS denotes the terminal diffusion step, distinct from the clip length TT. Inversion supplies a source-correlated initialization; how much of the source survives then depends on the sampling, feature reuse, and guidance applied during re-denoising. Figure 8.17 schematizes the five paradigms, with panels (a)–(e) keyed to the paragraphs below.

Training-Free (Zero-Shot) Methods. The lightest realization of Eq. (8.53) (Figure 8.17a) edits a video without any fine-tuning, analogous to zero-shot image editing [ju2023directinversionboostingdiffusionbased]: DDIM inversion encodes the source into latent codes and noise maps, and the denoising process is rerun on them under the edited prompt. Text2Video-Zero [Khachatryan_2023_ICCV] and Pix2Video [ceylan2023pix2videovideoeditingusing] established the category, and vid2vid-zero [wang2024zeroshotvideoeditingusing], I2VEdit [ouyang2024i2veditfirstframeguidedvideoediting], RAVE [kara2024rave], and FastVideoEdit [zhang2024fastvideoeditleveragingconsistencymodels] add latent-code warping and feature injection to improve temporal consistency without fine-tuning.

One-Shot Tuning Methods. Trading a little training for sharper fidelity (Figure 8.17b), Tune-A-Video [wu2023tune] fine-tunes a limited subset of a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model’s parameters on the frames of a single source video, so that the model learns its content and motion and can regenerate it under a new prompt. Dreamix [molad2023dreamixvideodiffusionmodels] builds on one-shot fine-tuning to improve both editability and fidelity to the original motion.

Training-Based Methods. The limited control and quality of inference-time editing have motivated editors that learn a reusable operator from editing data (Figure 8.17c), particularly for instruction-based editing. InsV2V [cheng2023consistentvideotovideotransferusing] extends the InstructPix2Pix [brooks2023instructpix2pixlearningfollowimage] framework directly to video; GenProp [Liu_2025_CVPR] propagates an edit from a user-modified first frame to the rest of the sequence; and VideoPainter [videopainter] uses a video inpainting model as an intermediary. UNIC [ye2025unicunifiedincontextvideo] handles many editing tasks in one model by concatenating the conditions into a sequence with task-aware positional embeddings, and EditVerse [ju2025editverseunifyingimagevideo] unifies video generation and editing by representing text, image, and video as one token sequence processed with self-attention, which permits in-context learning and flexible inputs.

Attention-Based Editing. To protect preservation within the inference-time recipe (Figure 8.17d), many techniques manipulate the cross-attention maps directly: following Prompt-to-Prompt in images, they blend the attention maps of the original and edited prompts so that the inverted source structure of Eq. (8.53) survives the re-denoising. FateZero [qi2023fatezerofusingattentionszeroshot] and Video-P2P [liu2023videop2p] were early examples, and Edit-A-Video [shin2023editavideosinglevideoediting], TokenFlow [tokenflow2023], UniEdit [bai2024uniedit], and AnyV2V [ku2024anyv2vtuningfreeframeworkvideotovideo] improve temporal consistency at the token or feature level, enabling localized edits such as changing an object’s material or color while the scene structure is kept.

Editing with Structural Guidance. At the explicitly guided end (Figure 8.17e), editing is conditioned on spatial signals extracted from the source video, the conditioning machinery of §8.3.2 repurposed for preservation rather than generation. Rerender A Video [yang2023rerender] feeds the source’s depth or edge maps to a ControlNet-like module during editing so that geometry and layout stay intact, and MagicEdit [liew2023magicedit] accepts a variety of spatial inputs (e.g., , pose, sketches, segmentation maps) for high structural fidelity, which suits style transfer and object replacement, where preserving structure is what prevents distortion and keeps motion coherent.

The paradigms trade cost against control: training-free editing avoids per-clip weight updates but may still need iterative inference, whereas a trained instruction editor is expensive to build but generalizes across edits.

8.3.5.3 Benchmarks

Video editing has no single canonical suite, and evaluation has moved from shared source-video collections toward purpose-built, fine-grained editing benchmarks. Early evaluations report on DAVIS [pont20172017], the de facto source set for object-centric edits, and on the LOVEU text-guided video-editing (TGVE) benchmark [wu2023loveutgve], which supplies prompt–clip pairs with human ratings; VPBench, released with VideoPainter [videopainter], adds masked clips with dense captions for inpainting-style edits. The most recent suites target instruction-guided editing and pair richer data with model-based scoring. FiVE [li2025five] contributes 7474 real clips (drawn from DAVIS) and 2626 generated clips across six fine-grained editing types, with 420420 object-level prompt pairs and masks, evaluated under a 1515-metric protocol spanning background preservation, text–video similarity, temporal consistency, video quality, and runtime. IVEBench [chen2026ivebench] scales this to 600600 source videos spanning seven semantic dimensions and clip lengths from 3232 to 1,0241{,}024 frames, across eight task categories (3535 subcategories) whose prompts are generated by LLMs and refined by experts, and adopts a three-dimensional protocol (video quality, instruction compliance, and video fidelity) that fuses traditional metrics with multimodal-LLM-based assessment.

Editing-fidelity Metrics.

Editing is judged on three axes that mirror the editability–preservation tension of Eq. (8.52). The classic metrics are, for edit adherence, the CLIP similarity between each edited frame and the target prompt; for temporal consistency, frame-to-frame CLIP similarity together with a warping error that flow-aligns adjacent frames and reports the photometric residual; and for structure and background preservation, PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS on the unedited regions against the source, atop the generic FVD [unterthiner2018fvd] quality score. These scalars correlate only loosely with human judgment on fine-grained edits (an object recolored but mislocalized can still score well), so the latest benchmarks add vision-language judges: FiVE-Acc [li2025five] uses a VLM to test whether the intended fine-grained edit succeeded, and IVEBench [chen2026ivebench] scores instruction compliance and fidelity with multimodal LLMs alongside the traditional metrics. Results are reported as an edit-versus-preservation pair, since ignoring the instruction trivially maximizes preservation.

8.3.5.4 Challenges and Trends

Three problems are specific to editing. Pushing the edit harder erodes the unedited regions and the source motion, while protecting them too strongly suppresses the requested change; this editability–preservation trade-off of Eq. (8.52) is what every paradigm above negotiates differently. The invert-and-re-denoise recipe of Eq. (8.53) is imperfect, and its reconstruction error compounds over long clips, so edits that are clean over a few seconds degrade over minute-scale video. And training-based editors follow only the edit types seen in their training pairs, so a flexible instruction editor that handles arbitrary edits remains open; the unified generate-and-edit models UNIC [ye2025unicunifiedincontextvideo] and EditVerse [ju2025editverseunifyingimagevideo], which treat the source clip as one stream among many in shared attention, are the current attempt.

8.3.6 Summary and Critical Challenges and Future Directions

Table 8.9 places the five control axes side by side: the control signal each introduces, the operator it instantiates over the shared sampler of Eq. (8.41), the paradigms it surveys, the methods anchoring each, and the benchmarks on which it reports.

The axes partition not by output domain, since all five decode a clip from the same 𝒵vid\mathcal{Z}^{\text{vid}}, but by the control fed to one shared sampler: text-to-video is the κ=∅\kappa=\varnothing limit, spatial, temporal, and other control progressively enrich κ\kappa, and editing alone reverses the direction of the map, taking an existing clip in place of pure noise. The injection mechanism converges across axes: the spatial residual branch (Eq. (8.47)), the temporal branch (Eq. (8.49)), and the multi-condition interface (Eq. (8.51)) are one idea, a trainable control pathway added to a pretrained backbone, generalized from one condition to many, and the most recent systems (VideoComposer, FullDiT, UNIC, EditVerse) go further by folding every axis, editing included, into a single token sequence processed by shared attention. Evaluation has not converged: no suite spans the five axes, each reports generic quality together with a channel-specific adherence score, and the newest editing benchmarks (FiVE, IVEBench) add vision-language and multimodal-LLM judges to improve human alignment.

Video generation inherits every difficulty of the 2D and 3D priors of §8.1 and §8.2 and adds the time axis, which turns several already-hard problems into open ones; the four below cut across all five axes.

Temporal coherence and long-horizon drift. The defining difficulty of video over image generation is keeping content stable across frames. The signature artifact is flicker, the high-frequency appearance instability between adjacent frames that plagues per-frame and early GAN-based methods (§8.3.1); over longer spans it gives way to identity drift, the gradual mutation of a subject’s appearance, color, or fine texture across a clip; and in autoregressive roll-outs to error accumulation, the compounding of small per-step mistakes that caps usable clip length. Latent video autoencoders with temporal compression [blattmann2023stable, blattmann2023align] and dedicated spatio-temporal attention suppress flicker, while autoregressive–diffusion hybrids such as CausVid [yin2025slow] and MAGI-1 [ai2025magi1autoregressivevideogeneration] combine sequential consistency with diffusion fidelity to push toward minute-scale generation; coherence over arbitrarily long horizons remains unsolved and is the binding constraint on the world-model applications that motivate the section.

Controllability versus fidelity under multi-condition fusion. As §8.3.2–§8.3.4 stack heterogeneous conditions (spatial scaffolds, camera paths, audio, style) onto Eq. (8.41), the conditions begin to conflict. Over-strong conditioning yields rigidity and texture collapse; weak conditioning ignores the control; and naive fusion produces control-signal dilution (summed adapters wash one another out), condition leakage across frames, and collapse to the dominant condition when one modality (e.g., , audio in talking-head generation) overwhelms the rest. Compositional and universal frameworks (VideoComposer [wang2023videocomposercompositionalvideosynthesis], OmniHuman [lin2025omnihuman1rethinkingscalinguponestage], and the unified-attention design of FullDiT [ju2025fullditmultitaskvideogenerative]) replace per-axis injection with joint token fusion and task-aware positional embeddings, but a principled account of how to weight and arbitrate competing conditions is still missing.

Physical and 3D plausibility. Even a temporally coherent, well-controlled clip may depict an impossible world, which is the bridge back to §8.2. Generated motion frequently violates object permanence (objects teleport, morph, or vanish), contact and rigid-body dynamics (rigid objects warp non-rigidly; feet slide; occlusions resolve implausibly), and multi-view consistency under camera motion, where the same scene is rendered inconsistently from successive viewpoints. Systems presented as steps toward “world simulators”, Sora [sora2024] among them, still exhibit these failures on closer inspection. Camera-control methods [he2024cameractrl, yu2024viewcrafter] and explicitly 3D-aware video diffusion (Diffusion-as-Shader [gu2025diffusionshader3dawarevideo] and GS-DiT [bian2025gsditadvancingvideogeneration]) narrow the gap by conditioning generation on geometry, which suggests that the more promising route to physical plausibility runs through the volumetric representations of §8.2 rather than through scale alone.

Compute, latency, and evaluation. Underlying all three is cost: a spatio-temporal latent is an order of magnitude larger than an image latent, so long, high-resolution clips strain memory and make iterative sampling slow, which in turn limits the context length available for coherence and the conditioning budget available for control. Consistency distillation and few-step samplers, together with sparse and causal attention, are the active responses. Evaluation compounds the problem: distributional scores such as FVD and per-frame FID are blind to temporal and control adherence, and automatic metrics correlate weakly with human judgment, so reported progress is hard to compare across methods; benchmarks and human-aligned protocols that jointly score fidelity, temporal coherence, and per-axis control adherence are a central near-term need.

Coherence and physical plausibility both demand longer temporal context, which inflates compute, and every added condition enlarges the evaluation surface, so progress on any one of the four is bounded by the others. Together they mark the last step of the progression traced across §8, from the static 2D prior of §8.1 through the static volumetric prior of §8.2 to dynamic, navigable models that consume spatial structure over time.

8.4 Motion Generation

Motion generation is the temporal, embodied output channel of spatial generation: where §8.1–§8.3 synthesize static images, volumetric assets, and controllable video, motion generation produces the articulated dynamics that an avatar, character, or robot can actually enact. A generated motion is a time series of body poses that must be believable in its dynamics, physically plausible (balance, ground contact, non-penetration), and faithful to its driving signal, whether a text description, audio, a scene, or a key frame. The conditional-sampler template that turns a prompt into pixels (Eq. (8.2)) is here instantiated over a sequence of poses in a structured kinematic space, so geometric priors meet physical constraints: the output must respect the biomechanics of an articulated body as well as the semantics of the condition.

The subsections are indexed by the moving agent and then by one cross-cutting operation: human motion (§8.4.1), animal motion with its cross-species morphology (§8.4.2), vehicle motion planning, where the body is rigid and the difficulty moves into the multi-agent traffic scene (§8.4.3), and motion editing (§8.4.4).

8.4.1 Human Motion Generation

Human motion generation produces natural, varied sequences of human body poses from intentions, environmental stimuli, or explicit conditions, and supports animation, virtual characters in film and games, AR/VR, and human–robot interaction.

8.4.1.1 Task Definition

Let a motion be a temporal sequence of body poses 𝐦1:T=(𝐦1,…,𝐦T)\mathbf{m}^{1:T}=(\mathbf{m}^{1},\dots,\mathbf{m}^{T}), where each frame 𝐦t∈𝒫\mathbf{m}^{t}\in\mathcal{P} is a pose in a chosen representation space 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℳ=𝒫T\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{P}^{T} is the resulting motion space. Writing ϕ\phi for the text encoder of Eq. (8.2) and κ:𝒞→𝒞′\kappa:\mathcal{C}\!\to\!\mathcal{C}^{\prime} for an encoder of a driving signal 𝐜∈𝒞\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C} (an action label, a text description, a music or speech track, or a scene), human motion generation learns a conditional sampler

Gθmot:𝒞′→ℳ,𝐦^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐦1:T∣κ⁢(𝐜)).G_{\theta}^{\text{mot}}:\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\!\to\!\mathcal{M},\qquad\hat{% \mathbf{m}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{m}^{1:T}\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})% \right). (8.54)

This is the conditional-sampler template of Eq. (8.2) instantiated over a temporal pose sequence rather than an image latent: with no driving signal (κ=∅\kappa=\varnothing) it reduces to unconditional motion synthesis, and the choice of 𝐜\mathbf{c} indexes the five conditioning settings surveyed in §8.4.1.2.

Figure 8.18 illustrates the pose representations that instantiate 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Broadly, representations fall into keypoint-based and rotation-based categories, and the two are convertible: joint rotations map to spatial keypoints via forward kinematics (FK), and keypoints recover joint rotations via inverse kinematics (IK).

Keypoint-based Representation.

The body is modeled as a collection of keypoints, each a distinct anatomical landmark (joints or salient surface locations) given by its 2D or 3D coordinates in a chosen frame (pixel space or world space), and motion is encoded as a temporal series of such configurations. Keypoint representations are directly available from many motion-capture systems and are highly interpretable, but many downstream uses (character animation, robotic control) require converting keypoints to joint rotations through the IK problem. Some works instead augment or replace sparse skeletal keypoints with dense body markers distributed across the body surface [WuWZZHYT22, TaheriCBT22], which carry richer information about body shape, limb twisting, and fine geometric detail.

Rotation-based Representation.

A pose is represented by joint angles, the rotations of body segments relative to their parent in a hierarchical kinematic tree. Most studies model these in three dimensions, treating each non-root joint as an element of SO⁢(3)\mathrm{SO}(3), parameterized as Euler angles, axis–angle vectors, or unit quaternions.

Skinned Multi-Person Linear Model.

Beyond pure joint rotation, statistical mesh models jointly capture pose and body shape, including non-rigid deformations associated with articulation. The Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) model [loper2015smpl] defines a template mesh with fixed topology (6,890 vertices, 23 joint rotations plus a root) and uses linear blend skinning augmented by learned blend shapes: identity (shape) blend shapes for inter-subject variation and pose blend shapes for rotation-dependent deformations such as muscle bulging and twisting.

8.4.1.2 Methodology

Methods for human motion generation are organized along two axes. The first is the learning paradigm: regression-based techniques learn a deterministic mapping from conditions to a single target motion, whereas generative approaches model the full conditional distribution of motion using GANs, VAEs, normalizing flows, or diffusion models (the generative paradigms themselves are detailed in §8.1.1). Formally, a regression model realizes Eq. (8.54) as a point estimate,

𝐦^1:T=fθ⁢(κ⁢(𝐜)),minθ⁡‖𝐦^1:T−𝐦1:T‖,\hat{\mathbf{m}}^{1:T}=f_{\theta}\!\left(\kappa(\mathbf{c})\right),\qquad\min_% {\theta}\ \big{\|}\hat{\mathbf{m}}^{1:T}-\mathbf{m}^{1:T}\big{\|}, (8.55)

which is simple and stable but collapses the inherently one-to-many condition–motion relationship onto an averaged trajectory. Generative models instead sample 𝐦^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐦1:T∣κ⁢(𝐜))\hat{\mathbf{m}}^{1:T}\!\sim\!p_{\theta}(\mathbf{m}^{1:T}\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})); the now-dominant diffusion instantiation trains a denoiser GθG_{\theta} to recover the clean motion at every noise level nn,

ℒ=𝔼𝐦1:T,n⁢‖𝐦1:T−Gθ⁢(𝐦n1:T,n,κ⁢(𝐜))‖2,\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m}^{1:T},\,n}\,\big{\|}\,\mathbf{m}^{1:T}-G_{% \theta}(\mathbf{m}^{1:T}_{n},\,n,\,\kappa(\mathbf{c}))\,\big{\|}^{2}, (8.56)

which preserves diversity and supports flexible conditioning, at higher sampling cost. The second axis is the conditioning modality 𝐜\mathbf{c}, which indexes the five settings below; each setting instantiates the same Eq. (8.54) and has migrated, broadly, from regression and adversarial models toward diffusion. Figure 8.19 previews this two-axis organization.

Action-to-Motion.

Given a discrete action label (e.g., , “walk”, “throw”), these methods generate a corresponding sequence. Early work used GANs with graph convolution and self-attention (SA-GAN [YuZLYC20], Kinetic-GAN [DegardinNLBY022]) for realism and diversity, while VAE/CVAE frameworks (Action2Motion [GuoZWZSDG020], ACTOR [PetrovichBV21]) produced probabilistic, controllable motions. More recent models adopt contrastive latent learning (ODMO [LuZLR22]), discrete autoregressive sequences (PoseGPT [LucasBWR22]), and diffusion (MDM [TevetRGSCB23], the latent-diffusion hybrid MLD [ChenJLHFCY23]). As most methods excel only at single actions, MultiAct [LeeML23] recurrently composes multiple action motions into long sequences via a canonicalization scheme.

Text-to-Motion.

Conditioning on free-form language exploits richer semantic cues than fixed labels allow. Early methods used GANs (Text2Action [AhnHCYO18]) or joint text–motion embeddings (JL2P [AhujaM19], two-stream encoder–decoders [GhoshCOTS21]); later ones added variational modeling and attention (TEMOS [PetrovichBV22], TEACH [AthanasiouPBV22]). For zero-shot generalization, MotionCLIP [TevetGHBC22] and AvatarCLIP [HongZPCYL22] align the motion latent space with CLIP. The current frontier combines VQ-VAE tokenization [GuoZWC22], autoregressive transformers (T2M-GPT [zhang2023generating]), and diffusion (FLAME [KimKC23]), with multimodal conditioning extensions such as MoFusion [DabralMGT23] fusing text and audio. More recent masked-generative models (MoMask [GuoMJW024]) push quality and inference speed further by predicting quantized motion tokens with a bidirectional, iteratively-refined masking schedule rather than left-to-right.

Music-to-Dance.

The goal is coherent, expressive dance aligned to a music track. Early approaches framed this as supervised sequence-to-sequence translation via LSTM autoencoders [TangJM18], transformers (AI Choreographer [LiYRK21]), and multi-person frameworks (GroupDancer [Wang0WXCMCW22], GDancer [LePDTT023]). Because music–dance is inherently one-to-many, generative models model the diverse distribution: MNET [0001OKT022] with style conditioning, Transflower [PerezHBHOA21], Bailando [SiyaoYGLW0L022] (VQ-VAE + GPT), and EDGE [TsengCL23] (diffusion). Graph-based methods (ChoreoMaster [ChenTLZGZ021], PC-Dance [GaoPZSZ22], ChoreoGraph [AuCJG22]) use motion graphs and shared music–motion embeddings for rhythmic coherence, while curriculum learning, dynamics-prior denoising, and hierarchical pose/motif/choreography modeling target long-term, genre-consistent full-song dances [HuangHWSZJ21, SunWHLJH22, AristidouYACSC23].

Speech-to-Gesture.

Co-speech gesture synthesis generates upper-body or full gesture sequences from speech (audio, sometimes text). Early adversarial methods modeled person-specific gesture patterns [GinosarBKCOM19]; subsequent work disentangled shared versus motion-specific variation [KucherenkoHHKK19] and decomposed body, hands, and face [HabibieXMLSPET21]. Recent methods employ diffusion [ZhuLLQLY23, AlexandersonNBH23, AoZL23], VQ-VAE quantization [YiLLCWBTB23], and style or speaker embeddings [AhujaLNM20] to handle diversity, identity, rhythm, and expression more robustly.

Scene-to-Motion.

Here the condition is a 3D scene, and most methods adopt a multi-stage pipeline that predicts a goal or interaction anchor, plans a trajectory, then generates motion along it. Early works predict a goal from 2D/RGB scene inputs and synthesize motion through trajectory-guided VAEs [CaoGMCVM20, WangYDL21], sometimes with scene-aware discriminators. SAMP [HassanCVSYZB21] models 3D paths and human–object interactions; later methods refine interaction with per-joint contact maps [D00010HS22] or path-search (A∗A^{\ast}) for trajectory diversity [0003RLYLD22], and GOAL [TaheriCBT22] and SAGA [WuWZZHYT22] target grasping via two-step goal-to-motion VAEs. Some assume given goals and stitch sub-goal motions hierarchically for long-term synthesis [WangXXL021], while refinement-based frameworks such as CIRCLE [AraujoLVAWGCL23] initialize by interpolation and refine with scene-geometry-aware modules.

8.4.1.3 Benchmarks

Human motion datasets group naturally by conditioning modality; Table 8.10 gives their representation, scale, and condition. Text- and action-conditioned corpora dominate, led by the language-annotated KIT Motion-Language [PlappertMA16] and HumanML3D [GuoZZ0JL022], BABEL [PunnakkalCAQB21]’s sequence- and frame-level labels over the AMASS [mahmood2019amass] aggregate, and the action taxonomies of UESTC [JiXYSSZ18], NTU-RGB+D 120 [LiuSPWDK20], and HumanAct12 [GuoZWZSDG020]. Audio-conditioned resources split into music-to-dance sets (AIST++ [LiYRK21], AIOZ-GDANCE [LePDTT023], and several genre-specific collections) and co-speech gesture sets (Trinity [FerstlM18], BEAT [LiuZIPLZBZ22], PATS [AhujaLNM20]), many built by fitting parametric body models to in-the-wild video. Scene-conditioned datasets (PROX [HassanCTB19], GRAB [TaheriGBT20], HUMANISE [WangCLZLH22], CIRCLE [AraujoLVAWGCL23]) capture human–scene and human–object interaction with synchronized geometry, from Vicon and IMU rigs to synthetic engines such as GTA-IM [CaoGMCVM20]. Across all three groups, the cost of high-quality capture forces a trade-off between scale and annotation fidelity.

Evaluation Metrics.

Evaluating synthesized motion is hard because the condition–motion map is one-to-many, judgments are partly subjective, and quality depends on high-level conditional cues, so the literature reports an ensemble of metrics along three axes. Fidelity captures naturalness, smoothness, and plausibility: distance-based measures such as NPSS [GopalakrishnanM19] and NDMS [TankeZG21], keypoint accuracy (PCK [YangR13]), motion-space statistics (AVE, Hellinger distance over speed histograms [yang2023qpgesture], Fréchet Distance over pose rotations [HassanCVSYZB21, 0003RLYLD22], PSKL [RuizGM19]), feature-space distributional distances led by FID (with IS [AhujaLNM20], MMD [YuZLYC20], and related scores), and physical-plausibility proxies for foot sliding and foot–ground contact (FCS [TsengCL23], non-collision ratios [WuWZZHYT22], contact accuracy [ZhangT22]), the last still lacking a standardized definition. Diversity guards against the long-sequence “freezing” failure via intra-motion variation and freezing rate [SunWHLJH22], inter-motion manifold coverage, and multimodality metrics (n-APD, ADE/FDE and their multimodal variants [YuanK20]) computed by sampling many motions per condition. Condition consistency measures alignment to the driving signal: recognition accuracy and R-Precision for text/action, feature-level text–motion distance (Multimodal Distance [GuoZZ0JL022], mCLIP and MID [KimKC23]), audio–motion beat metrics (beat coverage, hit rate [LeeY0WLYK19], beat alignment [LiYRK21], SRGR [LiuZIPLZBZ22], Semantic Score [AoZL23]), and, for scene conditioning, non-collision and human–scene contact scores [WuWZZHYT22, ZhangBSGP22]. No single metric is decisive, so methods are compared on a task-appropriate composition of the three.

8.4.1.4 Challenges and Trends

Data scarcity is the most basic constraint: high-quality motion capture is expensive and slow, so dataset scale trades against annotation fidelity, and heterogeneous pose representations and conditioning signals fragment the data that exist; fusing heterogeneous sources through weak supervision and multimodal foundation models is the main response. Semantic alignment is the second. Motion encodes culture, communication, and context, not only mechanics, and a model that fits joint trajectories while missing their relation to language, music, or environment produces motion that is kinematically clean but perceptually empty; semantic priors from language and foundation models help, but how to measure the result is unresolved. That is the evaluation problem: every objective metric above has blind spots, none replaces a user study, and the field still needs metrics that are both interpretable and better correlated with human perception. Controllability matters for practical use as much as in image generation, and joint masking, attribute prompts, and style conditioning are moving toward editing tools with textual, spatial, and temporal handles (§8.4.4). Interactivity remains underexplored: most methods animate one person in a static scene, and socially coupled groups (conversation, group dance) and motion grounded in dynamic, actionable scenes need both new corpora and new models.

8.4.2 Animal Motion Generation

Most motion-generation work targets the human body and ignores the diversity of animal behavior, although synthesizing animal motion matters for wildlife conservation, ecology, and biomechanics. Relative to §8.4.1, animal motion is harder on two fronts that the human setting never confronts: species vary widely in skeletal topology and morphology, so a single fixed-skeleton representation no longer suffices, and the same textual description (“walk stealthily”) maps to radically different gaits across species. These two pressures, i.e., , data scarcity and morphological heterogeneity, shape every method below, which is why animal motion generation borrows the architectures, datasets, and training recipes of human motion generation while adding species-conditioning machinery on top.

8.4.2.1 Task Definition

Animal motion generation extends the human sampler of Eq. (8.54) with an explicit species (morphology) descriptor. Let s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} index a species and let 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s} be its species-dependent pose space (its skeleton topology and joint count depend on ss), so that ℳs=𝒫sT\mathcal{M}_{s}=\mathcal{P}_{s}^{T} is the corresponding motion space. With κ\kappa encoding a driving signal 𝐜∈𝒞\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C} (an action class, a text description, an anchor pose, or past motion), the task is to learn

Gθamot:𝒞′×𝒮→ℳs,𝐦^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐦1:T∣κ⁢(𝐜),s).G_{\theta}^{\text{amot}}:\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\!\times\!\mathcal{S}\!\to\!% \mathcal{M}_{s},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{m}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{m}^% {1:T}\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c}),\,s\right). (8.57)

Restricting 𝒮\mathcal{S} to the single human morphology recovers Eq. (8.54) exactly; the open difficulty is that ss ranges over a heterogeneous, long-tailed set of skeletons for which paired text–motion data are scarce, so the species condition must do double duty as both a generation control and a regularizer that shares statistical strength across morphologies.

8.4.2.2 Methodology

Almost all animal motion generation is text-driven, and the methods share a common response to the data-scarcity and morphology problems of Eq. (8.57): transfer representations learned from abundant human motion, then specialize them to a species through feature modulation. Concretely, given a backbone feature 𝐡\mathbf{h} at some layer, species-aware modulation applies a FiLM-style affine transform conditioned on ss,

𝐡~=γ⁢(s)⊙𝐡+β⁢(s),\tilde{\mathbf{h}}=\gamma(s)\odot\mathbf{h}+\beta(s), (8.58)

where γ⁢(s),β⁢(s)\gamma(s),\beta(s) are predicted from the species descriptor, allowing one shared network to adapt its internal representation to diverse anatomical forms. The methods differ in how they obtain the shared representation and how strictly they enforce cross-species plausibility, as Figure 8.20 summarizes.

OmniMotionGPT [YangZSWXHBQ024] tackles limited animal data by jointly training motion autoencoders on human and animal corpora and aligning their latent encodings to text via CLIP embeddings; it relies most directly on transfer, and at inference it still depends on human-motion priors, which prevents truly text-only animal generation. Motion Avatar [0006W0CZH0F0024] uses SinMDM [RaabLTABC24] for data augmentation in its ZooGen pipeline (the route by which the Zoo-300K dataset is built) and extends the masked-motion modeling of MoMask [GuoMJW024] to animals, adding an LLM planner that orchestrates joint motion and 3D-avatar mesh generation; it makes little use of species-specific structure, which is what Eq. (8.58) addresses. AniMo [WangRZW25] makes that remedy central, injecting species-aware modulation into a joint-aware spatiotemporal tokenizer and learning, through masked modeling, a mapping from text plus species attributes to motion tokens; its AniMo4D dataset (78,149 sequences over 114 species) yields markedly better morphological and behavioral fidelity than transfer-only baselines. X-MoGen [abs-2508-05162] pushes toward a single model spanning humans and animals: it embeds motion into a shared space with graph-based VAEs and latent autoencoders, generates via masked modeling, and adds a morphological-consistency module that enforces skeletal plausibility across species, supported by the UniMo4D corpus (∼115{\sim}115 species, ∼119{\sim}119K sequences). OmniMotionGPT and Motion Avatar still lean on human priors, whereas AniMo and X-MoGen promote species morphology to a first-class, explicitly regularized conditioning variable, so the four together trace a progression from transfer toward native cross-species modeling.

8.4.2.3 Benchmarks

Animal motion resources fall into two groups (Table 8.11). Capture and pose-estimation corpora supply ground-truth articulated motion but no language: RGBD-Dog [Kearney0PKC20] and 3DDogs-Wild [abs-2406-14412] pair RGB-D or RGB video with marker-based mocap for canine pose, and DeformingThings4D [LiTTZN21] provides synthetic 4D sequences with dense mesh-deformation annotations across humanoid and animal categories. Text-to-motion corpora drive recent progress: AnimalML3D [YangZSWXHBQ024] is the first text–animal-motion dataset, and the field then scales sharply through Zoo-300K [0006W0CZH0F0024] (built by the ZooGen pipeline with SinMDM and LLM annotators), AniMo4D [WangRZW25] (normalized to a 30-joint cross-species skeleton), and UniMo4D [abs-2508-05162], which merges AniMo4D with HumanML3D and KIT-ML. Even the largest text-conditioned sets remain smaller and more morphologically fragmented than their human counterparts of §8.4.1.3, which is what forces the transfer-and-modulate methodology above.

Evaluation Metrics.

Animal motion evaluation reuses the three-axis human protocol of §8.4.1.3, adapted for species-specific biomechanics. Fidelity is measured by FID against real movement distributions and by MPJPE against ground-truth poses, augmented with physical-plausibility checks for gait-cycle regularity, ground contact, and the absence of foot sliding or limb penetration. Condition alignment carries over R-Precision and Multimodal Distance to score text-/action-to-motion correspondence, and diversity / multimodality metrics quantify behavioral variety within and across species. The animal-specific addition is perceptual and biomechanical judgment of naturalness, balance, and anatomical consistency, which matters more for quadrupeds and multi-limbed morphologies than for the single human skeleton.

8.4.2.4 Challenges and Trends

Physical realism is the most basic gap: most methods do not simulate ground-contact forces, quadruped balance, or the fluid dynamics of swimming and flight, so artifacts the human setting has largely learned to suppress reappear, and differently for every body plan. Behavioral diversity is harder than for humans because one instruction such as “walk stealthily” realizes into different gaits, postures, and speeds across species, so the conditional distribution to be captured is far wider while the data to capture it are scarcer. Unseen species and radical morphologies remain out of reach: species-aware modulation (Eq. (8.58)) and morphological-consistency constraints generalize across the skeletons seen in training, but insects and winged or aquatic creatures violate the shared-skeleton, fixed-topology assumptions on which current methods rest. AniMo and X-MoGen already move toward treating morphology as a variable rather than a template, and topology-flexible representations are the direction this points.

8.4.3 Vehicle Motion Planning

Where §8.4.1 and §8.4.2 generate the motion of an articulated body, vehicle motion planning generates the trajectory of a (near-)rigid agent moving through a traffic scene. The body is far simpler, since a vehicle has essentially no internal articulation, but the difficulty moves outward into the environment: a planned trajectory must obey vehicle dynamics, stay on the drivable surface dictated by an HD map, and remain socially compatible with the future motion of many surrounding agents whose intentions are unobserved. This is the setting where motion generation becomes inseparable from multi-agent spatial reasoning and physical feasibility: trajectory forecasting (predicting how others will move) and planning (deciding how the ego vehicle should move) are two readings of the same generative object.

8.4.3.1 Task Definition

Let a trajectory be a sequence of agent states 𝝉1:H=(𝐬1,…,𝐬H)\bm{\tau}^{1:H}=(\mathbf{s}^{1},\dots,\mathbf{s}^{H}) over a horizon HH, where each state 𝐬t\mathbf{s}^{t} collects position, heading, and velocity. The driving signal is now a structured scene context 𝐜=(𝐬−P:0,𝒢,𝒜)\mathbf{c}=(\mathbf{s}^{-P:0},\,\mathcal{G},\,\mathcal{A}) comprising the agent’s own past states, an HD-map / lane graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and the observed histories of neighboring agents 𝒜\mathcal{A}. With κ\kappa encoding this context, vehicle motion planning learns

Gθveh:𝒞′→𝒯,𝝉^1:H∼pθ⁢(𝝉1:H∣κ⁢(𝐜))s.t.𝐬t+1=fdyn⁢(𝐬t,𝐮t),G_{\theta}^{\text{veh}}:\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\!\to\!\mathcal{T},\qquad\hat{\bm{% \tau}}^{1:H}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{\tau}^{1:H}\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\right% )\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbf{s}^{t+1}=f_{\text{dyn}}(\mathbf{s}^{t},\mathbf{u% }^{t}), (8.59)

the conditional-sampler template of Eq. (8.54) with the pose sequence replaced by a state trajectory and an added kinematic-feasibility constraint fdynf_{\text{dyn}} (e.g., , a bicycle model) that distinguishes this setting from articulated-body generation. Dropping 𝒜\mathcal{A} recovers single-agent forecasting; supplying a goal or reward in place of 𝐜\mathbf{c} turns prediction into planning.

8.4.3.2 Methodology

Prediction methods vary along two axes: how the scene context is encoded and how the multimodal future is decoded. Early encoders rasterize the scene into a bird’s-eye-view image, but the field has converged on vectorized encoders that represent lanes and agent tracks as polylines: VectorNet [gao2020vectornet] and LaneGCN [liang2020lanegcn] build graph representations of the HD map, and transformer encoders such as Wayformer [nayakanti2023wayformer] and the Motion Transformer (MTR) [shi2022mtr] attend jointly over map and agents; graph-attention predictors [ZhangFWH22] model spatial and temporal interaction in the same spirit. On the decoding side, the defining property is multimodality, since a single context admits many plausible futures, so models predict a set of KK modes with probabilities,

pθ⁢(𝝉∣κ⁢(𝐜))=∑k=1Kπk⁢𝒩⁢(𝝉;μk⁢(κ⁢(𝐜)),Σk),p_{\theta}(\bm{\tau}\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c}))=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_{k}\,\mathcal{N}% \!\left(\bm{\tau};\,\mu_{k}(\kappa(\mathbf{c})),\,\Sigma_{k}\right), (8.60)

rather than the single point estimate of Eq. (8.55), which here would average distinct maneuvers (turning vs. going straight) into an infeasible mean. The earliest learned predictors modeled social interaction directly in agent-coordinate space, Social-LSTM [alahi2016social] through pooled recurrent states and Social-GAN [gupta2018social] through adversarial sampling, and Trajectron++ [salzmann2020trajectron] added dynamic feasibility to a graph-structured latent-variable model. Goal-based decoders make the modes explicit: DenseTNT [gu2021densetnt] samples dense candidate endpoints on the map and scores trajectories conditioned on them, exposing the maneuver structure that Eq. (8.60) captures only implicitly. Generative decoders replace the fixed mixture with a learned sampler: MotionDiffuser [jiang2023motiondiffuser] denoises whole multi-agent trajectory sets jointly.

Planning turns the same machinery on the ego vehicle. ChauffeurNet [bansal2019chauffeurnet] learns the ego policy by imitating expert driving and augments the demonstrations with synthesized perturbations and worst cases, so that the policy stays robust when it drifts off the data manifold. Figure 8.21 situates these families along the encode/decode axes.

8.4.3.3 Benchmarks

Progress is measured on large real-world driving logs that pair agent tracks with HD maps: nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes], Argoverse and Argoverse 2 [Argoverse-ChangLSSBHW0LRH19, wilson2023argoverse], and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset [ettinger2021womd], the last two offering the scale and interaction density that current transformer models require. Evaluation centers on the multimodal-aware displacement metrics that match Eq. (8.60): minimum average and final displacement error over the KK predicted modes (minADEK, minFDEK), miss rate (the fraction of scenes where no mode lands within a tolerance of the ground truth), and the soft mean-average-precision of the Waymo protocol, which jointly scores accuracy and the calibration of mode probabilities πk\pi_{k}. Off-road and collision rates further test the feasibility constraint fdynf_{\text{dyn}} that purely displacement-based scores ignore.

8.4.3.4 Challenges and Trends

A planner must assign trustworthy probabilities to the futures it enumerates, not merely list them: an over-confident missed mode of Eq. (8.60) is a safety failure rather than a metric error, so calibrated multimodality is the first open problem. Feasibility and safety are the second: displacement metrics reward trajectories a vehicle cannot physically execute, so feasibility has to be enforced inside the model (fdynf_{\text{dyn}}) rather than checked afterward, and the long tail of near-collision scenarios is exactly where data are scarcest. The third is closed-loop distribution shift: models trained to imitate logged, open-loop futures drift once their own predictions feed back into the scene, the difficulty ChauffeurNet’s worst-case synthesis was built to expose. Diffusion- and transformer-based scene-level samplers that forecast all agents jointly and run closed-loop are the current direction, and they connect directly to the controllable-video and world-model lines of §8.3 and §8.6, in which a driving world model both predicts and is conditioned on the ego plan.

8.4.4 Motion Editing

The subsections above synthesize motion from scratch; motion editing instead modifies an existing motion so that it satisfies a new constraint while leaving the rest intact. It is the temporal, articulated analogue of the image editing of §8.1.3 and the video editing of §8.3.5, and its demand is again selective preservation: change a targeted aspect (a trajectory, a joint, a style, a semantic action) while holding the body’s identity, timing, and untouched portions fixed, which makes editing the controllability layer that closes the generate-and-refine loop for motion.

8.4.4.1 Task Definition

Given a source motion 𝐦in∈ℳ\mathbf{m}^{\text{in}}\!\in\!\mathcal{M}, an edit region 𝐌∈{0,1}T×J\mathbf{M}\!\in\!\{0,1\}^{T\times J} over time TT and joints JJ, and an edit control 𝐜\mathbf{c} (a text instruction, target keyframes, a desired root trajectory, or a target joint), motion editing learns an operator

Eθ:ℳ×{0,1}T×J×𝒞′→ℳ,𝐦^=Eθ⁢(𝐦in,𝐌,κ⁢(𝐜)),E_{\theta}:\mathcal{M}\!\times\!\{0,1\}^{T\times J}\!\times\!\mathcal{C}^{% \prime}\!\to\!\mathcal{M},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{m}}=E_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{m}^% {\text{in}},\mathbf{M},\kappa(\mathbf{c})\right), (8.61)

which lifts the image-editing operator of Eq. (8.8) into the motion domain. As in image and video editing, Eq. (8.61) encodes two competing objectives, editability (the output must realize the control 𝐜\mathbf{c} inside 𝐌\mathbf{M}) and preservation (it must match 𝐦in\mathbf{m}^{\text{in}} outside 𝐌\mathbf{M} and remain a plausible, smooth motion), and methods differ chiefly in how they trade these off.

8.4.4.2 Methodology

Because a pretrained motion diffusion model already samples plausible motion, most editors realize Eq. (8.61) without retraining, by conditioning the sampler of Eq. (8.56) rather than learning a dedicated EθE_{\theta}. The simplest mechanism is masked infilling: at every denoising step the observed entries are overwritten with the (noised) source while only the masked entries are generated,

𝐦^=(1−𝐌)⊙𝐦in+𝐌⊙Gθ⁢(𝐦n,n,κ⁢(𝐜)),\hat{\mathbf{m}}=(1-\mathbf{M})\odot\mathbf{m}^{\text{in}}+\mathbf{M}\odot G_{% \theta}\!\left(\mathbf{m}_{n},\,n,\,\kappa(\mathbf{c})\right), (8.62)

which directly enforces preservation by construction. This is the basis of motion in-betweening, where 1−𝐌1-\mathbf{M} marks given keyframes: robust in-betweening [harvey2020robust] predates the diffusion era, and CondMDI [cohan2024condmdi] casts flexible keyframe-conditioned in-betweening as masked diffusion, while PriorMDM [shafir2024priormdm] reuses a frozen motion-diffusion prior for editing and composition tasks such as joining and in-filling. A second family handles spatial controls that masking alone cannot express (a target root path, or a specific joint at specific times) through classifier-style guidance: GMD [karunratanakul2023gmd] and OmniControl [xie2024omnicontrol] steer the denoiser toward arbitrary spatial constraints at any joint and time. A third, optimization-based family treats the initial diffusion noise itself as the free variable, solving min𝐳⁡ℒedit⁢(𝒟⁢(𝐳))\min_{\mathbf{z}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{edit}}(\mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z})) so that the decoded motion satisfies an arbitrary differentiable criterion: DNO [karunratanakul2024dno] shows this single mechanism serves editing, in-betweening, and refinement as one universal motion prior. Finally, semantic editors take a natural-language instruction in place of a geometric mask: MotionFix [athanasiou2024motionfix] learns text-driven edits from paired source–target motions, and LLM-driven approaches [goel2024iterative] decompose an instruction into a program of primitive edits applied iteratively. Figure 8.22 groups these four mechanisms by how they obtain EθE_{\theta}, paralleling the editing taxonomies of §8.1.3 and §8.3.5.

8.4.4.3 Benchmarks

Motion editing inherits the corpora of §8.4.1.3 (HumanML3D [GuoZZ0JL022] and BABEL [PunnakkalCAQB21] over AMASS), used in editing protocols where keyframes, joints, or trajectories are held out as the constraint, together with the dedicated MotionFix [athanasiou2024motionfix] benchmark of paired source–edit–instruction triples that supplies the ground truth most editing tasks lack. Evaluation must report the editability–preservation pair jointly: editability through control adherence (instruction-conditioned R-Precision, target-joint or trajectory error) and overall realism (FID, foot-skating), and preservation through the deviation from the source outside the edit region. As in video editing, single scalars correlate weakly with perceived edit quality, so reporting a tuple, and increasingly a learned or VLM-style judge of instruction compliance, is becoming standard.

8.4.4.4 Challenges and Trends

The central tension is the editability–preservation trade-off of Eq. (8.61): pushing harder on a control propagates unwanted change through the kinematic chain (editing one arm disturbs balance and foot contact), so a good editor must respect the body’s global coordination, not just the masked entries. This is compounded by sparse-control ambiguity: a single keyframe or a root path under-determines the full-body motion, and the model must fill the gap plausibly, which the guidance and noise-optimization families address with differing robustness. Underlying both is an evaluation gap sharper than in synthesis: because the “correct” edit is rarely unique, ground-truth-based metrics under-reward valid alternatives, motivating the paired-triplet and judge-based protocols above. The trend mirrors the rest of §8.4 and §8.3: from per-mechanism, training-free editors toward unified models that generate, control, and edit motion within a single conditional sampler, increasingly driven by natural-language instructions rather than geometric masks.

8.5 4D Spatial Generation

Generative modeling has moved outward from static images [rombach2022ldm, saharia2022photorealistic] to video [chen2024videocrafter2, chen2023videocrafter1, ho2022video, harvey2022flexible], multi-view imagery [shi2023mvdream, liu2023zero, shi2023zero123++, zhao2024sg, zhao2024chase], and static 3D assets [wang2023score, raj2023dreambooth3d], yet each stops short of a scene that is at once three-dimensional and alive. A 3D asset holds geometry but not motion; a video holds motion, but no view-consistent geometry one can navigate or simulate. 4D generation is where the two meet: the synthesis of dynamic 3D content whose geometry stays view-consistent as it moves and deforms over time [singer2023text, zheng2024unified, jiang2023consistent4d, ling2024align, wang2025moving]. This is the representation an embodied system needs to rehearse how a scene will unfold, and it underwrites photorealistic digital humans [guo2023vid2avatar, zhao2024sg, zhao2024chase], interactive AR/VR [zhao2024hfgs, miao2024pla4d], and high-fidelity simulation for autonomous driving and embodied AI [gao2024magicdrive3d, zhao2024efficient].

Two advances make this tractable. Temporal 3D representations, deformation-aware fields over NeRFs [mildenhall2021nerf], point clouds, and Gaussian splatting [kerbl20233d, zhao2024efficient], supply a geometry that can bend and move without losing view consistency, while the extension of generative diffusion into this domain supplies the realism and controllability to drive it. Together they open dynamic scene synthesis, 4D editing, and interactive agent simulation, at the cost of the difficulty this section returns to throughout: holding long-range temporal coherence while still granting flexible, user-driven control.

Formally, we cast 4D generation as the latent-generator framework of §8.1.1 unrolled along time over a shared 3D representation. Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the 3D-representation space of Eq. (8.9) (mesh, NeRF, 3DGS, point cloud, and so on), and let κ:𝒞→𝒞′\kappa:\mathcal{C}\!\to\!\mathcal{C}^{\prime} encode a conditioning signal 𝐜∈𝒞\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C} (text, an image, a video, a static 3D asset, or a combination thereof). 4D generation learns a conditional sampler

Gθ4D:𝒞′→ℛ[0,T],𝐫^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐫1:T∣κ⁢(𝐜)),G_{\theta}^{\text{4D}}:\mathcal{C}^{\prime}\!\to\!\mathcal{R}^{[0,T]},\qquad% \hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{r}^{1:T}\mid\kappa(% \mathbf{c})\right), (8.63)

that emits a time-indexed sequence of 3D representations 𝐫^1:T\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T} with view-consistent geometry and coherent motion. Two limiting cases anchor the framework: with a single time step (T=1T=1) Eq. (8.63) recovers the static 3D generator of Eq. (8.9), and rendering each frame 𝐫t\mathbf{r}^{t} to a 2D view recovers the video generator of Eq. (8.41), so 4D generation is precisely the 3D generator of §8.2 unrolled in time, or equivalently the video generator of §8.3 lifted from per-frame pixels to a shared, renderable geometry. The subsections are organized by the conditioning input (text, image, video, a static 3D asset, or several at once). Figure 8.23 previews this organization together with two methodological strategies that recur across all five, per-scene score distillation and explicit “generate-then-reconstruct” supervision; feed-forward generators and rig-based animation of meshes appear alongside them in the subsections where they apply.

8.5.1 Text-to-4D Generation

Text-to-4D generation synthesizes dynamic content directly from natural language, supporting text-driven asset creation and character animation [HongZPCYL22, chen2024ct4d]. Its progress has been propelled by large language models for semantic understanding and by video foundation models that supply motion priors.

8.5.1.1 Task Definition

Text-to-4D generation specializes the 4D sampler of Eq. (8.63) to a textual condition 𝐜=𝐱\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{x} encoded by the text encoder ϕ\phi of Eq. (8.2),

𝐫^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐫1:T∣ϕ⁢(𝐱)).\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{r}^{1:T}\mid\phi(\mathbf{% x})\right). (8.64)

Because language fixes only semantics and leaves geometry and motion grossly under-determined, the sampler must hallucinate both a plausible 3D shape and its temporal evolution from the prompt alone, the source of the semantic-to-motion ambiguity examined in §8.5.1.4.

8.5.1.2 Methodology

Two strategies recur throughout this section, implicit distillation and explicit supervision, implemented across various 4D representations (Figure 8.23). The more common implicit strategy leverages Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to indirectly optimize the geometry and motion of a 4D representation, using pre-trained diffusion models as frozen priors [singer2023text, zheng2024unified]. Formally, it applies a score-distillation update to per-scene parameters θ\theta [poole2022dreamfusion],

∇θℒSDS=𝔼s,ϵ,π⁢[w⁢(s)⁢(ϵϕ⁢(𝐳s;s,κ⁢(𝐜))−ϵ)⁢∂𝐱θ∂θ],𝐳s=αs⁢𝐱θ+σs⁢ϵ,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SDS}}=\mathbb{E}_{s,\epsilon,\pi}\!\left[w% (s)\left(\epsilon_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_{s};s,\kappa(\mathbf{c}))-\epsilon\right)% \frac{\partial\mathbf{x}_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}\right],\quad\mathbf{z}_{s}=% \alpha_{s}\mathbf{x}_{\theta}+\sigma_{s}\epsilon, (8.65)

where 𝐱θ=Render⁢(𝐫^θ1:T,π)\mathbf{x}_{\theta}=\mathrm{Render}(\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T}_{\theta},\pi) is a differentiable rendering at camera π\pi, ss indexes diffusion noise levels, and ϵϕ\epsilon_{\phi} is a frozen 2D/video diffusion prior. The update differentiates through the renderer while treating the prior noise residual as the supplied gradient signal; this lifts the static score-distillation objective of §8.2.1.2 to a temporal sequence. In contrast, explicitly supervised methods initialize the 4D generation from text-to-3D or text-to-video outputs and use these generated assets as direct supervisory signals [zhao2024efficient, wu20244d, yang2024deformable, ling2024align, blattmann2023align, xu2024comp4d]. This “generate-then-reconstruct” strategy first synthesizes target frames 𝐲^\hat{\mathbf{y}} with a fast generator 𝒢2D\mathcal{G}_{\text{2D}} and then fits the 4D asset to them,

𝐲^=𝒢2D⁢(𝐜),𝐫^1:T=arg⁡min𝐫1:T⁢∑π,t‖Render⁢(𝐫t,π)−𝐲^πt‖2,\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathcal{G}_{\text{2D}}(\mathbf{c}),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1% :T}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{r}^{1:T}}\sum_{\pi,t}\big{\|}\mathrm{Render}(\mathbf{r}^% {t},\pi)-\hat{\mathbf{y}}^{t}_{\pi}\big{\|}^{2}, (8.66)

replacing score-distillation guidance with explicit pixel targets; reconstruction may itself require per-scene optimization, so a speed advantage depends on the implementation. The two strategies are realized across mesh, NeRF, and 3DGS representations.

Mesh-based Methods. Meshes offer explicit geometric control, which suits precise text-driven shape manipulation and animation. CT4D [chen2024ct4d] implements a three-stage “Generate-Refine-Animate” pipeline in which a mesh is generated from text, its texture refined, and its vertices animated; TextMesh4D [dai2025textmesh4d] deforms a generated mesh through a per-face Jacobian deformation field under video-diffusion priors; and AvatarCLIP [HongZPCYL22] generates a static avatar zero-shot and animates it by registering motion to an SMPL skeleton.

NeRF-based Methods. NeRFs represent continuous geometry and complex temporal variation well. MAV3D [singer2023text] introduced multi-stage SDS optimization that refines texture, geometry, and motion with priors from both T2I and T2V diffusion models; 4D-fy [bahmani20244d] blends 3D-aware, image, and video score signals in a hybrid SDS; and Dream-in-4D [zheng2024unified] first generates a static asset with a multiview diffusion model and then adds dynamics with a video diffusion model.

Gaussian Splatting-based Methods. 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) [zhao2024hfgs, wu20244d] renders efficiently and differentiably, which speeds up text-driven dynamic scene synthesis. Early methods followed the two-stage implicit pipeline of Eq. (8.65): AYG [ling2024align] generates a static 3D Gaussian model from text via SDS and adds dynamics under a T2V prior, and Comp4D [xu2024comp4d] uses an LLM to parse a complex prompt into several dynamic objects and their trajectories for a compositional scene. Later works moved to explicit supervision (Eq. (8.66)): PLA4D [miao2024pla4d] aligns the 4D Gaussians pixel by pixel with generated video targets, and 4Real [yu20244real] uses generated multiview video frames as the reference for photorealistic scene-level generation. For digital humans, AvatarGO [cao2024avatargo] generates 4D human–object interactions zero-shot by animating a text-to-3D human with the SMPL-X skinning function.

8.5.1.3 Benchmarks

Text-to-4D, like the other subfields of this section, has no standardized benchmark, because large-scale dynamic 3D data with text descriptions is hard to capture and annotate. Training and evaluation instead adapt static 3D repositories (Table 8.12): Diffusion4D [liang2024diffusion4d] filtered Objaverse and Objaverse-XL [deitke2023objaverse, deitke2023objaversexl] down to 54K high-quality animated assets, and SV4D [xie2024sv4d] built ObjaverseDy by adaptive sampling and viewpoint adjustment. These are synthetic renderings and lack the multimodal annotations, text in particular, needed to train and evaluate text-conditioned models robustly.

Evaluation Metrics.

Evaluation across 4D generation combines user studies with metrics borrowed from image and video generation, and the subsections that follow use this same set. Semantic alignment with a prompt is measured by CLIP Score [radford2021learning] between rendered views and the text; fidelity by PSNR [hore2010image], SSIM [wang2004image], and LPIPS [zhang2018unreasonable] where a reference view exists; temporal quality and motion by the Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [unterthiner2018fvd]; and overall plausibility and aesthetics by user studies. None of these scores the two properties that make content 4D, cross-view consistency and long-range spatio-temporal coherence.

8.5.1.4 Challenges and Trends

The challenge specific to text-to-4D is semantic-to-motion ambiguity: a prompt such as “a dancing dog” admits endlessly many movements, styles, and trajectories, and methods that lean on generic T2V priors struggle to produce diverse, fine-grained motion that matches a nuanced description. One response uses LLMs for motion planning, as Comp4D [xu2024comp4d] does when it decomposes a prompt into a structured spatio-temporal plan for several interacting objects; another targets human–object interaction [cao2024avatargo], moving toward story-driven dynamic scenes.

8.5.2 Image-to-4D Generation

Image-to-4D generation synthesizes dynamic content from a single static image, combining the spatial information in the image with temporal priors learned by video models [yang2024diffusion, sun2024eg4d]. No large image–4D paired dataset exists, which has ruled out direct end-to-end training and pushed the field toward optimization and toward generated supervision.

8.5.2.1 Task Definition

Image-to-4D generation specializes the 4D sampler of Eq. (8.63) to a single-image condition 𝐜=I\mathbf{c}=I,

𝐫^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐫1:T∣κ⁢(I)),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{r}^{1:T}\mid\kappa(I)% \right), (8.67)

where the source view at t=0t=0 is fixed by II while every unseen viewpoint and time step must be inferred. Both the unseen 3D geometry and the entirely absent temporal dynamics have to be inferred from one 2D view, which requires combining the spatial cues of the input with temporal priors from large video models [ren2023dreamgaussian4d, zhao2023animate124, sun2024eg4d].

8.5.2.2 Methodology

Both strategies of §8.5.1.2 apply, and most methods use 4D Gaussian Splatting as the representation [ren2023dreamgaussian4d, yang2024diffusion].

Implicit Optimization with Diffusion Priors. These methods instantiate Eq. (8.65), typically combining a multiview diffusion model for geometric consistency with a video diffusion model for temporal coherence. Animate124 [zhao2023animate124] first generates a static NeRF from the image and then refines its dynamics with a video-diffusion SDS loss, and Diffusion2 [yang2024diffusion] reconciles the scores of heterogeneous priors (multiview and video) through Variance-Reducing Sampling, improving both multiview and temporal consistency of the resulting 4D Gaussians.

Explicit Supervision with Generated Data. The slow, iterative nature of SDS motivates the two-stage pipeline of Eq. (8.66), in which an image-to-video model first generates an intermediate video that then supervises the 4D reconstruction directly. DreamGaussian4D (DG4D) [ren2023dreamgaussian4d] generates a static 3D Gaussian model and learns a deformation field to animate it, using the generated video for texture refinement and dynamic supervision, and EG4D [sun2024eg4d] avoids SDS entirely by chaining image-to-video and image-to-multiview models into coherent image sequences that guide a fast reconstruction.

Unified and Tuning-free Generation.
