GenXD [zhao2024genxd] trains one model on both 3D and 4D data, using multiview-temporal modules that separate camera motion from object motion, and Free4D [liu2025free4d] builds a 4D scene from a single image without fine-tuning any model, distilling pretrained image-to-video and multiview priors into a consistent 4D representation.

Specialized Methods for Human Generation. Dynamic human avatars form a sub-domain in which strong body priors raise fidelity. Human4DiT [shao2024360] uses a hierarchical 4D transformer that integrates human-specific features, camera parameters, and temporal signals to generate 360-degree human animations from a single image, and Disco4D [pang2025disco4d] models the body with SMPL-X while representing clothing separately with Gaussian splats, allowing detailed animation of clothed humans.

8.5.2.3 Benchmarks

With no image–4D pairs, methods are evaluated on images from Objaverse [deitke2023objaverse] or on in-the-wild photographs chosen by the authors, which makes comparison across papers unreliable. The metric set is that of §8.5.1.3, applied to the source view and to pseudo-ground-truth novel views where available.

8.5.2.4 Challenges and Trends

Inferring a complete shape and a plausible motion from one viewpoint is extremely ill-posed, which shows up as geometric inconsistency in unseen views (e.g., , the “Janus problem”) and as unnatural or repetitive motion, since every dynamic detail must be hallucinated. Domain-specific priors are the main remedy: Human4DiT [shao2024360] and Disco4D [pang2025disco4d] regularize geometry and motion with parametric body models and reach much higher fidelity, at the cost of generality.

8.5.3 Video-to-4D Generation

Video-to-4D generation lifts a single-view video into a dynamic 4D representation that can be viewed from new angles with consistent geometry and motion, turning ordinary video into interactive 4D content. Annotated video-to-4D datasets are hard to curate, so current methods build on pretrained video diffusion priors, either as multi-view supervision or through score distillation.

8.5.3.1 Task Definition

Video-to-4D generation specializes the 4D sampler of Eq. (8.63) to a monocular video condition 𝐜=𝐯1:T\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{v}^{1:T},

𝐫^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐫1:T∣κ⁢(𝐯1:T)),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{r}^{1:T}\mid\kappa(% \mathbf{v}^{1:T})\right), (8.68)

so that re-rendering 𝐫^1:T\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T} from the input viewpoint reproduces 𝐯1:T\mathbf{v}^{1:T} while novel views remain geometrically consistent. Unlike image-to-4D (Eq. (8.67)), the temporal dynamics are now observed and the residual ambiguity is purely geometric: the unseen off-axis structure.

8.5.3.2 Methodology

Most methods densify the monocular input into multi-view supervision and reconstruct against it (Eq. (8.66)), some add score distillation (Eq. (8.65)), and the newest predict the 4D asset feed-forward.

Mesh-based Methods. Meshes are interpretable and efficient to animate. DreamMesh4D [li2024dreammesh4d] obtains a coarse mesh and drives it with a sparse deformation graph and linear blend skinning (LBS), reaching strong spatio-temporal consistency more cheaply than implicit volumetric methods, and V2M4 [chen2025v2m4] reconstructs an animated, textured mesh asset directly from a monocular video.

NeRF-based Methods. NeRF-based methods model the continuous volumetric content of a video well, and they overcome the single view by generating data. Consistent4D [jiang2023consistent4d] densifies the monocular input through temporal and multiview interpolation before optimizing a NeRF with SDS, 4Diffusion [zhang20244diffusion] fine-tunes a video diffusion model with a learnable motion module on synthetic multiview data so that it produces consistent multiview video to guide generation, and SV4D [xie2024sv4d] completes missing views and frames with a diffusion model and uses the resulting multiview video to supervise the reconstruction.

Gaussian Splatting-based Methods. 4DGen [yin20234dgen] grounds 4D Gaussian generation in the input video with spatial-temporal pseudo labels; Efficient4D [pan2024efficient4d] converts the video into a multiview image matrix with a multiview-consistent generator (SyncDreamer) for rapid reconstruction; SC4D [wu2024sc4d] first fits sparse control Gaussians for coarse shape and motion and then drives dense Gaussians through LBS; and L4GM [ren2024l4gm] predicts the 4D Gaussians of a whole clip in a single feed-forward pass, trained on rendered animated objects.

8.5.3.3 Benchmarks

Video-to-4D has the one dedicated evaluation set in this section, released with Consistent4D [jiang2023consistent4d]: synthetic and real monocular videos with training and test splits. The metrics are those of §8.5.1.3, with reconstruction fidelity measured at the input view and novel-view quality measured where synthetic ground-truth multiview video exists.

8.5.3.4 Challenges and Trends

The video constrains motion but not the unseen 3D structure, which leads to geometric distortion, depth ambiguity, and a “painted-on” look in novel views. Explicit geometric structure is the main remedy: DreamMesh4D [li2024dreammesh4d] and SC4D [wu2024sc4d] constrain the reconstruction with meshes or sparse control points under LBS, which improves both coherence and efficiency, and combining such structure with the appearance modeling of neural representations is the obvious next step.

8.5.4 3D-to-4D Generation

3D-to-4D generation animates a static 3D model, so that the geometry is given and only motion and deformation must be synthesized, which makes the large stock of existing 3D assets usable for simulation, virtual reality, and character animation. Unconditional generators of dynamic neural fields, such as HyperDiffusion [erkocc2023hyperdiffusion], which runs diffusion directly on the weights of neural fields, sample 4D content without a given asset; 3D-to-4D instead starts from one, either through explicit mesh deformation and rigging or through neural and physics-based deformation models.

8.5.4.1 Task Definition

Here the condition is itself a 3D representation 𝐜=𝐫0∈ℛ\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{r}_{0}\in\mathcal{R}, so only its temporal evolution must be generated. We therefore specialize Eq. (8.63) to a deformation operator that takes the static asset and an optional auxiliary driving signal 𝐜aux\mathbf{c}_{\text{aux}} (text, audio, or a motion sketch) to a sequence,

𝐫^1:T=𝒟θ⁢(𝐫0,κ⁢(𝐜aux)),𝐫^0=𝐫0,\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T}=\mathcal{D}_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{r}_{0},\,\kappa(% \mathbf{c}_{\text{aux}})\right),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{0}=\mathbf{r}_{0}, (8.69)

with the first frame pinned to the input asset. This places 3D-to-4D in the same family as the editing operators of §8.2.5 and §8.4.4: it transforms an existing representation rather than synthesizing one from scratch.

8.5.4.2 Methodology

Methods realize the deformation operator 𝒟θ\mathcal{D}_{\theta} of Eq. (8.69) either with explicit mesh structure, increasingly through learned rigging, or with neural and physics-informed deformation fields.

Mesh-based Methods. Meshes give explicit structure and precise control over deformation. Motion3DGAN [otberdout2022sparse] generates 3D facial animation from a static face mesh by first predicting the displacement of facial landmarks for a target expression and then deforming the full mesh, with a GAN keeping the sequence temporally coherent. A recent line makes arbitrary meshes animatable by predicting the rig itself: MagicArticulate [song2025magicarticulate] and RigAnything [liu2025riganything] predict skeletons and skinning weights feed-forward, Puppeteer [song2025puppeteer] rigs a mesh and then animates it by fitting the rig to videos generated from renderings of the mesh, and AnimateAnyMesh [wu2025animateanymesh] generates text-driven mesh animation in a single forward pass with a rectified-flow model over a dynamic-mesh latent.

NeRF-based Methods. ElastoGen [feng2024elastogen] generates physically grounded elastodynamic behavior: it rasterizes a static 3D model and then predicts and refines deformation fields iteratively with recurrent and 3D convolutional modules, so that the motion obeys physical principles.

8.5.4.3 Benchmarks

No benchmark with ground-truth dynamic sequences exists; methods are evaluated on a few individual assets, often faces or generic objects, mostly by user study and with the metrics of §8.5.1.3 where a reference animation is available. Physical plausibility, specific to this subfield, can be measured for physics-informed methods such as ElastoGen [feng2024elastogen] as deviation from a high-fidelity simulator or as violation of conserved quantities such as energy and momentum.

8.5.4.4 Challenges and Trends

Even with the geometry given, the space of plausible animations of a static model is unbounded, so without guidance the task is unconstrained, and current methods specialize to narrow categories such as faces. Physical priors constrain it (ElastoGen [feng2024elastogen] grounds motion in elastodynamics), learned rigging makes arbitrary assets animatable, and pairing the asset with text, audio, or motion sketches turns open-ended generation into controllable animation.

8.5.5 Multi-conditional 4D Generation

Multi-conditional 4D generation steers dynamic scene synthesis with several signals at once: semantic conditions (text), appearance conditions (images, video), structural conditions (skeletal poses, explicit trajectories), and rule-based priors (differentiable physics). The central design problem is to fuse them so that each is respected without one overpowering the others.

8.5.5.1 Task Definition

We generalize the single-condition cases of Eqs. (8.64)–(8.69) to a set of KK conditions, each mapped by its own encoder κk\kappa_{k} and fused into the shared embedding:

𝐫^1:T∼pθ⁢(𝐫1:T∣κ1⁢(𝐜1),…,κK⁢(𝐜K)),\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{1:T}\sim p_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{r}^{1:T}\mid\kappa_{1}(% \mathbf{c}_{1}),\dots,\kappa_{K}(\mathbf{c}_{K})\right), (8.70)

which recovers a single-modality sampler when K=1K=1. Users can then specify not only what is generated (semantics) but how it behaves (motion path, physical behavior, artistic style), which complex applications such as character animation and driving simulation require.

8.5.5.2 Methodology

Methods fuse the encoders κk\kappa_{k} of Eq. (8.70), usually combining score distillation (Eq. (8.65)) with explicit supervision (Eq. (8.66)) tailored to each condition.

Motion and Trajectory Control. TC4D [bahmani2024tc4d] lets users define a spline trajectory that guides both the global rigid transformation and the local deformation of an object, with text supplying the semantics. For human animation, skeletons are the natural condition: Beyond Skeletons [yang2024beyond] integrates text and image conditions with the skeleton to refine motion, and STAR [chai2024star] uses skeleton-aware SDS and motion retargeting so that avatar movement is both visually coherent and anatomically accurate.

Physics-Informed Control. Sync4D [fu2024sync4d] and Phy124 [lin2024phy124] integrate differentiable Material Point Method (MPM) simulation, so that the generated content follows realistic dynamics such as elasticity and collisions under video or text guidance.

User-Centric and Artistic Control. Generative Rendering [cai2024generative] uses a pre-existing dynamic mesh to guide a pretrained text-to-image model, giving precise control over the style and detail of the rendered output, and sketch-based interfaces [yang2024sketch] let users draw the dynamics they want.

Complex, Application-Specific Control. MagicDrive3D [gao2024magicdrive3d] generates dynamic driving scenes from 2D bounding boxes, Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) maps, agent trajectories, and text together, producing tightly controlled traffic scenarios.

8.5.5.3 Benchmarks

No benchmark exists; building one would require 4D assets annotated with several aligned conditions (e.g., , a clip with a description, a skeletal motion sequence, and a trajectory map). Text adherence is scored with the CLIP Score of §8.5.1.3, while adherence to sketches or trajectories relies on task-specific errors (e.g., , distance from the specified trajectory) or on user studies, which remain the only holistic judge of how well a combination of inputs was followed.

8.5.5.4 Challenges and Trends

Semantic guidance from text, geometric constraints from skeletons, and rule-based priors from physics can contradict one another, and keeping each respected without one overpowering the rest while preserving fidelity is the open problem. Domain-specific stacks such as MagicDrive3D [gao2024magicdrive3d] sidestep it by fixing the set of inputs for one application, and interactive interfaces such as sketches [yang2024sketch] point toward iterative creation in which several control channels are adjusted in turn.

8.5.6 Summary, Overarching Challenges and Future Directions

Table 8.13 compares the five subfields as specializations of the 4D sampler of Eq. (8.63): image- and video-to-4D progressively replace hallucinated structure with observed pixels, 3D-to-4D is given the geometry and generates only motion, and multi-conditional generation fuses several signals at once.

Data Scarcity and Generative Priors.

Large, annotated 4D datasets are the field’s main missing ingredient: real dynamic 3D data with multi-view consistency and multimodal annotation (text, motion capture) is expensive and technically hard to collect, which has largely ruled out end-to-end training. The field has therefore converged on distilling pretrained text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D models, the de facto way to guide 4D synthesis.

From Score Distillation to Explicit Supervision.

Score distillation [poole2022dreamfusion] converges slowly, is costly and unstable, and produces multi-faced geometry and flickering textures. The generate-then-reconstruct pipeline of DreamGaussian4D [ren2023dreamgaussian4d] and EG4D [sun2024eg4d], which first generates target videos and then reconstructs against them, is replacing per-prompt SDS, and feed-forward predictors such as L4GM [ren2024l4gm] and AnimateAnyMesh [wu2025animateanymesh] take the next step by removing per-scene optimization altogether.

4D Gaussian Splatting as the Default Representation.

NeRF-based works rendered well but trained and rendered slowly. 3D Gaussian Splatting [kerbl20233d] and its temporal extension offer real-time, high-fidelity rendering with efficient gradient-based optimization, and their explicit, point-based form is easier to edit and to couple with physical simulation, so 4DGS has become the representation of choice for current methods [wu20244d, ren2023dreamgaussian4d, ling2024align].

Consistency, Control, and Physical Plausibility.

Keeping geometry, appearance, and motion coherent across all viewpoints and over long horizons remains the central difficulty, and control is moving beyond single prompts toward fine-grained manipulation of motion, appearance, and interaction. Physical plausibility is the newest goal: integrating differentiable simulators, as PhysSplat [zhao2024efficient] and Phy124 [lin2024phy124] do, makes generated dynamics more realistic and predictable. Progress on all three is hard to measure while evaluation relies on small, author-curated test sets and on image and video metrics that ignore cross-view and long-range consistency; 4D-aware benchmarks and metrics are a prerequisite for the rest.

8.6 World Modeling

Despite its growing popularity across AI research, the notion of a “world model” does not yet enjoy a unified or universally agreed-upon definition. Its conceptual roots trace back to the psychologist Kenneth Craik, who argued in his 1943 monograph The Nature of Explanation that the mind “carries a ‘small-scale model’ of external reality and of its own possible actions within its head”. In its original form, a world model referred to an individual’s internal representation of external reality; contemporary AI has generalized the concept far beyond mental representations to structured models of physical and spatial environments.

Fei-Fei Li has framed the gap between current AI systems and physical understanding in these terms [Feifei2025spatial]: modern LLMs resemble “wordsmiths in the dark”, fluent in symbols but divorced from the physical world that gives them meaning, and capable AI must instead understand, act within, and reason about three-dimensional space. On this view world models are new-generation generative models that simulate, predict, and imagine the world’s dynamics rather than only describe it, which ties world modeling directly to spatial intelligence.

Complementing Li’s generative perspective, another influential formulation comes from Yann LeCun [lecun2022path]. He describes a world model as a system capable of predicting how the world will evolve given its current state and an action. Formally, it consumes the current state S⁢(t)S(t) and an action A⁢(t)A(t), and produces a prediction of the next state S′⁢(t+1)S^{\prime}(t+1); in many cases, it also integrates external sensory observations O⁢(t)O(t) to update its internal state. This predictive relation can be written compactly as

S^⁢(t+1)=Wθ⁢(S⁢(t),A⁢(t),O⁢(t)),\hat{S}(t+1)=W_{\theta}\big{(}S(t),\,A(t),\,O(t)\big{)}, (8.71)

where WθW_{\theta} denotes the learned world model parameterized by θ\theta. Read against the conditional-generation backbone of this chapter (Eq. (8.2)), WθW_{\theta} occupies the position of the generator, but its decoder is a state-transition predictor rather than a pixel or geometry renderer; this is the sense in which world modeling extends Chapter 8 from reconstruction toward prediction. What exactly constitutes a “state” remains open: some work defines it as a compact latent representation in which the world model operates at an abstract semantic level, much as human cognition forecasts events without simulating every physical detail.

Although no single definition of world modeling has been universally accepted, a survey of the literature [fung2025embodied, li2025comprehensive, ding2025understanding, kong20253d] reveals three recurring paradigms, three realizations of Eq. (8.71) that differ in what they predict. Representation world models learn abstract latent spaces that capture the state and dynamics of the environment. Generative world models explicitly simulate or generate future states of the world through data-driven or hybrid mechanisms. Mental world models aim to infer and represent the mental states of humans or agents, enabling social reasoning and Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities. Figure 8.24 contrasts them side by side.

8.6.1 Representation World Model
8.6.1.1 Definition

A representation world model learns an internal latent description of the environment by compressing multimodal observations into structured, predictive embeddings, prioritizing the extraction of physical and semantic regularities over the generation of photorealistic pixels. Much as LLMs learn abstract linguistic representations through self-supervised pretraining, representation world models are trained on “world data” to infer the principles that govern physical and semantic dynamics; the objective is to predict how the world evolves at an abstract level, not to reconstruct pixels. The latent state is meant to encode objects and their properties (shape, size, appearance, material), their spatial relations (topology, distance, configuration), the dynamics that govern how the scene evolves, and the causal dependence of outcomes on actions. With such a state, an agent can predict over long horizons, reason, and plan without operating in high-dimensional sensory space.

8.6.1.2 Multimodal Perception

A world model draws on several sensory streams, whose encoding is the subject of Chapter 6. Vision dominates: images and especially video carry objects, geometry, interaction, and temporal dynamics, and modern systems rely on high-capacity encoders trained with contrastive vision–language objectives for semantic and geometric priors. Audio adds direct evidence about events and the physical state of the surroundings, which language conveys only symbolically. Touch is indispensable where vision is unreliable, occluded, or unavailable (grasping inside a bag, fine manipulation, tool use), yet it remains underexplored because tactile sensors are limited and tactile data are hard to collect at scale.

8.6.1.3 World Representation Modeling
Vision-oriented Modeling.

A major line of representation world modeling builds latent spaces from visual observations: video frames are encoded into a compact latent space by self-supervised learning, and a transition model predicts future latent states from past latents and actions, which captures the dynamics of the visual world more efficiently than pixel-space prediction. Concretely, an encoder EϕE_{\phi} maps observations to latent states and a predictor PθP_{\theta} is trained to minimize a prediction loss defined entirely in latent space,

ℒrep⁢(θ,ϕ)=𝔼⁢[∥Pθ⁢(Eϕ⁢(O≤t),A⁢(t))−sg⁡(Eϕ¯⁢(Ot+1))∥2],\mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}}(\theta,\phi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\big{\lVert}P_{% \theta}\big{(}E_{\phi}(O_{\leq t}),\,A(t)\big{)}-\operatorname{sg}\!\big{(}E_{% \bar{\phi}}(O_{t+1})\big{)}\big{\rVert}^{2}\,\right], (8.72)

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operator and Eϕ¯E_{\bar{\phi}} a slowly updated target encoder. This objective instantiates the transition of Eq. (8.71) with the predicted state S^⁢(t+1)\hat{S}(t+1) taken to be an abstract embedding rather than raw pixels (Figure 8.24(a)), which is precisely what allows representation world models to capture dynamics efficiently while discarding perceptually salient yet predictively irrelevant detail.

The World Models architecture [ha2018world] decomposes the problem into a VAE-based vision model, an RNN-based memory model, and a lightweight controller; the vision and memory components learn latent dynamics from raw pixels without supervision, and the controller then learns its behavior inside the “dreamed” environment, which greatly simplifies policy learning. The Dreamer agents carry this idea into reinforcement learning at scale: Dreamer [hafner2019dreamer] learns a latent dynamics model from pixels and trains an actor and critic entirely on imagined latent trajectories, and DreamerV3 [hafner2023mastering] applies a single configuration across a wide range of domains. MuZero [schrittwieser2020mastering] learns a model that predicts only the quantities planning needs (reward, value, and policy) and plans with it by tree search, mastering Atari, Go, chess, and shogi without being given the rules.

Yann LeCun’s autonomous intelligence framework proposes the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) [lecun2022path] as the core mechanism for constructing world models. JEPA learns latent representations and predictions through self-supervised objectives rather than pixel-level reconstruction, and Eq. (8.72) is its generic form. I-JEPA [assran2023jepa] first instantiated it on images, predicting the embeddings of masked target regions from a visible context block, and V-JEPA [bardes2024vjepa] carried the same feature-prediction objective to video, predicting masked spatio-temporal embeddings in latent space with no pixel reconstruction, text, or negative examples, and so avoiding the cost and ambiguity of pixel prediction. V-JEPA 2 [assran2025vjepa] turns this encoder into a world model. Pretrained on more than a million hours of internet video, it is extended with an action-conditioned predictor, V-JEPA 2-AC, post-trained on less than 62 hours of unlabeled robot video; deployed zero-shot on Franka arms, it picks and places objects by planning actions whose predicted embeddings reach a goal image.

The stop-gradient and slowly updated target encoder in Eq. (8.72) exist only to keep the representation from collapsing, and the most recent JEPA work removes them. LeJEPA [balestriero2025lejepa] shows that an isotropic Gaussian is the optimal embedding distribution for downstream prediction and enforces it with a single sketched regularizer (SIGReg), leaving one trade-off hyperparameter and no teacher–student machinery. LeWorldModel [maes2026leworldmodel] uses the same regularizer to train an action-conditioned JEPA world model end to end from raw pixels with only two loss terms; at about 15M parameters it trains on a single GPU, plans up to 48 times faster than world models built on foundation-model encoders, and its latents encode physical quantities well enough to flag physically implausible events. The principle has also reached language: VL-JEPA [chen2025vl] predicts continuous embeddings of the target text instead of generating tokens, and LLM-JEPA [huang2026llmjepa] adds an embedding-prediction objective to the next-token training of language models.

DINO-World [baldassarre2025back] instead freezes DINOv2 as a universal visual encoder, whose features are already semantic, geometric, and object-centric, learns a latent-space predictor from large-scale unlabeled video, and adds action-conditioned prediction to model how interventions change future visual states.

Hybrid World Modeling.

Another important direction expands representation learning beyond vision by incorporating additional modalities such as LiDAR, camera trajectories, or multi-view geometric signals. These hybrid models aim to overcome the limitations of purely visual latent spaces by injecting explicit spatial structure, depth cues, and geometric consistency constraints. For instance, MUVO [bogdoll2025muvo] is a multimodal generative world model that learns jointly from synchronized camera and LiDAR streams. By integrating LiDAR-derived depth priors into the latent world representation, MUVO achieves more reliable 3D scene prediction, improved object motion modeling, and long-horizon forecasting in autonomous driving environments. UniWorld [min2023uniworld] introduces a unified pretrained architecture that merges 3D object detection, motion prediction, and scene representation learning. Through joint training of BEV features, temporal dynamics, and multisensor context, UniWorld produces a structured latent state that simultaneously supports perception and trajectory forecasting. Aether [zhu2025aether] proposes a geometry-aware unified world model where camera trajectories are treated as explicit action signals. This allows the model to learn action-conditioned scene transitions and perform predictive visual planning. By binding egomotion with geometric consistency constraints, Aether generates spatially coherent future predictions and supports counterfactual simulation within a 3D-aware latent space.

Language-oriented World Modeling.

A final category examines language as a central medium for latent world representation. This raises an important question: can LLMs themselves be viewed as world models? From a formal perspective, LLMs indeed share structural similarities with classical world models. They maintain internal states, treat textual context as observations, accept prompts as actions that alter these states, and generate predictions that correspond to inferred future states. Models such as Dynalang [lin2023learning] demonstrate that natural language can serve as a universal intermediate representation for encoding environment states, predicting transitions, and expressing causal relations. LLMs also exhibit emergent knowledge of commonsense physics, intuitive causality, and human behavior derived from massive text corpora. However, their limitations remain clear: they are trained on symbolic descriptions rather than direct interaction with the physical world; their internal dynamics reflect linguistic statistics more than physical laws; and their world representations tend to be sparse, fragmented, and disconnected from geometric or temporal continuity. Thus, while LLMs can be interpreted as language-driven world models, their predictive capacity is primarily symbolic and semantic, rather than grounded in spatial or physical understanding.

8.6.2 Generative World Model

In contrast to representation-based foundation models, generative world models focus on explicitly predicting future states or synthesizing the evolution of the environment over time. Rather than only learning compact latent encodings, these models aim to simulate how the world might change under different conditions, capturing temporal dynamics and causal structure. Whereas the representation paradigm of Eq. (8.72) predicts in an abstract latent space, generative world models learn an explicit conditional distribution over future observations and can be unrolled autoregressively over a horizon HH,

pθ⁢(Ot+1:t+H∣O≤t,At:t+H−1)=∏k=0H−1pθ⁢(Ot+k+1∣O≤t+k,A⁢(t+k)),p_{\theta}\big{(}O_{t+1:t+H}\mid O_{\leq t},\,A_{t:t+H-1}\big{)}=\prod_{k=0}^{% H-1}p_{\theta}\big{(}O_{t+k+1}\mid O_{\leq t+k},\,A(t+k)\big{)}, (8.73)

so that sampling from Eq. (8.73) realizes the transition of Eq. (8.71) directly in observation space (Figure 8.24(b)). This explicit synthesis is what allows generative world models to be rendered, inspected, and acted within, at the cost of having to model a high-dimensional output distribution. Broadly, generative world models can be grouped into two main families: physics-driven simulation, which relies on hand-crafted rules and equations, and learning-driven world generation, which learns world dynamics directly from data. The former can be viewed as the deterministic limit of the latter: it fixes the transition of Eq. (8.73) to a hand-specified rule set instead of a learned distribution, trading sample diversity and coverage for exact reproducibility and verifiability. A third route, growing quickly since 2024, sits between the two: a learned model writes the rules as code and a simulator executes them (Section 8.6.2.3).

8.6.2.1 Physics-driven Simulation

Physics-driven simulation builds interactive virtual worlds from human-designed physical, geometric, and logical rules rather than from learned latent spaces. The environment is governed by predefined physical laws, rendering rules, collision logic, and behavioral scripts, specified top-down as explicit mathematical formulations, so the same initial conditions always produce the same outcome; this determinism, together with interpretability and verifiability, is what makes such systems suitable for safety-critical engineering.

Game engines are the canonical example. Physics engines such as Bullet, Havok, PhysX, and Box2D implement Newtonian, rigid-body, soft-body, cloth, particle, and volumetric dynamics, and the engines around them add acceleration structures (e.g., , BVH trees), real-time ray tracing, and navigation meshes for path planning, which gives them a natural foothold in spatial-intelligence tasks. Film production relies on the same principle at higher fidelity: pipelines built on Pixar USD, Maya, or Houdini simulate cloth, hair, smoke, fire, and fluids with differential-equation and fluid solvers (e.g., , FLIP/MantaFlow) and physically based path tracing. Engineering, architecture, and scientific visualization extend rule-based simulation to structural mechanics, electromagnetics, illumination, and material response through finite element methods, computational fluid dynamics, and photonic simulation.

For embodied AI, physics-driven simulators such as CARLA [dosovitskiy2017carla], AirSim, and Isaac Sim [NVIDIA2021Isaac] remain the standard platforms for testing and training in autonomous driving, navigation, and manipulation, because they model lighting, collisions, dynamics, and sensor noise closely enough to yield data distributions near those of the real world. The same engines underpin digital twins built on platforms such as NVIDIA Omniverse, Unity, and Unreal Engine, which are discussed in Part IV, Section 11.1.

8.6.2.2 Learning-driven World Generation

In contrast to simulation frameworks based on explicit physical rules, learning-driven world generation seeks to acquire world structure, dynamics, and causal regularities directly from large-scale data, in a bottom-up fashion. These models do not encode Newtonian equations, lighting models, or geometric constraints by hand; instead, world behavior emerges as statistical patterns during training. For example, a model may never be given the analytic form of the gravity equation, yet by observing countless videos of falling objects, it can still infer the regularity that objects tend to accelerate downward. The resulting world models are probabilistic and can exhibit complex, emergent behaviors without explicit programming.

Current learning-driven world generation follows two technical directions: (1) video-centric generative models that learn dynamic world evolution in pixel or latent space, and (2) 3D/4D asset generation methods that directly model spatially structured worlds in three or four dimensions.

Video-centric Generative World Models.

Recent advances in video generation have renewed interest in the idea of a “world simulator”. Video models are intrinsically suited to encoding spatiotemporal structure, and when they produce sequences that are not only visually coherent but also consistent with basic physical intuition, they begin to resemble implicit world models. This became especially prominent with the release of OpenAI Sora [sora2024], whose generated videos demonstrate strong temporal consistency, long-horizon stability, and apparent physical plausibility, prompting the community to reconsider whether deep video generation might be converging towards a form of physical world modeling. Subsequently, Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 [genie3] extended video generation from passive “watchable” content to interactive experiences: the model updates the generated world in response to user actions, enabling agent-in-the-loop, closed-loop world simulation, complementing the action-conditioned scene generators surveyed in §8.2.2. World Labs’ RTFM [worldlabs_rtfm] further highlights real-time performance, achieving high frame-rate and low-latency prediction. Systems such as Wan [wan2025wan], Emu3.5 [cui2025emu35], OpenAI Sora 2 [sora2], and Veo 3 [veo3] continue this trajectory, gradually pushing video generation from mere visual fidelity towards world coherence, physical consistency, and interactivity. Action-conditioned diffusion has also turned games into testbeds: GameNGen [valevski2024diffusion] simulates the game DOOM interactively in real time, and DIAMOND [alonso2024diffusionworldmodelingvisual] trains reinforcement-learning agents entirely inside a diffusion world model of Atari games, while NVIDIA’s Cosmos [nvidia2025cosmos] offers pretrained video world foundation models intended to be post-trained as simulators for robotics and driving.

Video world models are particularly promising in autonomous driving. GAIA-1 [hu2023gaia] proposes a generative world model tailored for driving scenarios, built around a spatiotemporal Transformer that generates future multi-view scenes based on past observations. By implicitly capturing traffic patterns, pedestrian behavior, scene geometry, and multi-agent motion, GAIA-1 can support closed-loop evaluation, behavior prediction, and synthetic data generation, thereby reducing the cost and risk of traditional real-world testing.

3D/4D Asset Generation as World Modeling.

A complementary avenue is to build world models that operate directly on structured three- or four-dimensional representations, such as 3D geometry, occupancy fields, or 4D spatiotemporal volumes. Unlike video-based approaches that primarily model dynamics in pixel space, these methods explicitly parameterize geometry and temporal evolution, making it easier to represent interactive, spatially consistent worlds.

Genesis [Genesis] exemplifies this direction. It is not only a generative 3D/4D physics simulation platform, but also integrates a vision-language model-driven “world-building agent” that uses a tool API to create dynamic 4D environments (geometry plus dynamics). These generated worlds can be rendered into multiple modalities (RGB, depth, semantics, contact events, etc.), providing rich supervision for training embodied AI systems. Genesis thus combines a unified physics engine with generative agents for large-scale world construction.

Autonomous driving again serves as a natural application domain for 3D world models. DriveArena [yang2025drivearena] builds a closed-loop generative simulation platform, allowing planning modules to iteratively probe and learn within synthesized 3D driving environments. Its diffusion-model-based multi-agent scene generation can rapidly produce long, interactive driving episodes. OccWorld [zheng2024occworld] and OccSora [wang2024occsora] adopt 4D occupancy grids as the core representation, predicting future 3D occupancy over time from continuous video and sensor streams, thereby providing a unified motion-and-structure world model. Copilot4D [zhang2023copilot4d] tokenizes LiDAR scans and forecasts future LiDAR point clouds with discrete diffusion, learning a world model from unlabeled sensor data alone.

Generating interactive 3D worlds brings generative world models closest to their conceptual ideal. Marble [Feifei2025Marble] from World Labs combines action-conditioned generation, geometric consistency constraints, and multimodal inputs, so that users can act within the generated world and observe the consequences. Its next-generation model, Atlas [worldlabs2026atlas], is an omni world model pretrained from scratch on text, images, video, and 3D: an autoregressive diffusion transformer that conditions every generated image and depth map on an explicit camera pose and grounds them all in a shared 3D context, so that the same model generates camera-controlled video of up to a minute, reconstructs scenes from a handful of images, and exports its output as point clouds or 3D Gaussian splats. World Labs reports that it outperforms specialized open-source reconstruction models, and that it will power future versions of Marble.

8.6.2.3 Code-and-Simulator World Models

Between hand-written simulation and learned generation sits a route that has grown quickly since 2024: a language model writes the world model as executable code, and a simulator or engine runs it. The learned component is the author of the rules, not the rules themselves,

𝒫∼pθ⁢(𝒫∣c),S^⁢(t+1)=Sim⁢(S⁢(t),A⁢(t);𝒫),\mathcal{P}\sim p_{\theta}\big{(}\mathcal{P}\mid c\big{)},\qquad\hat{S}(t+1)=% \mathrm{Sim}\big{(}S(t),\,A(t);\,\mathcal{P}\big{)}, (8.74)

where cc is the conditioning context (a description, observations, or a history of interactions), 𝒫\mathcal{P} the generated program, and Sim\mathrm{Sim} the interpreter or engine that executes it: plain Python, a physics engine such as MuJoCo or PyChrono, or Blender. Compared with Eq. (8.71), the learned WθW_{\theta} is replaced by a program that can be read, tested, and repaired, so the resulting world keeps the determinism and verifiability of physics-driven simulation while gaining the open-endedness of a generative model. The scene programs of Section 8.7 rest on the same idea; the difference here is that 𝒫\mathcal{P} encodes how the world changes under actions, not only how it is laid out.

In one line of work, code is an agent’s transition model. Code World Models [dainese2024codeworld] synthesize Python implementations of reinforcement-learning environments with a generate, improve, and fix search over programs (GIF-MCTS), evaluated on a benchmark of 18 environments, and plan with them faster and more sample-efficiently than with learned dynamics; WorldCoder [tang2024worldcoder] builds its world model as a program from its own interactions and transfers knowledge to a new environment by editing that program.

In the other, code builds a simulated 3D world. SceneCraft [hu2024scenecraft] turns a description into Blender Python, planning with a scene graph, converting spatial relations into numerical layout constraints, and checking renders with a vision-language model. GenSim [wang2023gensim] and RoboGen [wang2023robogen] have language models write robotic simulation tasks, scenes, and rewards, making the simulator an open-ended source of training data, and the world-building agent of Genesis [Genesis] follows the same pattern. Recent systems close the loop with the simulator itself. Code2Worlds [zhang2026code2worlds] generates 4D worlds as Blender code refined by a vision-language motion critic; Code2Worlds-2 [zhang2026code2worlds2] compiles such worlds into physically valid MuJoCo scenes and revises them from penetration, contact, and stability signals; and ChronoAgentic [wang2026chronoagentic] has cooperating agents write and repair PyChrono simulations, meeting the joint semantic and physical correctness criterion on 82.5% of PhyWorldBench demos against 52.5% for the best of ten text-to-video models.

The price is coverage. A program can express only what its simulator supports, so photorealistic appearance, deformable and fluid materials, and open-ended visual variety still favor learned generators, while code-and-simulator models win where physical correctness has to be checked.

8.6.3 Mental World Modeling

Physical world models enable agents to understand and predict how the external environment evolves. However, intelligent behavior in real-world settings also requires an internal model of other minds. Humans naturally construct such models, i.e., , often referred to as mental models, to reason about others’ beliefs, desires, intentions, emotions, and social context. This ability, commonly associated with Theory of Mind (ToM) [astington1995theory], underlies human social interaction, collaboration, communication, and decision-making.

Craik’s “small-scale models” of reality are the origin of this notion too [nersessian1993theoretician, staggers1993mental], and Johnson-Laird later argued that human reasoning, problem solving, and causal inference rely on abstract internal representations of situations rather than on replaying detailed physical dynamics. These representations selectively capture the most relevant structure, i.e., , objects, relations, causal dependencies, and possible outcomes, while abstracting away low-level perceptual details. For example, when cycling, a human does not mentally simulate every joint torque or physical trajectory; instead, one imagines “whether I would fall or not” when encountering an obstacle. This high-level, conceptual simulation is a defining property of mental world modeling.

8.6.3.1 From Physical to Cognitive Mental World Models

Human mental simulation operates by combining current observations with stored knowledge to predict plausible futures. Perception provides the immediate sensory input, which is then transformed into an internal symbolic and probabilistic representation of the world. Within this representation, the brain runs rapid, approximate simulations that evaluate different hypothetical actions. These simulations are not physically precise but are cognitively meaningful: they help determine risks, anticipate others’ responses, or evaluate alternative courses of action. In this sense, mental models serve as a compact, abstract, and counterfactual “world engine” for decision making.

In artificial systems, the distinction between physical and mental world models mirrors that in human cognition. Physical world models predict state transitions in the environment (e.g., , dynamics, geometry, object motion), whereas mental world models encode the latent mental states of human users or other agents. These models allow an AI system to reason about what humans know, believe, want, or intend to do, capabilities that embodied agents, collaborative robots, intelligent tutors, and multi-agent planners all need.

Inspired by the Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) [rao1995bdi, georgeff1998belief] framework, a mental world model for AI typically includes a small set of structured variables. Beliefs. These are representations of what the human knows, perceives, or believes about the world. Desires. These capture user goals, preferences, motivations, and values. Intentions. These are planned or ongoing actions that the agent expects the human (or another agent) to follow. Such decomposition enables an AI system to explicitly reason about human rationality, goal pursuit, and action planning. Formally, a mental world model can be cast as the inference of a latent mental state M⁢(t)M(t), comprising the beliefs, desires, and intentions above, from observed behavior, followed by a prediction of the other agent’s next action,

M^⁢(t)=arg⁢maxM⁡p⁢(M∣O≤t),A^other⁢(t+1)=π⁢(M^⁢(t)).\hat{M}(t)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{M}\,p\big{(}M\mid O_{\leq t}\big{)},% \qquad\hat{A}^{\text{other}}(t+1)=\pi\big{(}\hat{M}(t)\big{)}. (8.75)

This formulation mirrors the transition of Eq. (8.71) but replaces the physical state with the inferred mental state of another agent (Figure 8.24(c)), so that the predicted quantity is no longer how the environment will evolve but how a human or peer agent is likely to act.

Machine Theory of Mind is now measured directly. ToMi [le2019tomi] tests false-belief reasoning in short stories with controls against shortcut solutions, BigToM [gandhi2023bigtom] generates controlled social scenarios with language models to probe whether models infer beliefs from percepts and actions, and MMToM-QA [jin2024mmtomqa] poses belief and goal questions about a person acting in a household from video and text together. Large language and multimodal models remain unreliable on these tests, whereas MMToM-QA’s BIP-ALM, which performs Bayesian inverse planning over a symbolic state with a language model scoring the likelihoods, does better; it is an explicit instance of the inference in Eq. (8.75).

Dimensions of Mental State Representation.

Beyond the belief-desire-intention core, a mental world model for embodied agents must span several further layers of internal state and social context. It has to read affect, recognizing emotional cues and how they shift a person’s risk tolerance and willingness to cooperate. It has to represent social dynamics: the relationships, roles, group structures, and cultural norms that shape behavior. And it has to interpret communication, both the verbal channel and the non-verbal one carried by tone, gesture, posture, and facial expression. These layers are what turn a bare goal estimate into a socially situated account of why a person acts as they do.

Human spatial reasoning is social as well as geometric, which ties mental modeling to spatial intelligence. To assist or collaborate with humans in homes, factories, classrooms, or vehicles, an agent must infer the intention behind a spatial action (e.g., , where a person intends to move next), anticipate trajectories from goals or habits, adapt navigation or manipulation to user preferences, and interpret spatial configurations that reflect what a person believes or misunderstands.

8.6.3.2 A Joint Physical-Mental Formulation

The benchmarks above still treat the mental state as something inferred next to a world model, not as part of it: Eq. (8.75) estimates another agent’s mind, but the environment it acts in is predicted separately. Mental World Modeling (MWM) [fei2026mental] makes the mental state part of the state that the world model of Eq. (8.71) rolls forward. We follow its notation, in which subscripts index time, so that sts_{t} and atϵa_{t}^{\epsilon} play the roles of S⁢(t)S(t) and A⁢(t)A(t) above. The case for a joint state is that neither half suffices alone. For a target agent ϵ\epsilon whose true action distribution is p⋆p^{\star}, a physical-only representation fails whenever

p⋆⁢(atϵ∣stphy,stment)≠p⋆⁢(atϵ∣stphy,s~tment),p^{\star}\big{(}a_{t}^{\epsilon}\mid s_{t}^{\mathrm{phy}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}% }\big{)}\neq p^{\star}\big{(}a_{t}^{\epsilon}\mid s_{t}^{\mathrm{phy}},\tilde{% s}_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}}\big{)}, (8.76)

that is, whenever two scenes that are physically identical but differ in what people believe or want (stments_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}} versus s~tment\tilde{s}_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}}) lead to different actions; the symmetric condition, with the mental state held fixed and the physical state changed, rules out a mental-only representation.

Joint State.

The world state is the pair

st=(stphy,stment)∈𝒮phy×𝒮ment,stment=({mti}i∈ℐ,{mtG}G∈𝒢,Rtment,αt).s_{t}=\big{(}s_{t}^{\mathrm{phy}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}}\big{)}\in\mathcal{S}^{% \mathrm{phy}}\times\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{ment}},\qquad s_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}}=% \big{(}\{m_{t}^{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}},\,\{m_{t}^{G}\}_{G\in\mathcal{G}},\,R_{% t}^{\mathrm{ment}},\,\alpha_{t}\big{)}. (8.77)

The physical part collects the objects, the embodied characters, their spatial and contact relations, and the environmental conditions of the scene. The mental part holds an individual state mtim_{t}^{i} for every agent ii in the set ℐ\mathcal{I}, optional states mtGm_{t}^{G} for groups G∈𝒢G\in\mathcal{G}, the social attitudes and role relations RtmentR_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}} between agents, and the atmosphere αt\alpha_{t} of the setting. Each individual state extends the belief-desire-intention core introduced above,

mti=(idti,bti,qti,gti,ιti,eti,dti,nti,cti),m_{t}^{i}=\big{(}\mathrm{id}_{t}^{i},\,b_{t}^{i},\,q_{t}^{i},\,g_{t}^{i},\,% \iota_{t}^{i},\,e_{t}^{i},\,d_{t}^{i},\,n_{t}^{i},\,c_{t}^{i}\big{)}, (8.78)

with identity attributes, beliefs, attention focus, goals, intentions, emotions, dispositions, norms, and behavioral constraints. Beliefs, goals, and intentions are the BDI variables; emotions, norms, and the relations RtmentR_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}} turn the affect and social-dynamics layers discussed above into explicit state variables.

Target-Specific Observation.

The model reasons from the perspective of one target agent ϵ∈ℐ\epsilon\in\mathcal{I}, which sees only a rendering of the joint state:

otϵ=Ωϵ⁢(st)=(Ωϵphy⁢(stphy;κtϵ),Ωϵment⁢(stphy,stment;ρtϵ)),o_{t}^{\epsilon}=\Omega_{\epsilon}(s_{t})=\Big{(}\Omega_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{% phy}}\big{(}s_{t}^{\mathrm{phy}};\,\kappa_{t}^{\epsilon}\big{)},\;\Omega_{% \epsilon}^{\mathrm{ment}}\big{(}s_{t}^{\mathrm{phy}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}};\,% \rho_{t}^{\epsilon}\big{)}\Big{)}, (8.79)

The mental part of the observation contains the target’s view of its own state and its estimates m^t,ϵj,(ℓ)\widehat{m}^{\,j,(\ell)}_{t,\epsilon} of every other agent jj, nested up to a depth LL; at the first level they are sampled as

m^t,ϵj,(1)∼Qϵ(1)⁢(mtj∣otϵ,phy,mtϵ,Rtment,αt),\widehat{m}^{\,j,(1)}_{t,\epsilon}\sim Q^{(1)}_{\epsilon}\big{(}m_{t}^{j}\mid o% _{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{phy}},\,m_{t}^{\epsilon},\,R_{t}^{\mathrm{ment}},\,% \alpha_{t}\big{)}, (8.80)

Spatial access enters the mental model directly through κtϵ\kappa_{t}^{\epsilon}: what the target can see from where it stands bounds what it can believe, so a poor decision can follow from an object outside its view as much as from a mistaken belief.

Action and Coupled Transition.

Each action has a physical carrier and a mental content, atϵ=(atϵ,phy,atϵ,ment)a_{t}^{\epsilon}=(a_{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{phy}},a_{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{ment}}) (approaching someone, and meaning to comfort them), and the policy factorizes as Πϵ⁢(atϵ,phy,atϵ,ment∣otϵ)=Πϵphy⁢(atϵ,phy∣otϵ)⁢Πϵment⁢(atϵ,ment∣atϵ,phy,otϵ)\Pi_{\epsilon}(a_{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{phy}},a_{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{ment}}% \mid o_{t}^{\epsilon})=\Pi_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{phy}}(a_{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{% phy}}\mid o_{t}^{\epsilon})\,\Pi_{\epsilon}^{\mathrm{ment}}(a_{t}^{\epsilon,% \mathrm{ment}}\mid a_{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{phy}},o_{t}^{\epsilon}). The world model then predicts the next joint state with a staged transition,

(8.81)

The asymmetry is deliberate. An intention moves nothing until it is carried out physically, so the physical factor ignores atϵ,menta_{t}^{\epsilon,\mathrm{ment}}; the mental factor depends on both components, because the same reassuring words land differently when the speaker is approaching than when walking away. The physical factor still conditions on the mental state, since what objects, space, and visibility allow is joined by what other agents intend to do. Those other agents are not controlled: their actions at−ϵa_{t}^{-\epsilon} are marginalized under the simulator’s predictive distribution,

Tθ⁢(st+1∣st,atϵ)=∫Tθ⁢(st+1∣st,atϵ,at−ϵ)⁢p⁢(at−ϵ∣st)⁢dat−ϵ,T_{\theta}\big{(}s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}^{\epsilon}\big{)}=\int T_{\theta}\big% {(}s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}^{\epsilon},a_{t}^{-\epsilon}\big{)}\,p\big{(}a_{t}^% {-\epsilon}\mid s_{t}\big{)}\,\mathrm{d}a_{t}^{-\epsilon}, (8.82)

with p⁢(at−ϵ∣st)=∏j≠ϵΠj⁢(atj∣Ωj⁢(st))p(a_{t}^{-\epsilon}\mid s_{t})=\prod_{j\neq\epsilon}\Pi_{j}\big{(}a_{t}^{j}% \mid\Omega_{j}(s_{t})\big{)} for simultaneous moves, so that every agent still acts on its own partial observation. The whole pipeline, st→Ωϵotϵ→Πϵatϵ→Tθst+1s_{t}\xrightarrow{\Omega_{\epsilon}}o_{t}^{\epsilon}\xrightarrow{\Pi_{\epsilon% }}a_{t}^{\epsilon}\xrightarrow{T_{\theta}}s_{t+1}, is Eq. (8.71) with a mental component added to the state and a perspective added to the observation.

Evaluating Candidate Futures.

Simulating each candidate gives a branch s^t+1k\hat{s}^{k}_{t+1}, and the predicted decision is the branch of highest value,

k^=arg⁢maxk∈{1,…,K}⁡rk.\hat{k}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{k\in\{1,\dots,K\}}\,r_{k}. (8.83)

In MENTIS, the training-free and fully inspectable baseline of MWM, the branch value rkr_{k} is a weighted combination of normalized scores for physical plausibility, mental consistency, and social appropriateness, and a binary safety and legality veto sets it to zero. Each formal component maps to a module: a state parser recovers s^t\hat{s}_{t}, an observation generator implements Ωϵ\Omega_{\epsilon}, an action parser structures the candidates, a world-state transitor implements TθT_{\theta}, and an evaluator assigns rkr_{k}. On situated decision scenarios presented as text, image, and sounding-video stories, experiments across eight LLM-based world models indicate that the explicit mental component is what makes a person’s actual decision predictable [fei2026mental].

8.6.4 Discussions and Challenges
Representation-based World Models as an Alternative Foundation Model Paradigm.

Representation world models may emerge as a parallel paradigm to current LLMs, functioning as large-scale foundational models trained through massive self-supervised representation learning to capture physical regularities, causal dynamics, and environmental constraints. Unlike LLMs, which learn the world indirectly through linguistic abstraction, representation world models aim to model the physical world directly from multimodal observations. Such models could serve video generation, action prediction in VLA systems, 3D and 4D understanding and generation, and decision-making in autonomous driving.

The Necessity of Multi-source Intelligence Integration.

World models will likely require the integration of heterogeneous informational sources. On the one hand, LLMs embody language-driven intelligence, while world models emphasize physically grounded intelligence; rather than being mutually exclusive, a truly capable world model must incorporate both forms of reasoning. On the other hand, accurate world understanding requires far more than visual perception alone: audio, speech, tactile signals, force feedback, and even proprioception provide essential supplementary cues about the dynamics and structure of the physical environment. Yet the current research community focuses overwhelmingly on visual-only modeling. Building world models that holistically integrate multimodal sensory information remains a major challenge.

Unifying Physical Modeling and Mental Modeling.

Another promising direction is the integration of physical and mental modeling within a unified world-modeling framework. Embodied agents operating in real environments must simultaneously reason about the physical evolution of the environment and the mental or behavioral responses of humans (or other agents). Recent work in multi-agent systems, social navigation, pedagogical reasoning, human-robot collaboration, and interactive LLM agents emphasizes the growing need for AI systems to build internal hypotheses about both external dynamics and human mental states. Mental World Modeling [fei2026mental] is an early formulation of such a joint state (Section 8.6.3.2). Ultimately, scalable general-purpose world models must simulate not only what will happen but also what others believe, intend, desire, or misunderstand.

Balance between Generative Fidelity and Physical Correctness.

A central challenge for learning-driven world models is reconciling generative expressiveness with physical accuracy. High-capacity video generators often produce visually stunning but physically implausible outcomes, while models optimized for strict physical consistency may underperform in realism or diversity. Achieving stable long-horizon predictions without temporal drift or compounding errors remains unsolved. Designing architectures, training objectives, and constraints that jointly enforce physical laws, spatial coherence, and generative flexibility is a key open problem for the next generation of world simulators.

Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Verifiability of World Models.

Unlike language models, which can be evaluated through perplexity, benchmarks, or task accuracy, world models lack standardized, reliable, and comprehensive evaluation protocols. Physical correctness, causal consistency, interactive fidelity, multimodal coherence, and long-horizon stability are difficult to quantify in a unified manner. Furthermore, world models that aim to simulate open-ended environments raise issues of verifiability, reproducibility, and safety: how can we assess whether a world model reliably generalizes to unseen real-world scenarios, or whether its internal dynamics exhibit hidden biases or unsafe behaviors? Establishing principled evaluation methodologies and shared benchmarks for both representation-based and generative world models is an urgent research direction.

8.7 Programmatic and Symbolic Spatial Generation

Programmatic and symbolic spatial generation synthesizes 2D and 3D scene structure through explicit rules, executable programs, and symbolic geometric abstractions. It generates the structural backbone of a scene (spatial layout, hierarchical organization, geometric constraints, executable logic) rather than its raw appearance, which gives it controllability, compositional generalization, global spatial consistency, and interpretability.

Where the largely neural samplers of §8.1–§8.6 map a condition directly to pixels, voxels, or a neural latent, programmatic methods emit an intermediate program that a deterministic renderer executes into the final scene. This intermediate layer is what makes the structure auditable, editable, and compositionally reusable, properties that flat neural outputs lack. Three paradigm families mark the historical and technical progression of the field: rule- and grammar-based procedural generation, symbolic graphics programs and domain-specific languages, and neuro-symbolic language-to-program synthesis driven by large language models.

8.7.1 Task Definition

Let 𝐜∈𝒞\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C} denote a conditioning intent, typically a natural-language description, a layout specification, or a partial constraint set, and let κ:𝒞→𝒞′\kappa:\mathcal{C}\!\to\!\mathcal{C}^{\prime} be its encoder. A programmatic generator GθG_{\theta} emits a symbolic program ρ\rho drawn from a graphics language or domain-specific language ℒ\mathcal{L}, which a deterministic executor RR evaluates into a concrete scene 𝐬^\hat{\mathbf{s}} (a raster image, vector graphic, UI specification, or 3D shape):

ρ=Gθ⁢(κ⁢(𝐜)),𝐬^=R⁢(ρ),ρ∈ℒ.\rho=G_{\theta}\big{(}\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{s}}=R(\rho)% ,\qquad\rho\in\mathcal{L}. (8.84)

This formulation inherits the conditional-sampler abstraction of Eq. (8.2) but replaces its learned decoder DD (Eq. (8.1)) over a continuous latent space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} with an interpretable, discrete program ρ\rho and an exact, non-learned renderer RR. The neural generators of §8 are recovered as the limiting case in which RR is itself a neural renderer and ρ\rho a continuous latent, whereas the symbolic case constrains ρ\rho to be a human-readable executable artifact. Two properties follow directly: errors are localizable to specific program statements, and structural constraints can be enforced or verified deterministically on ρ\rho before rendering.

8.7.2 Methodology

Figure 8.25 schematizes the three paradigm families that instantiate Eq. (8.84), contrasting how each obtains the program ρ\rho before the shared deterministic renderer RR executes it.

Rule- and Grammar-based Procedural Generation.

The earliest line of work, procedural content generation (PCG) [parish2001procedural] in computer graphics and game development, synthesizes scenes such as dungeon maps, terrains, architectural plans, or UI layouts from hand-crafted rules or parameterized procedural programs. Classical formalisms instantiate GθG_{\theta} as a fixed production system rather than a learned model. The Lindenmayer system (L-system) [lindenmayer1968mathematical], originally developed to model biological growth, employs parallel rewriting rules to simulate natural growth processes and fractal patterns, making it ideal for self-similar structures such as vegetation and complex terrain. Formally, the program evolves by repeated parallel application of a production set Π\Pi to an axiom ω\omega,

ρ0=ω,ρt+1=Π⁢(ρt),𝐬^=R⁢(ρT),\rho_{0}=\omega,\qquad\rho_{t+1}=\Pi(\rho_{t}),\qquad\hat{\mathbf{s}}=R(\rho_{% T}), (8.85)

where the generated symbolic string is not the geometry itself but a sequence of Turtle Graphics commands that the interpreter RR parses to draw the final shape in 2D or 3D space. Shape grammars, introduced by stiny1980introduction, provide another influential symbolic mechanism by defining geometric primitives and rewrite rules for composing architectural or engineered shapes. These early paradigms demonstrated a fundamental insight: spatial structures can be synthesized by executing symbolic generative rules, rather than by directly predicting raw geometry.

Symbolic Graphics Programs and Domain-Specific Languages.

Symbolic graphics programs (SGPs) encode spatial layouts and geometric configurations as formal programs that execute deterministically into images, vector graphics, UI designs, or 3D shapes, bridging abstract scene intent and concrete visual realization. Common languages such as SVG [bing2025learning], TikZ/LaTeX [ellis2018learning], and HTML/CSS [chen2025designcoder] already carry rich symbolic layout specifications in real-world use. In parallel, researchers have developed domain-specific languages (DSLs) tailored for fine-grained spatial and visual synthesis. Examples include hierarchical GUI-code generators [zhu2018automatic] that translate visual structures into programmatic UI specifications, and ShapeAssembly [jones2020shapeassembly], a 3D assembly language in which objects are represented as executable programs describing part composition, symmetry, and connectivity. Such DSLs make the advantages of explicit symbolic control concrete: precise geometry, modular design, verifiable constraints, and systematic compositionality.

Neuro-symbolic and Language-to-Program Synthesis.

A more recent direction couples symbolic programs with learned models, so that GθG_{\theta} becomes a trained synthesizer rather than a fixed rule set. The Scene Language [zhang2025scenelanguage] unifies neural and symbolic components: a program specifying relational and hierarchical layout structure, natural-language labels summarizing entity semantics, and learned embeddings capturing visual identity. Executable structure, rather than raw geometry, thus becomes a primary representational layer for scenes. Large language models [brown2020language, achiam2023gpt] have accelerated the move toward language-to-program spatial generation: instead of predicting images or layouts directly, LLM-based systems act as symbolic planners that synthesize the program by approximately maximizing its conditional likelihood,

ρ⋆=arg⁢maxρ∈ℒ⁡pθ⁢(ρ∣κ⁢(𝐜)),\rho^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\rho\in\mathcal{L}}\,p_{\theta}\big{(}% \rho\mid\kappa(\mathbf{c})\big{)}, (8.86)

mapping natural-language descriptions to executable layout programs [aguina2024open, hsu2025programs, yang2024holodeck]. These programs then guide downstream renderers to produce UI designs, graphic layouts, architectural plans, or 3D scenes with precise structural fidelity, and users can edit or refine the underlying program with fine-grained control.

The three families differ along two cross-cutting axes. The first is the representation of ρ\rho: a parallel string-rewriting system (grammar-based generation), an executable program in a general-purpose or domain-specific graphics language (SGPs and DSLs), or a hybrid structure that interleaves code, language, and learned embeddings (neuro-symbolic synthesis). The second is the inference procedure that produces ρ\rho: hand-authored production rules, human-written or template-instantiated programs, or learned program synthesis and LLM-based planning. Across all three, the target modality (2D raster, vector graphics, UI, or 3D) is determined solely by the renderer RR, which keeps the symbolic and rendering concerns cleanly separated.

8.7.3 Benchmarks

Evaluation in this area differs from the distributional metrics of §8 because the immediate output is a program, not an image, so quality is assessed along several complementary axes. Program validity measures whether the emitted ρ\rho parses and executes without error in its target language, a prerequisite that purely neural generators do not face. Rendered-output fidelity then compares the executed scene R⁢(ρ)R(\rho) against a reference, using pixel- or perceptual-level similarity for raster and vector targets and geometric agreement for 3D shapes. Constraint satisfaction checks whether explicitly specified spatial relations, counts, alignments, or symmetries hold in the rendered result, a property that symbolic methods are designed to guarantee. Controllability and editability assess how reliably localized edits to ρ\rho produce the intended localized changes in the scene without unintended global drift. Concretely, these axes are exercised across vector-graphics and SVG synthesis [bing2025learning], UI and GUI code generation [zhu2018automatic, chen2025designcoder], 3D program induction over part-structured shapes [jones2020shapeassembly], evaluated against part-hierarchy benchmarks such as PartNet [mo2019partnet], and full scene-program synthesis [zhang2025scenelanguage, yang2024holodeck], where the executable program serves simultaneously as the prediction and as the verifiable ground for measurement.

8.7.4 Challenges and Trends

The field has moved from entirely hand-authored rules toward neuro-symbolic integration with large models, driven by the demand for generators that are more controllable and interpretable than end-to-end neural methods.

Generalization. Automatically synthesized programs still struggle with novel constraints and complex semantic specifications [mao2025neurosymbolicconcepts]. Program synthesis has to infer the structural logic of a scene rather than memorize surface patterns if the generator is to extrapolate to compositions and constraint combinations absent from training.

Efficiency and differentiability. Neuro-symbolic programs that are both efficient and fully differentiable [guo2023efficientsymbolicpolicy] would let a rendering-level loss propagate back through the program, so that the whole pipeline, from symbolic planning to neural rendering, could be trained and fine-tuned end to end.

Embodied interaction. Procedurally synthesized interactive environments already supply large-scale embodied worlds [kolve2017ai2thor, procthor, wang2024pipeline], and the next step is for agents to generate or validate symbolic scene structure through active exploration rather than from static datasets alone, yielding symbolic representations of physical spaces that can be checked against what the agent observes.

8.8 Summary and Outlook

This chapter has surveyed spatial reconstruction and generation across seven subfields that, taken together, span an axis of increasing output structure and dimensionality: 2D images (§8.1), 3D objects and scenes (§8.2), video (§8.3), embodied motion (§8.4), 4D space-time content (§8.5), world models (§8.6), and interpretable symbolic programs (§8.7). Despite their different output domains, the subfields are unified by a single conditional-generation backbone, established in §8.1.1: an encoder κ\kappa maps a condition 𝐜\mathbf{c} into a latent code, a generator GθG_{\theta} samples structure from that code, and a decoder or renderer turns the sampled structure into a concrete artifact (Eq. (8.1), Eq. (8.2)). What distinguishes the subfields is not this backbone but the output space and the decoder that closes it: a pixel decoder for images, a volumetric or splatting renderer for 3D, a spatio-temporal decoder for video, a kinematic sampler for motion, a time-indexed 3D representation for 4D, a state-transition predictor for world models, and an exact, non-learned program executor for symbolic generation. Table 8.14 consolidates this view.

A shared backbone, specialized by output space. The progression from §8.1 to §8.7 is best read not as seven disjoint problems but as one generative abstraction instantiated against progressively richer codomains, and each section casts its own subtasks as conditional specializations of that common sampler. The symbolic case (§8.7) is the limiting instance in which the decoder degenerates to an exact program executor, trading the expressiveness of a learned renderer for interpretability and verifiable control.

The 2D prior as a reusable engine. The image generators of §8.1 recur throughout the chapter not as terminal systems but as priors to be distilled or lifted: 3D synthesis distills frozen 2D diffusion through score distillation and multi-view consistency (§8.2), video models inflate text-to-image backbones along the temporal axis (§8.3), and 4D pipelines compose both (§8.5). A single advance in the 2D substrate therefore propagates outward across every higher-dimensional subfield, which concentrates research leverage but also propagates the substrate’s failure modes.

Physical plausibility and fragmented evaluation. Across subfields, the recurring failure mode is not low visual fidelity but violated physics and geometry, manifest as multi-view inconsistency in 3D, temporal drift and flicker in video, foot-skating and interpenetration in motion, and dynamic implausibility in 4D. Evaluation remains correspondingly fragmented: each subfield has evolved its own metric tuples, and all are migrating toward learned and vision-language-model judges as scalar similarity scores prove insufficient for spatially structured output. A unified, physically grounded evaluation protocol that spans these subfields remains an open goal.

Outlook. These observations point toward convergence rather than further fragmentation. World modeling (§8.6) already acts as a conceptual capstone that absorbs reconstruction, generation, and dynamics into a single predictive substrate, while programmatic and symbolic generation (§8.7) supplies the controllability and interpretability that purely neural pipelines lack; their integration, neural generators steered and verified by symbolic structure, is a natural trajectory for the field. The capabilities surveyed here also form the generative substrate for the applications of Part IV, where embodied agents, digital twins, and interactive environments consume generated spatial content rather than producing it for its own sake.

Part IV Applications

The preceding parts built spatial intelligence as a set of capabilities; this part asks what those capabilities are worth once they leave the laboratory. Applications are not a victory lap over Parts II and III but a stress test: a method that reconstructs a scene cleanly on a benchmark must, in the field, do so under a latency budget, a safety constraint, a sensor that fails, or a cost of error measured in more than accuracy. What a domain demands of spatial intelligence, and what it reveals about the gaps that remain, is visible only at deployment.

This part is therefore organized by domain rather than by capability, because the interesting content lives in the delta each domain adds over a general treatment. The tour runs from embodied agents that must act in the physical world, through the extended-reality systems that render it back to a user in real time, to the geo-spatial and scientific settings that model it at the scale of planets and of cells, to the assistants that inhabit a person’s own environment, and out into a long tail of further fields. Each stresses spatial intelligence along a different axis: real-time action, on-device perception, metric fidelity, human-centered interaction. Read together, they make the case that spatial intelligence is not one more application but a horizontal foundation on which applications across science, industry, and daily life are increasingly built.

Chapter 9 Spatial Intelligence for Embodied Systems

Embodied systems are the arena in which spatial intelligence stops being a matter of analysis and becomes a matter of consequence. An embodied agent does not merely describe a scene; it occupies one, and every perception it forms and every inference it draws is ultimately answerable to an action it must take in the physical world, under real time budgets, sensor noise, and the cost of being wrong. This chapter turns from the capabilities of the previous part to their deployment, examining how perception, reasoning, and generation are brought to bear inside agents that move, manipulate, and assist.

What makes this more than a restatement is that embodiment changes the problem. The same spatial competence looks different in a manipulator closing a grasp, a car threading traffic, a wearable inferring its user’s intent, a drone holding position in wind, or a fleet of robots coordinating on a warehouse floor: each fixes its own sensors, latencies, safety margins, and notion of success. The chapter is organized by these domains rather than by capability, because the interesting content lives in the domain-specific delta, what each setting demands of spatial intelligence that a general treatment does not reveal.

9.1 Robotic Manipulation

9.1.1 Introduction

Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly, driven by strides in perception, learning, and control. Yet a significant gap remains between competent laboratory systems and robust, general-purpose robots capable of operating in unstructured settings. A central bottleneck is that manipulation is fundamentally spatial: every decision (where to reach, how to establish contact, how to route a trajectory through clutter, or how to use a tool) hinges on perceiving, representing, and reasoning about three-dimensional structure under uncertainty. Manipulation is thus a direct test of the spatial intelligence developed throughout Parts I–III: it demands that systems go beyond semantic recognition to build actionable 3D world models, ground tasks in geometric constraints, predict contact outcomes, and plan behaviors that respect the physical laws of the environment. The perception, reasoning, and generation capabilities that such systems presuppose are surveyed in Chapter 6, Chapter 7, and Chapter 8; this section focuses not on re-deriving those capabilities but on how they are composed, grounded, and constrained for physical manipulation.

9.1.2 System Overview

A manipulation system maps raw multimodal observations and a task instruction into executable, constraint-satisfying actions, and this section organizes that mapping into four strategic pivots, each a fundamental shift in how systems bridge perception and physical action. (i) Grounding Action in Spatial Anchors moves beyond raw pixels to vision priors and sparse spatial tokens (keypoints, dense correspondences) that stay consistent across viewpoints and instances; (ii) Inferring Functional Action Possibilities shifts from object classification to extracting affordances and tool-use capabilities, bridging perception with contact-rich execution; (iii) Encoding Spatial Reasoning in Generalist Models transitions from single-task policies to foundation models (VLMs/VLAs) that integrate explicit 3D representations and reasoning traces for cross-embodiment generalization; and (iv) Satisfying Geometric and Logical Constraints advances from simple trajectory generation to constrained optimization and neuro-symbolic planning (TAMP), ensuring actions respect strict safety limits and long-horizon logical structure. The four pivots are complementary and mutually reinforcing rather than strictly sequential: anchors and affordances structure the perceptual input, generalist models supply broad priors, and constraint-based planners check feasibility under the modeled geometric, physical, and logical assumptions. Figure 9.1 situates them as complementary capabilities within a closed-loop perception-to-action system, and the remainder of this section treats them in this order.

9.1.3 Pivotal Task-1: Grounding Action in Spatial Anchors

This pivot reframes visuomotor learning from operating over raw pixels to reasoning through explicit spatial anchors (sparse semantic keypoints, dense correspondences, point tracks, or affordance-based contact points) that compress high-dimensional observations into spatial tokens tied to object- or task-centric reference frames and designed to remain comparatively stable across viewpoint, instance, and clutter. As Figure 9.2 indicates, the approach follows a three-step logic: large-scale vision priors first produce the anchors, policies are then conditioned on them, and the payoff is read off as a generalization gap between seen and unseen instances.

The dominant methodology leverages large-scale vision priors to generate, propagate, or retrieve these anchors, then trains standard visuomotor learners on the resulting structured inputs. A common strategy prescribes anchor points in a few reference frames and propagates them across large datasets via off-the-shelf correspondence models: P3-PO [levy2024p3poprescriptivepointpriors] propagates manually specified keypoints using dense features from DINO [dino], DINOv2 [dinov2], or diffusion-based representations [tang2023emergentcorrespondenceimagediffusion, zhao2025high, zhang2023talefeaturesstablediffusion] (these visual representations are surveyed in Chapter 4). Relatedly, Robo-ABC [ju2024roboabcaffordancegeneralizationcategories] retrieves affordance contact points from an external memory and transfers them to novel scenes via dense semantic correspondence, while Track2Act [bharadhwaj2024track2act] learns long-term point tracks from Internet-scale video and uses them to infer object-centric transformations that serve as open-loop manipulation plans. Once anchors are obtained, policy learning conditions action prediction directly on them, through keypoint-conditioned behavior cloning (KALM [fang2024keypointabstractionusinglarge]), diffusion policies in object-relative frames (AffordDP [wu2025afforddpgeneralizablediffusionpolicy]), and shared human–robot 3D keypoint spaces (Point Policy [haldar2025pointpolicyunifyingobservations]). Across these variants, anchoring actions to spatial structure reduces perceptual ambiguity and improves robustness under distribution shift.
