Because the central claim is out-of-distribution generalization, evaluation pairs high-fidelity simulation with real-robot deployment rather than relying on either alone. In simulation, affordance-centric methods such as AffordDP [wu2025afforddpgeneralizablediffusionpolicy] run on IsaacGym [makoviychuk2021isaac] over articulated objects from GAPartnet [geng2023gapartnet] whose functional parts (handles, knobs, levers) vary widely in geometry, while imitation suites such as Robomimic [robomimic2021] and RoboTwin [mu2024robotwin] isolate trajectory tracking and dual-arm coordination, with P3-PO [levy2024p3poprescriptivepointpriors] using them for controlled spatial-anchoring ablations. Real-world suites then stress in-the-wild generalization on articulated (drawers, microwaves), deformable (towel folding), and tool-use (sweeping) tasks, as in Point Policy [haldar2025pointpolicyunifyingobservations] and Track2Act [bharadhwaj2024track2act], and a zero-shot cross-category protocol (train on one knife, test on spatulas or novel knives) is formalized by Robo-ABC [ju2024roboabcaffordancegeneralizationcategories] to measure how well retrieved anchors transfer without extra supervision. Performance is reported as Task Success Rate and, to isolate the contribution of anchoring, a Generalization Gap between seen and unseen instances. Spatially grounded policies outperform pixel baselines under shift in these studies: P3-PO reports large gains on cluttered, novel-object scenes [levy2024p3poprescriptivepointpriors], and Robo-ABC improves both affordance-retrieval accuracy and real-robot success without heavy robot-data collection, binding demonstrations to reusable spatial structure more effectively than classic one-shot imitation [duan2017oneshotimitationlearning].

9.1.4 Pivotal Task-2: Inferring Functional Action Possibilities

This pivot shifts from general object recognition to extracting object affordances, i.e., , the specific action possibilities implied by an object’s functional properties, and uses them as the intermediate representation that bridges raw perception and contact-rich execution. Whereas Pivotal Task-1 treats contact points as viewpoint-stable anchors for conditioning a policy, affordances here are studied as functional possibilities that specify what action an object supports. As Figure 9.3 shows, the thread runs from how affordances are represented, through the actions they drive (grasping, placement, tool use), to outcome-oriented benchmarks that score achieved function rather than imitated trajectory.

To capture functional properties beyond whole-object categorization, prior work builds object-centric representations (part-level segmentation [do2018affordancenet], dense visual descriptors [florencemanuelli2018dense], and keypoint-based encodings [manuelli2019kpam, qin2020keto, mo2021where2act]) that directly support action synthesis, and more recent vision–language models predict spatial affordance points directly from open-vocabulary prompts (RoboPoint [yuan2024robopoint], MOKA [liu2024moka]). These representations drive learning-based 6-DoF grasping [sundermeyer2021contact, zhao2025high, jiang2021synergies, zhao2024efficient, yuan2023m2t2, deshpande2025graspmolmo] and stable object placement [zeng2020transporter, liu2022structformer, zhao2025towards, yuan2023m2t2, zhao2025anyplace] by grounding generation in functional structure rather than raw geometry, and a specialized strand further models tool–behavior relationships, either learning tool–action–effect pairs [stoytchev2008learning] or predicting specific affordances such as pulling [tikhanoff2013exploring], so as to infer end-effector poses that achieve the intended functional outcome.

Benchmarks for affordance methods emphasize understanding object functionality over geometric matching: the property under test is functional generalization, not trajectory imitation. For grasping, YCB-based real-world evaluations [Calli2015YCB], GraspNet-1Billion [Fang2020GraspNet], and simulation suites such as Dex-Net [Mahler2017DexNet] score 6-DoF stability and contact validity across novel instances and viewpoints; placement benchmarks such as RLBench [james2020rlbench] and ManiSkill [mu2021maniskill] test stable stacking and insertion in cluttered, articulated scenes, and M2T2 [yuan2023m2t2] explicitly evaluates valid placement poses conditioned on object geometry and scene context. For articulated objects and tools, Where2Act [mo2021where2act] and PartNet-Mobility [xiang2020sapien] score the prediction of actionable parts and interaction parameters for pulling, pushing, and rotating, while tool-use tasks judge whether the inferred end-effector pose produces the intended causal effect (drawing, hooking, pulling) rather than reproducing a specific trajectory. Evaluation therefore centers on outcome-oriented success: stable grasps that lift and hold unseen objects under pose, scale, and appearance variation; placement success, pose accuracy, and post-release stability under clutter and occlusion; and, for articulated and tool interactions, whether the predicted parameters yield the desired functional result.

9.1.5 Pivotal Task-3: Encoding Spatial Reasoning in Generalist Models

This pivot moves from specialized, single-task policies toward generalist robotic foundation models. Existing Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models such as RT-2 [zitkovich2023rt2] and OpenVLA [kim2024openvla] show strong semantic understanding but often lack the spatial common sense needed for precise manipulation or robust generalization to novel viewpoints, so the central challenge is to strengthen spatial grounding during pre-training, enabling explicit reasoning about 3D geometry and generalization across environments and embodiments [chen2024spatialvlm]. The general foundation-model and spatial-reasoning machinery these policies inherit is treated in Chapter 7; here we examine only its manipulation-specific adaptation, which Figure 9.4 groups into three families: explicit 3D representations, view-invariant representations, and grounded reasoning traces.

The first family builds explicit 3D representations: models such as 3D-LLM [hong20233d] and 3D-VLA [zhen20243d] bridge point clouds and large language models, with 3D-VLA adding a 3D generative pre-training objective that lets the model reason about action outcomes in a consistent geometric space, effectively “imagining” future states. The second groups view canonicalization and spatial action encoding as distinct mechanisms: OG-VLA [singh2025og] projects multi-view observations into a point cloud and re-renders canonical orthographic views to reduce sensitivity to camera placement, while SpatialVLA [qu2025spatialvla] uses Ego3D position encoding for observations and Adaptive Action Grids to discretize spatial movement actions; adapting to new setups can involve re-discretizing the grids. The third injects spatial reasoning through grounded reasoning traces: “thinking” models such as Emma-X [sun2024emma], MolmoAct series [lee2025molmoact, fang2026molmoact2], closely related to TraceVLA [zheng2024tracevla], replace direct pixel-to-action regression with intermediate, grounded outputs (2D motion trajectories or relative depth maps) that explicitly condition the final action prediction.

These approaches are evaluated under method-specific zero-shot and adaptation protocols across embodiments, viewpoints, and environments, with key metrics including multimodal goal-generation quality, robustness to extrinsic camera perturbations, and skill transfer across robot morphologies such as from a fixed-base Franka arm to a mobile manipulator [team2024octo]. The reported gains point the same way: canonical orthographic views keep grounding consistent under viewpoint change (OG-VLA), spatially aligned action grids share 3D structure across setups through discretized movement (SpatialVLA), and intermediate visual or depth-aware reasoning traces act as a regularizer on action prediction (Emma-X, MolmoAct).

9.1.6 Pivotal Task-4: Satisfying Geometric and Logical Constraints

This pivot moves planning from heuristic trajectory generation toward formal constrained optimization that enforces geometric feasibility, fundamental physical laws (non-penetration, friction cones, force limits), and high-level logical task structure. By casting manipulation as multi-objective optimization, these methods seek to satisfy modeled hard constraints while optimizing soft task objectives, spanning both high-frequency control and long-horizon decision-making. Figure 9.5 organizes the thread along three fronts (symbolic–geometric planning, contact and trajectory optimization, and constraint-aware generative planning) before synthesizing the roles constraints play in learning-based systems.

Methodological progress has moved from purely symbolic planners toward neuro-symbolic, learning-augmented optimization frameworks that unify discrete logic with continuous physics. Classical Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and Logic-Geometric Programming (LGP) [toussaint2015lgp] provide the foundation by jointly reasoning over symbolic task structure and geometric feasibility, and recent systems augment them with Large Language Models and Vision-Language Models for scalability in open-ended domains; for example, VIZ-COAST [yan2025vizcoast] uses the spatial reasoning of VLMs to predict refinement failures before expensive geometric optimization, substantially reducing search complexity on long-horizon problems. At the level of physical interaction, contact-implicit optimization discovers contact schedules without explicit mode enumeration but is traditionally too slow for real-time control; GPU-parallelized systems such as SPaSM [chen2025spasm] compile constraint evaluation and gradient computation into CUDA kernels, accelerating joint optimization of object placements and robot trajectories. Beyond deterministic constraints, learning-based and generative models capture uncertainty and complex structure: differentiable physics engines [freeman2021brax] let gradients flow through physical interactions, stochastic implicit neural signed distance functions [quintero2024stochastic] model geometric uncertainty directly within the planning manifold, and diffusion-based planners such as JM2D [jung2025joint] couple model-free diffusion with model-based constraint optimization during sampling, rather than relying only on a sequential plan-then-filter interface.

Such systems are benchmarked on multi-stage re-grasping under uncertainty, forceful tool use, and tight-tolerance sequential interaction, since what they promise is reliability over long, contact-rich horizons; suites such as the Functional Manipulation Benchmark (FMB) [fmb2023] scoring not only task completion but constraint satisfaction under partial observability, external disturbance, and compounding execution error. In these systems constrained optimization plays three roles: it acts as a teacher, generating physically valid trajectories that supervise imitation and offline reinforcement learning; as a safety shield, where model-based projections map unconstrained neural or diffusion policy outputs onto constraint-satisfying sets at execution time [römer2025diffusionpredictivecontrolconstraints]; and as a structural prior that prunes physically infeasible regions of the action space and curbs compounding error in long-horizon tasks. Together these roles keep learned and generative planners grounded in geometric and physical reality, reducing physically implausible outputs and supporting interpretable, feasible plans under the modeled assumptions; real-world execution still depends on state estimation, model accuracy, solver convergence, and disturbance handling.

Table 9.1 consolidates the principal benchmarks, representative methods, and headline evaluation focus across the four pivots, situating the spatially grounded methods surveyed above within a common evaluation landscape.

9.1.7 Established Tools and Systems

Progress in spatially grounded manipulation has been inseparable from a maturing ecosystem of simulators, open software stacks, shared datasets, and, increasingly, commercial robot platforms that serve as common development and deployment substrates.

Simulation and physics engines. GPU-parallel engines such as NVIDIA IsaacGym and the newer Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab11 1 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim [makoviychuk2021isaac], articulated-object simulators such as SAPIEN [xiang2020sapien] (with its PartNet-Mobility assets), and general-purpose physics engines including MuJoCo [todorov2012mujoco], PyBullet22 2 https://pybullet.org, and the recent Genesis33 3 https://github.com/Genesis-Embodied-AI/Genesis provide high-throughput, contact-rich environments, while ManiSkill [mu2021maniskill], RLBench [james2020rlbench], Robomimic [robomimic2021], and RoboTwin [mu2024robotwin] package standardized task suites, demonstrations, and evaluation protocols that have become de facto testbeds for imitation and policy learning.

Open software stacks and datasets. On the software side, the Robot Operating System (ROS 2) with the MoveIt motion-planning framework44 4 https://moveit.ai remains the de facto middleware for real-robot integration, and Hugging Face’s LeRobot55 5 https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot packages datasets, pretrained policies, and training pipelines for low-cost reproduction. Large cross-embodiment efforts such as Open X-Embodiment66 6 https://robotics-transformer-x.github.io, which aggregates demonstrations and the RT-X policies across dozens of robot platforms, together with open generalist checkpoints such as Octo [team2024octo] and OpenVLA [kim2024openvla] and NVIDIA’s GR00T humanoid foundation models77 7 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/gr00t, expose pretrained weights and fine-tuning interfaces that lower the barrier to transferring foundation-model policies onto new morphologies.

Commercial and humanoid platforms. On the deployment side, a rapidly growing set of companies is moving spatially grounded manipulation out of the laboratory. Boston Dynamics88 8 https://bostondynamics.com (the electric Atlas and the Stretch warehouse robot), Tesla Optimus99 9 https://www.tesla.com/we-robot, Figure AI1010 10 https://www.figure.ai, 1X Technologies1111 11 https://www.1x.tech, Agility Robotics1212 12 https://agilityrobotics.com (the Digit humanoid, piloted in logistics), Physical Intelligence1313 13 https://www.physicalintelligence.company (the π0\pi_{0} generalist policy), and Sanctuary AI1414 14 https://sanctuary.ai each pair learned manipulation with humanoid or mobile-manipulator hardware, while firms such as Covariant1515 15 https://covariant.ai target warehouse pick-and-place at commercial scale. These platforms are the clearest evidence that the spatial-intelligence capabilities surveyed above are crossing from benchmark tasks into economically deployed systems.

Together these tools convert the representation and reasoning machinery of Chapter 7 into reproducible, physically grounded manipulation pipelines; their principal limitation remains the fidelity gap between simulated and real contact dynamics, which the following discussion revisits.

9.1.8 Challenges

Despite rapid progress across all four pivots, bringing spatial intelligence to robust, general-purpose manipulation remains bounded by a set of intertwined difficulties that cut across perception, policy, and planning. They cluster into four threads: keeping a persistent and calibrated internal model of the scene; closing the loop between contact physics and active sensing; transferring skills across embodiments while sourcing the data to do so; and meeting the reliability budget of a deployed system.

Persistent, calibrated world models. The first requirement is a persistent 3D belief: an actionable, temporally consistent world model that survives heavy occlusion, articulation, deformation, and sensor drift, and that is maintained at control rates rather than reconstructed from scratch each frame. Persistence alone is not enough if the model cannot say how much it trusts itself. Calibrated uncertainty asks that distributional beliefs over geometry, contact state, friction, and articulation propagate through perception, policy, and planner, so that a decision reflects confidence rather than a bare point prediction and a low-confidence grasp can trigger caution instead of failure.

Contact modeling, sensing, and active perception. Manipulation is ultimately about contact, yet most spatial models still reason about collision-free geometry rather than the physics of touch. Progress on contact modeling and sensing hinges on tightly integrating vision with force and tactile feedback to reason about stick–slip, compliance, and incipient failure. Because contact is often unobservable until it happens, this couples naturally to information-seeking control: interleaving manipulation with active perception and probing (touch-to-disambiguate, look-while-acting) inside tractable belief-space planners. And because contact is precisely where simulators diverge from reality, sim-to-real for contact stays open, demanding better material, friction, and compliance models together with fast system identification for on-robot adaptation.

Cross-embodiment transfer and data at scale. Skills learned on one platform rarely move cleanly to another. Cross-embodiment and cross-scene transfer requires aligning action spaces and spatial tokens across grippers, cameras, and environments without hand-tuned frames or retraining. Sustaining that transfer is a data problem as much as an algorithmic one: data and evaluation at scale calls for “long-tail” data engines that cover rare geometries, materials, and tools with counterfactual and safety labels, and for benchmarks that measure calibration, persistence, recovery, and long-horizon competence rather than success rate alone.

Systems reliability. Finally, a deployed manipulator must hold together as a system: meeting latency budgets, absorbing calibration drift, detecting out-of-distribution geometry, and enabling safe fallback and continual learning without catastrophic forgetting. Closing these gaps will require tighter couplings among 3D world models, affordance predictors, language-grounded objectives, and constraint-aware planners, so that spatial representations are not only expressive but actionable, calibrated, and safe in unstructured settings.

9.2 Autonomous Driving

9.2.1 Introduction

Autonomous driving sits at the intersection of spatial intelligence, transportation engineering, and human–machine interaction, and it is one of the most demanding real-world testbeds for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part III. A self-driving vehicle must continuously close a perceive–localize–decide–act loop: it has to recognize and track the surrounding traffic scene, estimate its own pose within a metric map, reason about how nearby agents will move, and commit to safe control actions, all under tight latency and safety budgets. Advances in deep learning, multi-sensor fusion, and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication have steadily pushed the boundaries of what vehicles can perceive, predict, and decide, while fundamental questions around robustness, trust, ethics, and regulation remain open. Perception and reasoning themselves are treated in Chapter 6 and Chapter 7; what is specific to driving is that each capability must hold up at speed, in all weather, and with lives at stake.

Figure 9.6 summarizes the SAE J3016 automation levels that frame this domain. The SAE J3016 standard 1616 16 https://www.sae.org/news/2019/01/sae-updates-j3016-automated-driving-graphic provides a widely adopted framework for defining automation levels, with most current production systems still operating at Level 2. Progress toward higher levels, especially full Level 5 autonomy, faces major technical [YurtseverLCT20], ethical [StahlTM16], and financial [fisher2020governmental] challenges.

Deep learning has driven most of this progress, from Transformers [WangLLLXLCLZH22] and graph networks [ZhangFWH22] that model multi-agent interaction to lifelong learning for open-world adaptation [ZhuBZZW24], but its opacity raises safety concerns compounded by sensor noise and the limited reach of vehicle-to-vehicle communication, and reaching Levels 4 and 5 depends as much on redundant hardware, large-scale data pipelines, and verifiable safety assurance as on model architecture.

9.2.2 System Overview

Modern self-driving stacks realize the perceive–localize–decide–act loop as a modular pipeline, sketched in Figure 9.7. A front-end perception module converts raw, multi-modal sensor streams (camera, LiDAR, radar) into a structured model of the scene: what objects are present, where the drivable surface and lane geometry lie, and which agents are most safety-critical. A localization and mapping module places the ego-vehicle within a metric, typically HD-map-anchored, representation of that scene, so that perception outputs can be expressed in a stable world frame. A decision and control module then predicts how the scene will evolve and selects the steering, acceleration, and braking commands that are sent to the actuators and fed back into the environment, closing the loop. Each of the three stages is a distinct spatial-intelligence problem with its own representations, benchmarks, and failure modes, and they are the pivotal tasks below, in pipeline order.

9.2.3 Pivotal Task-1: Perception and Detection

Perception is the front-end of the pipeline: it turns raw camera, LiDAR, and radar streams into a structured, layered model of the scene that every downstream module consumes, reusing the detection, segmentation, and 3D scene-understanding machinery of Chapter 6 but specializing it to the driving Operational Design Domain (ODD). It is best read as a set of complementary structured representations, sketched in Figure 9.8: object detection localizes traffic participants, semantic and occupancy prediction labels the surrounding space, lane detection recovers the road geometry that constrains motion, and pedestrian recognition isolates the most safety-critical agents.

The base layer is object detection, which identifies and localizes obstacles and is the most direct determinant of collision safety [FengHWD22]. Its central practical constraint is the ODD: environmental factors such as poor weather degrade sensor visibility and model accuracy [KoopmanF19], so recent work formalizes and iteratively validates the ODD through quantifiable environmental models and scenario catalogues, trusting a detector only within conditions it has demonstrably handled, though the absence of a standardized ODD specification still makes cross-system safety claims hard to compare. Robustness to adverse weather is therefore a first-class concern [zhang2023perception, TahirZACE24, HnewaR21]: rain, snow, fog, and glare corrupt LiDAR, radar, and camera signals alike, and because driving datasets under-represent these conditions, models trained on fair-weather data generalize poorly. Responses range from dedicated robust pipelines, such as multi-stage visibility enhancement coupled with deep CNN tracking [HassaballahKMM21], to new sensing hardware, e.g., , frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) LiDAR and high-dynamic-range cameras that recover usable signal in glare at higher cost. Moving from the image plane into metric space, 3D object detection localizes and tracks objects in the vehicle’s surroundings [LiWLXSLQD22], where the bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representation has become dominant because it yields a unified top-down map well suited to planning. BEVFormer [YangCTTZZHLQLZD23] fuses multi-camera and temporal cues with spatiotemporal transformers to approach LiDAR-level accuracy on nuScenes, while Fast-BEV [LiHCCLSLXSOS24] and SparseBEV [LiuTLWW23] trade marginal accuracy for the lightweight, sparse, query-based computation needed for real-time on-vehicle deployment, together tracing the field’s balancing of accuracy, latency, and deployability.

Detections tell the planner where objects are but not which space is free; that dense layer is supplied by semantic segmentation and its 3D extension, occupancy prediction [ZhouBWN20, NestiRNBB22]. The progression runs from 2D pixel labeling with FCN [long2015fcn] and DeepLab [chen2017deeplabv2] to volumetric reasoning: the Tri-Perspective View [HuangZZ0L23] lifts RGB into a 3D representation rivalling LiDAR, SurroundOcc [WeiZZZZL23] uses multi-camera 2D–3D attention to capture arbitrary shapes, and occupancy world models such as OccWorld [zheng2024occworld] extend this to forecasting how the 3D scene evolves, moving beyond the limits of bounding boxes. Because these dense predictors are data-hungry and domain-sensitive, robustness techniques such as the SePiCo pixel-contrast framework [XieLLLHW23] and GAN-based synthetic data [AbdollahiPSMA21] are used to survive scene variability, occlusion, and weather shift. On top of the free-space layer, lane detection recovers the road geometry that defines the lateral reference for lane-keeping and planning; early CNN- and YOLO-style detectors trace markings well in clear conditions but are brittle on curved, worn, or occluded lanes, motivating successors that lift lanes into 3D and use attention over global context to infer occluded segments. Finally, pedestrian recognition focuses on vulnerable road users whose behavior can be difficult to predict: CNN-, YOLO-, and SSD-based detectors deliver the required precision and latency, color–thermal fusion handles low-light scenes, and spatial–temporal models couple detection with motion prediction to anticipate crossing behavior.

Across all four layers, perception is benchmarked on large-scale driving datasets, KITTI [KITTI-GeigerLU12], the Waymo Open Dataset [WaymoOpen-SunKDCPTGZCCVHN20], and nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes] for 2D/3D detection, Cityscapes [cordts2016cityscapes] and BDD100K [yu2020bdd100k] for segmentation, dedicated lane benchmarks for lane detection, and CityPersons [zhang2017citypersons] for pedestrians, and scored with mean Average Precision (mAP) and the nuScenes Detection Score (NDS), mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU), and F1/accuracy, respectively (Table 9.2). Increasingly these metrics are reported on adverse-weather and out-of-distribution splits, precisely to measure behavior within and beyond the declared ODD.

9.2.4 Pivotal Task-2: Localization and Mapping

If perception answers what is around the vehicle, localization and mapping answer where the vehicle is and what the persistent structure of the world is. The two are tightly coupled: a metric, HD-map-anchored pose lets perception outputs be expressed in a stable world frame that planning can rely on, and the map itself is built and maintained from the same sensor streams. As Figure 9.9 shows, the problem decomposes into pose estimation against a known map (localization), the construction of that map (3D mapping and reconstruction), and the joint solution of both when no map exists (SLAM), with multi-sensor fusion the common thread that holds accuracy together when any single modality degrades.

Localization has moved from GPS-dependent positioning to learned matching of live camera or LiDAR observations against a pre-built map, reaching centimeter-level accuracy even in GPS-denied urban canyons; semantic cues such as roads and buildings further let a vehicle re-localize in changed environments without full remapping. Because no single sensor is reliable across occlusion, weather, and GPS dropout, sensor-fusion localization is the dominant paradigm: probabilistic estimators (particle filters, Kalman filters, and NDT scan matching) reconcile GNSS, IMU, and LiDAR, while learned vision–radar fusion compensates for modality-specific weaknesses in rain, fog, and glare. The recurring bottlenecks here are cross-sensor spatial/temporal synchronization and fault tolerance, which motivate Bayesian uncertainty weighting and online-adaptive fusion that recalibrates as conditions change.

3D mapping and reconstruction supply the persistent representation that localization matches against, turning LiDAR and stereo streams into metric models; for the place-recognition and loop-closure that keep maps globally consistent, transformer descriptors such as SeqOT [ma2022seqot] match sequential LiDAR scans faster than the sensor frame rate, trained on richly annotated corpora such as ApolloScape [wang2019apolloscape]. The open problems are the cost of processing dense point clouds at city scale and the handling of occluded or incomplete returns, which favor incremental map updating over full re-mapping. When the map is unavailable, SLAM solves localization and mapping jointly, which is critical in GPS-denied corridors; modern driving-oriented vSLAM hybridizes classical geometry with learned features (for example, extending ORB-SLAM [mur2017orb] with learned features, semantic labels, and learned depth to favor stable landmarks) and recovers from drift through loop closure with bundle adjustment.

These capabilities are evaluated on KITTI Odometry [KITTI-GeigerLU12], Oxford RobotCar [Maddern2017RobotCar], and ApolloScape [wang2019apolloscape] for long-horizon SLAM and place recognition, on nuScenes [caesar2020nuscenes] and Waymo [WaymoOpen-SunKDCPTGZCCVHN20] for map-relative pose, and on Argoverse [Argoverse-ChangLSSBHW0LRH19] for the trajectory forecasting that localization feeds, e.g., , with the Motion Transformer [shi2022mtr] (Table 9.2). The standard metrics, i.e., , Absolute and Relative Pose Error (ATE/RPE), recall@NN for loop closure, and minADE/minFDE for forecasting, are reported under GPS-denied, adverse-weather, and sensor-degradation conditions to stress exactly the robustness the fusion machinery is built to provide.

9.2.5 Pivotal Task-3: Decision Making and Control

Decision making and control is the action end of the pipeline: it consumes the scene model from perception and the pose from localization, predicts how the scene will evolve, and commits to the steering, acceleration, and braking that close the loop, drawing on the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter 7. As Figure 9.10 indicates, two architectural philosophies dominate, differing in how much of the perceive-to-act mapping is learned end-to-end versus decomposed into interpretable modules, and they are increasingly converging.

The first philosophy is learning-based decision making, centered on (deep) reinforcement learning, which acquires driving policies through trial-and-error interaction and is well suited to the sequential, interactive nature of driving. Representative methods illustrate its design axes: the stochastic latent actor-critic (SLAC) [lee2020stochastic] learns compact latent states from high-dimensional images, PPO [schulman2017proximalpo] within a nonlinear control framework handles sharp turns and obstacle avoidance, and the DeepSet-Q architecture [huegle2019dynamic], building on permutation-invariant set encoders [zaheer2017deep], ingests a variable number of surrounding agents for high-level lane-change decisions. Hybrids with explicit planning, such as Monte Carlo tree search guided by DRL or scene-representation transformers that forecast neighbor intentions, improve sample efficiency and situational awareness in dense traffic. The binding difficulty is that safety-critical episodes are rare in logged data, which pushes the field toward high-fidelity simulation for rare-event coverage and toward encoding hard safety constraints directly in the policy rather than trusting the reward signal alone. The second philosophy, end-to-end decision making, learns the mapping from sensors to trajectory or control directly, removing hand-designed interfaces between modules. Early instances learned state-to-action policies with DDPG [lillicrap2015continuous] in simulators such as TORCS, and multi-task backbones such as HybridNets [vu2022hybridnets] share computation across detection and segmentation without yet closing the loop to control. Current systems are trained by imitation on large driving logs: TransFuser [chitta2023transfuser] fuses camera and LiDAR features with transformer attention and predicts waypoints for a closed-loop agent, and UniAD [hu2023uniad] chains tracking, mapping, motion forecasting, and occupancy prediction through query interfaces inside one network optimized for planning. Driving world models such as GAIA-1 [hu2023gaia] generate future multi-view scenes conditioned on ego actions, giving such policies a learned simulator for training and evaluation. Opacity is the price of end-to-end training: attribution methods such as layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) [bach2015pixel] support interpretation but do not by themselves establish safety or regulatory compliance, which is why hybrid designs keep inspectable scene or trajectory intermediates together with explicit constraint checks, whose guarantees extend only as far as the modeled constraints.

Closed-loop driving policies are evaluated chiefly in simulation, i.e., , the CARLA urban simulator [dosovitskiy2017carla] (NoCrash, Longest6), the nuPlan planning benchmark [caesar2021nuplan], and highway-interaction simulators built on HighD/INTERACTION (Table 9.2), because rare, safety-critical events cannot be exercised safely on public roads. The headline metrics are the CARLA Driving Score (route completion penalized by infractions), collision and intervention rates, and route completion, complemented by comfort proxies such as jerk and, for the open-loop forecasting sub-problem, minADE/minFDE.

9.2.6 Established Tools and Systems

The systems on the road today populate a deployment ladder whose rungs are the SAE levels of Figure 9.6, but what separates one rung from the next is rarely a single breakthrough in perception accuracy. It is, instead, two coupled engineering choices: how wide an Operational Design Domain (ODD) the system claims, and where legal responsibility for the driving task sits. Three tiers are in genuine production, i.e., , supervised Level 2 assistance, certified Level 3 “eyes-off” automation, and driverless Level 4 robotaxis, and, as the following progression shows, moving up the ladder consistently means adding sensing and compute redundancy while narrowing the domain in which the autonomy guarantee holds.

9.2.6.1 Large-scale Production ADAS (SAE Level 2 / 2+)

The defining property of Level 2 is that the system performs continuous lateral and longitudinal control, yet the human remains the legal driver and the immediate fallback; consequently, every Level 2 product is fundamentally an exercise in bounding the ODD and enforcing driver attention rather than in achieving autonomy, and the deployed systems differ mainly in how they strike that balance. One design philosophy gates hands-free operation to pre-validated, HD-mapped limited-access highways and polices it with in-cabin driver monitoring: GM Super Cruise1717 17 https://www.gm.com/innovation/autonomous-driving, Ford/Lincoln BlueCruise1818 18 https://www.lincoln.com/technology/bluecruise/, and BMW Driving Assistant Professional1919 19 https://www.bmwgroup.com/en/news/general/2023/driver-assistance-systems.html all keep the vehicle centered, regulate following distance, and offer assisted lane changes, but escalate alerts and disengage the moment attention drifts or the car leaves a supported segment; their reliability is a direct product of this deliberately narrow envelope. A second philosophy trades map dependence for scale: Tesla Autopilot2020 20 https://www.tesla.com/en_gb/support/autopilot and FSD (Supervised)2121 21 https://www.tesla.com/en_gb/fsd rely on a camera-first vision stack refined through fleet-wide over-the-air training, which extends assistance to a far broader and less-bounded set of scenarios but, lacking comparable geofencing, still demands constant supervision and degrades on poor markings, construction zones, and adverse weather. At the conservative end, Toyota Safety Sense declines hands-free operation altogether, functioning as an always-on crash-avoidance layer (automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping, and adaptive cruise) that intervenes only to prevent or mitigate collisions. Despite these differing emphases, the binding limitation is identical across all of them: a bounded ODD coupled with a mandatory human fallback, and it is precisely that fallback which the next tier begins to remove.

9.2.6.2 Certified “Eyes-off” Conditional Automation (SAE Level 3)

Level 3 is the first tier at which, inside a defined envelope, the driver may legally divert attention and the manufacturer assumes liability for the driving task. This shift in responsibility, rather than any new perception capability, is what dictates the engineering. Mercedes-Benz Drive Pilot2222 22 https://www.mercedes-benz.co.uk/passengercars/technology/autonomous-driving.html and Honda Traffic Jam Pilot2323 23 https://global.honda/en/tech/Traffic_Jam_Pilot_TJP/ purchase the “eyes-off” guarantee by pairing complementary sensing (cameras, radar, and LiDAR with high-precision, HD-map-anchored localization) with redundant braking, steering, and power paths that retain control through a single-component failure. Both, tellingly, keep the envelope deliberately small (low-speed or traffic-jam flow on mapped, divided highways), and both center on the same safety mechanism: as conditions approach the ODD boundary, the system issues a timed takeover request and, absent a driver response, executes a minimal-risk maneuver such as a controlled stop with hazard signals. The narrowness of the Level 3 envelope is therefore not a marketing concession but the direct cost of guaranteeing safe behavior once the human is no longer continuously in the loop: a cost the next tier pays in full by removing the driver entirely.

9.2.6.3 Driverless Robotaxis and Autonomous Ride-hailing (SAE Level 4)

Level 4 removes the human from the loop entirely within a geofence: there is no driver to hand back to, so the vehicle must resolve every in-domain situation itself or bring itself to a safe state, with remote operators supplying only high-level guidance rather than moment-to-moment control. To meet this far stricter bar, Waymo One2424 24 https://waymo.com/ and Baidu Apollo Go2525 25 https://www.apollogo.com/ converge on essentially the same recipe: a dense, overlapping multi-sensor suite (lidar, radar, and camera vision) for redundant coverage, HD-map-anchored localization, and conservative prediction-and-planning that favors lawful, cautious maneuvers through dense urban traffic. Each makes the problem tractable not by claiming universal competence but by tightly restricting where and when it operates and validating performance city by city before extending the geofence. Across the three tiers, every step up the ladder buys wider autonomy by narrowing the operating domain and adding redundancy, until at Level 4 the system finally internalizes the fallback that Levels 2 and 3 delegated to the driver.

9.2.7 Challenges

Every tier of the deployment ladder works because it limits where it operates, and general, trustworthy autonomy requires lifting those limits. Four threads, each cutting across perception, localization, and decision, stand in the way: justifying life-critical decisions (safety and explainability), dependable behavior across the long tail of road, weather, and traffic conditions (resilience and robustness), adaptation to genuinely novel situations from little prior data (unfamiliar road scenarios), and continual learning on deployed vehicles without eroding mastered behavior (enhanced autonomy in complex scenarios).

Safety and Explainability.

Because driving decisions are life-critical, the inability to explain why a model selected a given maneuver is a first-order obstacle to certification and public trust. Post-hoc attribution methods such as layer-wise relevance propagation [bach2015pixel] and Shapley-value attribution expose which inputs drove a decision, supporting both engineering debugging and regulatory audit, while causal-inference models go further by separating mere correlation from the actual influence of factors such as road state and a maneuver’s effect on surrounding agents. The unresolved difficulty is that these explanations remain largely retrospective and local to individual decisions; converting them into guarantees that provably hold across the full operating domain is still an open problem.

Resilience and Robustness.

Robustness to the long tail of driving conditions is commonly pursued through curriculum learning, where a policy is trained on a graded sequence from simple navigation to dense mixed-traffic interaction, which improves sample efficiency and training stability relative to confronting hard cases directly. Its effectiveness, however, hinges on a scenario curriculum that faithfully spans the deployment distribution and on objectives that keep safety and comfort constraints satisfied at every difficulty level. The practical risk is that, absent a benchmark which deliberately surfaces rare but critical events, strong curriculum performance on common scenes can mask failures precisely on the cases that determine real-world safety.

Unfamiliar Road Scenarios.

A distinct difficulty is generalization to genuinely novel situations (an unseen sign, an irregular work zone, an atypical vehicle) where data-hungry models degrade but human drivers adapt from a single exposure. Approaches that target this gap include probabilistic program induction in a Bayesian framework, which represents a new concept as a compact program inferred from few examples, and the injection of compositional, causal, and meta-learning priors so that, for instance, a system can infer that a fallen obstacle will trigger sudden lane changes in adjacent traffic. The standing obstacle is validating such few-shot behavior to a safety standard, since the very rarity of these events makes their failure modes hard to measure and certify.

Enhanced Autonomy in Complex Scenarios.

Sustained operation in changing environments motivates lifelong learning [ZhuBZZW24], in which a deployed system keeps acquiring new knowledge (a new traffic pattern or road layout) without retraining from scratch and without overwriting prior competence. The central technical barrier is catastrophic forgetting, which is addressed by memory-augmented architectures and continual-learning regularizers that protect previously learned parameters, together with transfer mechanisms that reuse knowledge across tasks and cities. The harder, still-open requirement is to perform such updates on-vehicle under real-time and verification constraints, so that an update improving one scenario cannot silently regress a safety-critical behavior elsewhere.

9.3 Wearable AI System

9.3.1 Introduction

Wearable devices have become a central sensing modality for embodied and spatial intelligence, delivering continuous, fine-grained measurements of human motion, physiology, and physical interaction. Because they are worn on or integrated into the body, they access proprioceptive and kinesthetic cues, joint rotations, muscle activations, contact forces, and locomotion patterns, which exteroceptive sensors such as RGB-D cameras or LiDAR cannot capture directly. We use the term broadly, covering inertial measurement units (IMUs), surface electromyography (EMG) sensors, smart textiles, haptic interfaces, and wearable cameras: body-mounted technologies that together model human dynamics and embodied interaction in real-world settings. It is this egocentric, body-centric vantage point that makes wearables valuable for spatial intelligence, letting a system reason about how a person moves through, reads, and acts upon their surroundings, and it has driven rapid adoption across health monitoring, sports analytics, rehabilitation [patel2012review], industrial safety, and human–robot collaboration.

The signals wearables provide are especially valuable because they are anticipatory. Joint kinematics and muscle activity reveal what a person is doing and, crucially, what they are about to do next, which is what underpins intent recognition, action forecasting, and safe coordination in shared spaces. Wearable IMU arrays, for example, recover whole-body skeletal motion in cluttered or occluded settings where optical capture breaks down [huang2018dip, vonmarcard2017sparse], and EMG surfaces pre-activation patterns that precede any visible movement [atzori2014ninapro].

These devices are often bracketed with head-mounted XR hardware, yet their role in spatial intelligence differs in kind. XR headsets integrate sensing and display for immersive visualization and mixed-reality interaction, leaning on outward-facing cameras for SLAM and environment mapping. The wearables treated here look inward instead, supplying the biomechanical and physiological state, high-frequency, continuous, and on-body, that an XR headset does not observe.

The spatial-intelligence capabilities that wearables ultimately serve, pose estimation, action recognition, localization, and trajectory prediction, are formulated in Part III (spatial perception in Chapter 6, spatial reasoning in Chapter 7). This section does not re-derive them; it concentrates on the body-centric sensing layer, the devices that acquire embodied signals, the systems assembled around them, and the tasks, methods, and failure modes that surface once spatial intelligence must be grounded in continuous on-body measurement, spanning long-horizon activity and gait analysis, intention prediction for human–robot collaboration, and real-time safety in industrial and logistics settings.

9.3.2 Wearable Devices

Body-centric sensing spans a diverse device ecosystem, summarized in Table 9.3.

Motion and Body-State Sensing.

Inertial measurement units (accelerometers, gyroscopes, and often magnetometers) are the most widely deployed body-worn sensors. Consumer watches and bands such as the Apple Watch2626 26 https://www.apple.com/watch/, Samsung Galaxy Watch2727 27 https://www.samsung.com/global/galaxy/galaxy-watch/, Fitbit2828 28 https://www.fitbit.com/, and Xiaomi Band stream inertial data for activity and gait monitoring, while research and industrial systems place IMUs at specific anatomical sites and fuse them into full-body kinematics [vonmarcard2017sparse, yi2021transpose]; because they need no line of sight, they keep working under occlusion and poor lighting. Full-body motion-capture suits such as Xsens2929 29 https://www.movella.com/products/xsens, Rokoko Smartsuit Pro3030 30 https://www.rokoko.com/, and Noitom3131 31 https://www.noitom.com/ combine many IMUs, sometimes with pressure or stretch sensors, into accurate skeletal pose outside the studio, which has made them standard in biomechanics, sports, robotics, and character animation [trumble2017totalcapture]. Smart clothing embeds conductive fabrics, stretch sensors, or distributed pressure sensors in garments for unobtrusive, long-duration monitoring of posture, joint angles, and whole-body contact [luo2021learning], and physiological sensors (heart rate, galvanic skin response, respiration), foot-mounted inertial or pressure sensors, and ear-worn IMUs add workload, ground-contact timing, and head orientation [patel2012review].

Neuromuscular, Egocentric, and Interactive Wearables.

Electromyography (EMG) armbands and high-density arrays sense the muscle activations that precede visible movement, giving early cues for gesture recognition and intent estimation [atzori2014ninapro], and combining EMG with inertial data makes them more robust to arm posture and fatigue [atzori2016deep]. Wearable cameras add the exteroceptive, first-person view: egocentric RGB, depth, or fisheye streams supply scene geometry and activity context that can be fused with on-body signals [grauman2022ego4d, adt]. Two device families also act on the body. Haptic gloves such as HaptX3232 32 https://haptx.com/ and SenseGlove3333 33 https://www.senseglove.com/ and haptic vests such as bHaptics3434 34 https://www.bhaptics.com/ return tactile, vibration, or force feedback during manipulation, teleoperation, and training [pacchierotti2017wearable], and exoskeletons combine IMUs, torque and force sensors, and joint encoders with actuation, estimating user intent in real time to assist or rehabilitate movement [young2017state], which makes them a direct test of embodied spatial intelligence.

9.3.3 System Overview

Taken together, the devices above form the front end of a single body-centric perception-to-action loop that defines the wearable AI system as a whole. Raw on-body signals are first sensed (inertial, neuromuscular, tactile, and egocentric-visual streams), then modeled into geometric and biomechanical state (joint kinematics, body pose, contact forces), interpreted and predicted into higher-level behavioral and intentional descriptions (activities, gestures, short-horizon motion forecasts), and finally fed back to the wearer or to a collaborating agent through action channels (haptic cues, exoskeleton assistance, safety alerts, or shared-control commands). The loop then closes: the consequences of feedback alter the wearer’s motion, which the sensors observe anew.

Figure 9.11 schematizes this loop and situates the three pivotal tasks that organize the remainder of this section as complementary stages of it. Pivotal Task-1 (Embodied Motion Sensing and Pose Reconstruction) occupies the sense-to-model stage, turning body-centric signals into stable geometric descriptions of motion. Pivotal Task-2 (Behavioral Understanding and Intention Modeling) occupies the interpret-and-predict stage, mapping reconstructed motion and neuromuscular cues to recognized activities and anticipated actions. Pivotal Task-3 (Safe Collaboration and Embodied Interaction) closes the loop at the action stage, converting interpreted human state into coordinated, safe, and assistive responses in shared physical environments. Because all three stages must run under the power, compute, and reliability constraints of body-worn hardware, lightweight on-device inference is a cross-cutting concern that recurs throughout.

9.3.4 Pivotal Task-1: Embodied Motion Sensing and Pose Reconstruction

The first stage of the wearable loop turns raw body-centric signals into a geometric description of how the wearer moves. It is a bottom-up reconstruction problem: per-segment inertial and biomechanical measurements must yield joint angles, segment velocities, and ultimately a full-body pose that remains stable over long horizons and in settings where exteroceptive capture fails. This task subsumes full-body skeletal pose estimation, fine-grained limb tracking, real-world locomotion and gait analysis, and body-centric localization in GPS-denied spaces; the underlying pose-estimation formulations are developed in Chapter 6, so the emphasis here is on reconstruction from on-body sensing. Figure 9.12 illustrates this reconstruction stack from segment-level signals to full-body pose.

From signals to kinematics. Reconstruction begins with kinematic and dynamic modeling, which provides the physical grounding for interpreting inertial and pressure-based signals. Forward and inverse kinematics infer joint angles and segment orientations from inertial measurements, compensating for drift and sensor noise through optimization-based filtering and biomechanical constraints. Classical recursive estimators such as extended and unscented Kalman filters incorporate kinematic priors and temporal smoothness to improve stability in real-world settings [welch1995kalman, madgwick2011estimation], while articulated-body dynamics and parametric body models such as SMPL [loper2015smpl] enforce anatomical plausibility for complex motions such as rapid locomotion or limb coordination. Multi-IMU fusion against musculoskeletal models extends these ideas to full-body pose estimation in challenging environments where optical motion-capture systems fail [huang2018dip, yi2021transpose, yi2022pip], and recent systems fold in physics-based dynamics and inter-sensor ultra-wideband ranging to tighten accuracy and suppress jitter [armani2024ultra].

Learning-based reconstruction and sensor fusion. Where analytic models struggle with sparse or noisy sensing, data-driven approaches learn the mapping from raw inertial streams to pose directly [huang2018dip, yi2021transpose], and sensor fusion integrates heterogeneous modalities for drift-compensated estimates. IMU-and-vision fusion resolves ambiguities in inertial tracking by leveraging environmental context from egocentric cameras [grauman2022ego4d, adt], while drift-compensation techniques, including zero-velocity updates and constraint-based corrections, stabilize long-horizon wear. For body-centric localization, sparse-sensor systems couple inertial pose estimation with simultaneous localization and mapping, so that the wearer’s global trajectory is recovered together with body pose rather than left to drift freely [yi2023egolocate]; visual-inertial odometry that fuses the same inertial signals with first-person imagery offers a complementary route through GPS-denied indoor spaces, assessed on dedicated benchmarks [Schubert2018TUMVI].

Benchmarks and evaluation. The kinematic, learning-based, and fusion methods above are measured against the same yardsticks: large-scale motion-capture corpora such as AMASS [mahmood2019amass], which provides a canonical surface-and-skeleton reference for full-body pose, alongside dedicated inertial-pose datasets for sparse-IMU reconstruction [trumble2017totalcapture, huang2018dip], while body-centric localization is assessed separately on visual-inertial odometry benchmarks [Schubert2018TUMVI]. Reconstruction quality is reported as mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) and joint-angle error, and localization as absolute trajectory error and accumulated drift (Table 9.4). Read against the needs of real deployment, these numbers reveal a clear gap. On curated benchmarks, sparse-IMU systems now recover root-relative full-body pose to within roughly five centimeters of optical ground truth [yi2022pip], but global translation still drifts over long sequences unless it is anchored by SLAM or ranging [yi2023egolocate], and even the root-relative accuracy falls off in the wild, where fast or unseen motions and loose sensor placement push errors past the tolerance that downstream control or clinical gait analysis can absorb. The pose the next stage consumes is thus dependable on average yet brittle at exactly the fast, atypical movements that matter most.

9.3.5 Pivotal Task-2: Behavioral Understanding and Intention Modeling

Once motion has been reconstructed, the second stage of the loop interprets it: recognizing what the wearer is doing and anticipating what they will do next. Continuous neuromuscular and inertial cues feed activity recognition and segmentation and then short-horizon intention prediction, even in daily-life settings where visual systems face severe occlusion or field-of-view limits. Because the recognition and reasoning formulations themselves are treated in Chapter 7, the focus here is on how high-frequency wearable streams are modeled to support behavioral inference. Figure 9.13 sketches the path from multimodal time-series and body-graph representations to recognized activity and predicted intent.

Sequence models for wearable time-series. The availability of large-scale wearable recordings has driven deep models tailored to high-frequency temporal streams from IMU, EMG, and multimodal sensors. Recurrent networks, temporal convolutional networks, and Transformers are widely applied to gait classification, gesture recognition, and activity segmentation [ordonez2016deep]: temporal convolutions capture multi-scale dependencies for long-horizon pattern detection [bai2018tcn], while attention-based architectures learn complex correlations across sensor channels [attention]. Because labeled wearable data are scarce and expensive, self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled motion recordings has become the dominant route to transferable representations [haresamudram2021contrastive]: masked-reconstruction encoders such as LIMU-BERT learn compact IMU features from raw streams [xu2021limubert], and multimodal contrastive objectives such as IMU2CLIP align inertial signals with video and language, pointing toward wearable foundation models that generalize across tasks and users [moon2023imu2clip].

Graph-based body representations. Because human anatomy is structured as a kinematic tree, graph neural networks offer a natural representation for wearable-derived motion [kipf2017semisupervised], encoding relational dependencies between joints and limbs directly in graph space. Such formulations fuse IMU placements across body segments, propagate temporal features along skeletal edges, and remain robust to missing or corrupted sensor channels; combining graph convolution with temporal attention jointly models spatial structure and temporal evolution for activity recognition and biomechanical analysis [yan2018stgcn].

Neuromuscular cues and multimodal fusion for intent. Beyond recognizing observed motion, EMG-based wearables detect subtle neuromuscular activations that precede visible movement [atzori2014ninapro], providing predictive cues for early intention estimation and responsive human-robot collaboration. Fusing EMG with inertial data sharpens fine-grained gesture and anticipatory-command decoding [atzori2016deep], while fusing IMU with egocentric video grounds activity recognition in environmental context [stein2013combining, grauman2022ego4d]. A recent milestone shows how far this can scale: a surface-EMG wristband trained across more than a thousand users decodes gestures, clicks, and handwriting from neuromuscular signals alone and, critically, generalizes to new wearers without per-user calibration [kaifosh2025neuromotor], addressing the inter-user variability that has long limited EMG interfaces. Physiological and pressure cues additionally support inference of fatigue, balance, and abnormal gait over extended periods.

Benchmarks and evaluation. Taking the reconstructed motion of the previous stage as input, the sequence, graph, and fusion models above are evaluated on wearable human-activity-recognition corpora [reiss2012pamap2, chavarriaga2013opportunity], EMG gesture datasets [atzori2014ninapro], and egocentric activity datasets such as Ego4D [grauman2022ego4d] and EPIC-KITCHENS [EPIC-KITCHENS], with recognition reported as accuracy and macro-F1 and intention prediction as anticipation accuracy and prediction lead time (Table 9.4). Here the gap to maturity is one of generalization rather than peak score. Balanced locomotion corpora such as PAMAP2 are close to saturated, yet the same architectures score markedly lower on cluttered, null-dominated sets such as Opportunity and lose accuracy again under cross-user and cross-environment evaluation; reliable intention forecasting, meanwhile, still extends only to short, well-rehearsed horizons. This falls well short of the open-world, anticipatory understanding that the safe-collaboration stage below depends on, where the system must read unfamiliar users in unfamiliar settings.

9.3.6 Pivotal Task-3: Safe Collaboration and Embodied Interaction

The third stage closes the loop, converting interpreted human state into coordinated, safe, and assistive responses in shared physical environments. Contact- and force-level sensing of human–environment interaction supports real-time inference of effort and hazard, which in turn drives feedback for collaboration and shared autonomy. The collaboration and shared-control reasoning that this task builds on is developed in Chapter 7 and, for the manipulation setting specifically, in Section 9.1; here the emphasis is on the wearable feedback and safety layer. Figure 9.14 depicts this closing stage, from contact sensing to coordinated safety response.

Sensing interaction and effort. Haptic and tactile wearables capture contact forces, surface interactions, and manipulative behaviors, supplying the signals needed to model human–environment interaction and object handling [HOI4D, luo2021learning]. Exoskeletons equipped with torque and force sensors use these signals to infer user effort and detect hazardous conditions, adjusting assistive strategies accordingly [young2017state]; probabilistic fusion that integrates biomechanical priors and uncertainty estimates is central to robustness in such safety-critical settings.

Coordination, safety, and feedback. In industrial and shared-autonomy scenarios, on-body inertial and proximity sensors contribute to safety monitoring by detecting collision risks, unsafe postures, and sudden motion anomalies, while haptic channels return spatial alerts and force feedback that close the sensorimotor loop [pacchierotti2017wearable]. Combined with the intention forecasts of Pivotal Task-2, these signals form the basis for predictive safety mechanisms and shared-control frameworks that anticipate human motion rather than merely reacting to it.

On-device constraints. Because feedback must be timely, the action stage is where the wearable system’s power, memory, and compute limits bite hardest. Model compression (pruning, quantization, and distillation) [hinton2015distilling] and edge-optimized architectures [howard2017mobilenets] enable real-time inference on wearable microcontrollers or smartphone-class processors, and on-device adaptation mitigates inter-user variability without relying on remote servers, keeping safety-critical computation local and low-latency.

Benchmarks and evaluation. Closing the loop, the interaction-sensing, safety, and on-device methods above are assessed on human-object-interaction datasets such as HOI4D [HOI4D] and, for assistive control, on exoskeleton and teleoperation testbeds, with metrics spanning contact- and force-estimation error, collision-avoidance and safety-violation rates, and intention-anticipation lead time (Table 9.4). Evaluation here is the least mature of the three stages: it remains fragmented across hardware-specific testbeds with few shared protocols, so reported gains are hard to compare and seldom stress real safety guarantees. Current systems perform convincingly in instrumented demonstrations, but closed-loop, certified safety under the full variability of human partners, the bar that genuine shared autonomy must clear, is still an open target rather than a measured result. The robustness, generalization, and safety gaps that recur at each stage of the loop are what the challenges below take up directly.

9.3.7 Established Tools and Systems

Commercial wearables have converged on the head and the wrist, and what separates current products is less their sensors than where perception runs and whether anything is shown back to the wearer. Full augmented-reality headsets are covered with the XR platforms in Section 10.1; here the focus is on everyday-wearable glasses, neural input bands, and the research platforms and chips behind them.

AI glasses without a display. By volume, the dominant wearable AI device is a pair of ordinary-looking glasses carrying a camera, microphones, open-ear speakers, and an IMU, with a multimodal assistant running on the paired phone or in the cloud. Meta’s line with EssilorLuxottica3535 35 https://www.meta.com/ai-glasses/ defines the category: the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta (2025) records 3K video from a 12-megapixel camera and runs up to eight hours per charge, and the Oakley Meta Vanguard adapts the design to sport with a 122-degree camera. Display-less models made up 96% of AI-glasses shipments in the first half of 2026, almost all of them Meta’s3636 36 Counterpoint Research, global AI glasses shipments, H1 2026., while Xiaomi’s AI glasses (2025) and Alibaba’s Qwen-based Quark AI glasses3737 37 https://www.quark.cn/ (November 2025) lead a fast-growing Chinese segment. Google and Samsung previewed Gemini-based Android XR glasses3838 38 https://www.android.com/xr/ with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker in May 2026, with the first display-less models due in the fall. Spatially, these devices answer questions about what the wearer is looking at one camera frame at a time; most keep no persistent map of the surroundings, so the continuous body and scene tracking of Pivotal Tasks 1 and 2 is still largely absent from shipping products.

Display glasses and neural input. Adding a display makes the glasses an interface, and input then becomes the hard problem. Meta Ray-Ban Display3939 39 https://www.meta.com/ai-glasses/meta-ray-ban-display/ (September 2025) puts a small monocular display, with a 20-degree field of view, in the right lens and ships with the Meta Neural Band, a surface-EMG wristband that decodes finger gestures and handwriting; it is the commercial form of the generic neuromotor interface described in Pivotal Task-2 [kaifosh2025neuromotor]. In waveguide display glasses, Rokid4040 40 https://global.rokid.com/ led shipments in the first half of 2026, ahead of Meta and Even Realities4141 41 https://www.evenrealities.com/, whose glasses favor a minimal text display over cameras.

Research platforms and on-glass compute. Much of the egocentric data behind the methods of this section was recorded on research glasses rather than consumer products. Meta’s Project Aria [engel2023projectaria]4242 42 https://www.projectaria.com/ provides glasses with RGB, tracking, and eye-tracking cameras, IMUs, and spatial microphones, together with machine-perception services for trajectories, eye gaze, and hand tracking; its second generation (2025) adds a heart-rate sensor and a contact microphone in the nosepad, alongside on-device perception. The platform underlies Aria Digital Twin [adt]; Ego-Exo4D [grauman2024egoexo4d], which pairs egocentric Aria recordings of skilled activities with synchronized exocentric cameras over 1,422 hours; and Nymeria [ma2024nymeria], which adds full-body ground-truth motion from a motion-capture suit to 300 hours of everyday activity, the kind of supervision the pose reconstruction of Pivotal Task-1 needs. Ego4D [grauman2022ego4d] gathered its 3,670 hours from several head-mounted cameras, and remains the main benchmark for egocentric activity understanding. On the compute side, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon AR1+ Gen 14343 43 https://www.qualcomm.com/products/mobile/snapdragon/xr-vr-ar (2025) runs a one-billion-parameter language model on the glasses without a phone, a first step toward the on-device inference that the latency and power constraints of Pivotal Task-3 call for.

9.3.8 Challenges

Wearable sensing is coupled to the dynamics and variability of the human body in a way that external sensing is not, and that coupling is the source of its hardest problems. The four below track the loop of the System Overview: signal quality at the sense stage, robustness under partial observation, fusion across heterogeneous modalities, and generalization across users.

Signal Instability and Drift.

On-body signals are inherently unstable. IMU drift, EMG noise, and calibration shifts arise continuously from motion artifacts, sensor displacement, and soft-tissue deformation, and they strike precisely the quantities that pose estimation, trajectory tracking, and dynamics reconstruction integrate over time, so small per-step errors compound into large ones across a long recording.

Incomplete and Intermittent Sensing.

Sensing is rarely continuous in practice. Sweat, motion, and wireless dropouts cause brief losses of contact and stretches of degraded signal, leaving the system to reconstruct reliable motion from partial and sometimes corrupted segment-level data, a demand that clean-benchmark evaluation rarely exercises.

Heterogeneous Multimodal Fusion.

The modalities that make wearables powerful are also mismatched. IMU, EMG, pressure, and egocentric-visual streams differ in sampling rate, latency, noise, and coordinate frame, and fusing them under real-world variability, without letting one noisy channel corrupt the whole estimate, remains an open integration problem rather than a solved preprocessing step.

Inter-User Variability.

Finally, the body itself is the confound. Anatomy, muscle-activation patterns, and movement style vary enough between people that a model tuned on a small or homogeneous population transfers poorly, and the effect is sharpest exactly where wearables matter most, in motion reconstruction, intent prediction, and gait analysis, where individual biomechanics dominate the sensor signature. Personalization, domain adaptation, and larger, more diverse training corpora are the levers for closing this gap, and how far they succeed will decide whether wearable spatial intelligence moves from convincing demonstrations to dependable deployment.

9.4 Aerial Agents

9.4.1 Introduction

Aerial agents (satellites, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs)) acquire rich, dynamic, large-scale observations from the sky and near space and, increasingly, perceive, decide, and act on them autonomously through onboard processing and adaptive control (Table 9.5). The aerial domain is a demanding testbed for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part III: it stresses perception across extreme scale and viewpoint changes (Chapter 6) and decision-making under partial observability and tight latency budgets (Chapter 7), across platform tiers that differ in altitude, resolution, endurance, and latency by orders of magnitude.

Satellites supply the global tier. Navigation constellations, namely GPS [enge1994global, leick2015gps] within the broader Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), Russia’s GLONASS [ivanov1992glonass], the European Union’s Galileo, and China’s BeiDou [yang2019introduction, yang2020basic], provide the positioning, navigation, and timing on which vehicles [li2022real], smartphones [zangenehnejad2021gnss], network synchronization [hasan2018gnss], and every lower aerial tier rely. Earth-observation satellites operate continuously over years, which suits long-term, wide-area monitoring that neither ground sensors nor short-endurance UAVs can provide: seasonal vegetation dynamics [malingreau1986global], wildlife migration [dobrynin2017integration], river-basin ecosystem health [ferreira2013estimating], deforestation [tucker2000strategies, finer2018combating], desertification [del1998status, collado2002satellite], biodiversity loss [turner2015free], and climate indicators such as land surface temperature, ocean color, and atmospheric composition [yang2013role, kaufman2002satellite], together with ecological conservation [pettorelli2014satellite, boyle2014high], multispectral and hyperspectral resource discovery [pettorelli2019satellite], precision agriculture [guo2018multi] and crop-yield estimation [maas1988using, ferencz2004crop], and the detection of algal blooms [fang2022global] and pollutant leakage [pandey2019satellite].

Differently, UAVs, commonly known as drones, have gained widespread popularity due to their agility, low operational cost, and capability for autonomous operation. Equipped with onboard sensors and processing units, UAVs can perceive their surroundings, plan flight paths, and adapt to dynamic conditions in real time. This unique perspective allows UAVs to capture high-resolution imagery and video from flexible vantage points, enabling frequent revisits and reduced occlusions in complex environments. Compared to satellites, UAVs excel in capturing fine-grained, localized data, and can be rapidly deployed to areas of interest, including hazardous or otherwise inaccessible regions. They now serve aerial photography [zhao2023ms, shao2022efficient], cinematography [pitas2022autonomous, dang2022path], environmental mapping [zheng2020university, wang2021each, lin2022joint], precision agriculture [goodrich2023placement], geolocalization [liu2019lending, shi2019spatial, shi2020optimal, shi2020looking, shi2022beyond, shi2022accurate, shi2022cvlnet, shi2023boosting, song2023learning], and last-mile delivery [sorbelli2023wind, dissanayaka2023review].

Filling the altitude gap between satellite systems and UAVs, emerging platforms such as stratospheric balloons, solar-powered high-altitude platform stations, and small satellite constellations (e.g., , CubeSats [lemmer2017propulsion]) are increasingly being integrated into aerial observation networks. These high-altitude platform stations (HAPS) offer complementary advantages: HAPS [gonzalo2018capabilities] provide persistent regional coverage with higher spatial resolution than satellites, while orbital systems [cunningham2004national] enable global, long-term monitoring at varying temporal and spectral scales. Together, they form a multi-tiered aerial ecosystem capable of capturing heterogeneous multimedia data, from visible and thermal imagery to hyperspectral and LiDAR scans, across spatiotemporal scales unattainable by any single platform alone. For instance, solar-powered HAPS such as Airbus Zephyr [kothe2019flight] or HAWK30 by AeroVironment/HAPSMobile [fladeland2019demonstrating] can operate autonomously in the stratosphere (about 20 km altitude) for weeks, offering persistent observation and communication relay services with sub-meter resolution, which is superior to most Earth observation satellites and at lower cost than maintaining UAV fleets.

A growing trend is the coordination of heterogeneous aerial agents into cooperative networks, where satellites offer global context, HAPS serve as communication relays or edge computing nodes, and UAVs execute localized missions, enabling real-time, closed-loop intelligence. The utility of these systems is further amplified by advances in artificial intelligence, including machine learning, computer vision, big data analytics, and transfer learning [wang2024multiple, wang2022learning, zheng2022adaptive]. These technologies empower intelligent processing of massive aerial datasets, enabling automated image and video analysis [liu2023robust, li2021uav, 9854892, zheng2019unsupervised, wang2023context, ju2025video2bev], real-time object detection and tracking [zhang2019eye, wen2021detection], predictive modeling for urban dynamics [fang2022cognitive, shi2022geometry], natural language-based control interfaces [chu2024towards], and city-scale digital twin simulations [zheng2022citysim]. Data privacy, airspace integration, energy efficiency, and operational robustness remain open, and are taken up in the Challenges below.

9.4.2 System Overview

An aerial agent realizes a sensing-to-action loop that spans the multi-tier ecosystem of Table 9.5: satellites supply global context and positioning, HAPS act as persistent regional relays and edge-computing nodes, and UAVs execute localized, low-latency missions at the point of interest. Across this stack, spatial intelligence is exercised through three complementary stages, which constitute the pivotal tasks of this section. Cross-view perception anchors aerial and ground observations to a common geographic frame, so that what a drone sees can be matched to a map or a street-level query (Pivotal Task-1); remote-sensing detection and environmental understanding turn that imagery into structured scene knowledge about objects, layouts, and human activity (Pivotal Task-2); and autonomous navigation and decision making convert perception into flight plans and control actions in unseen environments (Pivotal Task-3). Figure 9.15 sketches this pipeline, with a feedback path from action back onto sensing that ties the three stages into one closed loop rather than a feed-forward chain.

9.4.3 Pivotal Task-1: Ground-Air Collaborative Perception and Visual Geolocalization

A foundational requirement of any aerial system is to place its observations on the map: the integration of ground-level and aerial views for cross-modal understanding enables visual geolocalization, determining the geographic location of a query image by matching it against a reference database. This task anchors the perception stage of the system and is particularly challenging due to the large modality gap between ground street-view images and overhead (aerial or satellite) imagery, an instance of the cross-view correspondence problem treated more generally in Chapter 6. For instance, the University-1652 dataset [zheng2020university] has become a benchmark for this task, offering ground, drone and satellite image triplets of campus buildings, thus facilitating research on cross-view matching and localization. Such capabilities are critical for urban search-and-rescue, augmented reality, and infrastructure monitoring, where precise alignment between ground observations and aerial maps is essential. Progress has come from bridging the modality gap, encoding spatial structure into a viewpoint-invariant representation, and exploiting multiple views per location (Figure 9.16).

Bridging the modality gap. Most extant research frames geolocalization as a cross-view image retrieval problem, where the core challenge is to learn a viewpoint-invariant representation that effectively bridges the disparity between images captured from different perspectives. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the widespread application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) for extracting robust visual features. One prominent line of inquiry employs metric learning to construct a shared latent space for images acquired from diverse platforms. Workman et al. [workman2015location] show that a CNN pre-trained on the Places dataset [zhou2014learning] can, by itself, yield highly discriminative features without explicit fine-tuning for the task. The integration of contrastive loss, which minimizes the distance between positive pairs in the feature space, further enhances geolocalization performance [workman2015wide, lin2015learning]. Liu et al. [liu2019stochastic] introduce the Stochastic Attraction and Repulsion Embedding (SARE) loss, which minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the learned and actual data distributions, and more recently Deuser et al. [deuser2023sample4geo] show that hard negative sampling strategies also significantly influence the final discriminative power.

Encoding spatial structure. Another significant body of work addresses the problem of spatial misalignment in ground-to-aerial matching, injecting geometric priors into the representation. Vo et al.evaluate various network architectures and propose an orientation regression loss to train an orientation-aware network [vo2016localizing]. Zhai et al. [zhai2017predicting] utilize semantic segmentation maps to facilitate semantic alignment, while Hu et al. [hu2018cvm] incorporate a NetVLAD layer to extract more discriminative features. Subsequently, Liu et al. [liu2019lending] propose a Siamese Network to explicitly integrate spatial cues, such as orientation maps, into the training process, and Shi et al. [shi2020optimal] introduce a spatial-aware layer to improve localization performance. Given that each location has multiple training images from different viewpoints, Zheng et al. [zheng2020university] train a multi-branch CNN as a base model. Building upon this multi-branch architecture, Wang et al. [wang2021each] further partition the feature map into multiple segments to improve matching discriminability, while Lin et al. [lin2022joint] incorporate keypoint detection into the learning process.
