More recently, researchers resort to ViT structures: L2LTR [yang2021cross] adopts a hybrid CNN-ViT architecture, leveraging CNNs to extract high-level semantic features and ViTs to encode them into global representations; GeoDTR [zhang2023cross] further enhances geometric reasoning by introducing a ViT-based layout extractor that generates geometry-aware attention maps; and TransGeo [zhu2022transgeo] advances the paradigm with a two-branch ViT model and a two-stage coarse-to-fine learning strategy.

From image pairs to multi-view benchmarks. The maturation of these methods is closely tied to the datasets that score them (see Table 9.6). The majority of prior geolocalization datasets are based on image pairs, designed for matching images from two distinct platforms such as terrestrial cameras and satellites. One of the earliest contributions [lin2015learning] leverages public sources to create 78,000 image pairs spanning a 45-degree bird’s-eye perspective and the ground. In a similar vein, Tian et al. [tian2017cross] compile image pairs for urban localization, positing that buildings are crucial for this task and thus incorporating building detection into their pipeline. The CVUSA [zhai2017predicting] and CVACT [liu2019lending] datasets instead address matching panoramic ground-view images with satellite-view images, which is particularly useful for user localization when GPS data is unavailable. A key distinction is one of objective: the latter two focus on localizing the user who captures the photograph, while the former focus on localizing a specific target within the image, so that multiple views of the target are more beneficial for the target-localization datasets (Lin et al., Tian et al.) because they encourage the model to learn the target’s structure. However, most existing datasets typically provide only two views of a given location. The University-1652 dataset [zheng2020university] addresses this by including a greater number of views per target, thereby fostering more robust viewpoint-invariant features; SUES-200 [zhu2023sues] follows a similar multi-view strategy with drone-captured real-world data. Wang et al. [wang2024multiple] further extend University-1652 to multi-weather evaluation (rain, fog, and other complex conditions), while Chu et al. [chu2024towards] introduce linguistic annotations and a language-based query setting for a more intuitive user experience.

Metrics. These benchmarks are scored by retrieval metrics that reflect their gallery structure. Several datasets [liu2019lending, zhai2017predicting, vo2016localizing] adopt Recall@K, defined as 1 if a correct match appears within the top K retrieved images; Recall@K is highly sensitive to the rank of the first correct match and is best suited for test sets containing only a single ground-truth match in the gallery. In contrast, datasets such as University-1652 [zheng2020university] and SUES-200 [zhu2023sues] include multiple ground-truth matches from various viewpoints, where Recall@K fails to comprehensively reflect retrieval performance; they therefore also employ Average Precision (AP), as used by Lin et al. [lin2015learning] and Tian et al. [tian2017cross]. AP, defined as the area under the Precision-Recall (PR) curve, considers all ground-truth images in the gallery, and recent evaluations usually report both Recall@K and the mean Average Precision (mAP) across all queries.

9.4.4 Pivotal Task-2: Remote Sensing Detection and Environmental Understanding

Once observations are geolocalized, the next stage turns aerial imagery into structured scene knowledge. Aerial platforms are integral to large-scale environmental monitoring and public safety, facilitating fine-grained object detection in complex scenes, a specialization of the detection and segmentation machinery of Chapter 6 to the aerial viewpoint. Prominent datasets such as DOTA [xia2018dota], DOTA-v2 [xia2018dota, ding2021object], and VisDrone [du2019visdrone] provide comprehensive annotations for detecting various objects, including vehicles and pedestrians, under a wide range of weather, illumination, and scale conditions. These benchmarks have spurred the development of robust detection models specifically engineered to address challenges inherent to aerial perspectives, such as extreme aspect ratios, dense object clustering, and diminutive object sizes. A significant application is found in UAV-based wildlife monitoring, where systems are deployed for animal census in conservation areas [vermeulen2013unmanned], highlighting the utility of aerial technologies in promoting ecological sustainability. Figure 9.17 relates the aerial-specific difficulties of orientation, scale, and density to the detectors built for them and to the human-centric understanding that aerial video enables.

Beyond object detection, as shown in Table 9.7, with the proliferation of UAVs in smart-city and other human-centric applications, human behavior understanding [li2021uav] has emerged as a critical and formidable research challenge, including person re-identification and action recognition. For instance, the UAV person re-identification (re-ID) task [albaluchi2025uav] is designed to address cross-drone identity matching amid substantial viewpoint and illumination variations, thereby motivating the creation of view-invariant feature representations. In conjunction with resources like VisDrone, which contains multi-target tracking sequences from mobile UAVs, these datasets facilitate the design of intelligent video analytics systems capable of performing long-term human behavior analysis and anomaly detection in dynamic environments.

Remote sensing object detection is primarily challenged by the prevalence of arbitrarily oriented objects and substantial scale variations [xia2018dota, ding2021object, sun2022fair1m, liu2016ship, cheng2022anchor, yao2023automated], and existing research can be broadly organized along two corresponding fronts. Detection of arbitrarily oriented objects. A significant line of work focuses on developing specialized oriented object detection (OOD) methods. Early approaches often augment horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) with an angle parameter, employing techniques such as feature refinement in the detector neck [yang2019scrdet, yang2021r3det], extraction of rotated regions of interest (RoIs) [ding2019learning, xie2021oriented], or designing specific OOD heads [hou2022shape, han2021redet, ming2021dynamic]. However, these methods frequently suffer from boundary discontinuity and representation ambiguity due to their reliance on angle parameters. To mitigate these issues, subsequent research has explored more flexible object representations: some methods describe oriented objects using points [fu2020point, li2022oriented] or gliding vertexes [xu2020gliding], while others model them with Gaussian distributions [yang2021rethinking, yang2021learning, cheng2022dual] and design corresponding loss functions [qian2021learning]. Handling substantial scale variations. Another research direction designs specialized backbones and feature extraction strategies to cope with large scale variations in remote sensing images (RSIs). A common strategy is multi-scale feature learning, achieved through data augmentation [zhao2019multi, shamsolmoali2021rotation, chen2020stitcher], multi-scale feature integration [zhang2019hierarchical, zheng2020hynet, 9382268, liu2016ssd], enhanced feature pyramid networks (FPNs) [lin2017feature, hou2022refined, zhang2021laplacian, guo2020rotational], or multi-scale anchor generation [guo2018geospatial, hou2021self, qiu2019a2rmnet]. Other works focus on ensuring equivalent receptive fields for objects of different orientations [han2021redet, pu2023adaptive]. More recently, some methods [Li_2023_ICCV] have employed large kernel convolutions [liu2022convnet, ding2022scaling, liu2022more] to enlarge the spatial receptive field for large objects, though this can introduce background noise for smaller ones, while others harness multi-scale convolution kernels and attention to address scale variance [guo2022segnext, dai2023multi, zhang2022multiscale, cai2024poly].

These method fronts are evaluated on a complementary set of benchmarks and metrics. The VisDrone dataset [du2019visdrone] provides a comprehensive benchmark for drone-captured imagery, featuring urban and rural scenes with challenges like varying altitudes and occlusions; DOTA-v2 [xia2018dota, ding2021object] focuses on oriented object detection in high-resolution satellite images, emphasizing rotated bounding boxes for objects like planes and ships; and UAV-Human [li2021uav] targets human behavior understanding from UAVs, with multi-modal sequences for pose and action analysis. Complementary datasets, such as UAVDT [du2018uavdt] for traffic surveillance and iSAID [waqas2019isaid] for instance segmentation, broaden the scope of aerial detection tasks and collectively enable cross-dataset fine-tuning to mitigate domain gaps. Evaluation extends standard metrics to address orientation, scale, and density: the primary metric, mean Average Precision (mAP), is computed as the area under the precision-recall curve, typically at an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 (mAP@0.5) or across 0.5:0.95 for stricter assessment [lin2014microsoft], and for oriented detection, as in DOTA-v2, rotated IoU variants ensure alignment with object headings [xia2018dota]. Per-class and per-size Average Precision exposes imbalances, and small objects (<32×32<32\times 32 pixels) remain the main source of error on drone imagery [du2019visdrone]. Additional metrics include precision, recall, and F1-score to assess false positives (e.g., , background clutter) and misses (e.g., , occlusions), while Frames Per Second (FPS) is critical for real-time UAV deployment, targeting 30+ FPS [yang2023laiyolo]. Video-specific metrics like Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) are used for dynamic scenes in datasets like UAV-Human [li2021uav]. Modern real-time detectors of the YOLO family [wang2024yolov9] are increasingly adapted to the aerial setting, though aggregated aerial mAP still trails their COCO-level performance owing to small-object and orientation hardness, keeping open gaps such as multi-modal fusion and zero-shot adaptation active.

9.4.5 Pivotal Task-3: Autonomous Aerial Navigation and Decision Making

The final stage closes the loop, converting perception into action. Traditional UAV geolocalization addresses basic aerial navigation by matching a query (e.g., , a satellite image or textual description) to a database of historical flight paths or geographic points [zheng2020university, chu2024towards]. However, a critical distinction exists between such perception-oriented tasks and the overarching goal of autonomous navigation: the latter requires complex decision-making and control to bridge perception to action, drawing on the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter 7. In practical scenarios, the objective is often for an aerial agent to autonomously locate a destination, particularly an unexplored target, through environmental exploration and, when available, collaboration with a map. This goal introduces significant challenges in generalization to unseen environments, including novel objects, unmapped regions, and interaction with the environment. For instance, recent benchmarks adapted from general Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) have begun to address this by requiring models to output a detailed flight plan with 6-DoF control signals [wang2024towards]. Figure 9.18 follows the problem from the perception-to-action gap to foundation-model-driven VLN and multi-agent extensions.

From visual perception to language-guided planning. Recent years have witnessed significant progress in UAV navigation, with a primary focus on visual perception [loquercio2018dronet, kang2019generalization, giusti2015machine, smolyanskiy2017toward, fan2020learn, bozcan2020air, majdik2017zurich] and collision avoidance [xu2025navrl, singla2019memory]. Building on this aerial-perception foundation, Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) for UAVs remains an emerging area of research. To address it, recent efforts have leveraged Large Multi-modal Models (LMMs) to harness general knowledge for navigation planning: STMR [gao2024aerial] builds upon AerialVLN [liu2023aerialvln] with a zero-shot LLM-based framework utilizing a Semantic-TopoMetric Representation for enhanced spatial reasoning. A parallel line reframes UAV autonomy as a full agentic loop rather than one-shot instruction following. AeroVerse [yao2024aeroverse] assembles a simulator, real-virtual pre-training corpora, and five downstream tasks, i.e., , scene awareness, spatial reasoning, navigational exploration, task planning, and motion decision, to train aerospace embodied world models, and proposes SkyAgentX as a unified perception-reasoning-navigation-planning agent; AirVista-II [lin2025airvista] pursues zero-shot dynamic-scene semantic understanding via agent-based task scheduling and adaptive keyframe selection; and PRPSearcher [ji2025uavsearch] casts aerial visual object search over the CityAVOS benchmark as a perception-reasoning-planning problem solved by a multimodal LLM agent. Complementary systems such as NeLV [yuan2025nelv] operationalize the language-to-flight pipeline end to end, chaining an LLM parser, route and path planners, and a control platform across short-, medium-, and long-range missions. Beyond single-agent setups, some works have begun to explore multi-drone systems; for instance, Wu et al. [wu2025aeroduo] deploy two drones flying at different altitudes to facilitate planning.

Datasets and simulators. As shown in Table 9.8, several foundational frameworks and datasets have been established. One of the early works, i.e., , UAVA [albanis2020dronepose], leverages the panorama images in the Matterport3D dataset [chang2017matterport3d] to render the indoor environment, while harnessing the camera viewpoints as physically available flight anchors to generate trajectories. AerialVLN [liu2023aerialvln] introduces a large-scale dataset with an effective baseline, and further infrastructure contributions include datasets such as CityNav [lee2024citynav], AVDN [fan2022aerial], and OpenFly [gao2025openfly]. Notably, UAV-Need-Help [wang2024towards] provides a realistic UAV dynamics simulator, i.e., , OpenUAV, alongside its evaluation protocol; OpenUAV is further used in HaL-13k [wu2025aeroduo] to simulate two drones at different altitudes. Additional observation agents, such as road infrastructures and vehicles with depth sensing, have also been incorporated to enrich environmental understanding [gao2025airv2x].

Metrics. Evaluation metrics for UAV aerial navigation, especially VLN, measure how well a model navigates a drone based on visual inputs and language instructions. Common metrics include Success Rate (SR), which checks if the UAV reaches the target location within a specified distance, and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), which balances success with how efficiently the drone travels (shorter paths score higher). Path Length (PL) measures the total distance traveled, while Navigation Error (NE) calculates the distance between the final position and the goal. Together these metrics assess both accuracy (reaching the target) and efficiency (taking an optimal route), providing a clear way to compare model performance across datasets like UAVA, AerialVLN, and CityNav.

9.4.6 Established Tools and Systems

Beyond the methods and benchmarks above, the aerial domain rests on a real-world layer of simulators, platforms, and infrastructure that turns research prototypes into deployable systems; we group it into three tiers.

Simulation environments and benchmarks. Because flight data is costly and safety-critical to collect, high-fidelity simulation underpins much of the field. The OpenUAV simulator released with UAV-Need-Help [wang2024towards] supplies realistic UAV dynamics and a continuous 6-DoF evaluation protocol, and is reused to simulate multi-altitude drone teams in HaL-13k [wu2025aeroduo]; OpenFly [gao2025openfly] targets large-scale real-to-sim transfer across diverse scenes; and AerialVLN [liu2023aerialvln] pairs a city-scale synthetic environment with a navigation baseline. Photorealistic indoor rendering for UAV tasks is provided through Matterport3D [chang2017matterport3d] in UAVA [albanis2020dronepose], while V2X-style multi-agent simulation combines CARLA and Microsoft AirSim4444 44 https://microsoft.github.io/AirSim/ in AirV2X [gao2025airv2x].

Commercial platforms and vendors. On the hardware side, consumer and enterprise drones from DJI4545 45 https://www.dji.com/ (whose Matrice series collects datasets such as UAV-Human) and autonomy-focused vendors such as Skydio4646 46 https://www.skydio.com/ dominate the UAV tier. In the stratospheric tier, solar-powered HAPS such as Airbus Zephyr [kothe2019flight] and AeroVironment/HAPSMobile’s HAWK30 [fladeland2019demonstrating] provide persistent regional coverage, complemented by small-satellite constellations built on CubeSat platforms [lemmer2017propulsion] and broader HAPS programs [gonzalo2018capabilities].

Connectivity and positioning infrastructure. Aerial autonomy ultimately depends on shared positioning and communication backbones: the GNSS constellations introduced above (GPS [enge1994global], GLONASS [ivanov1992glonass], Galileo, and BeiDou [yang2019introduction]) supply global timing and localization, while space-based broadband relays such as Starlink [michel2022first] and orbital observation systems [cunningham2004national] increasingly serve as the connectivity layer for coordinated, real-time aerial operations.

9.4.7 Challenges

Aerial autonomy is limited less by any single model than by the gaps between platforms, scales, and operating conditions. Four threads follow the pipeline in order: fusing heterogeneous platforms into a coherent situational model, perceiving small objects and complex activities reliably, navigating unseen and GPS-denied environments, and meeting the ethical and operational constraints under which any of this can be deployed.

Heterogeneous-Platform Fusion.

A primary obstacle lies in integrating aerial agents with heterogeneous platforms for robust environmental perception. Coordinating a UAV with ground-based sensors or satellite systems to construct a cohesive situational-awareness model remains complex, particularly in dynamic or cluttered settings where the platforms differ in resolution, latency, and viewpoint (Table 9.5). Reconciling these asynchronous, multi-resolution streams into a single consistent representation, without one modality’s noise corrupting the fused estimate, is the standing difficulty, and it motivates the V2X-style cooperative-perception efforts that incorporate road infrastructure and ground vehicles as additional observers.

Small-Object and Complex-Activity Understanding.

Aerial perception is defined by extremes of scale and density. The recognition of small objects, such as identifying debris in disaster zones or distinguishing wildlife in ecological surveys, demands high-resolution imaging and detectors robust to dense clustering, which often strain onboard computational resources. Understanding complex activities, such as discerning human behavior during search-and-rescue missions, compounds the problem by requiring nuanced spatio-temporal and contextual analysis that current systems struggle to deliver consistently. Closing this gap calls for detectors and activity models that remain accurate at extreme scale variation while fitting a UAV’s tight compute and power budget.

Navigation in Unseen and GPS-denied Environments.

Autonomous operation in unseen or GPS-denied environments, such as dense urban canyons or subterranean spaces, further complicates the action stage, as agents must rely on real-time mapping and obstacle avoidance without pre-existing data. The core requirement is generalization: a navigation policy must extend to novel objects, unmapped regions, and genuinely interactive scenarios, rather than replaying matched trajectories. This is precisely the gap that foundation-model-driven VLN and multi-altitude cooperative planning aim to narrow, but validating such behavior to a safety standard in the open world remains open.

Privacy, Airspace, and Operational Robustness.

Beyond perception and navigation, several ethical and operational challenges persist. Data-privacy concerns arise when aerial agents capture high-fidelity multimedia data, potentially compromising individual rights without stringent safeguards, motivating privacy-preserving approaches such as federated learning. Airspace integration poses another hurdle, as regulatory frameworks struggle to accommodate the proliferation of aerial agents alongside traditional aviation, necessitating harmonized protocols to ensure safety. Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck, since prolonged missions demand lightweight yet powerful power sources and motivate renewable solutions such as solar-powered propulsion. Finally, operational robustness is challenged by environmental uncertainties, such as extreme weather or electromagnetic interference, that can disrupt system reliability. Advances in artificial intelligence and sensor fusion that address these constraints, rather than perception accuracy alone, are what will let aerial agents move from bounded demonstrations toward dependable, large-scale deployment.

9.5 Warehouse and Industrial Logistics

9.5.1 Introduction

Warehouse and industrial logistics is one of the most mature real-world testbeds for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part III: it demands perception-to-action pipelines that interpret complex, dynamic environments such as dense shelving systems populated with diverse stock keeping units (SKUs), pallets, forklifts, and human workers. These systems construct and maintain spatial memory representations (semantic maps, object and pose states) to support downstream planning and manipulation for tasks including inventory counting, order picking, pallet handling, and coordinated fleet operations. Perception and reasoning themselves are treated in Chapter 6 and Chapter 7; logistics adds throughput targets, engineered but crowded layouts, and people sharing the floor with fleets of robots. Performance is judged in terms of throughput, order accuracy, safety, and operational cost, especially under high SKU diversity, visual clutter, elongated aisles, and human-robot collaboration. Dense shelving and manipulation in clutter remain the hardest cases, as the Amazon Picking Challenge made plain [Correll2016AmazonChallenge], and they demand that perception, pose estimation, mapping, and multi-agent planning be integrated rather than tuned in isolation.

9.5.2 System Overview

The complete warehouse automation pipeline, sketched in Figure 9.19, integrates five complementary capabilities into a closed loop. Perception converts raw multi-sensor streams into semantic object information (what is present, where, and in what pose); localization and mapping grounds that information in a metric spatial map and keeps it consistent over time; reasoning and planning consume these representations to allocate tasks and generate optimized fleet schedules; manipulation and control physically execute the resulting picking and transport actions; and a human-robot collaboration and safety layer adapts behavior dynamically in mixed human-robot environments. Integration is achieved via middleware such as ROS 2 and industrial protocols like Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC-UA), while digital twin platforms such as NVIDIA Omniverse4747 47 https://www.nvidia.com/en-gb/omniverse/ support simulation and validation before deployment. The five capabilities are the pivotal tasks below, taken in pipeline order.

9.5.3 Pivotal Task-1: Perception and Recognition

Perception constitutes the sensory foundation of the pipeline: it transforms raw sensor data into actionable knowledge, reusing the detection, segmentation, and pose-estimation machinery of Chapter 6 but specializing it to the warehouse Operational Design Domain. Core capabilities include detecting and classifying objects (packages, pallets, tools), estimating their 3D poses, and tracking their motion and state over time. Unlike outdoor environments, warehouses impose distinct perceptual challenges: dense clutter, heavy occlusion, visually similar items, reflective packaging, narrow aisles, and continually changing layouts, which together make robust perception a central and ongoing research focus [Tubis2023IntelligentWarehouse, redmon2016yolo]. Formally, perception is a structured mapping from a synchronized multimodal stream Xt={ItRGB,ItDepth,PtLiDAR,RtRFID}X_{t}=\{I_{t}^{\text{RGB}},I_{t}^{\text{Depth}},P_{t}^{\text{LiDAR}},R_{t}^{% \text{RFID}}\} (together with calibration parameters and a prior map MM) to a scene graph Gt={oi,ci,𝐛i,𝐩i,Σi}G_{t}=\{o_{i},c_{i},\mathbf{b}_{i},\mathbf{p}_{i},\Sigma_{i}\}, in which each detected object oio_{i} carries a class label cic_{i}, a bounding box or segmentation mask 𝐛i\mathbf{b}_{i}, an estimated pose 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i}, and an uncertainty measure Σi\Sigma_{i} that grounds subsequent manipulation, navigation, and decision making. Figure 9.20 sketches this representation stack.

Detection and recognition form the base layer. Convolutional and transformer-based architectures, i.e., , YOLO [redmon2016yolo], RetinaNet [lin2017focal], and the transformer-based DETR with deformable attention [Zhu2021DeformableDETR], have steadily improved accuracy and efficiency under clutter, and are scored on COCO [lin2014microsoft], whose mean Average Precision (mAP) broken down by object size is particularly informative for the small-SKU and barcode-label cases that dominate warehouse failure modes. Pose estimation lifts these 2D detections into the metric space that manipulation requires: PoseCNN [xiang2017posecnn], DenseFusion [Wang2019DenseFusion], and CosyPose [Labbe2020CosyPose] fuse visual and geometric cues to infer six-degree-of-freedom (6D) orientation and position even under occlusion, and are evaluated on YCB-Video [xiang2017posecnn] for textured household and industrial objects and on T-LESS [Hodan2017TLESS] for textureless, industry-relevant parts, with Average Distance (ADD) the standard accuracy measure and MOTA/MOTP reporting tracking quality in dynamic scenes. The Amazon Picking Challenge [Correll2016AmazonChallenge] couples perception with manipulation in real warehouse scenarios, stressing generalization across novel object sets and thereby anticipating the manipulation task of §9.5.6 below. Representative benchmarks across the section are consolidated in Table 9.9. In industrial practice, perception pipelines are increasingly standardized and modularized; the deployed software stacks that realize them are surveyed in the Established Tools and Systems subsection.

9.5.4 Pivotal Task-2: Localization and Mapping

If perception answers what is around the robot, localization and mapping answer where the robot is and what the persistent structure of the warehouse is, forming the spatial backbone on which fleet coordination rests and drawing on the same scene-construction techniques as Chapter 6. Automated guided vehicles (AGVs) and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) require centimeter-level accuracy to navigate narrow aisles, dock precisely at shelves, and operate safely alongside workers. The problem is conceptually the SLAM problem of autonomous driving, yet it faces warehouse-specific constraints: highly repetitive structures (rows of identical shelves), dynamic obstacles (workers, pallets, forklifts), and low-light or GPS-denied indoor conditions. Formally, a sequence of odometry and sensor measurements Z1:t={IMU,LiDAR,cameras,wheel encoders,UWB beacons}Z_{1:t}=\{\text{IMU},\text{LiDAR},\text{cameras},\text{wheel encoders},\text{% UWB beacons}\}, optionally supplemented by a prior map M0M_{0} or fiducial anchors, is fused into a pose graph 𝒳t={x1,…,xt}\mathcal{X}_{t}=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}\} that estimates the trajectory and an evolving semantic map MtM_{t} fusing geometric structure with storage zones and restricted areas. Beyond navigation, this map underpins the digital twins (spatial models synchronized with the facility whose simulations feed back into its operation; §11.1) that increasingly govern modern facilities [Cadena2016SLAMSurvey]. Figure 9.21 casts the task as a multi-sensor fusion problem.

A family of SLAM algorithms has been tailored to these conditions. ORB-SLAM3 [Campos2021ORBSLAM3] extends visual SLAM with inertial and multi-camera support for accurate visual-inertial localization; LIO-SAM [Shan2020LIOSAM] provides real-time LiDAR–IMU fusion through factor-graph optimization that stays robust under fast motion and partial occlusion; and RTAB-Map [Labbe2019RTABMap] supports online RGB-D mapping and loop-closure detection with memory management suited to long-term operation, all expressible within the unified factor-graph framework of GTSAM [Dellaert2012GTSAM]. Multi-modal fusion is the common thread that holds accuracy together when any single modality degrades, and is also the dominant emerging research direction, alongside learning-based estimation (neural depth prediction, differentiable bundle adjustment, and learned place-recognition embeddings) and the migration of SLAM computation to the edge for fleet-scale latency. These capabilities are evaluated on KITTI [Geiger2013KITTI] for outdoor visual and LiDAR odometry and loop closure, on the indoor visual-inertial EuRoC MAV dataset [Burri2016EuRoC] whose challenging motion and illumination mirror warehouse conditions, and on the high-fidelity Replica reconstructions [straub2019replica] for dense mapping and semantic labeling, with Absolute and Relative Pose Error (APE/RPE) and loop-closure precision/recall the standard metrics and, for warehouse use, semantic-zone IoU and map completeness (Table 9.9).

9.5.5 Pivotal Task-3: Reasoning and Planning

Reasoning and planning form the decision-making core of warehouse automation, transforming the perceptual and localization outputs into task assignments and motion plans, and instantiating the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter 7. This layer determines which robot executes which task, how tasks are sequenced, and how routes and schedules are optimized for safe, efficient, coordinated operation. In contrast to autonomous driving, where planning typically focuses on individual vehicles, warehouse reasoning must address multi-agent coordination across fleets of dozens or hundreds of robots in constrained indoor space [Veloso2015CMUCoBot], maximizing throughput and minimizing latency while maintaining safety under dynamic obstacles, human interactions, and stochastic task arrivals. Formally, the perceived states GtG_{t}, a task list 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the fleet state FtF_{t} (positions, capabilities, battery levels), and the warehouse map MtM_{t} are mapped to a task-allocation matrix AA, optimized motion paths ℛ\mathcal{R}, and temporal schedules π\pi that jointly specify when and how tasks execute. Figure 9.22 contrasts the two solution families.

The first family is combinatorial optimization. Traditional methods (the Hungarian algorithm, branch-and-bound, and mixed-integer linear programming) remain widely used for task allocation and scheduling in small- to medium-scale deployments, while Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) formulations [Cordeau2007VRP] and their multi-depot and time-window variants are central to modeling fleet movement. The second family is learning-based coordination: reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-agent RL (MARL) handle dynamic environments and real-time uncertainty [Sartoretti2019PRIMAL, samvelyan2019smac], with toolkits such as Google OR-Tools [Perron2019ORTools] and PyMARL enabling rapid experimentation across both families. Emerging research couples the two: hierarchical and hybrid frameworks combine symbolic reasoning with learned components, graph neural networks and differentiable optimization accelerate multi-agent coordination and transfer policies across layouts, and digital-twin integration enables simulation-informed, predictive re-planning, increasingly under multi-objective criteria that balance throughput, energy, and human safety. Planning systems are benchmarked on Solomon’s VRP suite [Solomon1987VRP] for static routing and scheduling and on the Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL) [Sucan2012OMPL] for continuous-space motion planning, complemented by synthetic multi-robot testbeds; common metrics are throughput (items/hour), task-completion latency, total travel distance or time, collision rate, and re-planning latency (Table 9.9).

9.5.6 Pivotal Task-4: Manipulation and Control

Manipulation constitutes the physical execution layer, enabling robots to interact directly with objects, containers, and infrastructure such as bins, shelves, and conveyors. In industrial logistics this typically involves robotic arms performing grasping, placing, sorting, or palletizing, as well as AGVs docking to pallets or workstations. Manipulation bridges high-level symbolic or geometric plans with continuous motor control, and therefore demands both precision and robustness to the inherent variability in packaging, geometry, and material properties [Levine2016DeepGrasp]; the grasping and control techniques here connect directly to the robotic-manipulation treatment of §9.1 and the planning paradigms of Chapter 7. Formally, estimated object poses 𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i} and task descriptions (grasp targets, placement goals, trajectory constraints) are mapped to low-level motor commands 𝐮t\mathbf{u}_{t} that ensure stable grasping, precise placement, and compliant, collision-free motion. Figure 9.23 contrasts modular grasp-and-plan systems with learned visuomotor control.

Grasp synthesis anchors the methodology: Dex-Net combines synthetic grasp data and analytic robustness metrics to train a grasp-quality predictor for candidate selection [Mahler2017DexNet], while learned visual control can predict grasp success from camera images and candidate task-space motions, then select actions for adaptive manipulation [Levine2016DeepGrasp]. Motion planning then realizes the chosen grasp: sampling-based algorithms such as RRT* [Karaman2011RRTStar] remain fundamental for generating collision-free trajectories in high-dimensional configuration spaces, exposed through frameworks like MoveIt [Sucan2010MoveIt]. These capabilities are benchmarked on the Amazon Picking Challenge [Correll2016AmazonChallenge], which established a standardized testbed for picking under clutter and uncertainty, and on the YCB Object and Model Set [Calli2015YCB], a diverse collection of everyday items with physical models for grasping and manipulation; grasp success rate, cycle time per pick, placement accuracy, and task-completion rate are the headline metrics (Table 9.9). Hybrid control frameworks that combine analytical models with data-driven adaptation are emerging as the practical route to generalizing across variable geometries and grasp contexts, complemented by tactile sensing and force control for slip detection and contact regulation.

9.5.7 Pivotal Task-5: Human-Robot Collaboration and Safety

Even in highly automated warehouses, human workers remain indispensable for complex, dexterous, or exception-handling tasks that require contextual understanding and flexible decision making, so the final stage of the pipeline is safe and efficient human-robot collaboration (HRC). HRC systems must balance productivity with stringent safety guarantees, enabling mixed teams (robots handling repetitive or heavy-load work, humans managing fine-grained, judgment-based activities) to share workspaces without physical or operational interference [Lasota2015HRC]. The task maps multimodal human-detection and intent signals (pose, gesture, gaze, and trajectory data from vision, LiDAR, wearables, or motion capture) to adaptive robot behaviors such as dynamic speed modulation, path re-routing, stop-and-wait actions, or task reallocation in response to predicted human movement. Figure 9.24 sketches this predict-then-adapt loop.

Intent recognition lets robots anticipate human motion: sequence models based on hidden Markov models or recurrent networks predict trajectories and proactively adjust behavior [Mainprice2016Intent], while proxemics-aware planning maintains socially acceptable distances and re-routes trajectories under human proximity [dragan2013legibility], with multimodal sensing (vision-based detection fused with wearable or RFID localization) improving reliability. These principles are embodied in force- and speed-limited collaborative robots and safety-rated AMRs (see Established Tools and Systems), governed by international standards such as ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066. Evaluation combines quantitative safety metrics with qualitative interaction assessment: human-motion corpora such as Human3.6M [IonescuPOS14] supply sequences for intent prediction, and key indicators include intervention frequency (safety-triggered stops per hour), near-miss rate, human-detection accuracy, and compliance with ISO-defined safety zones.

9.5.8 Established Tools and Systems

The pivotal tasks above are realized in production through a layered ecosystem of simulators, middleware, optimization services, and robot hardware that together constitute the real-world delta over the methods of Part III.

Simulation and middleware form the integration substrate. Digital-twin and physics platforms such as NVIDIA Omniverse Isaac Sim [NVIDIA2021Isaac] and Gazebo provide realistic environments for developing and validating perception, localization, and planning pipelines before deployment, while perception SDKs such as NVIDIA Isaac, the Intel RealSense SDK, and Zebra RFID/barcode platforms supply end-to-end sensing support in real facilities. Interoperability across heterogeneous hardware is provided by ROS [Quigley2009ROSIndustrial], ROS 2, and ROS-Industrial, with commercial localization stacks such as SLAMcore4848 48 https://www.slamcore.com/ and BlueBotics ANT4949 49 https://bluebotics.com/ delivering optimized multi-sensor fusion, map management, and fleet coordination for AGVs and AMRs.

Warehouse management and fleet orchestration sit at the enterprise layer. Large-scale optimization services such as SAP Extended Warehouse Management5050 50 https://www.sap.com/products/scm/extended-warehouse-management.html, Blue Yonder WMS5151 51 https://blueyonder.com/, and Manhattan Associates5252 52 https://www.manh.com/ integrate task allocation and scheduling with enterprise resource planning, while open toolkits such as Google OR-Tools [Perron2019ORTools] and PyMARL support the underlying combinatorial and learning-based planners.

Robot hardware and manipulation close the loop physically. High-throughput pick-and-place arms from ABB5353 53 https://new.abb.com/products/robotics, FANUC5454 54 https://www.fanuc.com/, and KUKA5555 55 https://www.kuka.com/ are widely deployed and integrated through ROS-based middleware, mobile manipulators such as those from Fetch Robotics5656 56 https://fetchrobotics.com/ unify navigation and grasping, and motion-planning frameworks such as MoveIt [Sucan2010MoveIt] and NVIDIA cuMotion provide inverse kinematics and trajectory optimization. For shared workspaces, collaborative robots from Universal Robots5757 57 https://www.universal-robots.com/ and AMRs from Locus Robotics5858 58 https://locusrobotics.com/ provide the safety-rated platforms on which the HRC layer is built.

9.5.9 Challenges

Deployed warehouse systems work because they fix the SKU sets, layouts, and operating conditions they handle, and each stage of the pipeline has its own obstacle to relaxing those limits: small-object and cluttered perception, perceptual aliasing in repetitive aisles, multi-agent scalability under uncertainty, manipulation of variable objects, and the safety–throughput trade-off in human–robot collaboration.

Cluttered and Small-Object Perception.

Barcode labels and compact SKU packages often occupy only a few pixels in high-resolution images, leading to frequent misdetections, while occlusion and clutter compound the difficulty as items overlap within bins and shelves. A further persistent issue is domain shift: models trained on synthetic or generic data degrade under real-world variation in lighting, reflective surfaces, and packaging. Research responses include domain adaptation and self-supervised learning for generalization [Tzeng2017DomainAdversarial], active perception that deliberately adjusts viewpoints or sensing to resolve occlusion [Bajcsy2018ActivePerception], and continual learning that lets perception adapt over time without exhaustive retraining, increasingly combined with multi-sensor fusion and neuro-symbolic representations for higher-level causal and semantic reasoning.

Perceptual Aliasing in Repetitive Environments.

Localization and mapping are degraded by dynamic obstacles (humans, forklifts) that generate transient or misleading landmarks corrupting loop-closure hypotheses [Cadena2016SLAMSurvey], and above all by perceptual aliasing: repetitive shelving and low-texture surfaces produce ambiguous place recognition and false data associations in feature-based SLAM [Campos2021ORBSLAM3, Labbe2019RTABMap]. High-speed AGV and AMR operation further demands low-latency, sub-centimeter pose updates that sensor delays, occlusion, and monocular scale drift can readily violate. Robust multi-modal fusion, learning-based estimation, and tighter integration of SLAM with semantic perception and digital twins are the leading mitigations.

Scalability and Uncertainty in Multi-agent Planning.

The combinatorial complexity of multi-robot coordination grows exponentially with the number of agents and tasks, rendering exact optimization intractable for large fleets, while real-world uncertainty (new order arrivals, blocked aisles, unpredictable human movement) necessitates adaptive re-planning and decentralized decision making under partial observability [Veloso2015CMUCoBot, Sartoretti2019PRIMAL]. Hierarchical and hybrid planners, graph-neural and differentiable coordination, and simulation-informed multi-objective optimization are the active directions toward scalable, resilient fleet behavior.

Manipulation of Variable and Deformable Objects.

Many SKUs exhibit deformable, reflective, or transparent surfaces that interfere with perception and grasp stability [Calli2015YCB, Mahler2017DexNet], and deformable handling remains especially difficult because grasp dynamics and contact points resist rigid-body modeling [Levine2016DeepGrasp]. Tactile sensing and force control improve slip detection and grasp robustness but face cost and calibration barriers in industrial deployment, motivating hybrid control that combines analytical models with data-driven adaptation for generalization across geometries and grasp contexts.

Safety–Throughput Trade-off in Collaboration.

Robust human detection under occlusion, variable lighting, and cluttered aisles continues to hinder reliable intent estimation [dragan2013legibility, Mainprice2016Intent], and the trade-off between throughput and safety remains unresolved: conservative margins reduce efficiency while aggressive planning risks unsafe interaction [Lasota2015HRC]. Emerging work emphasizes predictive and explainable safety models that justify decisions in human-interpretable terms, and adaptive safety frameworks that fuse learned intent models with certified control policies for dynamic risk assessment and shared autonomy on the warehouse floor.

Chapter 10 Spatial Intelligence for Virtual Realities

Virtual realities are the media in which spatial intelligence becomes constitutive rather than optional: an extended-reality (XR) device cannot draw a single pixel until it knows where it is, what surrounds it, and where the user is looking and reaching. This makes XR the most demanding real-time deployment target for the perception, reasoning, and generation capabilities of the previous part, specialized to run egocentrically, on-device, and within a hard latency budget.

Beneath everything in XR sits the platform itself, the runtime that localizes the device, maps and registers the surrounding world, senses the user’s body, and composites the result in real time; layered on top is the application that has driven the medium hardest, entertainment, spanning live AR and VR experiences and virtual production as well as the offline, high-fidelity reconstruction and performance capture that supply them with authored content.

10.1 AR/VR/XR

10.1.1 Introduction

Augmented, virtual, and mixed reality (collectively, extended reality or XR) form a continuum of media in which a head-worn display couples the user’s egocentric viewpoint to a computational world that is registered to, or substituted for, the physical surroundings. What distinguishes XR from screen-based media is that spatial intelligence is not an optional feature but a constitutive requirement: before any pixel can be drawn, the system must know where the headset is, what geometry surrounds it, and where the user is looking and reaching. XR is therefore the most demanding real-time deployment target for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part III. The perception machinery (detection, depth, pose, reconstruction) of Chapter 6, the spatial reasoning and planning of Chapter 7, and the neural reconstruction and rendering of Chapter 8 all reappear here, but specialized to run egocentrically, on-device, and within a hard latency budget.

This section treats the XR medium itself as a spatial-computing platform: the runtime engine that localizes the device, maps and registers the world, senses the user’s body, and presents a composited result. The neighboring section on entertainment (§10.2) builds on top of this engine, treating entertainment as an application domain: its real-time AR/VR experiences and virtual production, together with the offline, high-fidelity reconstruction and performance capture that supply them with authored content; here we focus on the platform that makes such experiences run at interactive rates. Concretely, a headset must continuously answer three coupled questions, i.e., , where am I (6-DoF self-localization), what is around me (geometry and semantics), and how do I fuse virtual content into that reality so that it appears physically present, while simultaneously sensing the user and refreshing the display. Early systems answered the localization question with outside-in tracking, using external base stations or cameras (SteamVR Lighthouse, the original Oculus constellation), but the dominant modern paradigm is inside-out tracking, in which visual–inertial SLAM runs entirely on the device, as in Meta Quest, Apple Vision Pro, and Microsoft HoloLens. The three pivotal tasks below correspond to the stages of this loop.

10.1.2 System Overview

As sketched in Figure 10.1, an XR device closes a tight real-time loop. Egocentric sensors first sense the device and the user (outward cameras and an inertial measurement unit for head pose; inward-facing cameras for eyes and outward- or downward-facing cameras for hands and body). The system then tracks and maps the environment, recovering a 6-DoF pose and a persistent geometric model, and registers virtual content into that model with correct anchoring, occlusion, and lighting. Finally, it renders and displays the composite back through the headset optics, after which the user moves and the loop repeats. The pipeline shares an end-to-end motion-to-photon budget; roughly 2020 ms at a display refresh of 9090 Hz or higher are the commonly cited targets, though the right values depend on device and application, and exceeding them degrades presence and comfort. The three pivotal tasks map onto this loop directly: Task-1 is the world-facing engine (track, map, register), Task-2 is the user-facing input (egocentric sensing and interaction), and Task-3 is the user-facing output (display and rendering).

10.1.3 Pivotal Task-1: Spatial Tracking, Mapping, and Registration

The first task is the medium’s spatial backbone: it answers where the device is, what surrounds it, and how virtual content is pinned to the world so convincingly that the illusion holds. It proceeds in three steps: localize the device, model the environment, and register synthetic content into that model. Figure 10.2 sketches this progression from inside-out tracking to a persistent scene map and finally to anchored, occluded, and relit virtual content.

Inside-out 6-DoF tracking. The foundational layer estimates the headset’s six-degree-of-freedom pose at high rate by fusing visual features with inertial measurements. Feature-based visual SLAM with loop closure and relocalization remains the academic standard, exemplified by the ORB-SLAM lineage and its visual-inertial extension ORB-SLAM3 [Campos2021ORBSLAM3], while tightly-coupled visual–inertial odometry such as VINS-Mono [qin2018vins] underpins many mobile and headset stacks; direct (photometric) methods such as DSO [engel2017direct] and the earlier LSD-SLAM [engel2014lsd] offer an alternative that does not depend on sparse keypoints. More recent learned dense systems, including DROID-SLAM [teed2021droid] and transformer-based geometric matchers [mast3r], trade computation for robustness in low-texture and fast-motion regimes. These methods are evaluated chiefly on EuRoC [Burri2016EuRoC] and TUM-VI [Schubert2018TUMVI], with absolute trajectory error (ATE) as the headline metric, but the binding constraints in XR are drift accumulation, recovery from tracking loss (the kidnapped-device problem), and the power and thermal envelope of on-device inference.

Spatial mapping and scene understanding. The tracked stream is consolidated into a usable model of the environment: dense depth and mesh, planar surfaces (floor, wall, table), and semantic labels. Real-time volumetric fusion in the KinectFusion tradition [newcombe2011kinectfusion] provides the geometric substrate, on top of which plane and mesh extraction expose the surfaces that gameplay and user interfaces attach to. (The offline, high-fidelity reconstruction of such scenes as navigable content is treated in §10.2 and Chapter 8; here the map is a means to localization and registration, not an end in itself.) Semantic and instance understanding is benchmarked on indoor datasets such as ScanNet [dai2017scannet] and Matterport3D [chang2017matterport3d], with mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) for segmentation, and increasingly on mobile-captured data with laser ground truth such as ARKitScenes [baruch2021arkitscenes] and high-quality reconstructions such as Replica [straub2019replica] for depth and geometry evaluation.

Persistent and shared anchors. For content to survive across sessions and to be experienced jointly by co-located users, the map must be persistent and shareable. Cloud-hosted and peer-to-peer world maps let a device relocalize against a previously built model, and at city scale a Visual Positioning System anchors content to real landmarks in well-mapped areas. The open problems are relocalization under appearance change (lighting, season, rearranged furniture), the memory footprint of on-device maps, and the privacy implications of uploading scans of private spaces, a thread we return to in the challenges.

Registration and realistic compositing. Finally, virtual content must be registered both geometrically and photometrically so that it appears to occupy the scene. Geometric registration pins objects to anchors and planes in the SLAM frame; depth-based occlusion lets real geometry correctly hide virtual pixels, as in the per-pixel depth produced for mobile interaction by DepthLab and the ARCore Depth API [du2020depthlab]; and lighting estimation predicts the dominant light direction and an ambient environment map from a single image so that virtual objects are shaded and shadowed consistently [gardner2017learning]. Small errors here are perceptually unforgiving: a few centimeters of depth error at an object boundary, or a mismatched shadow, immediately reveals the composite as synthetic, which is why robust occlusion and real-time inverse lighting remain active research problems.

10.1.4 Pivotal Task-2: Egocentric Human Sensing and Spatial Interaction

The second task closes the loop from the user’s body back into the system: it senses the hands, eyes, and posture from inside-out cameras and turns those signals into spatial intent. Low-level egocentric estimates of hands, gaze, and body are fused into selection, manipulation, and locomotion. As Figure 10.3 indicates, the same headset sensors that localize the device are repurposed to track the user, and the resulting estimates drive a gaze-and-gesture interaction model.

Hand tracking. Articulated 3D hand pose (commonly 2121 joints, often a full mesh) is regressed from headset cameras under heavy self-occlusion and truncation. The standard hand model is MANO [romero2017mano], and on-device pipelines such as MediaPipe Hands [zhang2020mediapipe] combine a palm detector with a landmark regressor to run in real time. Methods are benchmarked on FreiHAND [zimmermann2019freihand] and the two-hand InterHand2.6M [moon2020interhand2], with 3D mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) in millimeters as the headline metric; robust two-hand interaction and egocentric truncation remain the hard cases.

Eye and gaze tracking. Estimating 3D gaze from infrared eye images serves three roles: calibration, gaze as a pointing modality, and as the driver for foveated rendering (Task-3). Appearance-based estimation in the iTracker and GazeCapture tradition [krafka2016gazecapture] established that gaze can be regressed from commodity cameras, and headset-specific datasets such as OpenEDS [garbin2019openeds] provide near-eye infrared imagery with dense eye-region segmentation, with the later OpenEDS2020 track adding gaze prediction (angular error in degrees). The decisive interaction consequence is that gaze targets quickly but lacks a natural trigger, a long-standing difficulty known as the Midas-touch problem, which motivates the gaze-plus-pinch pattern discussed below.

Full-body pose from sparse signals. Driving a full-body avatar from a headset and two controllers is an underconstrained inverse problem, since the lower body is unobserved and must be synthesized. Recent methods infer plausible full-body motion from these three tracked points, including the transformer-based AvatarPoser [jiang2022avatarposer] and the diffusion-based AGRoL [du2023agrol], while a parallel line recovers pose from sparse body-worn inertial sensors, as in DIP [huang2018dip], TransPose [yi2021transpose], and the physics-aware PIP [yi2022pip]. These models are trained on large motion corpora such as AMASS [mahmood2019amass] and evaluated with MPJPE and temporal jitter. This sparse, live setting is distinct both from the wearable-IMU body sensing of §9.3 (which instruments the body more densely) and from the studio performance capture that drives authored avatars in §10.2; the XR-specific challenge is plausibility from radically incomplete observation.

Multimodal interaction and locomotion. The recovered signals are fused into spatial actions. The foundational idea of combining a deictic gesture with a complementary modality dates to Bolt’s “Put-That-There” [bolt1980putthatthere], and the modern instantiation decouples targeting from confirmation: the eyes select while a hand pinch or a voice command commits, sidestepping the Midas-touch problem. Locomotion through a virtual space larger than the physical room is handled by redirected walking, which applies imperceptible rotational and translational gains to steer the user within a confined area [razzaque2001redirected], with teleportation as the common non-natural fallback. Spatial user interfaces, in turn, must choose a reference frame (world-locked, body-locked, or head-locked) and increasingly anchor panels to scene semantics so that content lands on appropriate surfaces. Learning these interaction behaviors at scale is increasingly grounded in large egocentric corpora such as Ego4D [grauman2022ego4d], which supply the first-person video of hands, objects, and activities that egocentric-understanding models are trained and benchmarked on.

10.1.5 Pivotal Task-3: Spatial Display and Real-Time Rendering

The third task presents the composited world back to the user within the perceptual budget that the previous two stages must respect. Three questions decide it: where to spend rendering effort, how to hide system latency, and how to display the result comfortably. Figure 10.4 previews this pipeline, from gaze-contingent shading through latency compensation to the optics that place the image before the eye.

Foveated rendering. Because acuity falls off sharply outside the fovea, rendering effort can be concentrated at the gaze point. Foveated 3D graphics established multi-resolution shading driven by eye tracking [guenter2012foveated], and subsequent work added temporal stability and contrast preservation to make the quality reduction imperceptible [patney2016foveated]. Eye-tracked foveated rendering now ships on consumer headsets, materially reducing shading cost on thermally constrained hardware.

Latency compensation. Even an efficient renderer cannot meet the motion-to-photon budget on every frame, so the last stage warps the rendered image to the most recent head pose. Asynchronous time warp applies a rotational reprojection at display refresh, asynchronous space warp adds depth-aware frame extrapolation, and head-mounted optical-see-through systems use per-pixel late-stage reprojection [vanwaveren2016timewarp]. These techniques keep the world stable under fast head motion and are essential to comfort.

Passthrough versus optical see-through. Two display regimes trade off differently. Video passthrough mixed reality (as on Meta Quest 3 and Apple Vision Pro) renders the real world from cameras, granting full control over occlusion and relighting at the cost of camera-to-display latency, parallax, and limited dynamic range; optical see-through (as on HoloLens 2 and Magic Leap 2) presents the real world with zero latency at its true focal depth (though the virtual overlay still incurs render latency and a fixed focal plane) but cannot occlude real light or match real-world brightness. The choice propagates back into the registration problem of Task-1.

Depth-correct rendering and visual comfort. Conventional stereo displays fix the focal plane while vergence varies with content, producing the vergence-accommodation conflict and the eye strain that limits session length. Varifocal, light-field, and holographic near-eye displays aim to restore correct focus cues [maimone2017holographic], but remain largely at the prototype stage.

Neural rendering for telepresence. Finally, photoreal social presence requires driving a faithful avatar of a remote user from headset-mounted cameras that see only oblique crops of the face. The codec-avatar line, beginning with deep appearance models [lombardi2018deep], learns a person-specific decoder that is driven on-device, a direct specialization of the neural rendering of Chapter 8 to the constrained, real-time XR setting.

10.1.6 Established Tools and Systems

A mature ecosystem implements these tasks across mobile AR, standalone headsets, and the web, and it is organized into developer frameworks, cross-platform standards, hardware, and the companies that drive them.

SDKs and standards. At the device level, Apple’s ARKit11 1 https://developer.apple.com/augmented-reality/ and Google’s ARCore22 2 https://developers.google.com/ar expose plane detection, anchors, depth, light estimation, and people occlusion, with ARCore’s Geospatial API localizing against world imagery for outdoor anchoring; Vuforia33 3 https://developer.vuforia.com specializes in robust image and object targets for industrial AR. Cross-engine abstraction layers such as Unity AR Foundation44 4 https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.xr.arfoundation@6.0/ and the Meta Presence Platform and Spatial SDK55 5 https://developers.meta.com/horizon/develop/spatial-sdk present the common subset (planes, anchors, meshes, occlusion, hand and body tracking) over multiple devices, while 8th Wall and WebXR66 6 https://immersiveweb.dev bring markerless AR into the browser. These abstractions matter because XR content is expensive to author and must migrate across devices and sessions; this is the role of cross-platform standards, principally OpenXR77 7 https://www.khronos.org/openxr/ as a unifying runtime API and glTF together with OpenUSD and USDZ88 8 https://openusd.org as asset and scene-description formats. Without a shared runtime and shared asset formats, the ecosystem fragments into incompatible walled gardens.

Hardware. Current headsets divide along the passthrough versus optical-see-through axis. Apple Vision Pro99 9 https://www.apple.com/apple-vision-pro/ (2024) and Meta Quest 3 and 3S1010 10 https://www.meta.com/quest/ use high-resolution video passthrough, with the Quest line the consumer volume leader; Microsoft HoloLens 21111 11 https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/hololens/ (optical see-through, with production ended in 2024) and Magic Leap 21212 12 https://www.magicleap.com target enterprise, and Varjo1313 13 https://varjo.com and Pico1414 14 https://www.picoxr.com serve high-fidelity simulation and the Asian consumer market respectively. Lightweight true-AR glasses, such as Snap Spectacles1515 15 https://www.spectacles.com and Meta’s Orion and Project Aria research prototypes, signal the all-day-glasses horizon toward which the field is converging.

Companies and platforms. Meta leads consumer volume and the most aggressive glasses research bet; Apple defines the premium spatial-computing tier and the USD content pipeline; Google supplies world-scale localization through ARCore and Android XR; Microsoft has pivoted from first-party HoloLens hardware toward OpenXR software and enterprise cloud services; Niantic1616 16 https://www.nianticspatial.com operates a city-scale Visual Positioning System for persistent, multi-user AR; and Snap, Varjo, and ByteDance’s Pico round out the social-AR, high-fidelity, and consumer-standalone niches.

10.1.7 Challenges

XR runs every spatial capability egocentrically and on-device under a perceptual real-time budget, and its open problems follow from that constraint: holding the motion-to-photon budget, fitting perception into the compute and thermal envelope of glasses, keeping tracking and registration robust in the wild, sharing persistent maps without compromising privacy, and making extended wear visually comfortable.

Latency and the Motion-to-Photon Budget.

Meeting the motion-to-photon targets of the System Overview is increasingly difficult as pipelines add wireless or split rendering, cloud offload, and learned perception in the loop, each of which contributes its own delay that the reprojection stage of Task-3 can only partially mask.

On-Device Compute, Thermal, and Power.

All-day glasses face a hard energy and heat envelope: a lightweight form factor leaves little room for the silicon that SLAM, hand and eye tracking, and scene understanding demand. The frontier is partitioning perception across on-device accelerators, companion devices such as wristbands or pucks, and edge offload, without violating the latency or thermal budget.

Robust Tracking and Registration in the Wild.

Visual–inertial SLAM and relocalization degrade in dynamic scenes, textureless rooms, repetitive structures, low light, and outdoors, exactly the conditions that curated benchmarks such as EuRoC and ScanNet underrepresent [Burri2016EuRoC, dai2017scannet]. Persistent Visual Positioning Systems push toward city-scale anchoring, but globally drift-free, cross-device localization, together with convincing occlusion and lighting registration, remains unsolved.

Persistent, Shared Maps and Privacy.

Co-located multi-user AR requires a shared, persistent spatial map, an “AR cloud”, which collides directly with privacy: always-on egocentric cameras continuously scan private spaces and bystanders. Designing maps that support shared anchoring while minimizing the retention of raw imagery, and that admit meaningful consent, is both a research and a policy frontier.

Visual Comfort.

Beyond latency, fixed-focus stereo optics decouple vergence from accommodation, causing eye strain that limits session length, and poorly designed locomotion induces cybersickness. Varifocal and holographic displays, gaze-contingent depth-of-field, and accurate interpupillary-distance matching are promising but immature, leaving comfort a gating factor for mainstream adoption.

Because XR subjects the perception, reasoning, and generation capabilities of Part III to egocentric, on-device, real-time constraints, it exposes failure modes that offline settings rarely reveal.

10.2 Entertainment

10.2.1 Introduction

In entertainment, spatial intelligence is exercised chiefly as the ability to perceive and reconstruct 3D environments, objects, and human bodies, and to embed virtual content into the physical world so that it is geometrically and physically consistent. Spatial entertainment (AR games, VR experiences, location-based attractions, and virtual production for film) differs from screen-based media in that it must compute camera pose, scene geometry, and user state continuously and within strict latency limits, without sacrificing aesthetic quality or narrative coherence; the perception and reconstruction machinery involved is treated in Chapter 6 and Chapter 8.

The field has followed the same arc as the capabilities it borrows: commodity depth sensing made real-time dense mapping practical for AR games, neural radiance and Gaussian representations made captured sets photoreal and navigable, parametric body models made full-body avatars routine, and world-scale visual positioning let location-based games such as Pokémon GO anchor characters to real landmarks across sessions and players. Each of these threads returns in the pivotal tasks below.

10.2.2 System Overview

Entertainment sits on top of the XR platform of §10.1: it does not re-implement that runtime but builds on it, and its distinctive demand is production-quality spatial content, whether rendered live or authored offline. The domain spans two regimes. Real-time interactive experiences (AR games, VR titles, location-based attractions, and live virtual production) close the tight sensing-to-display loop sketched in Figure 10.5, whereas offline high-fidelity creation (scanning sets, capturing performers, building volumetric footage) supplies those experiences with assets. Across both, three spatial tasks recur as the frequent bottlenecks. World reconstruction builds the geometric and radiance model of the environment, supplying localization and occlusion for live experiences and navigable captured content for authored ones; embodied performance capture digitizes the user or performer into a controllable avatar; and spatial content authoring decides where virtual elements appear and how cameras move so that the result is both consistent and expressive. The interactive regime runs all three under hard latency budgets, while offline authoring trades that latency for fidelity.

10.2.3 Pivotal Task-1: World Reconstruction and Spatial Mapping

The first task builds and maintains an accurate, consistent model of the environment that supports localization, occlusion, and physics for live experiences and navigable content for authored ones, specializing the dense-reconstruction and scene-understanding techniques of Chapter 6 and Chapter 8 to interactive rates. Where §10.1 treated mapping as a means to on-device localization, here the reconstruction is itself the deliverable: the navigable set or stage that players and film-makers inhabit. Figure 10.6 contrasts geometric fusion, neural and point-based scene representations, and world-scale localization as complementary capabilities rather than obligatory sequential stages.

Geometric reconstruction forms the base: geometric SLAM and dense methods fuse depth or RGB data into volumetric maps, as in KinectFusion [newcombe2011kinectfusion] and the reconstructions underlying datasets such as ScanNet [dai2017scannet], while DynamicFusion extends this to moving users by tracking non-rigid deformations [newcombe2015dynamicfusion]. Neural and point-based representations such as NeRF, instant-NGP, and 3D Gaussian Splatting then represent scene radiance to produce compact, high-fidelity reconstructions that render at interactive rates [mildenhall2021nerf, muller2022instant, kerbl20233d]; dynamic and 4D extensions that deform or time-index the primitives carry this to moving scenes, so a performance or an entire set can be captured as free-viewpoint volumetric video for later replay [yang2024deformable, wu20244d]. At global scale, visual positioning systems (VPS) combine local reconstructions into a worldwide map that lets a mobile device localize from a single image, as in Niantic’s Lightship platform. These methods are evaluated on indoor datasets such as ScanNet and Matterport3D, which provide large-scale reconstructions with semantic labels for scene understanding [dai2017scannet, chang2017matterport3d], and on NeRF-style view-synthesis benchmarks (e.g., , synthetic Blender scenes) for photometric fidelity; the latter, however, rarely capture entertainment-specific constraints such as rapid camera motion or cluttered living rooms, so practitioners often fall back on custom internal datasets (Table 10.2). The standard metrics are absolute trajectory error (ATE) for localization, surface reconstruction error for geometry, and PSNR/SSIM for neural rendering [mildenhall2021nerf, kerbl20233d], but in entertainment these are complemented by interaction-centric measures: the accuracy of occlusion masks, the physical plausibility of collisions, and user reports on realism (for instance, whether a virtual character convincingly hides behind a sofa).

10.2.4 Pivotal Task-2: Embodied Performance Capture and Avatar Control

The second task estimates full-body pose, shape, and facial expression to drive avatars in real time, specializing the human pose and motion machinery of Chapter 6 (and the motion-generation methods of Chapter 8) to live interaction. Unlike the sparse three-point body tracking of §10.1, driven from a headset and two controllers, entertainment capture targets studio-grade, fully-observed performance. As Figure 10.7 indicates, approaches range from skeleton-based joint prediction to surface-based model fitting and full volumetric capture.

Skeleton-based methods predict joint positions from sensors, while surface-based approaches fit parametric models such as SMPL directly to video [loper2015smpl], with datasets like Human3.6M and AMASS supplying the supervised motion priors that make this robust [IonescuPOS14, mahmood2019amass]. Volumetric capture systems such as Holoportation go further, streaming textured 3D avatars into VR/AR scenes by combining reconstruction with tight time synchronization [orts2016holoportation]. More recent Gaussian-splatting avatars learn drivable, photorealistic humans from multi-view capture, with rigged 3D Gaussians giving expressive control over head avatars [qian2024gaussianavatars] and pose-dependent Gaussian maps modeling full-body avatars with dynamic clothing [li2024animatablegaussians], narrowing the gap between a captured performance and a real-time renderable asset. These capabilities are benchmarked chiefly on Human3.6M, which offers millions of 3D poses with calibrated cameras [IonescuPOS14], and on AMASS, which provides over forty hours of motion data for learning priors [mahmood2019amass]; commercial scenarios remain underrepresented, however, since common cases such as players using controllers in small rooms or performers in costumes lack sufficient public benchmark data (Table 10.2). Quantitative evaluation uses metrics like mean per-joint position error (MPJPE), but for interactive entertainment latency and temporal stability are decisive, as even minor jitter breaks the sense of embodiment, and user studies show that enjoyment depends on the alignment between perceived and actual motion [dongas2023vrrhythm]; production systems therefore pair algorithmic metrics with feedback from expert animators.

10.2.5 Pivotal Task-3: Spatially-Aware Content Authoring and Virtual Production

The third task helps creators decide where virtual elements appear and how cameras move, turning the reconstructed world and captured performers into a coherent, expressive scene, and connecting to the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter 7. Figure 10.8 previews the spectrum from SDK-level authoring primitives to camera-tracked LED-wall virtual production and AI-assisted cinematography.

Engine-level authoring provides designers with high-level primitives such as plane detection and anchors through AR SDKs in real-time engines like Unity and Unreal. Virtual production links physical cameras to 3D scenes on LED walls so that lighting and parallax respond correctly to camera movement, and intelligent cinematography research is exploring AI-assisted camera planning that respects film grammar while adapting to dynamic user actions [azzarelli2025intelligentcine]. Standardized benchmarks for spatial authoring are rare: some studies evaluate camera planning on synthetic storyboards, but most assessment happens internally at studios, and virtual-production workflows are typically tested on complex reference sequences rather than public datasets, which makes objective comparison of authoring tools difficult (Table 10.2). Evaluation accordingly mixes system metrics such as rendering latency with expert judgment on cinematic quality, with intelligent-cinematography studies often convening expert panels to analyze framing and continuity [azzarelli2025intelligentcine]; for AR/VR tools usability is paramount, and HCI evaluations measure how quickly a user completes a level-design task or how rich the resulting spatial layouts are under different tool abstractions. Generative world models are beginning to bypass authoring by synthesizing playable worlds directly: GameNGen [valevski2024diffusion] simulates the game DOOM interactively in real time with a diffusion model, and Genie 3 [genie3] generates navigable environments that respond to user actions, so that creating content starts to mean conditioning a world model (§8.6).

10.2.6 Established Tools and Systems

A robust set of tools implements these tasks for games, film, and live events. At the engine level, Unity’s AR Foundation1717 17 https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.xr.arfoundation offers a unified API over ARKit, ARCore, and other SDKs, exposing essential features such as point clouds and depth meshing, while Google’s ARCore Geospatial API1818 18 https://developers.google.com/ar/develop/unity-arf/geospatial/developer-guide adds global localization, allowing applications to attach anchors to outdoor landmarks with meter-level accuracy. These abstractions let designers build AR gameplay around real-world surfaces without managing low-level sensor fusion.

Niantic’s Lightship platform packages spatial mapping and multiplayer synchronization into turnkey services: Reality Blending1919 19 https://nianticlabs.com/news/realityblending-announcement in Pokémon GO uses learned depth to let virtual creatures move behind real-world obstacles, and Pokémon Playgrounds2020 20 https://nianticlabs.com/news/pokemon-playgrounds extends this to persistent AR, where players leave virtual items at specific locations for others to find, with Niantic’s Visual Positioning System (VPS) keeping that content anchored consistently across users and times.

In VR gaming, consumer headsets with inside-out tracking enable room-scale interaction; games like Beat Saber use precise 6-DoF tracking to create rhythm gameplay that doubles as exercise, and studies show a strong link between spatial design choices and player exertion, underscoring the connection between tracking quality and user experience [dongas2023vrrhythm]. Virtual production stages have likewise transformed film and sports broadcasting: productions such as The Mandalorian (built on ILM’s StageCraft) and sports studios such as ESPN’s Catalyst Stage2121 21 https://espnpressroom.com/us/press-releases/2023/06/catalyst-stage-disneys-new-immersive-espn-studio-opens-storytelling-and-production-frontiers/ use LED volumes driven by tracked cameras, where spatial intelligence involves calibrating physical cameras to digital scenes and maintaining low-latency tracking. Finally, neural capture tools inspired by NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting are entering the pipeline, letting artists scan a location with a phone and import navigable 3D assets into game engines [muller2022instant, kerbl20233d]; while this bridges scouting and production, it introduces new challenges around lighting control and integration.

10.2.7 Challenges

Entertainment asks for production-quality spatial content at interactive rates, and its open problems stem from that demand. The tension between real-time performance and visual fidelity is the most immediate; close behind come robustness once the system leaves controlled spaces, the cognitive load that authoring places on creators, and the human-factors and ethics questions that surface the moment these systems scan real users and real rooms.

Real-time Performance versus Fidelity.

Neural representations have improved visual quality, but many methods remain too computationally heavy for mobile or standalone VR. While techniques such as 3D Gaussian Splatting achieve real-time rendering on high-end hardware [kerbl20233d], porting them to thermally constrained devices is difficult, and entertainment applications must additionally handle variable network conditions while guaranteeing stable frame rates, since frame drops that are acceptable in research benchmarks can cause physical discomfort in VR.

Robustness in the Wild.

Existing benchmarks such as ScanNet focus on standard indoor spaces, yet entertainment experiences often occur in unpredictable environments such as festivals, dim clubs, or crowded stadiums. World-scale AR platforms address this by training on millions of crowdsourced scans, which raises questions about coverage bias (particularly toward urban areas) and the difficulty of maintaining maps as the world changes; designing models that remain robust under these shifts is an open research area.

Authoring Complexity.

Although modern SDKs are powerful, creating high-quality spatial experiences imposes a high cognitive load, as creators must simultaneously manage geometry, interaction, cinematography, and technical constraints. Intelligent-cinematography tools attempt to assist by suggesting camera paths [azzarelli2025intelligentcine], but these are not yet standard in creative workflows; there is a pressing need for tools that let designers specify high-level intentions (for example, “the character should hide behind the sofa”) which the system then realizes via underlying planning modules.

Human Factors and Ethics.

Spatial systems frequently scan users and private spaces.
