While datasets like AMASS demonstrate the utility of large-scale motion capture, collecting similar data in the wild raises privacy concerns, and from an HCI perspective issues such as cybersickness and fatigue limit the duration of VR and AR sessions, while physically active titles introduce comfort and safety considerations that spatial layout must respect. Addressing these problems requires a collaborative approach spanning algorithm design, user-feedback systems, and clear data governance.

Chapter 11 Spatial Intelligence for Geo-spatial Systems

Geo-spatial systems operate on spatial structure at the scale of assets, cities, and the planet, where the task is to build a faithful model of a physical system and keep it aligned with live observation. This chapter applies the spatial intelligence of the previous part to that task, across three settings that share the same closed loop between model and world but differ in scale and stakes.

The digital twin binds a metric, physically grounded replica to a specific asset through a live bidirectional loop, so that the physical system and its model track each other. GeoAI widens the frame to the planet, where streams of Earth-observation data drive perception and decision-making over terrain, infrastructure, and environmental change. Aerospace systems carry the same loop off the planet, where a spacecraft or rover must perceive, reason about, and act on its surroundings with little or no ground support.

11.1 Digital Twins

11.1.1 Introduction

A digital twin is a 3D representation faithful enough to stand in for its physical counterpart in analysis and operation. Building one requires more than accurate geometric reconstruction and photorealistic appearance under varying illumination; it requires realistic modeling of physical properties and interaction, so that the replica behaves as the original would. What separates a digital twin from any other 3D asset, however, is not fidelity alone but coupling. Following the now-standard taxonomy of Kritzinger et al. [kritzinger2018digital], a digital model carries no automated data exchange with the physical object, a digital shadow carries an automated one-way flow from the physical to the virtual, and only a digital twin closes the loop with an automated, bidirectional flow: the virtual model is continuously synchronized to the physical asset, simulated forward to predict, and used to act back upon it.

A digital twin therefore reuses, but specializes, much of the machinery surveyed earlier in this handbook. The perception stack of Chapter 6 supplies the captures from which a twin is built, and the neural reconstruction and generation methods of Chapter 8 supply its geometry and appearance; what the twin adds is metric accuracy, physical grounding, and a persistent correspondence to a specific real object over its lifecycle. Entertainment (§10.2) builds the same high-fidelity captures as creative content; here they become an operational engineering model wired to a live counterpart, and the city- and planet-scale twins that recur below connect to the GeoAI methods of §11.2. The concept itself traces from Grieves’ product-lifecycle lectures, formalized with Vickers [grieves2017digital], through its aerospace codification for NASA and U.S. Air Force vehicles [glaessgen2012digital], to its industrial maturation [tao2019digital, wang2023survey], where the five-dimension model of Tao et al.makes the data connections between physical entity, virtual entity, and services a first-class element of the architecture.

11.1.2 System Overview

Figure 11.1 draws the twin as a closed loop around its physical asset. Sensing (images, LiDAR, RGB-D scans, onboard IoT telemetry) feeds the construction of a replica that carries geometry, appearance, materials, and physical properties; the replica is simulated forward, kept synchronized by live data assimilation, and queried to predict, and its decisions operate the asset, which is then sensed anew. The three pivotal tasks map onto this loop directly. Task-1 builds the twin (sense and construct), Task-2 makes it behave (model and simulate), and Task-3 keeps it synchronized and turns it to use (assimilate, predict, and act). Table 11.1 collects the benchmarks on which the first two are evaluated; synchronization has no shared benchmark.

11.1.3 Pivotal Task-1: High-Fidelity Twin Construction

The first task builds the twin from sensor captures, and it must deliver four properties that a generic one-shot reconstruction does not guarantee. The twin must be metric (correct at real-world scale), relightable (its appearance separable from capture-time illumination), physically grounded (carrying mass, material, and friction), and actionable (its movable parts and joints encoded so a simulator can drive it). Figure 11.2 sketches the progression from raw captures through geometry and material recovery to a simulatable model.

Geometry and appearance acquisition. The earliest replicas were built by photogrammetry: multiple overlapping photographs of an object, terrain, or structure are captured, and a Structure-from-Motion algorithm recovers camera poses and a sparse metric point cloud, as systematized in COLMAP [schonberger2016structure], after which dense multi-view stereo and meshing produce a surface. Real-time RGB-D fusion in the KinectFusion tradition [newcombe2011kinectfusion] yields metric, watertight geometry over the observed region, and neural implicit-surface methods such as NeuS [wang2021neus] and the detail-preserving Neuralangelo [li2023neuralangelo] recover watertight meshes as the zero-level-set of a learned signed-distance field. A second family optimizes for view synthesis rather than surface quality: NeRF [mildenhall2021nerf], its hash-grid acceleration Instant-NGP [muller2022instant], and the explicit, real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting [kerbl20233d] render novel views with high fidelity but historically produced no clean surface and bake appearance into the representation; surface-aligned variants such as SuGaR [guedon2024sugar] and 2D Gaussian Splatting [huang20242d] narrow this gap by extracting watertight meshes directly from a Gaussian field. Because a twin requires metric scale and an extractable surface, the photogrammetric and implicit-surface lines are load-bearing, with meshing operators such as Poisson surface reconstruction [kazhdan2006poisson] and Marching Cubes [lorensen1998marching] converting a field or point set into geometry; the radiance-field family enters as an appearance and speed substrate, treated in full in Chapter 8.

Inverse rendering and relightable materials. A captured asset whose appearance is baked at scan time only reproduces the object under the one illumination it was scanned in, because each pixel entangles albedo, geometry, and lighting. A twin, by contrast, lives in a simulator where viewpoint and illumination change every frame, so its construction must recover separated physically based rendering (PBR) channels (albedo, roughness, normals) together with an estimate of the environment lighting. Inverse-rendering methods supply exactly this factorization: NeRFactor decomposes a captured radiance field into shape, reflectance, and a single environment light [zhang2021nerfactor], while the differentiable, engine-ready NVDiffRec jointly extracts a triangle mesh, an SVBRDF, and a lighting estimate directly optimizable for downstream rendering [munkberg2022extracting]. The same factorization has been ported onto explicit Gaussians, as in Relightable 3D Gaussians, which attaches normals and a BRDF to each primitive and ray-traces shadows for real-time relighting [gao2024relightable]. Relightability is what lets a twin be composited under novel lighting and rendered consistently inside a physics or sensor simulation.

Physical-property and articulation estimation. A static mesh is viewable but not operable: it has no notion of which surfaces move, with what effort, or under what dynamics. Closing this gap requires a movable-part inventory and the kinematic joints (revolute or prismatic, with axes and limits) that a physics engine can integrate, together with physical parameters such as mass and friction. Ditto recovers part geometry and an articulation model jointly from before-and-after observations of an interaction [jiang2022ditto], and URDFormer predicts a full URDF, the standard interactive description, from a single real image, turning a photograph into a simulatable articulated twin [chen2024urdformer]. Dynamical parameters can be identified directly in a differentiable field representation, as in PAC-NeRF, which estimates geometry and physical parameters together through a differentiable material-point simulator [li2023pacnerf], and PhysGaussian, which integrates Newtonian dynamics into a Gaussian representation so that what is reconstructed can also be simulated [xie2024physgaussian]. Such methods lean heavily on articulated-object datasets, principally the PartNet-Mobility models exposed through the SAPIEN simulator [xiang2020sapien], the fine-grained part hierarchy of PartNet [mo2019partnet], and the cross-category, actionable parts of GAPartNet [geng2023gapartnet]. The resulting articulated, parameterized model is the input to the behavioral simulation of Task-2.

Datasets and metrics. Construction quality is measured against scanned-object and scene corpora (Table 11.1). At the object level, the recent Digital Twin Catalog provides a large set of digital-twin-quality scans with millimeter geometry, photorealistic materials, and an explicit relighting evaluation [dong2025dtc], complementing the real-scanned OmniObject3D [wu2023omniobject3d], the simulation-ready Google Scanned Objects [downs2022googleGSO], the artist-authored, PBR-annotated ABO [collins2022abo], the large Objaverse collection [deitke2023objaverse], and the in-the-wild Common Objects in 3D [reizenstein2021common]. At the scene level, twins are evaluated on ScanNet [dai2017scannet], Matterport3D [chang2017matterport3d], the photorealistic Replica reconstructions [straub2019replica], and the commodity-LiDAR ARKitScenes [baruch2021arkitscenes], with metric-geometry benchmarks such as Tanks and Temples supplying laser-scan ground truth [knapitsch2017tanks]. Geometry is reported with Chamfer distance, F-score at a stated threshold, and normal consistency; appearance with PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; and, for twins specifically, an added relighting error that penalizes appearance that fails to transfer across illumination.

11.1.4 Pivotal Task-2: Physics-Based Modeling and Behavioral Simulation

The second task makes the constructed replica behave. Geometry is not behavior: a twin must reproduce its asset’s dynamics, not merely its shape, so the static model of Task-1 is coupled to a physics, behavioral, or surrogate engine and run forward as an executable model whose parameters are fit to the real asset (Figure 11.3).

Physics engines. The behavioral substrate of a twin is a simulator that integrates its dynamics. MuJoCo provides accurate rigid-body contact dynamics and is the de facto standard for model-based control [todorov2012mujoco]; the open-source PyBullet offers a widely used free alternative spanning rigid and soft bodies [coumans2021]; and SAPIEN specializes in part-level interaction with large articulated objects [xiang2020sapien], the natural runtime for the actionable twins of Task-1. GPU-accelerated platforms couple photorealistic rendering with physics at scale, exemplified by NVIDIA Isaac Sim11 1 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim on the Omniverse stack and its successor Isaac Lab22 2 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab, with newer GPU-first simulators such as Genesis33 3 https://genesis-embodied-ai.github.io/ and the accelerator-native MuJoCo MJX pushing throughput further; deformable phenomena such as cloth and fluids are handled by unified particle and material-point (MPM) solvers.

Differentiable simulation and system identification. A twin is only behaviorally faithful if its physical parameters match the real asset, which makes parameter estimation central. Differentiable simulators expose gradients of simulated outcomes with respect to physical parameters, turning system identification into gradient-based optimization: DiffTaichi compiles differentiable physical simulators from high-level code [hu2020difftaichi], Brax provides massively parallel differentiable rigid-body dynamics on accelerators [freeman2021brax], and gradSim couples differentiable simulation with differentiable rendering to backpropagate from video pixels all the way to mass, friction, and elasticity [jatavallabhula2021gradsim]. A twin can thus be calibrated to its counterpart from observation rather than hand-tuned.

Surrogate and physics-informed models. High-fidelity simulation is often too slow to run in the synchronization loop of Task-3, so twins frequently substitute a reduced or learned surrogate. Physics-informed neural networks embed governing partial differential equations directly in the training loss, solving forward and inverse problems with scarce data [raissi2019physics], a strategy situated within the broader programme of physics-informed machine learning [karniadakis2021physics]. Reduced-order modeling, identified early as a key enabling technology for digital twins, compresses a high-fidelity simulation to real-time evaluation [hartmann2018model], and the hybrid-twin paradigm couples such a physics-based reduced model with a data-driven correction term to absorb unmodeled effects [chinesta2020virtual].

Real-to-sim for policy learning. A faithful behavioral twin is also the substrate on which robot policies are trained and validated before deployment, which connects this task to the manipulation methods of §9.1 and the reasoning of Chapter 7. The reality gap between simulation and the physical world is bridged by randomizing visual appearance [tobin2017domain] and dynamics [peng2018sim] during training, and recent real-to-sim-to-real pipelines build a twin of the workspace from a quick scan and use it to robustify learned policies, as in RialTo [torne2024reconciling]. A complementary line argues that an exact twin is not always necessary: ACDC instead generates geometrically and semantically similar “digital cousins,” trading exact correspondence for robustness and zero-shot transfer [dai2024automated], sharpening by contrast what a true digital twin provides.

11.1.5 Pivotal Task-3: Real-Time Synchronization and Predictive Operation

The third task is the one that earns the name twin: it maintains the automated bidirectional coupling between model and asset that defines a twin [kritzinger2018digital], and turns that coupling to use. Figure 11.4 previews the pipeline, from a live sensor stream through data assimilation to prediction and a control signal fed back to the physical asset.

Data assimilation and state estimation. Keeping the twin synchronized is a state-estimation problem: the model’s latent state must be continually corrected toward the incoming measurements. The classical recursive estimator is the Kalman filter [kalman1960new], and for the nonlinear, high-dimensional systems typical of physical twins the ensemble Kalman filter provides a Monte-Carlo data-assimilation scheme that propagates an ensemble of states to forecast error statistics [evensen1994sequential]. At the level of an entire engineered system, a probabilistic graphical model casts data-driven model adaptation as Bayesian state estimation with end-to-end uncertainty quantification [kapteyn2021probabilistic], so that predictive twins can be assembled and updated at scale and their predictions carry calibrated confidence rather than point estimates.

Predictive operation across domains. The synchronized twin is queried to anticipate rather than merely to monitor, and the applications follow the asset. In manufacturing, the twin couples machine geometry to live telemetry for prognostics and health management, estimating remaining useful life and scheduling maintenance before failure [tao2018digital]. At urban scale, a city digital twin fuses a semantically rich 3D model with sensor and simulation layers to support planning and what-if analysis, as in the Herrenberg study [dembski2020urban] and national programmes built on CityGML foundations [soon2017citygml], a layer that connects directly to the GeoAI methods of §11.2. In healthcare, patient-specific anatomical twins driven by physiological models support precision diagnosis and treatment planning, with cardiology an early exemplar [corralacero2020digital] and a growing body of work surveyed across the field [katsoulakis2024digital]; the medical twin is developed in §12.1. In aerospace, where the paradigm was first codified, a structural twin mirrors an as-flown airframe to predict fatigue [glaessgen2012digital]; and in agriculture, field and crop twins fuse geospatial layers with growth models for precision management [verdouw2021digital].

11.1.6 Established Tools and Systems

Capture, authoring, and render runtimes. The construction stage is served by spatial-capture products such as Matterport44 4 https://matterport.com/ for interiors and sites, the mobile scanner Polycam55 5 https://poly.cam/, the photogrammetry pipelines RealityScan66 6 https://www.realityscan.com/ (formerly RealityCapture) and Agisoft Metashape77 7 https://www.agisoft.com/, and, as an integrating substrate, NVIDIA Omniverse with OpenUSD88 8 https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/, which provides the scene description and real-time rendering on which twins are assembled. Game and render engines such as Unreal Engine99 9 https://www.unrealengine.com/ and Unity, the latter packaged for industry as Unity Industry1010 10 https://unity.com/products/unity-industry, serve as the interactive runtimes for the resulting models.

Industrial twin platforms. The operational layer is dominated by enterprise platforms that wire CAD geometry to live telemetry. Siemens Teamcenter1111 11 https://plm.sw.siemens.com/en-US/teamcenter/ drives product twins from a PLM backbone; Ansys Twin Builder1212 12 https://www.ansys.com/products/digital-twin/ansys-twin-builder couples reduced-order models to 3D physics; Dassault’s 3DEXPERIENCE markets sensor-driven “virtual twin” experiences1313 13 https://www.3ds.com/virtual-twin; and cloud services including PTC ThingWorx1414 14 https://www.ptc.com/en/products/thingworx, AWS IoT TwinMaker1515 15 https://aws.amazon.com/iot-twinmaker/, Azure Digital Twins1616 16 https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/digital-twins, and Bentley iTwin1717 17 https://www.bentley.com/software/itwin-platform/ maintain live twin graphs of factories, buildings, and infrastructure, with GE Vernova1818 18 https://www.gevernova.com/software/ specializing in energy-asset twins.

City-scale systems and interoperability standards. At geo-scale, procedural and streaming platforms such as Esri ArcGIS CityEngine1919 19 https://www.esri.com/en-us/arcgis/products/arcgis-cityengine/overview, Cesium with 3D Tiles2020 20 https://cesium.com/, Google’s photorealistic 3D Tiles2121 21 https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/tile/3d-tiles, and NVIDIA Earth-22222 22 https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/high-performance-computing/earth-2/ build and serve city- to planet-scale twins, with national programmes such as Virtual Singapore as flagship deployments. What keeps such twins portable across this fragmented tooling are open standards: OpenUSD for scene description, IFC (ISO 16739) for building information, CityGML for semantic city models, and OGC 3D Tiles for streaming massive geospatial geometry, alongside the framework and terminology standards ISO 23247 and ISO/IEC 30173. The data layer feeding these geo-scale twins is the subject of §11.2.

11.1.7 Challenges

A twin must be high-fidelity, live, and scalable at once, and these three demands pull against one another. The open problems follow from that tension: scaling construction from an object to a city, keeping the twin current, validating that it is accurate rather than merely photorealistic, coupling several physical domains in real time, and making twins interoperable without exposing the spaces they capture.

Scalability to Large and City Scale.

Building a twin of a single object is now routine; building one of a city is not. City twins must convert heterogeneous source data into semantically structured models (CityGML levels of detail) and stream them efficiently (3D Tiles), and the reconstruction itself must scale, motivating divide-and-conquer pipelines for large-scene Gaussian splatting [liu2025citygaussian]. Data integration and cross-format interoperability remain the named bottlenecks at this scale.

Synchronization Latency and Data Assimilation.

A twin is only as useful as it is current, and maintaining real-time correspondence across an edge-fog-cloud hierarchy is hard: assimilation must keep pace with the asset’s dynamics, and the “liveness gap” between the asset’s true state and the twin’s estimate degrades every downstream prediction. Scaling data assimilation to high-dimensional physical systems without violating the update budget is an open problem.

Model Fidelity, Validation, and the Photorealism-Accuracy Tradeoff.

Verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification are the maturity frontier for twins used in consequential decisions. A specific tension recurs: methods such as vanilla Gaussian splatting optimize visual fidelity, not metric accuracy, so a photorealistic reconstruction can still fail a metric tolerance check; surface-aligned variants [guedon2024sugar, huang20242d] narrow but do not close this gap.

Multi-Physics and Multi-Scale Coupling.

Real assets couple mechanics, thermics, fluids, and electromagnetics across scales, and no universal model spans them; coupled systems risk solver instability, and the reduced-order and physics-informed surrogates [hartmann2018model, raissi2019physics] that make twins real-time must do so without discarding the cross-domain interactions that matter.

Standardization, Interoperability, Privacy, and Security.

The proliferation of scene and asset formats (USD, IFC, CityGML, 3D Tiles) keeps twins from composing across vendors, and the always-on capture that a live twin requires raises acute concerns: scanning private interiors and urban space implicates bystanders, and a compromised twin server can leak an asset’s dynamics, configuration, and credentials [wang2023survey]. Designing twins that interoperate while minimizing retained raw data is both a research and a policy frontier.

11.2 GeoAI

11.2.1 Introduction

Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) applies machine learning to geographic data (satellite and UAV imagery, LiDAR, GNSS traces, and IoT sensor streams) to model and act on processes that unfold over terrain, cities, and the Earth system. It makes the geospatial domain a large-scale deployment target for the perception and scene-understanding capabilities surveyed in Part III: the detection, segmentation, and remote-sensing techniques of Chapter 6 (and the aerial and remote-sensing setting of Section 9.4) are here specialized to Earth-observation data and decision workflows at planetary scale.

11.2.2 System Overview

A GeoAI workflow couples heterogeneous geospatial data to models that turn raw observations into spatially explicit decisions (Figure 11.5). Following the application taxonomy of the review by Boutayeb et al. [boutayeb2024geoai], we treat six domains as pivotal tasks: precision agriculture, the urban built environment, environmental monitoring, water resources, disaster management, and public health. The six share their inputs, largely the free Sentinel, Landsat, and MODIS archives, and until recently they shared a modeling pattern as well: a task-specific supervised network or tree ensemble trained for one region and one target, which the foundation models at the end of the section are beginning to replace. Table 11.2 samples representative data sources, methods, and reported results across the six.

11.2.3 Pivotal Task-1: Precision Agriculture

Precision agriculture tailors irrigation, fertilization, and pest control to the conditions of each field, or each plant, instead of managing a field uniformly. GeoAI supplies the maps and predictions this requires through the complementary mapping, yield-estimation, and irrigation tasks of Figure 11.6.

Crops Mapping. Crop mapping turns a time series of satellite or UAV imagery into a per-pixel crop-type label, and the accuracy gains in recent work track the richness of the temporal signal. Han et al. [han2023spatio] combine a ResNet feature extractor with cross-attention and spatio-temporal self-attention over Sentinel-1 SAR series, reaching 96% overall accuracy on the Brandenburg benchmark. 3D convolutional networks over Sentinel-2 [gallo2023season] and Landsat [MOHAMMADI2023272] series treat time as a third convolution axis, and fusing Sentinel-1 SAR with Sentinel-2 optical data maps rice phenological stages within the season [tiwari2024automated]. Multi-season and SAR–optical inputs consistently beat single-date classification, in part because SAR sees through the cloud that interrupts optical series. At the other end of the resolution range, UAV imagery supports row-level segmentation, where U-Net outperforms LinkNet and PSPNet on sugarcane crop lines [ribeiro2024automated].

Yields Prediction. Yield prediction regresses a continuous productivity estimate from the same imagery, and the usual design has two stages: extract a vegetation index or phenotype, then regress. Random forests over Sentinel-2, RTK GPS, and LiDAR variables predict cotton yield [carneiro2023soil], and an ensemble over Landsat-8 NDVI and agro-meteorological data reports R2 0.99 for tea yield on its test set [ramzan2023multimodal]. UAV imagery earns its extra cost where the target is a fine-grained phenotype: Mask R-CNN extracts wheat-spike phenotypes that feed a yield regressor [PengWZYLRLSX23], and a linear mixed-effect model on fixed-wing UAV multispectral imagery estimates rice leaf-area index and biomass [rs11111371].

Precision Irrigation. Irrigation closes the loop, turning maps and estimates into water-delivery decisions [AbioyeAMBIROOR20]. One line of work detects irrigation infrastructure at scale, such as center-pivot systems in Sentinel-2 series with Mask R-CNN [AlbuquerqueCSLB21] or irrigation types in NAIP aerial images with a U-Net and transfer learning [RaeiANSPA22]. The other controls water locally: a drone system fuses RGB, thermal-infrared, and GPS data to find the driest zones of a field and sets valve flow with a random forest [JalajamonyNMF23].

11.2.4 Pivotal Task-2: Urban Planning, Logistics, and Transport

The second task turns GeoAI on the built environment. Figure 11.7 presents five complementary tasks on a shared urban context, from built structure and temporal change to services, transport, and green infrastructure.

Urban Data Extraction. Land use and built form are classified from overhead and street-level imagery, and fusing the two views resolves ambiguities that neither settles alone. A fine-tuned EfficientNet classifies the 21 land-use classes of the UC Merced set [AlemK22], while a dual-branch network that pairs dilated convolutions on Google Earth imagery with an attention-based multi-view network on Street View detects informal urban villages [ChenFNYGYGL22].

Urban Dynamics. Temporal models capture how urban form changes over time. An LSTM with attention simulates urban densification from land-use rasters of 2000, 2010, and 2020 [el2023long], and a pix2pix GAN predicts land-use and land-cover change by conditioning Landsat imagery on planning indicators [SunMFWH21]. A static quantity such as urban solar exposure needs no temporal model; a feed-forward network on building geometry, occupancy, and orientation suffices [tehrani2024predicting].

Smart Cities. The service layer turns these representations into live operation: video georeferencing and small-object detection inside an urban digital twin [HuLYHCYLY23], LSTM parking-occupancy prediction served to a mobile application [CanliT21], and detection of commercial signage in Street View imagery to map urban commerce [YeWKXC19].

Logistics and Transport. Movement through the city splits into two problems with different tools. Flow forecasting is temporal: bus arrival times are predicted from a traffic-density matrix with recurrent and convolutional models [PanovskiZ20], a hybrid GRU–LSTM forecasts traffic from OpenStreetMap and GIS features [ZafarHSCM22], IODRNN decomposes its outputs incrementally to remove the lag in GNSS-based forecasts [LuMPXC24], and itinerary recommendation adds a denoising autoencoder with collaborative learning [ChenZCWC20]. Infrastructure mapping is a segmentation problem: open LiDAR point clouds inventory rockfall-prone road slopes [RuaNAM23], SegNet on RapidEye imagery updates rural road networks [kearney2020maintaining], and U-Net with PointNet++ performs panoptic segmentation of railway environments from multimodal LiDAR [grandio2023multimodal].

Green Infrastructure and Bio Security. Vegetation monitoring moves from coverage to function to threat, and each step demands finer spatial and spectral resolution than the last. A semi-supervised DeepLabv3+ maps urban tree cover nationwide from high-resolution satellite imagery [guo2023nationwide]; a Faster R-CNN tree inventory identifies seven canopy species and, through geographically weighted regression, their effect on land-surface temperature [das2022geoai]; and biosecurity surveillance of invasive forest pests uses multispectral aerial imagery, where an instance-segmentation model reached an F1-score of 79% against 58% for a tile classifier [carnegie2023airborne].

11.2.5 Pivotal Task-3: Environmental Monitoring

The third task observes the Earth system itself, across the three fronts of Figure 11.8.

Climate Change. Long-term land-surface change is read mostly through vegetation records spanning decades of Landsat, Sentinel, and MODIS data, and the methods trade spatial detail against record length. Lou et al. [lou2023deep] map land use and land cover on Google Earth Engine with a deep network and find rapid greening of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau from 1988 to 2018. Deep-learning-enhanced spatiotemporal fusion reconstructs long-term NDVI in the Danjiang River Basin [wang2023applying], random forests retrieve vegetation phenology from MODIS more accurately than rule-based methods [XinLLLZ20], and a bidirectional LSTM produces the GLASS 250 m leaf-area-index product (version 6) from MODIS reflectance [ma2022development].

Atmospheric Chemistry. Atmospheric composition is retrieved by learning the map from satellite radiances and meteorology to ground-measured concentrations. Nitrogen dioxide is the most studied target, estimated hourly from Sentinel-5P, meteorology, and sensor data with XGBoost [kim2021importance] and daily across China with a random forest and K-means clustering over OMI data [dou2021estimates]. A convolutional autoencoder coupled to WRF-Chem models volcanic SO2 dispersion [opio2023modeling], AQNet fuses Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-5P to predict NO2, O3, and PM10 [rowley2023predicting], an LSTM forecasts five pollutants from ground-station series [seng2021spatiotemporal], and a deep network derives aerosol absorption from the OMI ultraviolet aerosol index, validated against AERONET [SunVVL21].

Environmental Impacts. Impact assessment links land-use change to ecological outcomes, and it is judged not only on accuracy but on whether it can name the responsible driver, which is why explainability recurs here. Neural networks on multi-temporal Landsat land-cover maps assess urban ecological quality [alqadhi2024applying]; multiscale geographically weighted regression, random forests, and SHAP relate agricultural land to PM2.5 concentrations [gianquintieri2024implementation]; and interpretable ensembles measure the effect of climate change on agricultural land suitability [ShevchenkoLTBGKNSKM24].

11.2.6 Pivotal Task-4: Water Resources Management and Precipitation Forecasting

The fourth task addresses four complementary aspects of water resources in Figure 11.9.

Hydrological Modeling. Convolutional models dominate local surface geometry. Space-time image velocimetry on UAV video estimates river velocity and discharge, validated with LiDAR-derived terrain [islam2023mutual]; U-Net extracts drainage ditches from LiDAR in low-relief terrain [du2024drainage]; quadtree decomposition with multi-scale CNNs extracts coastlines at lower cost than FCN and U-Net baselines [sun2024quadtree]; and a reflectance-transformation CNN maps bathymetry from Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery [ChanZX0WA24]. At basin scale, where streamflow depends on several precipitation products (MODIS, CHIRPS, MSWEP), super-ensembles that weight multiple regressors take over [wegayehu2023super].

Groundwater. No optical sensor sees the water table, so groundwater models work from proxy variables and gravimetry. Static delineation of recharge or shallow-groundwater zones uses tree ensembles and deep networks over hydrogeological and remote-sensing variables [al2024hybrid, sahour2022identification, nhu2024new]. GRACE/GRACE-FO measures total-water-storage changes; isolating groundwater requires auxiliary estimates of other water-storage components. Storage forecasting uses these gravity-derived anomalies, which a CNN–LSTM forecasts with an RMSE of 44.92 mm/month [seo2021predicting] and which machine-learning regressors downscale to catchment resolution [sabzehee2023enhancing].

Water Quality. Water quality is regressed from spectral reflectance against in-situ samples, and accuracy follows the optical signature of the constituent. Pigments with a clear signature are tractable: fusion of data and classifiers through higher-order SVD estimates chlorophyll-a in Lake Nicaragua [sun2021ensemble], and on UAV multispectral and hyperspectral data of a karst wetland, transformers and gradient boosting predict phycocyanin, dissolved oxygen, and chlorophyll-a, interpreted with SHAP [yang2023monitoring]. Dissolved nutrients remain harder because their optical fingerprint is faint, whether estimated from MODIS with a spatiotemporal deep belief network [wu2022spatiotemporal] or from Landsat-8 with an ANN [vakili2020determination]. Optical water types themselves can be classified from Sentinel-2 with an SVM [dasilva2021machine].

Precipitation Forecasting. Precipitation nowcasting predicts the next radar frames from the current sequence. HST-AFP fuses radar echoes with weather forecasts through attention [niu2023heterogeneous], STIN adds humidity, wind, and temperature [jin2023spatiotemporal], and PFST-LSTM adds pseudo-flow estimation to follow echo motion [luo2020pfst]; at longer range, multi-model ensembles post-process numerical weather prediction [sengoz2023machine].

11.2.7 Pivotal Task-5: Disaster Management

The fifth task covers the disaster lifecycle (hazard or susceptibility mapping, event observation, and damage assessment) for earthquakes, floods, and forest fires, arranged as a grid in Figure 11.10.

Earthquakes. For earthquakes the lifecycle includes hazard mapping, event-related observation, and damage assessment; these tasks should not be equated with reliable prediction of an exact earthquake. A CNN over elevation, vector, and attribute data maps seismic risk in north-eastern India [jena2021earthquake], and encoder–decoder LSTMs [xiong2022gnss] and neural networks [hafeez2021possible] detect ionospheric anomalies in GNSS total-electron-content data around events such as the 2019 Pakistan earthquake. After the event, LiDAR, orthophotos, and multispectral imagery estimate building vulnerability [torres2019integration], and change detection on multi-temporal photogrammetric point clouds classifies structural damage into grades [zahs2023classification].

Floods. Floods lean on radar. Forecasting fuses meteorological, hydrological, and crowdsourced data, either comparing classical learners under cross-validation [PuttinaovaratH20] or with a ConvLSTM that learns spatial rainfall patterns and their temporal dynamics jointly [MoishinDPRA21]. Inundation mapping falls to SAR segmentation, which sees through cloud, as in an attention-augmented U-Net on dual-polarized Sentinel-1 imagery [LiWCWJG22].

Forest Fires. Fire has the fullest lifecycle. Susceptibility is predicted from drone imagery with temperature and humidity sensing [rathod2023multipurpose], or from elevation, vegetation indices, and hydrometeorology with a neuro-fuzzy system tuned by an artificial bee colony [PHAM2024102392]. Detection is trained on drone RGB and infrared imagery such as the FLAME 2 dataset [ChenHWOARFCRW22] and can be distributed across sites with federated learning [SiddiqueADBAA24]. Burn scars are delineated afterward by a U-Net on PlanetScope RGB and near-infrared imagery, with F1 up to 0.94 [ChoPKKLS23].

11.2.8 Pivotal Task-6: Healthcare

The sixth task brings GeoAI to public health, where spatial signals couple disease and environment (Figure 11.11).

Infectious Diseases and Toxins. Disease surveillance gains most from leading indicators, since search queries and geotagged posts surface an outbreak before clinical reporting does. Influenza forecasting combines CDC surveillance data with Google Flu Trends and climate in a multi-stage LSTM [DBLP:journals/access/VennaTGRMN19], with geotagged Twitter posts in a neural network tuned by an artificial-tree algorithm [hu2018prediction], and with search frequencies and health records in a network-based regression that exploits synchrony across U.S. states [lu2019improved]; dengue in China is forecast from climate and weekly case counts, with support-vector regression performing best [guo2017developing]. FINDER shows the payoff most clearly: it geolocates web-search signals of foodborne illness to restaurants, and the restaurants it flagged were three times more likely to pose food-safety risks than those found by complaint-based inspection [SadilekCDMSBJRG18].

Pandemics. A pandemic shifts the question to transmission across geography. Geospatial similarity learning predicts respiratory-virus spread in new regions [ZhaoHJCWWYR23], and spatio-temporal regression tracks COVID-19 in Brazil [da2021covid]. Detection networks catch what an epidemic curve misses: gatherings of people and vehicles in satellite imagery [atek2022geospatial], proximity between re-identified individuals in video [ZhangLCZJ23], and the drop in PM2.5 during lockdown, measured from MODIS and Sentinel-5P [TanLGJ22].

Public Health. Chronic exposure links where people are to what they breathe. On the mobility side, mobile health uses wireless devices for clinical and public-health purposes [kahn2010mobile], and the MD2K center turns mobile-sensor streams into markers of smoking, craving, and stress [KumarAAaBCCCEEG15]. On the pollutant side, a geographically weighted gradient-boosting machine [zhan2017spatiotemporal] and a neural network over MODIS aerosol optical depth and land-use features [di2016assessing] map daily PM2.5 across China and the United States. Exposure assessment is only as sharp as the coarser of the two spatial scales.

11.2.9 Established Tools and Systems

Cloud geospatial platforms provide planetary-scale storage and analysis next to the data. Google Earth Engine2323 23 https://earthengine.google.com/ offers a petabyte-scale archive of satellite imagery with server-side analysis, Microsoft’s Planetary Computer2424 24 https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/ pairs open Earth-observation data with a Python/STAC API, and commercial providers such as Esri ArcGIS2525 25 https://www.arcgis.com/ and Descartes Labs2626 26 https://www.descarteslabs.com/ deliver hosted GeoAI pipelines for enterprise and government users.

Open-source GIS and ML toolkits carry the modeling layer. QGIS2727 27 https://qgis.org/ is the de facto open desktop GIS, while deep-learning libraries tailored to raster geospatial data, such as TorchGeo2828 28 https://github.com/microsoft/torchgeo and Raster Vision2929 29 https://rastervision.io/, bridge PyTorch to satellite imagery, and Sentinel Hub3030 30 https://www.sentinel-hub.com/ streamlines on-demand access and processing of Copernicus archives.

Open Earth-observation programmes supply the data foundation: the European Copernicus programme’s Sentinel constellation and NASA/USGS Landsat provide free, calibrated, multi-decadal imagery, complemented by gravimetric (GRACE/GRACE-FO), atmospheric (OMI, Sentinel-5P), and high-resolution commercial (WorldView, PlanetScope) sources that recur throughout the methods above.

11.2.10 Toward Geospatial Foundation Models and GeoLLMs

Almost every method surveyed above is a task-specific supervised model: a CNN, random forest, LSTM, or GAN trained from scratch for one crop, one hazard, or one pollutant. That design is being displaced by the same pretraining-and-transfer paradigm that reshaped the rest of the field (Chapter 7), and the geospatial community has begun building its own foundation models. Masked-autoencoding backbones lead the shift: SatMAE [cong2022satmae] adapts the masked image model to the temporal and multi-spectral structure of satellite imagery, Scale-MAE [reed2023scalemae] makes the pretext task explicitly scale-aware so a single backbone serves the huge ground-sample-distance range Earth observation spans, and Prithvi [jakubik2023foundation] packages such a backbone as a generalist model fine-tunable across flood mapping, burn-scar delineation, and crop segmentation. A single pretrained encoder thus stands in for the dozens of bespoke feature extractors that populate the tasks above.

The language side is moving just as fast. RemoteCLIP [liu2024remoteclip] aligns remote-sensing imagery with text, giving open-vocabulary retrieval and zero-shot classification without per-class labels; GeoChat [kuckreja2024geochat] grounds a large vision-language model on overhead imagery so an analyst can query a scene, ask for region-level descriptions, and obtain referring localizations in dialogue; and SegEarth-R1 [li2025segearth] pushes further into pixel-level geospatial reasoning, generating segmentation masks from implicit, reasoning-heavy queries rather than fixed class names. These systems inherit the multimodal reasoning and world-model machinery of Part III and specialize it to Earth observation, pointing toward GeoAI workflows driven by natural-language instructions rather than hand-built per-task pipelines.

11.2.11 Challenges

Most of the methods above were trained and tested in one region on one sensor, and that pattern shapes the open problems: whether a model transfers across regions and sensors, how heterogeneous and uneven data are reconciled, whether pipelines run at the scale and latency that operations need, and what new failure modes the geospatial foundation models bring.

Generalization across Regions and Sensors.

Few of the studies surveyed test a model outside the region, season, or sensor it was trained on, so their reported accuracies say little about transfer. Crop calendars, building styles, and spectral responses vary from place to place, and a crop map or flood segmenter trained on one country or one satellite can degrade sharply on another. Pretrained backbones such as Prithvi [jakubik2023foundation] are motivated by exactly this gap, but systematic cross-region benchmarks remain rare.

Data Heterogeneity and Quality.

Geospatial workflows combine imagery, sensor streams, vector layers, and crowdsourced inputs that differ in resolution, revisit time, and reliability, and the volume of these archives makes curation itself demanding [boutayeb2024geoai]. Open-access data needs quality control before it can serve as training labels. Geospatial data is also strategically sensitive, which raises questions of data sovereignty, and adversarial manipulation of inputs is a threat that none of the methods above addresses.

Scale and Latency.

Operational services such as flood mapping during an event, precipitation nowcasting, and traffic forecasting must ingest new acquisitions continuously and update their models as satellites deliver data, which strains pipelines built around one-off training runs. When several models are chained in one workflow, validation and deployment cost grow with each link, pushing systems toward distributed, modular architectures.

Open Problems for Geospatial Foundation Models.

The foundation models of the previous subsection bring problems of their own: pretraining that fuses radar, optical, and hyperspectral sensors at very different resolutions; evaluation benchmarks that test geospatial reasoning rather than image-level recognition; and grounding language output in physically consistent, georeferenced coordinates, which dialogue systems such as GeoChat [kuckreja2024geochat] do not yet guarantee.

11.3 Aerospace Engineering

11.3.1 Introduction

Aerospace engineering designs and operates systems that work within and beyond the Earth’s atmosphere, and its missions are spatial problems at their core. Rendezvous and docking (RVD), on-orbit servicing (OOS), debris inspection, and planetary landing and roving all depend on estimating three-dimensional structure and relative motion, often of a non-cooperative target that carries no markers, while communication delays rule out continuous ground control. Both spacecraft autonomy (e.g., , guidance, navigation, and control) and human-in-the-loop operations (e.g., , situational awareness for ground controllers) therefore rest on spatial perception and reasoning over geometry, relative motion, semantics, and physical constraints.

Aerospace engineering is thus a demanding deployment target for the perception and reasoning capabilities surveyed in Part III: the detection, segmentation, pose-estimation, and 3D-reconstruction techniques of Chapter 6 and the planning and decision-making methods of Chapter 7 are here specialized to non-cooperative orbital targets, extreme illumination, and long-horizon autonomy under radiation-hardened compute and communication latency.

11.3.2 System Overview

The value of spatial intelligence in aerospace lies less in any single perception module than in the closed autonomy loop it serves (Figure 11.12): onboard and ground-based sensing (monocular and multi-view cameras, LiDAR, telemetry) feeds a perception-reasoning-decision core, whose commands change the scene that is sensed next. The four pivotal tasks treated below are complementary stages of this loop. Satellite pose estimation supplies the geometric anchor, recovering where a target is and how it is oriented; spacecraft detection, segmentation, and parts recognition enrich that anchor with structural semantics, identifying what the target is and which functional components it exposes; operator agents lift this perceptual state into high-level reasoning, planning, and human-facing decision support; and planetary robotics closes the loop on the surface, coupling perception, localization, and planning into physical exploration and sampling. Table 11.5, after Task-4, consolidates representative benchmarks and metrics across all four.

11.3.3 Pivotal Task-1: Satellite Pose Estimation

Vision-based satellite pose estimation predicts the 6-DoF relative position and orientation of a target spacecraft from monocular or multi-view imagery; it is the geometric anchor of the autonomy loop and a prerequisite for rendezvous, docking, and on-orbit servicing. It specializes the 6-DoF estimation problem of Chapter 6 to a hostile setting: harsh illumination, specular reflections, little texture, and a severe gap between the synthetic images models are trained on and the real images they meet in orbit. Figure 11.13 traces the pipeline from method to evaluation.

Traditional methods relied on hand-engineered features (e.g., , Harris corners, SIFT, SURF, and ORB) or model-based tracking [d2014poseestimationuncooperativespacecraft], which are sensitive to noise and domain shift, and deep learning has since become dominant [proencca2020deepURSO]. The first deep models regress the pose directly with CNNs [garcia2021lspnet], as in the Spacecraft Pose Network (SPN) [sharma2020neuralposeestimation], a GoogLeNet-based network [phisannupawong2020vision], and a VGG backbone [sonawani2020assistive], trained on synthetic data and on laboratory imagery that simulates an on-orbit assembly operation. SPNv2 [park2024robustspacecraftposeestimation] made multi-task learning the prevailing design: its shared encoder jointly predicts keypoints, a direct pose regression, and foreground segmentation, and it narrows the synthetic-to-real gap by online domain refinement, adapting the network’s normalization layers on unlabeled target imagery at deployment. Hybrid pipelines estimate a coarse pose with a deep model and refine it with geometry-based optimization, keeping the final estimate physically consistent; early work classified discretized viewpoints with a CNN [sharma2018pose], and the same coarse-to-fine pattern now extends to 6-DoF tracking with stereo event cameras [liu2025stereo].

SPEED [Sharma2019SpacecraftPE] and SPEED+ [park2022speed+] are the standard testbeds (Table 11.3): both pair a large synthetic training set with laboratory hardware-in-the-loop test images, so that the synthetic-to-real gap is measured rather than assumed, and the Satellite Pose Estimation Challenge built on them fixed common training regimes, input formats, and metrics [kisantal2020satellitechallenge]. CubeSat-CDT [musallam2022cubesatcdt] adds trajectories of a symmetric target, so that temporal methods and pose ambiguity can be evaluated. Evaluation reports translation and rotation error as defined for SPEED [Sharma2019SpacecraftPE], often with 2D reprojection or keypoint error [garcia2021lspnet]; results are given separately on synthetic and real test sets, and robustness to illumination, occlusion, and background clutter is probed explicitly [park2024robustspacecraftposeestimation].

11.3.4 Pivotal Task-2: Spacecraft Detection, Segmentation, and Parts Recognition

Detection, segmentation, and parts recognition enrich the geometric anchor of Task-1 with structural semantics, telling what the target is and which functional components it exposes; proximity operations, on-orbit servicing, debris inspection, and collision avoidance all depend on this. The detection and segmentation machinery of Chapter 6 meets the obstacles of Task-1 here (strong illumination variation, specular metallic surfaces, little texture) and, in addition, a scarcity of annotated real imagery. The stack runs from coarse presence to fine structure: detection localizes the spacecraft, segmentation delineates its silhouette, and parts recognition resolves its components, as Figure 11.14 illustrates.

Convolutional and transformer architectures now carry all three stages [shao2023satellite]. Detection is formulated as bounding-box or keypoint localization, with lightweight saliency-driven detectors for onboard compute, while encoder–decoder networks, pyramid attention modules, and hybrid 2D/3D architectures delineate silhouettes and component boundaries [zhao20223dnoncooperativespacecraft]. Parts recognition (solar panels, antennas, thrusters, reflectors) often adds semantic priors or 3D geometric reasoning to stay robust under occlusion. Two recent lines reduce the dependence on manual labels: prompt-guided Segment Anything (SAM) automates the annotation of space targets [zhang2024automaticspacetarget], and diffusion priors support few-shot segmentation and adaptation to unseen spacecraft [li2025exploitingdiffusion].

The datasets in Table 11.4 differ along a few axes. Labels range from whole-object masks (SwissCube [hu2021widedepthrange], a pose dataset that also provides CubeSat masks, and SPARK [musallam2021spacecraft]) and object-level boxes (STAR-24K [zhang2022star24K]) to component labels, from a single component (the solar panels of the Tsinghua dataset [li2020noncooperativeobjectdetection]) up to nine (Spacecraft-DS [cao2024spacecraftds]). Most are rendered (Unity3D for SPARK, Unreal Engine 4 for UESD [zhao2023intelligentUESD]), whereas Spacecraft-DS uses hardware-in-the-loop capture to narrow the synthetic-to-real gap. The Adelaide dataset [dung2021spacecraftdataset] fixed the common three-component scheme (solar panel, main body, antenna), which Shao et al. [shao2023satellite] extended to video sequences rendered under three illumination conditions and several relative-motion modes; Zhao et al. [zhao20223dnoncooperativespacecraft] carried the same labels to 3D point clouds, and NCSTP [liu2025largencstp] raised the scale to 200,000 images of satellites, debris, and rocks. Detection is scored by mean average precision and segmentation by IoU, as in Chapter 6.

11.3.5 Pivotal Task-3: Operator Agents

Operator agents lift the perceptual state recovered by Tasks 1 and 2 into reasoning, planning, and decision support, monitoring, interpreting, and controlling spacecraft systems to reduce operator workload and allow more autonomous mission execution. They are the aerospace instance of the planning and decision-making capabilities of Chapter 7. Rooted in rule-based and model-driven architectures, their role has expanded from health monitoring and scheduling to high-level control in dialogue with human experts, a history that runs from symbolic planning through multi-agent coordination to foundation-model reasoning (Figure 11.15).

Early operator-agent architectures were built on symbolic reasoning, constraint-based planning, and expert-system principles. The Remote Agent Experiment [bernard1998designremoteagent] and early autonomous spacecraft-agent prototypes [pell1997autonomousspacecraftagent] demonstrated onboard planning, diagnosis, and execution in deep-space missions. As autonomy requirements grew, multi-agent planning frameworks [colby2016autonomousmultiagent, picard2021autonomousAgents] were introduced to coordinate heterogeneous spacecraft, manage distributed sensing, and schedule jointly across satellite constellations. Large language models changed the design: recent work [rodriguez2024languagemodelsspacecraft, carrasco2025visualoperatoragents] uses LLMs as operator agents that interpret telemetry, generate action plans, respond to anomalies, and follow natural-language mission specifications, and fine-tuned LLMs [zucchelli2025finetunellmSpace, carrasco2024finetuneAutonomousSpacecraft, foutter2024spacellava, carrasco2025llmAutonomousSpacecraft] have been tested in simulators such as Kerbal Space Program (KSP) for guidance, navigation, and control. To meet the interpretability and safety requirements of mission-critical decisions, other studies integrate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [belo2025languageragSpaceSpace], domain knowledge graphs [powell2025questionknowledgegraphssatellite], and structured symbolic reasoning, while hybrid architectures such as MCP-based multi-component agents [wu2025spacemind] combine small specialized models with foundation models to balance computational cost and reasoning depth, particularly for on-orbit servicing.

Evaluation environments followed the same path. The Remote Agent Experiment [bernard1998designremoteagent] supplied real mission scenarios for onboard planning and diagnosis, and multi-agent planning studies [colby2016autonomousmultiagent] supply constellation-level scheduling, resource-allocation, and communication constraints. LLM agents are tested in simulation, chiefly in KSP [carrasco2025llmAutonomousSpacecraft] and in the KSPDG suite of SpaceGym [allen2023spacegym], a set of multi-agent pursuit–evasion differential games built in the KSP engine. Classical agents are scored on planning optimality, constraint satisfaction, fault-diagnosis accuracy, and task completion; LLM agents are additionally judged on adherence to safety constraints, robustness to shifts in telemetry or mission context, and the interpretability of their decisions, which is why uncertainty estimation and human-in-the-loop verification recur throughout this work.

11.3.6 Pivotal Task-4: Planetary Robotics

Planetary robotics closes the autonomy loop on the surface, coupling the perception, localization, and planning capabilities of Chapters 6 and 7 into exploration, navigation, and sampling on the Moon, Mars, and small bodies. Unlike orbital operations, surface missions face uneven and unstructured terrain, delayed and limited communication, restricted sensing, and long stretches of autonomy without continuous human supervision. Figure 11.16 layers the autonomy stack from perception and mapping through hierarchical decision-making to vision-guided manipulation.

Surface robots are organized around a mobility stack that couples perception, localization, mapping, planning, and control, with manipulation and science operations integrated at the task level. Feature tracking, visual odometry, and stereo reconstruction estimate rover motion and build local 3D models of rugged terrain, a capability flown since the Mars Exploration Rovers [maimone2007two]. The Enhanced AutoNav (ENav) system on NASA’s Perseverance rover [toupet2025enav] builds onboard 3D terrain maps, evaluates hazards, and plans safe local traverses under severe computational and communication constraints, and it evaluated terrain over a large majority of the rover’s traversed distance. This autonomy remains embedded in a human-supervised workflow: ground operators specify science goals and route segments, and onboard autonomy resolves local navigation and hazard avoidance.

Research and analogue-testbed systems extend these capabilities to multiple robots, where cooperative visual navigation and shared mapping improve coverage and robustness [bahraini2021autonomousplanetaryrobots]. Hierarchical frameworks decompose behavior across temporal and functional layers, balancing reactive locomotion and obstacle avoidance with deliberative path planning, task scheduling, and mission-level reasoning under safety, power, communication, and resource constraints.

Vision-guided manipulation supports sample collection and instrument deployment by coupling image-based pose estimation with position-controlled or compliant manipulation suited to contact with natural terrain [nickels2010visionplanetaryrobotics]. Learning-based methods are increasingly explored for terrain classification, slip prediction, and traversability estimation, but model-based perception, localization, and planning remain central: safety requirements are stringent, mission-representative labeled data is scarce, onboard computation is constrained, and purely data-driven methods are hard to validate for mission-critical use. Evaluation therefore combines physics-based simulators, mission-derived datasets, and laboratory or analogue-field testbeds that model illumination, dust, wheel–soil interaction, and communication delay, and it reports localization accuracy, map quality, hazard-aware traversal, task completion, and energy use.

11.3.7 Established Tools and Systems

Simulators and rendering engines. Because real orbital imagery is scarce and flight opportunities are expensive, most perception research is trained and validated in simulation. General-purpose game and physics engines have been repurposed as space testbeds: Unity3D and Blender drive the synthetic rendering pipelines behind the SPARK [musallam2021spacecraft] and satellite-component [shao2023satellite] datasets, while the Kerbal Space Program3131 31 https://www.kerbalspaceprogram.com/ engine underpins LLM-agent guidance-navigation-control studies [carrasco2025llmAutonomousSpacecraft]. For decision-making, SpaceGym3232 32 https://github.com/mit-ll/spacegym-kspdg [allen2023spacegym] packages its OrbitDefender2D gridworld games and the KSPDG suite as standardized non-cooperative game environments, and robotics simulators such as NVIDIA Isaac Sim3333 33 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim and Gazebo3434 34 https://gazebosim.org/ provide the wheel-soil and sensor models used to prototype planetary-rover autonomy.

Public challenges. The Satellite Pose Estimation Challenge [kisantal2020satellitechallenge], run by Stanford’s Space Rendezvous Laboratory and the European Space Agency on its Kelvins platform3535 35 https://kelvins.esa.int/, set the protocols that pose estimation now follows, and its SPEED+ edition [park2022speed+] made the synthetic-to-real gap the explicit test.

Flight-proven autonomy systems. The NASA Remote Agent [bernard1998designremoteagent], flown on Deep Space 1, remains the canonical reference for onboard planning, diagnosis, and execution. On planetary surfaces, rover visual odometry [maimone2007two] and the Enhanced AutoNav stack flown on Perseverance [toupet2025enav] set the operational baseline against which hierarchical-autonomy and learning-augmented methods are measured, and current work pairs such flight-qualified stacks with foundation-model agents [wu2025spacemind].

11.3.8 Challenges

Orbital and planetary environments differ from terrestrial ones in ways that terrestrial data does not cover, and the open problems follow the pipeline: the data gap that limits perception, the compute budget that limits deployment, and the trustworthiness requirements that limit certification.

The Unresolved Sim-to-Real Domain Gap.

Autonomous space systems, such as those performing on-orbit servicing or debris removal, are trained largely on simulated data, and simulators do not reproduce the high-dynamic-range lighting of orbit (e.g., , solar glare and deep shadow), intricate material reflections, or sensor degradation such as radiation noise. Models consequently lose accuracy on real imagery, as the hardware-in-the-loop test sets of the pose-estimation challenges show [kisantal2020satellitechallenge, park2022speed+], which keeps domain adaptation and domain randomization central to the field.

Computational Constraints and Real-time Operation.

Spacecraft hardware is bound by size, weight, and power (SWaP) limits and must use radiation-hardened processors that are far less powerful than ground-based GPUs. Running 6-DoF pose estimation or SLAM at the update rates that proximity operations require on such computers calls for model compression, lightweight architectures, and hardware-aware optimization that preserve accuracy while cutting latency and power consumption.

Assuring Trustworthiness and Robustness in Extreme Conditions.

Space missions are safety-critical, so perception must hold up under extreme visual ambiguity, such as estimating the pose of highly symmetric targets like CubeSats [musallam2022cubesatcdt] or navigating where standard reference signals are unavailable. Deployed systems also explain little about their own failures, so operators cannot easily trace a perception anomaly (e.g., , a pose error caused by sensor saturation) to its root cause in time to intervene. Formal verification and interpretable models that guarantee predictable behavior across operating extremes remain open problems.

Chapter 12 Spatial Intelligence for Biomedicine and Natural Sciences

Biomedicine and the natural sciences are, at their core, spatial disciplines: their objects are structures in space, from organs and tissues down to cells and molecules, and understanding them means reasoning about shape, arrangement, and interaction in three dimensions. This chapter turns the spatial-intelligence capabilities of the previous part onto that setting, where in both of its cases the unit of value is the same: a metrically faithful 3D model of a specific physical system, kept in correspondence with real measurements.

In medicine, that model is patient-specific, and it drives a closed loop running from imaging through planning to image-guided intervention. In the natural sciences the same perception and reconstruction machinery operates several orders of magnitude smaller, at the molecular and cellular scale, where the structures reconstructed are the very objects of scientific explanation.

12.1 Medicine and Clinical Healthcare

12.1.1 Introduction

Anatomy is a three-dimensional arrangement of organs with shape, volume, and topology; disease is localized, so that a lesion is a position and an extent in the body frame rather than a label on an image; and intervention is fundamentally an act of navigation, guiding an instrument to a target through tissue that must not be harmed.

The perception machinery of Chapter 6 (detection, segmentation, depth, pose) and the reconstruction and generation of Chapter 8 reappear here, specialized to volumetric data, to registration across modalities and time, and to a regulatory setting in which a wrong answer harms a patient. The unit of analysis is the individual patient and the individual procedure: the molecular and cellular scale belongs to the natural sciences (§12.2), the generic digital twin, of which the patient-specific medical twin below is a specialization, to §11.1, and the population scale of spatial epidemiology to the GeoAI of §11.2.

12.1.2 System Overview

Figure 12.1 draws clinical spatial intelligence as a closed loop around the patient: multimodal imaging (computed tomography, magnetic resonance, ultrasound, endoscopy, pathology) is acquired and the anatomy perceived, a patient-specific 3D model is built and a plan formed, the plan is executed under image guidance, and the outcome is imaged anew. Registration connects the image, patient, and instrument frames throughout this pipeline; the recurring difficulty is keeping the virtual model aligned with the physical patient as tissue moves and deforms. The three pivotal tasks map onto the loop directly (Task-1 perceives, Task-2 models and plans, Task-3 acts), and Table 12.1 collects their benchmarks.

12.1.3 Pivotal Task-1: Volumetric Medical Image Perception

The first task perceives the anatomy. Medical perception is intrinsically volumetric: it converts a voxel grid into delineated 3D anatomical objects with measurable shape and volume, localizes disease in the body frame, and aligns observations across modalities and time. Figure 12.2 illustrates three complementary outputs: segmented organs, a localized candidate finding, and a cross-modal alignment; these tasks need not form a serial pipeline.

Volumetric segmentation. Segmentation is the spatial core of medical imaging, and its history is a move from two-dimensional slices to full volumes. The encoder-decoder U-Net [ronneberger2015unet] founded the area, and its volumetric successors, the 3D U-Net [cciccek20163d] and the V-Net [milletari2016vnet] (which introduced the now-ubiquitous Dice loss to handle voxel class imbalance), moved it into three dimensions. The self-configuring nnU-Net [isensee2021nnunet] adapts preprocessing, architecture, and training to each dataset and remains the baseline that is hard to beat, while transformer encoders such as UNETR [hatamizadeh2022unetr] and Swin-UNETR [hatamizadeh2022swinunetr] add global context. At the whole-body scale, TotalSegmentator [wasserthal2023totalsegmentator] delineates more than a hundred anatomical structures in a single CT, functioning as a spatial atlas in routine use. These methods are evaluated by the Dice similarity coefficient for volumetric overlap and by boundary-geometry metrics, the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance and the average symmetric surface distance, that capture shape errors which overlap alone misses [taha2015metrics].

Medical foundation models. The recent shift mirrors the rest of vision: from per-task specialists to promptable foundation models that segment arbitrary anatomy from spatial prompts. The Segment Anything Model [kirillov2023sam] catalyzed the move, and MedSAM [ma2024medsam] adapted it by fine-tuning on more than a million medical image–mask pairs. Because anatomy is volumetric, the decisive step is into 3D: SAM-Med3D [wang2023sammed3d] replaces the slice-wise encoder with a fully three-dimensional one, and SegVol [du2024segvol] supports both spatial and textual prompts over hundreds of anatomical categories. Much of this work is built on the open MONAI framework [cardoso2022monai], whose medical-aware 3D transforms and model zoo have become standard infrastructure.

Detection and landmark localization. Detection localizes a finding in the body frame, and landmark localization fixes canonical anatomical coordinates; both are spatial tasks distinct from whole-image classification. Lung-nodule detection is anchored by the LIDC-IDRI reference database [armato2011lidcidri] and the LUNA16 benchmark [setio2017luna16], which standardized evaluation on the free-response operating characteristic (sensitivity against false positives per scan). Anatomical landmarks can be found by treating localization as a sequential spatial search, as in the reinforcement-learning agent of Ghesu et al. [ghesu2016landmark] that navigates the volume to a target.

Registration as spatial alignment. Registration brings two images into a common coordinate frame and is foundational for multimodal fusion, atlas-based labeling, longitudinal tracking, and surgical planning. Learning-based methods reframe it as predicting a dense deformation field in a single forward pass: VoxelMorph [balakrishnan2019voxelmorph] established the unsupervised CNN formulation, and TransMorph [chen2022transmorph] added a transformer backbone. These build on classical diffeomorphic and intensity-based methods, principally the symmetric diffeomorphic SyN [avants2008syn] and the intensity-based toolbox elastix [klein2010elastix], and are measured by the target registration error between corresponding landmarks. Segmentation and detection are benchmarked on generalist suites such as the Medical Segmentation Decathlon [antonelli2022msd], the brain-tumor benchmark BraTS [menze2015brats], the abdominal multi-organ datasets AMOS [ji2022amos] and BTCV [landman2015btcv], the kidney-tumor KiTS19 [heller2021kits19], and the cardiac ACDC [bernard2018acdc].

12.1.4 Pivotal Task-2: Anatomical Reconstruction, Modeling, and Surgical Planning

The second task turns the perceived anatomy into a patient-specific 3D model that can be measured, simulated, and planned upon, bridging from pixels to clinical decisions. Figure 12.3 previews this progression from a segmentation to an anatomical mesh, a patient-specific simulation, and a surgical plan.

3D anatomical reconstruction. A segmentation becomes a usable model once it is turned into geometry. The classical route extracts an isosurface mesh by Marching Cubes [lorensen1998marching], optionally constrained by a statistical shape model that encodes anatomical priors as a learned distribution over landmarks, an idea founded by Active Shape Models [cootes1995asm] and surveyed for medical use by Heimann and Meinzer [heimann2009ssm]. Deep methods deform a template mesh directly from the volume, as in Voxel2Mesh [wickramasinghe2020voxel2mesh] and the whole-heart reconstruction of Kong et al. [kong2021meshdeformnet]. Implicit neural representations supply a continuous alternative, with DeepSDF [park2019deepsdf] and Occupancy Networks [mescheder2019occupancy] as the substrate (Chapter 8) and medical adaptations such as the neural attenuation fields of NAF [zha2022naf] reconstructing volumes from sparse-view cone-beam CT.

Patient-specific modeling and the medical digital twin. A geometric model becomes a twin when it is endowed with patient-specific physiology and kept faithful to a particular patient, a medical specialization of the generic digital twin of §11.1. What is clinically specific is that the model is built from the patient’s own imaging and physiological signals, governed by mechanistic physiology rather than CAD, and bound by regulatory credibility. Cardiac twins are the most mature instance: the vision was set out by Corral-Acero et al. [corralacero2020digital], the mechanistic backbone is the multiscale cardiac modeling reviewed by Niederer et al. [niederer2019cardiacmodels], and a personalized virtual heart built from scar imaging has been used to guide ablation of ventricular tachycardia [prakosa2018personalized]. Hemodynamic twins compute fractional flow reserve from coronary CT by simulating blood flow [taylor2013ffrct], and the paradigm extends to the brain, where a virtual epileptic patient estimates the epileptogenic zone to guide surgery [wang2023vep]. Such models also underwrite in-silico trials, in which virtual patient cohorts partially substitute for physical ones [viceconti2016avicenna], a route that regulators have begun to accept, as in the VICTRE imaging trial [badano2018victre]. The broader landscape is surveyed in recent reviews of digital twins for health [katsoulakis2024digital].

Surgical and treatment planning. The patient model is finally used to plan. Open platforms such as 3D Slicer [fedorov2012slicer] assemble segmentation, registration, and 3D modeling into a planning workflow, and real-time finite-element engines such as SOFA [faure2012sofa] support interactive surgical simulation and rehearsal on deformable tissue. In radiotherapy, planning is increasingly cast as a learning problem of predicting an achievable dose distribution from anatomy, standardized by the OpenKBP challenge [babier2021openkbp]. Across these settings the plan is a spatial object, a trajectory, a dose map, or a resection boundary, defined on the patient’s own anatomy.

12.1.5 Pivotal Task-3: Image-Guided Intervention and Surgical Navigation

The third task brings the plan into the operating room and acts within the patient’s live coordinate frame. The central problem is patient-to-image registration under real-world deformation and latency: the preoperative model must be aligned to the physical patient, and instruments tracked within that frame, in real time. Figure 12.4 previews registered preoperative anatomy and augmented-reality guidance alongside the complementary reconstruction of a deforming endoscopic scene.

Surgical navigation. Navigation aligns the preoperative model to the patient and tracks instruments within that frame, typically by optical tracking, which is sub-millimeter but requires line of sight, or electromagnetic tracking, which tolerates occlusion but is perturbed by metal. The defining difficulty is deformation: in neuronavigation, the brain shifts by up to centimeters once the skull is opened, invalidating the rigid preoperative registration, which is why intraoperative imaging and learning-based compensation are active concerns.

Augmented-reality guidance. Rather than divert the surgeon’s gaze to a screen, augmented reality overlays the segmented anatomy directly on the surgical field, a use of the XR runtime treated in §10.1. The approach is most mature in spine surgery, where the Augmedics xvision system, the first FDA-cleared augmented-reality navigation platform, projects the patient’s CT-derived spine onto a transparent head-mounted display for pedicle-screw placement [molina2021xvision].

Endoscopic spatial perception. Minimally invasive surgery presents a hard perception problem: a monocular, moving camera views a deforming, specular, poorly lit scene. Surgical workflow and instruments are recognized from video, as standardized by the Cholec80 dataset and the EndoNet architecture for joint tool and phase recognition [twinanda2017endonet]. Geometry is recovered by self-supervised depth and visual odometry, benchmarked by the SCARED challenge [allan2021scared] and the EndoSLAM dataset [ozyoruk2021endoslam], and the deforming surgical scene is reconstructed in 3D by dynamic neural rendering, as in EndoNeRF [wang2022endonerf], a clinical specialization of the neural reconstruction of Chapter 8.

Surgical robotics. Robotic systems execute the plan within the patient frame; their manipulation and control are the subject of §9.1, and the concern here is the spatial perception and autonomy they enable. The da Vinci Research Kit [kazanzides2014dvrk] is the standard open research platform, and autonomy is commonly graded on a six-level scale from teleoperation to full autonomy [yang2017autonomy]. Most deployed systems remain teleoperated, but the frontier of autonomous spatial action is exemplified by the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot, which performs supervised-autonomous soft-tissue suturing using 3D tissue tracking [shademan2016star] and has been extended to in-vivo intestinal anastomosis [saeidi2022star].

12.1.6 Established Tools and Systems

Open-source frameworks. The research stack runs from voxels to a planned model: 3D Slicer11 1 https://www.slicer.org/ and MITK22 2 https://www.mitk.org/ provide segmentation, registration, and planning environments over the lower-level ITK and SimpleITK33 3 https://itk.org/ engines; MONAI44 4 https://monai.io/ supplies 3D-native deep-learning components and nnU-Net55 5 https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet the standard segmentation pipeline; and the web viewer OHIF66 6 https://ohif.org/ renders and annotates volumes in the browser.

Navigation and surgical-robotics vendors. The clinical stack carries the model from preoperative registration to constrained in-OR action. Navigation systems from Brainlab77 7 https://www.brainlab.com/, Medtronic (StealthStation)88 8 https://www.medtronic.com/, and Stryker99 9 https://www.stryker.com/ register and track instruments, and Augmedics1010 10 https://augmedics.com/ adds an augmented-reality head-mounted overlay. Surgical robots span teleoperated soft-tissue systems (Intuitive da Vinci and Ion1111 11 https://www.intuitive.com/, Medtronic Hugo, CMR Surgical Versius1212 12 https://cmrsurgical.com/) and CT-planned, haptically constrained orthopedic systems (Stryker Mako, Zimmer Biomet ROSA1313 13 https://www.zimmerbiomet.com/).

Imaging-AI and clinical platforms. A deployed layer turns spatial findings into care. Aidoc1414 14 https://www.aidoc.com/ triages critical findings on CT, Viz.ai1515 15 https://www.viz.ai/ alerts stroke teams to large-vessel occlusions, HeartFlow1616 16 https://www.heartflow.com/ computes non-invasive fractional flow reserve from coronary CT, PathAI1717 17 https://www.pathai.com/ quantifies biomarkers on whole-slide pathology, and Tempus1818 18 https://www.tempus.com/ fuses imaging with genomic and clinical data.

12.1.7 Challenges

Every capability in the clinical loop must be accurate, robust to deformation, and trustworthy enough to act on a patient. The open problems follow from those demands: generalizing across scanners and sites, obtaining labels under privacy constraints, registering deforming tissue during surgery, earning regulatory and clinical trust, and meeting real-time budgets while fusing imaging with non-imaging evidence.

Generalization across Scanners and Sites.

Models trained at one institution degrade at another, because scanner vendor, reconstruction kernel, and acquisition protocol induce a covariate shift that curated benchmarks underrepresent. Domain generalization and adaptation are therefore prerequisites for deployment, and leaderboard results routinely overstate performance at a new site.

Data Scarcity, Annotation Cost, and Privacy.

Volumetric expert annotation is slow and expensive, and patient data is locked in privacy-restricted silos. Self-supervised pretraining reduces the labeling burden [huang2023ssl], and federated learning trains shared models without moving data across institutions [rieke2020federated], but label efficiency and privacy-preserving collaboration remain limiting.

Non-Rigid Intraoperative Registration.

The hardest open spatial problem is keeping the model aligned with the patient as tissue moves.
